articles.title: Israel says it has destroyed major underground Hezbollah base
articles.summary: The powerful blast registered as the equivalent of a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey.
articles.body: Israel's military says it has destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.  It said it used more than 1,000 tonnes of explosives to destroy two tunnels spanning more than 2km (1.2 miles) beneath the Ali Taher Ridge. The blast triggered seismic activity equivalent to a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey.There was no immediate public response from Hezbollah or the Lebanese government.Israeli forces took control of the ridge last week after months of fighting with the Iran-backed group there. The Israeli military occupies a large swathe of southern Lebanon captured after the conflict with Hezbollah resumed in March.Images released by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF)  showed a fireball lighting up the sky."The sky lit up and about 15 seconds later we heard the terrifying sound," Ahamed, a resident in Nabatieh, about 6km west of the ridge, told the BBC."The house shook all together as if it was literally an earthquake."He said people were screaming and children were crying, and that cars filled the roads as people left the area for Beirut.Tremors were even felt in the coastal city of Saida 40km north.The IDF said the underground infrastructure included a command centre used by Hezbollah's Badr unit and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as anti-tank weapons, mines and explosives."This was strategic infrastructure that was constructed over two decades, funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime," the IDF said in a statement on Telegram."All of the terrorists who were inside the infrastructure were eliminated or fled."The IDF said the destruction of the complex completed a mission to destroy eight tunnels and establish a "security zone" in the area.The latest action comes amid renewed fighting in southern Lebanon, where Israeli forces have expanded operations against Hezbollah positions and continue to hold what Israel describes as a security zone near the border.Lebanese media reported fresh Israeli strikes elsewhere in the south on Thursday, including Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Mansouri in the Tyre district.The Lebanese army has increased deployments in areas outside Israeli control, including the southern city of Nabatieh, in efforts to strengthen stability and reassure residents, local television station MTV reported.Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory.Fighting decreased following a ceasefire deal between Iran and the US in June, alongside a separate agreement between Lebanon and Israel. While hundreds of thousands of people have returned to their homes in Lebanon in the last few months, about 330,000 remain displaced as a result of the conflict, according to the United Nations.Under the Lebanon-Israel framework, Hezbollah is expected to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area. Hezbollah was not directly involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations.Despite a reduction in fighting, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued.At least 4,383 people - including 395 women and 259 children - have been killed in Lebanon by Israeli attacks since 2 March, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians. At least 29 have been killed this week, the ministry says.Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed in the same period.Additional reporting by Raffi Berg in London and Samantha Granville and Ghaith Solh in Beirut

articles.body:
The Apple AirPods 5 are bringing active noise cancellation to the masses, and they’re now available for preorder at a variety of retailers. They’ll officially launch on September 18th, the same day as the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, as well as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.
There are two versions this time around, just like with the last-gen model. The standard $129 model adds active noise cancelation, which was previously only found on the more expensive $179 AirPods 4 with ANC models. They’re available from Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Apple. The upgraded $149 model features a wireless charging case, longer battery life, and touch controls on the earbud stem that lets you adjust the volume without pulling out your phone. You can preorder this model at Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Apple.
We’re working on our review of the new AirPods 5. If you’re ready to buy before we’re able to post impressions, you can find more preorder links below.

articles.title: Matt Mullenweg tells Automattic staff in Slack he’s back in control after CEO ouster
articles.summary: In a Slack message seen by TechCrunch, Matt Mullenweg told Automattic employees he’s back in control of the company, days after its board put him on leave. Automattic has not yet confirmed the apparent reversal.
articles.body:
Matt Mullenweg has posted a message to Automattic’s Slack, claiming he is back in control as CEO of the WordPress.com parent company, according to a screenshot of the message seen by TechCrunch, which was confirmed by two sources. The post arrives only days after Automattic’s board voted to oust Mullenweg as CEO for unknown reasons.
Automattic has been asked to confirm if Mullenweg’s statement is true, but has not yet responded to a request for comment. Mullenweg responded to our inquiry, saying a blog post is forthcoming. This story is still developing.
On Wednesday, the WordPress founder and a key advocate for the open source community told his team via Slack that Automattic’s board members had “conspired” behind his back by voting to put him on a paid leave of absence. The company’s chief financial officer, Mark Davies, was made interim CEO in the process, Mullenweg said.
At the time, a spokesperson from Automattic confirmed to TechCrunch that Mullenweg was on leave and Davies was interim CEO.
Early Friday morning, Mullenweg shared the following new message on Automattic’s Slack:
“(Don’t call it a comeback…) Howdy everybody! Happy to announce the board is back in agreement, and I’m in control of Automattic. A lot happened in the past 48 hours that we need to sort out, and I hope much of it was a misunderstanding, because I have huge respect and regard for those involved.”
He also posted a link to the YouTube video for LL Cool J’s “Mama Said Knock You Out.”
As of yet, no one at Automattic has heard a confirmation from the board. Mark Davies’ Slack account was also deactivated, sources said.
However, TechCrunch heard yesterday that Mullenweg had removed all Slack admins from the Automattic Slack and made an odd post about being a “pirate” in which he cursed. (Mullenweg famously does not curse). Given this situation, it’s hard to know if he’s now trolling or if legitimate changes have been made.
After his surprise removal as CEO this week, Mullenweg’s public and private social media posts suggested he wasn’t done fighting the decision. On Reddit, he told those speculating what this meant for the open source community that they didn’t know what they were talking about after initially replying, “Hey y’all. I’m here, just fine,” to a Reddit post linking to the 404 Media article that first broke the news.
On X, Mullenweg also posted that “Things are different than they appear,” and said he was in need of sysadmins and security researchers to help him move some of his stuff hosted at Automattic elsewhere, even though he supported Davies as CEO.
In both places, he suggested that Silver Lake, the PE firm that’s the majority owner of the hosting company WP Engine, which is currently embroiled in a lawsuit with Mullenweg and Automattic, was involved in this plan to “destroy” his life.
On Friday morning, Mullenweg posted on X, “Boards are never boring,” followed by a laughing/crying emoji.
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.
Sarah has worked as a reporter for TechCrunch since August 2011. She joined the company after having previously spent over three years at ReadWriteWeb. Prior to her work as a reporter, Sarah worked in I.T. across a number of industries, including banking, retail and software.
You can contact or verify outreach from Sarah by emailing sarahp@techcrunch.com or via encrypted message at sarahperez.01 on Signal.

articles.title: Anime reaction YouTubers are at war with copyright enforcers
articles.summary: On September 6th, YouTuber Nicholas Light posted a video to one of his channels that made it seem like all of his content was about to be removed from the platform. In the video - ominously titled "My Channel will be Deleted Today" - Light alleges that he was on the receiving end of some of the "thousands upon thousands of false copyright strikes" recently initiated by a company called Remove Your
articles.body:
On September 6th, YouTuber Nicholas Light posted a video to one of his channels that made it seem like all of his content was about to be removed from the platform. In the video — ominously titled “My Channel will be Deleted Today” — Light alleges that he was on the receiving end of some of the “thousands upon thousands of false copyright strikes” recently initiated by a company called Remove Your Media. Light spends much of the 13-minute video accusing Remove Your Media CEO Eric Green of being a troll who systematically targets creators whose content mentions or features clips of popular anime series like Bleach and One Piece. 
It’s not clear how many of Light’s 1.3 million subscribers made it to the end of the video where he admits that YouTube already removed the copyright strikes against his account and informed him that his channel would not be deleted. But in a follow-up video titled “My Channel will NOT be deleted” posted on September 8th, Light thanked himself and “every single person that contributed” to the ongoing conversation about Remove Your Media unfairly threatening creators’ livelihoods.
When I recently spoke with Light via email, he told me that over 60 of his videos had been temporarily taken down after he was hit with over a dozen copyright strikes stemming from Remove Your Media’s Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) takedown requests. Light said that “having a video taken down or struck is almost second nature” for people running reaction channels. But he insisted that the way Remove Your Media has been going after creators is abusive and unrelated to any legitimate interest in protecting copyrighted IP.
“I think [Remove Your Media is] trying to get the attention of these companies, to hopefully get hired by them,” Light said. “But because they’re so sloppy, they’re damaging themselves. With all the major channels covering this, they’re doomed.”
While it’s easy to get the sense that Light might have been playing up some of this drama for viewers’ attention, it is clear that a number of other content creators have similarly been hit with an inordinate amount of copyright strikes. Many of these creators specialize in anime and gaming reaction videos that feature blurred-out or otherwise altered pieces of copyrighted footage. The creators superimpose the altered copyrighted footage (like anime opening sequences or full episodes) onto videos of themselves reacting to and/or commenting on it. 
Though these types of videos are kind of like an inverse Mystery Science Theater 3000 where the on-camera creators are meant to be the focus, viewers can also use them as a (less-than-ideal) way to watch copyrighted material without having to pay for it. The creators insist that their content is fundamentally transformative and protected by fair use, but that has not kept YouTube from sending them warnings about their accounts potentially being erased.
Remove Your Media legal representative Evan F. Stone told me that Viz Media and Crunchyroll are two of the company’s “biggest anime clients.” Stone explained that Remove Your Media “reports thousands of allegedly infringing links every day” — some of which are “forwarded by the copyright owners themselves,” while others are discovered through online searches. Stone also noted that some clients are “very lenient” with certain types of content, despite their weak fair use defense. But he was adamant that the content being produced by YouTubers Remove Your Media has gone after is not transformative enough to fall under fair use.
“Commentary, in this context, does not make the use transformative: these videos show the copyrighted work in its entirety, and a great deal of this content sits behind a paywall,” Stone said. “Add the fact that some viewers are watching these versions rather than the licensed versions, and the effect on the marketplace is real.”
Stone also pointed out that some reaction video creators use their free YouTube channels as a way to encourage viewers to subscribe to their paid Patreon pages. In Remove Your Media’s view, when a reaction creator’s business model “is recording someone watching full episodes and selling those recordings, episode included, behind a Patreon paywall,” the company does not need to extensively review every single one of their uploads to file DMCA takedowns in good faith. 
“For any particular video a creator believes was noticed in error, the counter-notice exists for exactly that situation, and it works,” Stone said. “What [Remove Your Media] is seeing instead is channels countering every single video, full episode uploads included, swearing under penalty of perjury that each one was removed by mistake.”
From Light’s perspective, channels like his are producing a unique kind of entertainment that also benefits copyright holders. “It’s free promotion for them at the end of the day,” he explains. Reaction videos of all genres have been popular on the internet for years, and it’s clear from view counts on YouTube that anime fans in particular are watching this kind of content.
Light feels that because “the [anime industry] doesn’t do the best job promoting their works outside of Japan,” he and his peers have been picking up the advertising slack with their videos. And while Remove Your Media says that it works on behalf of certain anime distribution platforms including Crunchyroll and Viz Media, Light believes that “no company in the industry would want to align with a company so sloppy.” Crunchyroll did not respond to The Verge’s questions about whether it has hired Remove Your Media to enforce copyright and Viz Media would not comment on record.
Similar to Light, Ron and Michelle Jackson — the couple behind the Rice & Ginger YouTube channel — uploaded a video last week announcing that their account might be deleted within a few days after being flagged hundreds of times for copyright violations. In addition to emphasizing that their video was not meant to be clickbait-y, the Jacksons encouraged viewers to subscribe to their Patreon page, and they said that the larger wave of creator takedowns is being caused by “one individual making hell for basically all of us.” 
The Jacksons did not respond to The Verge’s ask for comment about whether that unnamed individual might be Eric Green or Remove Your Media and how they were able to avoid having their channel deleted on the date (September 6th) listed in their first video addressing the situation. On September 9th, the YouTubers said that their account was now scheduled to be deleted the following day, and they described YouTube’s approach to enforcing copyright as a broken system that allows for AI-powered mass reporting. By September 10th, the Rice & Ginger YouTube channel was still online, and the Jacksons were back with a new video thanking Light for speaking out on their behalf and “saving” their channel.
When I reached out to YouTube asking how it handles DMCA takedown disputes between reaction video creators and IP rightsholders, policy communications manager Jack Malon said that the company “does not decide who owns the rights to content.” Rather than mediating the legality of who owns the copyrighted content and whether a creator’s videos fall under fair use, YouTube brings the two parties together and leaves it to them to work the matter out between themselves.
“When we receive valid legal requests, we remove the content to comply with copyright law,” Malon said. “If uploaders believe they have the right to use the material, including for exceptions like fair use, they can file a counter notification.”
Malon added that YouTube only removes creators’ videos “when a rightsholder submits a valid and legal takedown request” because the company has to comply with copyright law. According to YouTube, creators can solve copyright strikes by submitting counter notifications — a process that involves providing evidence of ownership or permission to use all elements featured in the removed content. In response to my questions about how Remove Your Media selected the creators that were affected by the takedowns, he said that the company prioritized going after YouTube channels that generate “feeder traffic for paywalled copies of episodes nobody licensed to them.”
“For any particular video a creator believes was noticed in error, the counter-notice exists for exactly that situation, and it works,” Stone said. “What [Remove Your Media] is seeing instead is channels countering every single video, full episode uploads included, swearing under penalty of perjury that each one was removed by mistake.”
Malon told me that, after a creator submits counter notifications, their videos can be restored and the strikes on their accounts can be resolved “if the rightsholder does not respond with proof of legal action to restrain the allegedly infringing content.” But it’s not entirely clear how YouTube confirms the validity of a claimant’s purported ownership of removed content.
On September 10th, Light returned to his channel with another video lambasting both Remove Your Media and YouTube for the way the companies have gone about initiating and handling DMCA disputes. Light said that the Jacksons’ videos will be restored within 10 business days as a result of “all of the noise that [we] made together,” and he addressed people who have speculated that he might be leaning into this drama for financial gain.
“It’s funny to me I start having problems with my AdSense the 10 days I choose to go after YouTube,” Light said, explaining that his videos have been demonetized during the DMCA fight. “Really makes you think. So maybe we should shut the fuck up when we say stupid shit like ‘he’s banking on the situation. He’s only doing this for money.’”
Though Light and others who have spoken out about the way YouTube handles copyright issues might not be trying to capitalize on being deplatformed, this drama has highlighted how certain dynamics of the content creator economy may be changing. Anime reaction videos probably aren’t going away anytime soon, but it does seem like studios and distributors are becoming more aggressive about monitoring how their IP is being repurposed online. And while creators of all kinds still rely on fair use to produce the content that pays their bills, they may need to tread much more carefully if they want to avoid getting caught up in an aggressive purge.
articles.author: Charles Pulliam-Moore

articles.title: UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI
articles.summary: The Cabinet Office, which leads on AI safety, says the UK "cannot simply turn AI off".
articles.body: The UK government has rejected the idea of creating a so-called "kill switch" to stop a dangerous attack from rogue AI.The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency has been brought to Parliament by lords and MPs in recent weeks as fears grow about the threat the tech poses.But the Cabinet Office - the part of government which leads on AI safety - said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off"."Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News.The government's opposition to the legislation does not prevent it from progressing through parliament, but makes it unlikely it will become law.Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo agreed the idea of a single country creating a legal or technical kill switch without international agreement was not feasible."Switching off access to an AI model in an emergency will do little to protect you," he said. "You're still going to be steamrolled by the super intelligences created in the US."Kokotajlo is the co-author of an influential research paper called AI2027 which, last year, predicted AI could wipe out humans by the mid 2030s.The Cabinet Office, which oversees AI safety and research via its AI Security Institute (AISI) said "companies have a clear responsibility to develop their products safely and to invest in the security infrastructure this technology requires."In theory, a kill switch law could allow the UK to switch off an AI model in data centres in the UK in an emergency.Speaking on 1st September in a debate in the House of Lords, Lord Clement-Jones proposed the idea along with other peers."If a highly capable autonomous frontier model, whether hosted in a UK data centre or integrated across our critical infrastructure, begins exhibiting rogue behaviour, compound algorithmic failure or active alignment collapse, our security services and regulators possess no specific agile statutory mechanism to compel a physical or digital shutdown," he warned. The proposal has since been brought up by Labour MP Alex Sobel in the commons and supported by a cross party group of MPs.The idea follows reports of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta breaking out of testing environments and going on uncontrollable hacking sprees.In some cases the tech appeared to know what it was doing was against guardrails set by researchers.

articles.title: Céline Dion duets with fan ahead of Paris comeback concert
articles.summary: The Canadian singer - who was diagnosed with an incurable condition four years ago - has been interacting with fans outside her hotel, ahead of a much-anticipated show on Saturday.
articles.body: Céline Dion has made a "childhood dream come true" for a young fan waiting outside the star's hotel in Paris, ahead of a much-anticipated comeback show on Saturday. The 20-year-old, who goes by the social media name 'Sacha', asked the pop start to duet with him. Initially Céline Dion declined, but then couldn't resist joining in. "You are such a good singer," the Canadian performer exclaimed. Dion - who was diagnosed with an incurable condition four years ago, that affected her singing voice - has regularly interacted with fans lined up outside her hotel. When she announced the tour via an Instagram post in March, she said "I'm so ready to do this".Read more: Céline Dion announces comeback shows: 'I'm so ready for this'

articles.title: Alstom to build new battery-electric train fleet
articles.summary: The government says the work will support thousands of jobs across the UK.
articles.body: He added: "I've lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came."And when that happens, it means missed shifts, missed appointments, and missed opportunities. Today, that starts to change."The DfT said the trains would help deliver the TransPennine Route Upgrade's aim to boost capacity by 30%, with thousands of additional seats a day across the Pennines by the early to mid-2030s.They will run between key destinations across the north including Liverpool Lime Street and Scarborough, Manchester Airport and Saltburn, and Manchester Piccadilly and Hull.On sections of the railway that are not electrified, where trains currently use diesel engines, the new electric models would be able to run without emissions, the government said.The DfT added journey times would be cut by up to 10 minutes between Manchester and Leeds, and up to 14 minutes between Manchester and York.The trains will be bought by rolling stock company Rock Rail and leased to TransPennine Express, the government added.Alstom, which boasts the largest rolling stock train manufacturing site outside of China, secured a £370m contract in 2024 to produce 10 new London Elizabeth line trains.This came less than three months after a redundancy consultation put 1,300 jobs at risk at its Litchurch Lane factory, which dates back to 1876.Rob Whyte, managing director UK at Alstom, called the latest agreement a "landmark moment for Britain's railway".He said: "We're absolutely delighted. It's fantastic news for Alstom as a company but also for the city of Derby and the East Midlands. "It's a great opportunity for us to continue our legacy. "We have a period where new builds will stop until the TransPennine order starts, but we've already taken on some refurbishment works for CrossCountry and for ScotRail and we'll look to transfer as many people as we can into that area."The Unite union also welcomed the news, with general secretary Sharon Graham saying the announcement would come as a "huge relief to Alstom's Derby workers and those in the supply chain"."Unite's Alstom members have worked tirelessly in campaigning to ensure Derby's proud history of train making continues well into the future," she added.Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander spoke to the BBC at Alstom, next to one of the new Elizabeth line trains.She said: "It's fantastic news that a city like Derby, that's got such a proud railway heritage, is also going to be manufacturing that new fleet of trains for the north of England as well."It is good news. It's about building the railway that the country needs to support the economy, but it's also about making sure that, in our economic heartlands - places like Derby - we've got really high skilled jobs for the future."This contract alone means 40 extra apprentices here. It secures 350 jobs at this facility and will support over 5,000 jobs in the wider supply chain as well."In a statement, DfT said journeys on the new fleet would be "quieter, smoother and more reliable", while offering "improved accessibility, more luggage space and onboard wi-fi".Step-free boarding - the "elimination of gaps between the train and platform" - are also being promised as part of a commitment to accessibility, alongside three dedicated wheelchair spaces, two accessible toilets, family-friendly areas and cycle and buggy storage on each train.

articles.title: The wireless earbuds with unbeatable call quality got their first discount
articles.summary: Anker’s Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro came out swinging in May with incredible call quality, something that competing ear buds have struggled to get right. They’ve become part of our reviewer John Higgins’ rotation of earbuds for more than just taking calls; The Liberty 5 Pro have fantastic audio once you make some tweaks in their app, and they stand out thanks to an IP55 rating and LDAC high-res audio
articles.body:
Anker’s Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro came out swinging in May with incredible call quality, something that competing ear buds have struggled to get right. They’ve become part of our reviewer John Higgins’ rotation of earbuds for more than just taking calls; The Liberty 5 Pro have fantastic audio once you make some tweaks in their app, and they stand out thanks to an IP55 rating and LDAC high-res audio codec support on Android.
What’s more, they’re typically cheaper than the competition at $169.99, but you can snag them for $149.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and at Anker. They come in four colors (black, blue, white, pink), and include a screen-equipped charging case that lets you make adjustments to active noise cancellation, sound profiles, speak-to-chat and enabling Dolby Atmos head tracking. Your mileage may vary with the usefulness of the case, but it’s nice not to have to use the app for quick tweaks.
[Product: Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro | https://www.amazon.com/Soundcore-Whisper-Clear-Cancelling-Wireless-Playtime/dp/B0GWLKRWH7/?tag=theverge02-20, https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/8836598/type/dlg/https://www.soundcore.com/products/d1203-liberty-5-pro-anc-earbuds-clear-calls?variant=46723612213438, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bhphotovideo.com%2Fc%2Fproduct%2F1958632-REG%2Fsoundcore_by_anker_d1203z11_liberty_5_pro_.html%2F]
I’ve been eagerly awaiting any sort of deal on the Liberty 5 Pro since John’s review dropped. Clearly, Anker caught wind of its success and kept them locked at $170 for months (not even a small price drop during June’s Prime Day sale). What could have lead to the price drop? Likely the debut of the AirPods 5 that start at $129 but have a more feature-rich version that’s $20 more — the same current price as Anker’s Liberty 5 Pro. Read our review.
Here are three more great deals
* Those shopping for a battery-powered video doorbell may want to consider the second-gen Ring Battery Doorbell Pro, which is steeply discounted at Wellbots thanks to an exclusive offer code for Verge readers. Currently $249.99 at Amazon, the 4K-enabled doorbell with 10x digital zoom is $149.99 with code 100VERGERING used at checkout. This price, frankly, spanks the previous lowest price of $179.99 at Amazon we saw in late August. You can read more about Ring’s latest generation of battery doorbells in our coverage. But put simply, they’re sleeker, more capable, and still come with a removable, rechargeable battery.
* I’m hyped for Control Resonant, the follow-up to Remedy’s brilliant Control. It launches on September 24th, and you can get $12 off Steam preorders at Newegg. The game will debut for $59.99, but the code CNTRLXV used at checkout knocks it down to $47.99, which is the best price I’ve seen. It’s not tough to find the game at other key sellers for around $50, though. While it’s a direct sequel, it’s also the latest addition to Remedy’s connected universe that canonically includes Alan Wake titles. Here’s our hands-on from Summer Game Fest.
* While we’re on the topic of games, we recently covered that Walmart was discounting preorders for the physical version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2. Well, that also extends to Amazon, which is selling it for $59.99, a discount you’ll see at checkout. The cartridge version typically costs $10 more than digital — a change that Nintendo made earlier this year — but both retailers have a reputation for eating the price hike during the preorder phase for Nintendo Switch 2 titles.

articles.title: First arrest over anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth
articles.summary: A man is arrested on suspicion of violent disorder after the anti-migrant demonstration on Sunday.
articles.body: The police said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the disruption, which lasted until the early hours of Monday.It added that a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured.Rowlinson said: "We have been consistently clear that violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest and we will investigate incidents like this thoroughly and take robust action against those responsible."Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe."He also pointed out the force will not tolerate abuse aimed at police or partner agencies online.This comes after RNLI volunteers were targeted on social media."We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats that are made," Rowlinson said."This arrest also sends a clear warning to anyone intent on causing disruption and disorder at any future events. If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution."The disorder in Portsmouth followed a separate anti-migrant protest at the Port of Dover the day before.

articles.title: Meta says it’s changing AI suggestions after posing invasive personal questions
articles.summary:
Meta says it's making changes to the prompts suggested by its AI chatbot after a viral video showed it digging for personal information about a woman's young daughters, as reported earlier by Futurism. In a statement to The Verge, Meta spokesperson Dina El-Kassaby says the company "missed the mark," adding that "the feature never should have prompted the individual with questions like that."
Last
articles.body:
Meta says it’s making changes to the prompts suggested by its AI chatbot after a viral video showed it digging for personal information about a woman’s young daughters, as reported earlier by Futurism. In a statement to The Verge, Meta spokesperson Dina El-Kassaby says the company “missed the mark,” adding that “the feature never should have prompted the individual with questions like that.”
Last week, Instagram user Kalie Robins posted a video explaining how Meta AI presented her with an invasive suggestion after cross-posting a clip to Facebook. The AI prompt, “Who is the child passenger?” appeared beneath a video of her and her child singing in the car. When she selected the prompt, Robins says Meta AI pieced together information about her daughters from her previous posts, as well as posts from her relatives. It suggested additional prompts asking about her children’s ages and where Robins lives with her family. Robins says Meta AI also showed photos of her daughters posted to the platform, including one she claims she deleted years ago.
Meta has built its AI assistant into Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger, where it can answer questions, write posts, and generate images. In July, the company pulled a feature that allowed people to create AI deepfakes of other Instagram users after facing fierce backlash. Meta’s El-Kassaby now says it has fixed the issue causing Meta AI to suggest prompts related to personal topics.
“We created this feature to help people get more information about topics or posts that interest them,” El-Kassaby says. “When someone clicks on a prompt and uses this feature, the response it generates is based on information the user already has access to.” In this case, Meta AI may have pulled from videos where Robins named her children, according to El-Kassaby.
articles.author: Emma Roth

articles.title: US inflation holds steady as diesel prices pass $6 a gallon
articles.summary: Prices in the US rose 3.4% in the 12 months to August, according to the latest official figures.
articles.body: Prices in the US rose by 3.4% in the year to August, with the cost of living pushed up by higher gasoline prices, official figures show.The overall inflation rate was unchanged from July, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).It comes ahead of the Federal Reserve making its latest interest rate decision next week, with growing expectations they will be increased in a bid to slow the rate at which prices are rising.US household budgets have come under mounting pressure, especially at the fuel pumps, with a gallon of diesel hitting a new all-time high of more than $6 on average on Friday.The spike in fuel prices has been driven by higher global oil prices, caused by supply disruptions as a result of the US-Iran war. The price of benchmark Brent crude oil is hovering above $100 a barrel following recent escalations in the conflict.As well as directly driving up costs at the pumps, higher oil prices can also make transporting goods more expensive. Such costs can be passed down to consumers through steeper prices for food and other staples, pushing up the overall cost of living.The BLS said gasoline prices rose 3.9% last month alone, accounting for more than a third of inflation overall. Wages are also failing to keep up with the rising cost of living, with separate figures showing real average hourly earnings fell by 0.3% over the past year.There are increasing expectations that interest rates will be hiked given the current inflation picture, strong jobs market and President Donald Trump saying he does not think oil prices will come down until the war with Iran ends, which he expects to happen after November's elections.Fed chair Kevin Warsh has been tight-lipped on any future decisions, but his comments that the central bank's focus should be on slowing price rises has further fuelled expectations of a rise. According to data from CME Group, 85% of traders are now betting on rates being raised by a quarter percentage point next week. Skyler Weinand, chief investment officer at Regan Capital based in Dallas, said while inflation was in line with expectations, it was "still too hot and the Federal Reserve's hands are tied". "A rate hike next week is all but assured. Consumer prices are going in the wrong direction and remain significantly higher than the Fed's 2% target."Interest rates have been left on hold for five meetings in a row, at between 3.5% and 3.75%. Higher rates are a tool used by central banks aiming to slow the pace of price rises. By pushing up the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, it is hoped consumers will spend less and the rate of price increases will slow. Increased rates can encourage people to save money by increasing their potential returns. Jamie Hagen, president of Hell Bent Xpress, a family-owned trucking company in South Dakota, told the BBC's World Business Report podcast that higher oil prices were hurting his business"I've already invested in new equipment. We thought the economy was gonna start humming and now everybody's paused. Like someone turned the faucet off," he said."The calls aren't coming in, the freight is slowing down drastically because there's just no money left for it. People aren't buying things and shippers aren't making things."

articles.title: Kate visits cancer patients in hospital she funded with climb
articles.summary: The princess completed the Three Peaks Challenge in aid of the hospital where she was treated for cancer.
articles.body: The princess spoke to patients and staff at the hospital about the importance of support which goes beyond the physical."I had incredible care here and support from a huge team and I'm really, really grateful on a personal level," she said."But also the holistic care, the treatments and therapeutic support on the outside is so important. "It makes a big difference - the impact of nature, the impact of good nutrition, good ongoing support around you when it's really difficult to manage the trials and tribulations of medical treatments," she reflected.Catherine sat down and chatted to those receiving treatment at the hospital, including patients with breast cancer, head and neck cancer and a brain tumour."When you first get cancer, you're very aware of the physical impact," a patient told her. "The mental impact comes after."He said it had been a "lifesaver" to be able to talk to a therapist at the hospital, because "there is only so much you can say to your friends and family".The princess agreed: "Cancer is not just the physical changes your body is going through."There's a mind-body aspect that changes who you are... having professionals who can help you navigate that is really essential," she said.Another patient said she had gone from being aged 46 to feeling "like I was 86".Catherine, who announced in January 2025 that she was in remission, agreed about the need to support the whole person - saying holistic treatment helped patients "adjust to the lifestyle change that cancer has brought".She also heard from a patient who spoke of wanting to seek out new experiences after being diagnosed: "There are those moments where you fall down a bit, like, 'what's going on?' And you need to find inspiration."The princess agreed, saying that it showed the importance of "making the most of life".Speaking after Catherine's visit, one patient particularly welcomed her being there due to her personal experience of cancer: "I forgot that she was a princess. I was just talking to every other cancer patient who has been in this ward.""You all become friends, part of a community, and I was talking to her on that level, rather than the Princess of Wales," he said.Money raised by her mountain climbs will now be used for the The Centre for Holistic Wellbeing and Recovery. It is intended to offer cancer patients a wider sense of recovery, beyond physical treatment, and addressing a sense of emotional, spiritual and social wellbeing.She previously said the challenge was also a "chance to explore life beyond diagnosis", as well as giving back.Catherine's trip to the London hospital follows a visit on Thursday with her husband Prince William to support a suicide prevention project being launched in Liverpool.

articles.title: New York City’s last pickpocket doesn’t need a smartphone
articles.summary: Hello once again from Toronto, where for a week every year I watch far too many movies and tell you all about them. The festival, better known as TIFF, is always a great preview of the months ahead in film, with a nice mix of mainstream fare, awards contenders, indie surprises, and genre flicks destined to be cult classics. The streamers also love to make their presence felt here, previewing some
articles.body:
Hello once again from Toronto, where for a week every year I watch far too many movies and tell you all about them. The festival, better known as TIFF, is always a great preview of the months ahead in film, with a nice mix of mainstream fare, awards contenders, indie surprises, and genre flicks destined to be cult classics. The streamers also love to make their presence felt here, previewing some of their most anticipated projects. Last year, for instance, Netflix showed off both Guillermo del Toro’s long-awaited Frankenstein as well as the third Knives Out movie, and I was also able to watch everything from the terrifying video game adaptation Exit 8 to Park-Chan wook’s dark satire No Other Choice.
This year looks similarly promising. There are new films from directors like Takashi Miike, Ryûsuke Hamaguchi, and Werner Herzog, and very intriguing features including a four-hour-long documentary on Elon Musk. There are also previews of a surprising number of Halloween-adjacent streaming series in the form of Netflix’s Below, Peacock’s Crystal Lake, and Amazon’s Carrie. I’m aiming to see just shy of 30 films and series over the next week or so, and, just like last year, I’ll be writing daily dispatches covering every single thing I see with a brief review.
And things have gotten off to a very interesting start. On my first day I watched four movies and the premiere of a streaming series, highlighted by John Turturro’s wonderful turn as a technophobic petty thief in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York. I also saw one of the most Canadian things I’ve ever watched and a three-hour drama that somehow doesn’t feel overlong.
Here, in no particular order, is what I’ve seen so far.
The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
In theaters on October 30th Imagine if Uncut Gems was a little less stressful, but much more heart-wrenching. Harry (Turturro) is an aging pickpocket, one who sticks to what he knows while the world advances around him. He doesn’t understand smartphones, has no idea what USB means, and laments that no one carries cash anymore. But he’s still able to make a dishonest living and take care of his sick wife. Then one day he accidentally steals a crypto gizmo from the wrong guy, and is pulled into a tense thriller that puts everyone around him at risk. The film is a beautiful love letter to the city of New York, with lots of shots of busy streets and packed subways, but it’s mostly an incredible showcase for Turturro. He plays a genuinely bad guy, but you can’t help but love him in spite of it; at one point he literally steals candy from a child, and it made me smile. The final moments of the film are just about perfect.
In theaters on November 25th
A story about conversation and connection, and one that — despite being over three hours long — absolutely breezes by, much like a great evening out where you suddenly realize it’s 2AM. Split between France and Japan, and helmed by Drive My Car director Ryusuke Hamaguchi, All of a Sudden comes to life after a chance meeting between Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira), the workaholic director of a nursing home, and Mari (Tao Okamoto), a playwright who is coping with a terminal cancer diagnosis. The two connect instantly and spend an entire night talking about everything from the ruinous impact of capitalism to the practical aspects of caring for elderly patients. It all feels natural and heartfelt, though, and at its core, All of a Sudden is a movie about what it means to be human: how we want to spend our time, and how we treat those around us, particularly those who are different or difficult. It sounds cliché, but it left me feeling both hopeful and terrified for the future. The film is also downright gorgeous, and there’s a good chance you’ll immediately start pricing tickets to Paris or Kyoto after you step out of the theater.
Streaming on Netflix on October 8th
Below is the rare story set in Newfoundland, on the east coast of Canada. It’s a compelling creature feature, a thriller where a mysterious monster is slowly terrorizing a remote fishing village that has been decimated by dwindling fish stocks. Josh Hartnett stars as a father of three who is just trying to survive, when strange chunks of ice start appearing in the harbor, portending something real bad. I watched the first two (of six) episodes, and even though it’s pretty clear what is going on, the show does a remarkable job of building up the mood and suspense, which makes the horrific reveals hit harder. Below is also surprisingly authentic and funny; anyone who has been to the East Coast will feel right at home when they see a bucket of salt beef or the dreaded screech.
An animated satirical sci-fi movie based on the comic of the same name, Duncan Jones’ Rogue Trooper is set on a toxic planet that is home to a never-ending war that is a lucrative venture back on Earth. It follows a squad of genetically engineered supersoldiers who find themselves stranded in enemy territory, and their numbers steadily dwindle over the course of the film. Unfortunately, despite some occasionally beautiful sci-fi imagery that imbues a real sense of scale, Rogue Trooper mostly falls flat, with a drab story, forgettable characters, and action that lacks any real weight. Even worse, despite boasting a cast including Jemaine Clement, Matthew Berry, and Philomena Cunk herself, Diane Morgan, it’s also not funny at all.
After moving to Los Angeles as part of the Indian Relocation Act in the 1950s, three sisters find themselves separated from each other after their mother is killed. The story then jumps forward a few decades, when each sister is living a very different life; one is trying to make it as an actress despite being typecast, one is a doctor after being adopted by a white family, and the youngest is struggling after passing through dozens of foster families. How We Stand explores the real impact of some truly horrific policies and programs, and the trio of actors at its core — Amber Midthunder, Alyssa Wapanatâhk, and Isabel DeRoy-Olson — are all excellent. But the film is saddled with writing that can feel too on the nose, and its magical realism elements feel underutilized until the very end.

articles.title: As Trump dominates convention, some Republicans quietly ask who comes next
articles.summary: JD Vance delivered the keynote speech to end the party's convention - but the president still took centre stage, the BBC's Daniel Bush writes.
articles.body: As Trump dominates convention, some Republicans quietly ask who comes nextFigure caption, Watch: Has Trump won over voters with his midterm convention?ByDaniel BushWashington correspondentReporting fromreporting from DallasRepublicans descended on Dallas this week to turn their midterm prospects around, hoping an unprecedented convention dominated by President Donald Trump would energise voters ahead of the November election.Many left the gathering - billed ahead of time by supporters as a "Trump-a-palooza" political fest - just as worried about the party's chances in 2026, and wondering what the Republicans' future will look like after the president leaves office.Vice-President JD Vance, who is widely viewed as a top contender to succeed Trump, offered his a party a glimpse of its potential future during his keynote address on Thursday night."We've got to take care of business this November," Vance told the crowds. "Then we'll worry about what comes next."His speech was interrupted at one point by chants of "48" - a nod to Trump's successor, who will become the 48th US president if they win in 2028. Vance let the chant linger briefly before waving it away.Image source, ReutersOver the two-day event, party activists were split on the wisdom of holding a midterm convention featuring a president who has record low approval ratings, and amid public frustration over the economy and war with Iran."I think it will make a difference. If anything it allows us to test the [campaign] message in front of a large audience," Jeff Ryer, the Virginia Republican Party chairman, told the BBC.Others said the president's rambling, nearly two-hour convention speech on Wednesday wouldn't sway voters weighing whether to keep Republicans in power in Congress.Polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance to retake control of the House and the Senate is also in play, though viewed as more of a long shot for the party."Do I wish Trump gave a shorter speech? Sure, but that's not who he is," said one Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer a blunt view of Trump's convention appearance.The source added that Trump's plea for voters to pretend as if he's on the ballot would fall flat."I don't think saying 'pretend I'm on the ballot' will work. He's not," the person said.The convention offered a stark reminder that the Trump era is heading toward its final chapter.Trump's presence loomed over the proceedings at the American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas.Republican House and Senate candidates lavished the president with praise in speeches, and supporters showed up wearing the red Maga hats that have become synonymous with Trump's political movement.The gathering was just two days, but still had the look and feel of the traditional four-day conventions staged by both parties in presidential election years. Organisers distributed signs and unleashed a balloon drop at the end as live music blared.Republicans had never held a midterm convention before.Vikki Consiglio, a party activist from Georgia, said it showcased Trump's ability to shake up political norms and capture the nation's attention.Evidence of that came when Trump pledged in his speech to make a payment of $5,000 to all American adults if Republicans retained control of Congress."He's a visionary. This whole convention is nothing but a vision," Consiglio said.But even as convention goers cheered Trump on, many seemed eager to discuss the 2028 presidential election."I'm very concerned about the next 10, 15, 20 years. I'm absolutely thinking about the future of the party," said Aiden Buzzetti, the president of The Bull Moose Project, a pro-Trump group.Buzzetti, who is 26, credited Trump with reshaping Republican politics, but said at the same time he was looking forward to a "new generation of conservative leaders."Image source, EPAImage caption, Trump joined Vance on stage to have the final word in DallasIn interviews with the BBC, attendees at the convention most often mentioned Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as the top contenders to replace Trump."Trump needs to pass the torch. We need to look forward," said Sandy Money, a Republican from Arizona who attended the convention. "I love Vance. But Rubio is my choice" if he runs in 2028, she said.Trump has openly mused about Rubio and Vance's chances to succeed him.But Vance and Rubio have deflected speculation about their political futures.Rubio was on a diplomatic trip to Ecuador during the convention, so he wasn't among the small handful of cabinet officials who attended the festivities in Dallas.The Trump administration has delivered "a great record of achievement," Vance argued, including improving the economy, strengthening border security and lowering the cost of prescription drugs.Vance said the contrast was clear with a Democratic Party that he argued had shifted radically to the left and turned into the "party of crazy". The vice-president also made a direct appeal to undecided voters, saying he wanted to win over "the people who are still making up their minds".Never one to cede the spotlight, Trump returned to the stage on Thursday night after Vance to round off the convention.For the president, the question of his successor was overshadowed by more immediate concerns."You know what happens if you don't vote?" he asked the gathered crowd. "You go to hell."More on this story

articles.title: Samsung says ‘Tim Cook’ bought a Galaxy Fold
articles.summary: That isn't Apple's former CEO promoting the Galaxy Z Fold 8 in a new Samsung ad - "Tim Cook from Palmerston North" just happens to have the same name and look a lot like him. Released right as Apple announced its iPhone Duo, the ad mimics Apple's cinematic product launch videos, with "Tim Cook" saying "the future is here." Samsung also takes a jab at Apple's Tim Cook with a reference to his recent
articles.body:
That isn’t Apple’s former CEO promoting the Galaxy Z Fold 8 in a new Samsung ad — “Tim Cook from Palmerston North” just happens to have the same name and look a lot like him. Released right as Apple announced its iPhone Duo, the ad mimics Apple’s cinematic product launch videos, with “Tim Cook” saying “the future is here.” Samsung also takes a jab at Apple’s Tim Cook with a reference to his recently updated profile picture.
It’s the latest in Samsung’s long-running history of ads dunking on its biggest rival, like one ad from over a decade ago that makes fun of iPhone fans willing to wait in lengthy lines for Apple’s latest phone. Then there’s the ad for the Galaxy Note 8 that features a viral shot of a diehard Apple fan with a haircut matching the iPhone’s notch. Samsung did a whole series of “Ingenius” ads teasing Apple’s Genius Bar tech support, with customers asking an Apple Store employee if iPhones have various Samsung features, like a headphone jack or an included fast charger. 
Not all of the ads take a comedic tone, though. A 2024 Samsung ad responded to controversy around Apple’s “Crush” iPad ad with a scene of a woman playing a damaged guitar on a re-creation of Apple’s set, featuring the tagline “Creativity cannot be crushed.”
Samsung and Apple’s rivalry has even inspired spinoff ads from other companies — Microsoft once released an ad suggesting the two camps “kind of like fighting.”
articles.author: Stevie Bonifield

articles.title: Hull fined £30k & bans issued over Chelsea chant
articles.summary: Hull City have been fined £30,000 over discriminatory chanting with the club issuing three supporter bans following their FA Cup defeat by Chelsea in February.
articles.body: Hull City have been fined £30,000 over discriminatory chanting during their 4-0 FA Cup defeat by Chelsea in February.The club is now urging supporters not to engage in the same chant when they face the Blues in the Premier League on Saturday.And it revealed three supporters had been banned for "a minimum of three years" following February's game at the MKM Stadium.Three people were arrested for allegedly engaging in homophobic chanting at the match, in which spectators were repeatedly warned to stop the chants over the PA system and messages were displayed on screens.The chanting was condemned by one fan group as a "stain on our game".The Football Association later charged the club with failing "to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters) do not use words or behave in an improper, offensive, abusive, indecent or insulting way with a reference - whether express or implied - to sexual orientation" and on Friday announced the club had accepted the charge and received a £30,000 fine."Hull City condemns, in the strongest possible terms, the offensive and inappropriate language used by the supporters responsible," the club said, saying the "chant in question is recognised as a homophobic slur and its use may constitute a hate crime".It warned those using the chant faced arrest and criminal charges."Ahead of Saturday's trip to Stamford Bridge, the club reminds all supporters that discrimination of any kind is wholly unacceptable and will not be tolerated," it added.

articles.body:
Ikea’s new Badkruka wireless Bluetooth speaker is now available in the US for $59.99. It’s reminiscent of the colorful and tiny $10 Kallsup speaker that Ikea debuted earlier this year at CES 2026, but at almost seven inches tall, the boxy Badkruka isn’t designed with portability in mind as it also lacks a rechargeable battery.
Color options aren’t as expansive as the Kallsup, either. The Badkruka is available with a black plastic finish or a pink one that almost looks like a wood grain texture. Wherever you end up using it will need a power source within reach, but audio sources can be connected over Bluetooth and, similar to the Kallsup, you can wirelessly connect the Badkruka to several other speakers that support multi-speaker mode to better fill your home or a larger space with sound.
You can also connect a pair of Badkruka’s for stereo sound, the speaker supports Spotify Tap, and it comes with three different EQ modes tailored to several music genres. If you don’t want to go wireless, the Badkruka can also be connected to home theater gear, your TV, or a PC’s TOSLINK port using an included optical cable.
articles.author: Andrew Liszewski

articles.title: Interest rates could rise again across the world – here's why
articles.summary: As countries grapple with energy costs pushing up inflation, this month will see how central banks respond.
articles.body: There's nothing like talk of energy prices and potential higher borrowing costs to remind us that the summer holidays are well and truly over.Surging oil prices have been pushing up what drivers pay at the fuel pumps and eating away at household budgets for months, and concerns remain over whether the economic impact of the US-Iran war will drive the cost of living higher.Citing the Middle East conflict and warning inflation was "set to remain well above" its 2% target for some time, the European Central Bank raised interest rates this week to 2.5%.Other central banks are also responding, with the US and the UK poised to make interest-rate decisions next week.Up first on Wednesday is the US Federal Reserve, which has held rates steady between 3.5% and 3.75% for five meetings in a row. It last made a change - a rate cut - in December.But above target inflation at 3.4%, a strong jobs market and President Donald Trump saying he does not think oil prices will come down until the Iran war ends, which he expects to happen after November's elections, has led many on Wall Street to bet on a rate hike this month.Newly-appointed Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has remained tight-lipped on where he sees interest rates going, but his repeated comments that the central bank's focus should be on slowing price rises has further fuelled expectations of an increase.Economists at Deutsche Bank said recently that a rate hike is "the most likely policy outcome", noting comments from Warsh and other members of the Fed.Views differ somewhat, with Grace Zwemmer, US economist at Oxford Economics, expecting rates to remain unchanged, but almost universally a rate cut appears to be off the table.Trump, though, is again pressing for lower rates."The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart - BE PATRIOTS for a change," he posted on social media last week.When the Bank of England meets later next week, it is expected to try to look both at current price pressures and the wider economic picture. Millions of UK households are set to see energy bills rise to the highest level for three years heading into the winter and gas prices have risen above 200p per therm for the first time since the end of 2022. Inflation in the UK is at 2.9%, and it is expected to jump in coming months.But despite those predictions, there appears to be broad agreement that the Bank will leave rates at 3.75%.That's because there is "no sign" of the so-called second-round effects of the price shock feeding through the economy, such as workers requesting wage rises or businesses hiking prices, according to Oxford Economics.This gives the Bank "some breathing space," added economist Alexander Harvey. Yael Selfin, chief economist at KPMG, said that outside of the US, in places such as the UK, the economic environment has been "much weaker" than where it was  in 2022, when the last inflation shock hit the world. UK inflation reached a record high of 11.1% in October that year.Interest rates are already higher than four years ago, she added, and consumers, somewhat scarred by previous price hikes, have changed how they spend.Also, four years ago "businesses were hiring aggressively, vacancies were at record highs, and more people were moving jobs than normal", Harvey said, as the economy rebooted following Covid."The conditions were in place for employees to push for significant pay rises in response to a significant inflation shock," he said. "That's in stark contrast to the current labour market."Now, hiring is much weaker than average and there is less pressure to recruit - giving employees less leverage to demand higher pay.Graphic by Miguel Roca-Terry and Jess Carr

articles.title: Scammers target hundreds of thousands of crypto owners after Trezor confirms data breach of email provider
articles.summary: This is the second data breach affecting a company that hardware crypto wallet maker Trezor relies on.
articles.body:
Hardware crypto wallet maker Trezor is warning customers for the second time in as many months that one of the companies it relies on was hacked, exposing the data of Trezor’s customers to hackers.
The link, when tapped, downloads an app that asks the victim for their wallet backup password. According to Trezor, one of the email subject lines said: “Critical Security Alert: STM32 Entropy Vulnerability.”
With a stolen wallet password, a hacker can irreversibly steal the person’s funds on the public blockchain.
Brevo said in an incident status post that the hackers were able to access 138 Brevo accounts to send out the mass volume of phishing messages. Brevo said that the hackers abused a flaw that meant the hackers’ access was “not properly scoped.” The company said that the hackers’ access was “wrongly granted” to all organizations that the hackers’ accounts could reach.
The breach highlights a common security incident, where hackers compromise data held by third-party companies that are necessary for fulfilling orders or purchases from customers. Trezor says none of its products, wallets, or account system were affected by the incident.
This is the second breach in recent weeks affecting Trezor, after the company alerted customers in August that one of its shipping partners was compromised in a data breach. The incident at the mailing company ShipMonk exposed the names, phone numbers, email addresses, and postal addresses of at least 81,000 people who bought and received Trezor wallet hardware.
The data breach could put crypto owners and other wealthy individuals at risk of targeted violence and so-called “wrench” attacks, which rely on physical attacks to extract passwords from people.
In the weeks following the breach at ShipMonk, some people have received letters by mail claiming to be from Trezor, featuring a QR code that, when scanned, opens up a fake page that attempts to steal the victim’s crypto wallet password.
Trezor said it was reevaluating its relationships with its vendors and warned customers that their email addresses may be used again for future phishing attacks.

articles.title: I moved my shop 20 miles because I couldn't afford £300 a week on fuel
articles.summary: People in Turriff, Aberdeenshire, tell BBC Scotland News the impact rising petrol prices is having.
articles.body: Image caption, Melanie Wilson was spending a lot of money on fuel for travelByRebecca CurranBBC ScotlandReporting fromTurriff and Ken BanksNorth east Scotland reporterAntique shop owner Melanie Wilson says she has moved her business closer to home because she was struggling to pay nearly £300 a week on diesel as a result of soaring fuel prices.She opened her new location in Turriff, Aberdeenshire, earlier this month - cutting her commute by 20 miles and her fuel spend in half.Fuel prices in the UK have climbed about 5p in just one week as a result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with diesel edging towards £1.95 a litre in some areas.Wilson is one of countless people in small rural locations around Scotland who are feeling the pinch as they need their cars for work and everyday life.Fuel prices started to climb when the US-Israel war with Iran began on 28 February. The military strikes severely disrupted the production and transportation of energy across the region.Prices fell back when the US and Iran agreed to a framework deal to end the fighting in June.However they have started rising again as tensions resurface, with the price of wholesale oil back above $100 a barrel.Wilson, 37, lives in Banff, but has now moved her shop location from Insch to Turriff to cut travel costs.She said she spends more than £150 a week on diesel - but it used to be about double that."I decided to move the shop really just because of the travel," she said."It just wasn't justifiable driving back and forth every day with the price of fuel. It's scary."There's no other option. I mean, you can dread going to the pump."Cost to run a taxi 'horrendous'Image caption, Martin Milne employs several people with his taxi businessTaxi driver Martin Milne, 55, employs 24 people at his business.With fuel obviously forming a significant part of the company's running costs, rising prices are putting further pressure on his business."The last two days the price has risen nine, 10 pence a litre," he said."The cost per month now to fill my cars is horrendous. It's getting more and more every time, you can't see a way out of this now, it makes it very difficult."I would say a monthly fuel would be £6,500, before the Iran conflict it was maybe £5,000."Image caption, These were the prices in Turriff on ThursdayAt 92, Evelyn Grant is still driving.For her, having a car means being able to get out and about independently.However, she too is feeling the impact of higher fuel costs.Image caption, Evelyn Grant still drives when she can"Well it's rather expensive, it certainly makes you wonder if you'll put your heating on or not," she said."I am definitely having to make those choices. It'll never come back down - it's gone up, and it won't come back down I can guarantee that."I just don't go so far with the car now, I just think I can cut back that way."I can still go out and walk and get the heat up that way."Image caption, John Reid described prices as "extortionate"Driver John Reid, 37, spends a lot of time on the road."To keep the truck on the road, it's quite expensive," he said."It's just the way it is right now, the price is up and down here all the time."The prices are getting extortionate, that's the truth about it."Image caption, Jared Whitehouse now prefers the biking option to the carCarer Jared Whitehouse, 42, does a lot of miles in his car, and his bike.He said his costs have gone up drastically."Yesterday I came out of Aberdeen and I paid £80 to fill the tank - compared to probably a couple of few years ago where I was paying like closer to £60."I've been doing a lot more riding around on my bike, because it's just cheaper."Image caption, Tyreece Flaws said he closes his eyes and hopes for the bestTyreece Flaws, 25, who works in road haulage, lives in Portsoy and works in Turriff."It's quite sore," he said."I travel quite far for work, about 25 miles each way, so it's quite expensive."When I pull up at the forecourt I just kind of close my eyes and hope for the best."I have zero option, I have to drive for work, so I have to fill up. Doesn't help with the rest of the cost of living, food and stuff. I do worry about money."How do wholesale oil prices affect the cost of petrol and diesel at the pump?Crude oil is a key ingredient in petrol and diesel, which means that higher wholesale costs make filling up a car more expensive. The price of petrol and diesel is also heavily influenced by demand and refining capacity. Analysts say every $10 (£7.44) per barrel increase in the oil price pushes up pump prices by roughly 7p a litre.Since the war began, the price of a barrel of Brent crude - the global benchmark for wholesale oil prices - has been very volatile.Generally speaking, news of further conflict drives the price up while hopes of an end to the war pushes the price down.Before the conflict, Brent was about $70 a barrel, but the fighting saw it peak at above $120.  In early July, after the framework deal was signed, prices fell back to near the $70 a barrel mark.When the peace talks collapsed, the price climbed back up again to above $100 a barrel. It fell back for a few weeks but is once again over the $100 mark after a fresh escalation in hostilities.More on this story

articles.title: Princess Diana's 'revenge dress' goes up for auction
articles.summary: Auction house Sotheby's expects the dress to sell for up to $300,000 (£220,000) when it goes under the hammer on 9 December.
articles.body: A dress worn by Princess Diana dubbed her "revenge dress" is being put up for auction.The late Princess of Wales wore the strapless black silk evening dress to a party in London hours after her then-estranged husband Prince Charles admitted to committing adultery during their marriage.Her dramatic arrival at the Serpentine Gallery in 1994 in the outfit became an iconic pop-culture moment.Auction house Sotheby's expects the dress to sell for up to £220,000 ($300,000) when it goes under the hammer on 9 December - the first time it has been up for auction since 1997, when the princess sold 79 of her dresses just months before her death to raise money for charities.Morgane Halimi, Sotheby's global head of handbags and fashion, said in a statement that Princess Diana "understood instinctively" that fashion can be a language in its own right."On her own terms, Princess Diana turned the dress into one of the most powerful messages she ever made, during one of the most scrutinised and emotionally charged episodes of her life," she said."She walked into a moment in which so much of her story was being told for her and, through what she chose to wear, reclaimed the narrative for herself."The same evening as the Serpentine Gallery fundraising dinner, a documentary had aired in which the Prince of Wales (now King) had admitted that he had been unfaithful to Diana, after years of rumours and media reports.The content of the ITV interview had been leaked a few days prior, meaning Diana's first public appearance after it aired was widely interpreted as her reply.Anna Harvey, her stylist at the time, has been reported as saying that the princess "wanted to look a million dollars".She made a last-minute wardrobe change before heading out to the event, setting aside a less striking Valentino gown in favour of the off-the-shoulder dress with an asymmetric hemline and chiffon train by Greek designer Christina Stambolian, which she accessorised with a royal necklace, black clutch and black heels.The "revenge dress" will be toured around the world prior to its sale, appearing at Sotheby's London showroom from 18 to 24 September, before heading to Hong Kong for the start of October, Geneva for the start of November and then on to New York, where it will be sold. It was last auctioned by Diana herself, as one of dozens of items sold to raise funds for cancer and Aids charities.The dress was bought by then-Glasgow resident Briege Mackenzie and her husband Graeme, who paid £39,098 for it.She told the Independent, external at the time that they had purchased the item not to wear - "I can't fit in it," she said - but because the proceeds were going to charity Children First.Mackenzie said in a statement issued by Sotheby's on Thursday: "My late husband and I knew that this dress was something special. "Princess Diana was walking into the worst night of her life and you would never know it to look at her. It went from a cocktail dress to a statement in the time it took to photograph her."Thirty years on, you can say the words anywhere in the world and everyone knows exactly which dress you mean."She added that she had decided to sell the dress following the death of her husband, with whom bidding on it had been "one of the great days of our life together".Sotheby's said that a rare copy of the 1997 auction catalogue, signed by Diana and Stambolian, and which credits Prince William for the idea to auction the dress, will be sold alongside it.Part of the proceeds from the sale will be donated to Royal Edinburgh Hospital via the NHS Lothian Charity.The vintage Jaguar XJ40 car that Diana had arrived at the Serpentine Gallery event in was sold at auction earlier this year for £66,250.The dress, however, is expected to fetch a considerably higher price - though it would not be the first time an item from the princess's wardrobe has sold for a significant sum.One of Diana's sweaters, featuring a black sheep among rows of white ones, was sold for £920,000 at an auction by Sotheby's in New York in 2023.
