articles.title: Hull City footballer in crash near training ground
articles.summary: Premier League winger Sorba Thomas's Land Rover overturns in Cottingham.
articles.body: Premier League winger Sorba Thomas has been involved in a car crash close to Hull City's training ground, the club has confirmed.The 27-year-old walked away from the crash, which happened on Millhouse Woods Lane in Cottingham on Friday morning. His vehicle, a grey Land Rover Defender, was pictured on its roof, with broken windows.Humberside Police said emergency services remained at the scene and asked people to avoid the area.In a statement, the club said it was "relieved" to hear its player, who joined the Tigers from Championship side Stoke City earlier this month, was unharmed.The club added: "The club is aware of images of Sorba's car circulating on social media and can reassure supporters that he has sustained no injuries and emerged from his vehicle completely unscathed."A woman who lives at the scene said the crash, which happened at about 08:30 BST, woke her up."I was laid in bed [and] heard a noise – crash, bang," she said."I got up, come down and the car is in my hedge."An NHS worker who lives on the road said the incident had left him unable to go to work as the road was blocked."There will be patients who will miss appointments because of this," he said."It's one road in and one road out. It was an accident waiting to happen."

articles.title: Insta360 launches a single-lens Osmo Pocket rival you can actually buy in the US
articles.summary:
I saw the Luna Pro briefly at the IFA trade show, and it looks and feels a lot like the Ultra. | Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge	

Insta360's first compact steadycam, the Luna Ultra, made a splash this year by beating DJI to launch with two lenses. Now it's followed the Ultra with a slightly stripped back Pro model, which drops to one lens but has a unique advantage: It can shoot vertical video
articles.body:
Insta360’s first compact steadycam, the Luna Ultra, made a splash this year by beating DJI to launch with two lenses. Now it’s followed the Ultra with a slightly stripped back Pro model, which drops to one lens but has a unique advantage: It can shoot vertical video in 4K. Plus, unlike DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4, you can buy it in the US.
At its heart, the Luna Pro is mostly an Ultra with the telephoto lens stripped out. It uses the same 1-inch-type 8K sensor as the Ultra’s main camera, and has a similar design including the detachable 2-inch touchscreen that doubles as a remote, and the same four-hour battery life and NFC tag for quicker file transfers. It’s a bit smaller and lighter thanks to dropping the second lens, but that’s about it. 
Insta360 has given the Pro one crucial upgrade though: It can use that 8K sensor to record 4K vertical video at 30fps. The Luna Ultra — like both of DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4 and 4P models — is limited to 3K resolution when you record in portrait, forcing some people to hold the whole gimbal sideways to get the footage they need. It’s a relief to see the Pro fix that omission, and Insta360 told me that it will also be added to the Luna Ultra in a firmware update, currently expected to be released on September 20th.
The Luna Pro is out now in the US for $599.99, compared to $769.99 for the Luna Ultra. In Europe it starts at £469 / €529, just a little more than the £429 / €479 DJI Osmo Pocket 4, which is (officially) unavailable in the US following a ban on the company.
Update, September 11th: Added confirmation that the Luna Ultra will receive a firmware update to add 4K vertical video.
articles.author: Dominic Preston

articles.title: Polanski selected as Green Party candidate for Starmer's former seat
articles.summary: The Green Party leader said the party is the "underdog" in Holborn and St Pancras but "can win".
articles.body: Green Party leader Zack Polanski has been selected as the party's candidate in the by-election for Sir Keir Starmer's former seat in Parliament.Polanski, who is a London Assembly member, will stand in Holborn and St Pancras on 8 October as he seeks to become an MP.He was voted to be the party's candidate by members of the Camden Green Party ahead of local councillor Hamza Chowdhury.Polanski said the Greens "might be the underdog in this election but we have the momentum and we can win".He also spoke of how he made Camden "my home" when he first moved to London 20 years ago, adding he has "lived and worked across Holborn and St Pancras for many of the years since".Polanski said: "I love this place but I also know times are tough here in Holborn and St Pancras. My story of constantly moving around flats is such a common story for Londoners and I know so many people are struggling right now."He argued that voting Green "sends a clear signal" to the council and government that "we demand better for our communities".Polanski added he is "confident but not complacent" about his chances. He also said the election is about "putting pressure" on Prime Minister Andy Burnham, noting a Green MP would "work with him constructively to challenge him on the gaps in his plans".Announcing the result, Green MP Hannah Spencer said members had "overwhelmingly" chosen Polanski.The Greens finished second to Labour at the elections for Camden Council earlier this year.The by-election is an early test of Burnham's popularity with the public and whether Labour under his leadership is able to fend off the challenge from the Greens in inner-city constituencies. For Polanski, it will be a test on whether he can provide evidence that he can deliver on his ambition for the Greens to "replace" Labour.Labour has held the inner London seat since it was created in 1983 and the party's candidate for the by-election is Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali.The seat became vacant after former Prime Minister Sir Keir announced he was standing down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.

articles.title: AI boom helps drive surprise UK growth in July
articles.summary: The economy expanded by 0.4%, official figures show, whereas analysts had predicted no growth.
articles.body: The UK's economy grew faster than expected in July partly helped by businesses using artificial intelligence (AI).The economy expanded by 0.4%, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, whereas analysts had predicted no growth.Growth in July was helped by a strong performance from the services sector, and particularly computer programming.Experts said the figure showed the UK economy was proving resilient in the face of shocks such as the war in Iran, but they expect growth to slow in the months ahead as high energy prices affect households.July's figure follows growth of 0.3% in June and zero growth in May.According to the ONS director of economic statistics, Liz McKeown, there was evidence that businesses involved with AI and related technologies helped to boost the sector, not just in July but in May and June as well.The ONS said many of the IT businesses reporting the largest turnover "appear to be involved with AI", though it said it is difficult to quantify the exact impact of AI.McKeown also said some businesses had said that the warm weather and football world cup had affected activity in July, although she said the effects "differed across industries, benefitting some businesses while creating challenges for others".The ONS said that in the three months to July, which gives a better underlying picture, the economy grew by 0.4% compared with the previous three months.Rob Arnold, co-founder of Ascendea, an AI firm which employs nine people, believes the UK hasn't seen the real economic growth potential from the technology yet.He says his company is able to develop apps for other businesses "100 times quicker at a 50th of the cost" because of AI, but that the UK government needs to do more to invest in the sector as there are currently better opportunities in the US.He knows a few small UK-based AI firms that have either moved to the US or are thinking of doing so due to a lack of UK government support.Alongside grants and funding, he says the government also needs to invest in training companies on how to use AI as it can be dangerous if not understood properly. "It's like playing with a weapon," he says.Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said July's data showed "the resilience of the economy in the first half of the year continued into the second half".However, he added that higher energy prices and borrowing costs would soon start to hit growth, especially if the rises seen this week are sustained.The Iran war has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices - affecting households and businesses.This rise in energy costs has led to fears that inflation will remain high, and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep price rises under control.The Bank of England is meeting next week to discuss interest rates. Economists widely expect rates to be held, but some have predicted an increase before the end of the year.Chancellor John Healey said the economy, was "demonstrating a welcome resilience, despite serious global uncertainty"."Our growth although still fragile was the fastest in the G7 in the first half of the year," he added."But, the conflict in the Middle East does have impacts here at home - from the cost of the weekly family shop to the cost of government borrowing."Healey is to present his first Budget in October. He told BBC News this week that he wants people to confident about the economy, despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs.Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said nobody in the government "should be high-fiving themselves" over the latest figures. "Our construction and production sectors are shrinking, unemployment is up under Labour, and we've got the highest government borrowing rates in almost 30 years."Yael Selfin, chief economist at KPMG, said while July's headline growth figure was strong, it "masks a weaker picture for households"."Consumer-facing services contracted in July, as retail and hospitality activity fell following earlier increases in activity in the summer," she said."Higher energy and fuel prices are likely to place further pressure on household budgets, while elevated mortgage rates will continue to weigh on housing activity and wider consumer spending."Richard Carter, the head of fixed interest research at investment firm Quilter Cheviot, said the growth seem in July "may not last, especially as activity is likely to stall ahead of the Budget."The war in the Middle East continues to drive a lot of the economic data, but the UK is the most exposed to the fallout," he said."Calls for pro-growth measures will get louder as the Budget nears, but whether or not the government has the room to act remains to be seen."Additional reporting by Mitchell Labiak

articles.title: Girls given legal right to wear trousers in Northern Ireland schools
articles.summary: Guidelines stipulate that school uniform policies for the 2027/28 school year onwards must include the option for girls to wear trousers.
articles.body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The guidelines stipulate that school uniform policies for the 2027/28 school year onwards must include the option for girls to wear trousers throughout the school year, including for PEByAdam MandevilleBBC News NIGirls in Northern Ireland are to be given the legal right to wear trousers in school if they wish to do so.  Revising guidelines, Education Minister Paul Givan said that, from the start of the 2027/2028 academic year, schools will be banned from prohibiting girls wearing trousers. There are already laws on school uniform in Northern Ireland, and Givan had previously said they give girls the legal authority to challenge their schools. Education committee members, however, had called on the minister to go further.Some assembly members have now accused the minister of making a "U-turn", with "substantial sums of public money" spent on drafting legislation "to fix his error of judgement".Guidelines 'legally binding'It comes after assembly members passed a new law last year, aimed at addressing the cost of school uniforms in Northern Ireland - with these updated guidelines on wearing trousers now legally binding under the School Uniforms Act.Speaking on BBC Radio Ulster's The Nolan Show, Givan said the change would come into immediate effect ahead of the next academic year. "I don't need to go through the assembly to give effect to this," he said. "Today, I am taking that decision, that will be formally communicated, schools will be hearing from me, and as of the next academic year...schools will be required that this has to be available if it is requested upon."The minister explained that this change will not apply during the 2026/27 academic year, in order to allow schools to change their uniform policies.Givan added that the change will also apply to physical education.'Embarassing U-turn'Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The education minister says the changes will come into effect next yearIn a statement, Sinn Féin MLA Cathy Mason described Givan's decision as a "welcome but embarrassing U-turn"."This is an important win for girls and for all those who campaigned for this simple choice," she said."The minister had the opportunity to guarantee this right in his own school uniforms legislation but failed to do so. It should not have required further legislation from the Education Committee to force movement on something so basic."Mason added that girls' right to wear trousers "should never have been controversial and it should not have taken this long"."We welcome that the minister has finally acted and will be watching closely to ensure he follows through and that girls are not let down."'Error of judgement'In a statement, Alliance's education spokesperson, and chair of the Education Committee, Nick Mathison also described the decision as a "U-turn"."I want to thank all of the young campaigners who have been bravely raising their voices about this, and whose dedication will lead to seeing this wrong righted," he said."The committee will be doing their full due diligence to guarantee the wording used in this update will ensure all girls are granted the right to wear trousers as part of their school uniform."Mathison added: "Minister Givan will have to explain why he took so long to move on this issue. Substantial sums of public money have been spent on drafting legislation to fix his error of judgement, and we have said all along that he could have avoided this with the stroke of a pen."A statement published on the Department of Education website said: "The guidelines issued today stipulate that school uniform policies for the 2027/28 school year onwards must include the option for girls to wear trousers throughout the school year, including for PE and Games."The guidelines are legally binding under the School Uniforms Act which came into operation earlier this year."It added: "The Act is designed to help reduce the cost of school uniforms and ensure that affordability, comfort, practicality and sustainability are at the centre of school uniform policies."More on this story

articles.title: I was in the epicentre - I'm so lucky to have lived
articles.summary: Paul Berriff says his life expectancy has been cut short because of being buried under rubble.
articles.body: 'I survived the epicentre of 9/11 - I'm so lucky'Image source, Paul BerriffImage caption, Paul Berriff went to film the aftermath of 9/11 but ended up buried under rubbleByAmy OakdenBBC Radio Tees and Seb CheerYorkshireWarning: This story contains graphic details of the aftermath from the 9/11 attacks.On 11 September 2001, photographer and documentary filmmaker Paul Berriff was living and working in New York City.He was caught up in the 9/11 attacks and still remembers the day in vivid detail.More recently, he has become one of thousands of survivors to be diagnosed with terminal illnesses connected with the long-term effects of that day.Now aged 80 and living near Northallerton in North Yorkshire, Berriff has recalled the events."Somebody came into the office and said a plane had hit the twin towers," he said.First thinking it was likely to be a light aircraft or helicopter, often seen flying around the landmark, he phoned his wife who was at their home in Lower Manhattan.She told him about "fire engines and people running around" and his "news instinct kicked in" and he travelled to the scene to document the events on camera.As Berriff, a sound recordist and assistant producer approached, they could see "both towers were on fire"."We could see these black dots coming down from the side of each building and we wondered what it was," he said."As we got nearer, we could see it was people jumping, so we knew it was pretty serious."They headed to the base of the towers, where assistant fire commissioner Steve Gregory was sending firefighters in.Image source, Paul BerriffImage caption, Assistant fire commissioner Steve Gregory arrived at the base of the towers at the same time as Berriff"Suddenly, there was this loud explosion to my left," Berriff said."The camera was on and I turned it round and looked up, just to see the top of the south tower peeling away, like a massive umbrella opening."Whilst firefighters shouted for everybody to run away, Berriff said he "stayed there, looking through the small viewfinder on my camera to see 250,000 tonnes of metal and girders hurtling towards me".After "about two seconds", he and sound recordist Lulu "started running down the street"."The next thing I remember was my camera leaving my hand in slow-motion and everything goes black."He was unconscious for approximately 35 minutes, during which time the second tower also collapsed.After regaining consciousness, Berriff said his "mouth was full of all this cement gunge stuff"."I could hardly breathe. I was hot, I was sweating, my trousers were burning. Total blackness, I've never seen blackness like it."After many minutes of crawling to try and escape the "hell hole that I was in", Berriff emerged from under the rubble."I could see everything's gone from colour to black and white," he said."It was like ash from a volcano."Figure caption, Watch: Berriff filmed the first tower collapsing in 2001After realising Lulu was no longer with him, Berriff returned to the area where he had been buried under the rubble."In the road about 100 yards ahead of me, there was bits of the tower embedded in the roadway," he said."The police later said I was probably the first alive person in the epicentre of it - it was just total devastation."He found Lulu's sound mixer and his camera, which he picked up before returning to his apartment block, where Lulu was waiting."She'd been grabbed by one of the fire officers and they'd run into an underground garage so she'd escaped all the major impact."It was at this point he realised he was injured, with blood covering his back.His wife accompanied him to hospital, where he was decontaminated as a precaution as emergency services were concerned that there "might have been anthrax or other toxic chemicals that the terrorists may have put in all the planes"."So by now, they knew."Following treatment, they had no keys or other belongings so stayed at the home of a nurse, whose husband loaned Berriff clothes."I went into the sitting room and I'd still got the camera with me," he said."I pressed play and up came all this imagery of what had happened to me."Image source, Paul BerriffImage caption, Berriff visited Ground Zero as searches were still being carried outBerriff founded the Humber Rescue lifeboat charity in his back garden in Hessle, near Hull, in 1989.Six years later, he established a lifeboat station on the bank of the Humber.He was appointed OBE for his work in 2016 and volunteers now attend more than 100 callouts each year.'I'm so lucky'Twenty-five years on from 9/11, he is still feeling its impact."All of us that escaped that day thought we'd done well, then about three or four years ago, we started developing these illnesses," he said."All of us had ingested the cloud which contained body parts, glass, aviation fuel, you name it."We'd eaten all this, ingested it all."It had laid dormant for 20 years and we've all developed these fatal diseases."He was diagnosed three years ago with pulmonary fibrosis."My consultant said I've only got five years to live," he said."That was quite a shock actually, having survived it all that close and then 'bang' this happens."According to the 9/11 Memorial,, external tens of thousands of people have been diagnosed with illnesses linked to the attack.After 9/11, Berriff said he "lives every day as full as I can"."The only thing that stays with me is that I actually survived it and I shouldn't have done," he said."I ran down the street with the sound recordist. I went straight down the street."Those that went to the left or right of us, they died."I'm so lucky."Get in touch

articles.title: My experience of tragedy gave me a second family
articles.summary: Louise Rayner is still friends with the wife and children of Bob Lawrence, who died in South Tower.
articles.body: 'My experience of tragedy on 9/11 gave me a second family'Image source, Louise RaynerImage caption, Louise Rayner with her two former charges, Bobby and Toland Lawrence, pictured in New JerseyByHayley CoyleReporting fromBaildon"It was a series of sliding doors moments that led us to each other and from something so tragic, came an enduring, special friendship."On 11 September 2001, Louise Rayner was living with the Lawrence family in Summit, New Jersey. Then in her mid-20s, she was working as a nanny for Bob and Suzanne Lawrence's two children.Louise was a photography student from Bradford, but ended up forming a lifelong bond with the Lawrences after Bob, 41, was killed in the attacks on the World Trade Center, just one day after starting a new job on the 104th floor of the South Tower.She ended up staying with the Lawrences for a further two and a half years to help in the aftermath of the atrocity and they remain close today.On the 25th anniversary of the attacks, Louise, 52, told the BBC how 9/11 changed the "whole direction of my life" and gave her a second home in the US. Image source, Louise RaynerImage caption, Louise, Bobby and Toland have a deeply special bond, Louise said She met the Lawrence family by chance - she changed her original flight to the US by two weeks and on the plane met another au pair who introduced her to Bob, Suzanne and their children Bobby and Toland. The couple sponsored Louise to study while working as their nanny."Toland was about eight and Bobby was six - I got on really well with them and they were really cute and lovely. "A lot of Bob's family lived in Summit, so there was loads of cousins and it never felt like a job."On the day of the attacks, Suzanne was working away and Bob had left early that morning to get a lift into New York, where he worked for an investment bank in the South Tower.Image source, BBC/Hayley CoyleImage caption, Louise said 9/11 changed the the whole direction of her life but gave her a second family "I had taken the kids to school and hadn't seen Bob as he left so early and I went back to bed - and I remember the landline went and started ringing and ringing. "It was a nanny friend who lived two towns over and she said, 'are you watching the news?'," Louse recalled. "It had been such a beautiful, perfect morning with clear skies and what unfolded was so surreal. "We were watching it together live and I was talking to her as the second plane hit. "And then my mobile started to ring." Figure caption, 'My experience of tragedy on 9/11 gave me a second family'Louise said that some of Bob's family did not even know he had taken a new job at the World Trade Center and Suzanne, who was in another state, could not fly home as aircraft were grounded, so it was her who had to pick the children up from school. For weeks, Louise said there was lots of "clinging to hope" about missing people being found but it was understood that anyone on or above the 77th floor of the South Tower had died. The plane struck the building between the 78th and 84th floors. "And of course, no one expected the towers to fall; the skyline, it was like a child losing its tooth - it was just so stark to see it. "Everyone was presumed dead."I tried to just be a stable presence for the children - but I don't think it was officially confirmed for a long time that Bob had died," she added.  Image source, Louise RaynerImage caption, Louise pictured with Suzanne and the hosts of Ground Force, when they filmed in the USWhat followed for Louise was a feeling of "tiptoeing through someone else's grief" as the family navigated the loss of Bob, who she described as "bigger than life" and an "incredible family man". He was a keen athlete who loved tennis and hockey."But I wasn't going anywhere. I didn't even need to say it - Suzanne and the family needed me," Louise added.  Suzanne, who worked in finance, had to return to work shortly after so for two and a half years Louise helped with the cooking, cleaning and homework and kept Bob's family informed about the children. "I just knew that they were grateful for that", she said. Louise left New Jersey in 2003 due to her visa expiring and even though there are more than 3,000 miles between her home in the village of Baildon and New York, her friendship with the Lawrences was cemented. Suzanne, who is "so strong but not overly sentimental", sent her an engraved miniature picture frame out of the blue years later simply thanking Louise for being there when she was needed. She is especially close to Toland, now in her 30s, a coach and human design specialist who is "very cosmic". "She says to me 'you were meant to be there, it wasn't just anybody...it was you that was meant to be there you were sent to help'.Image source, SubmittedImage caption, Toland (far right), Suzanne and Bobby pictured at Louise's wedding"She is right - if I had gone on that original flight I would never have met the girl who introduced me, so there's all these ripples, all these like sliding doors moments that led us to that and I so feel so close to them even now," Louise added. Suzanne, Bob and Toland have been to Bradford and Toland was even Louise's bridesmaid when she married.Toland said the "love and care" Louise showed her family changed the course of her life for the better. Louise's own three children, aged 19, 17 and 14, also met the Lawrences in New York, which was "two worlds coming together". Louise said that experiencing something so catastrophic almost first hand has altered the way she sees the world."9/11 absolutely changed the course of my life, it gave me these friendships with the family with two close friends who were there with me when it happened, we share it."So much kindness came out of it, such a sharp contrast to what happened. "I've got this family in New Jersey that wouldn't have happened if it wasn't for 9/11."Toland added: "Her kindness and patience during those years is a resource I carry with me always and I'm so glad she is a part of my life."Get in touch

articles.title: Bed at 6:45am - US Open semi-finalists fight effects of late-night finishes
articles.summary: New York is known as the city that never sleeps. But that comes at a price for US Open stars - including men's semi-finalists Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev.
articles.body: Bed at 6:45am - US Open semi-finalists fight effects of late-night finishesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ben Shelton reached the US Open semi-finals after beating Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set thriller finishing at 3:34am ByBBC Sport tennis news reporterNew York is known as the city that never sleeps - and so it has been at this year's US Open.A number of matches have started late and finished in the early hours, backing up the city's reputation as a playground for the nocturnal.But when some players - including men's semi-finalists Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev - are heading to bed as Manhattan commuters are waking up for work, it raises questions about fairness.Three of top seed Zverev's five matches over the past fortnight have finished past 1am."I've been to bed as late as 6:45am in the past week so I'm kind of a bit jet-lagged," Zverev said."I feel like I'm playing the Australian Open in New York right now."Friday's semi-final against Karen Khachanov - not before 15:00 local time/20:00 BST - will be the first time the German has played in the day at this year's US Open.By contrast, unseeded Khachanov has not been on court beyond midnight. He also has slightly longer to prepare after his quarter-final against Alexander Blockx finished shortly before 19:00 local time on Wednesday.American eighth seed Shelton did not complete his last-eight victory over Carlos Alcaraz until 3:34am on Wednesday.Shelton faces 11th seed Frances Tiafoe, who wrapped up his quarter-final about 19:00 on Tuesday after beating US compatriot Alex Michelsen in a five-set epic."The advantage of the opponent who has played earlier in the day will be big - they've had that full evening's rest and a good night's sleep," Matt Little, who was Andy Murray's long-time strength and conditioning coach, told BBC Sport."We can all relate to it - if you have one really bad night's sleep, you have the knock-on effect of that for the coming days."Little saw the effects first hand when Murray infamously finished a match at 4am at the 2023 Australian Open, with the former world number one managing only three hours sleep before returning to Melbourne Park about 11am the following day.Zverev did not go to bed until gone 5am following his opening three victories at Flushing Meadows and stayed up to watch Shelton beat Alcaraz on his night off.Shelton, who meets Tiafoe in Friday's night session (19:00 local time/00:00 BST, Sat), insisted he would pull up "all right" after two days off court."He'll have to be napping to catch up some sleep," said Little."On the nutritional side, he'll be making sure he gets as many carbs and as much protein as he can in for that next match, and trying to get back to a bit of a routine."It's about making sure you can optimise the hydration and get as much sleep as possible without completely going into a full slumber."Murray described the situation in Melbourne - where he beat Thanasi Kokkinakis in the second-latest finish in Grand Slam history - as a "farce".Few disagreed, and slight tweaks have been made in an attempt to limit matches finishing at the crack of dawn.In response to Murray's match, the Australian Open cut the number of day-session matches on the main courts from three to two to reduce the risk of night sessions being delayed.In early 2024, the ATP and WTA created new rules which prevented tour matches  - played over three sets and not five like the Slams - starting after 23:00. These rules, however, do not apply at the majors.Image source, BBC SportImage caption, Zverev and Shelton have each played in two of the top-five latest finishes at this year's US OpenLast week, former world number one Venus Williams and her opponent Sofia Kenin began their first-round match at 12:13am - the latest start in US Open history.It was one of three matches which finished post-2am in the first seven nights, with three others ending after 1am, while Shelton's victory over Alcaraz was the latest finish in US Open history."Something has got to give," said 18-time Grand Slam singles champion Martina Navratilova. "This is not OK and it is not normal."Some argue these occasions are the essence of the US Open - and a raucous sporting representation of the city which never sleeps.The volume of early-morning matches has increased at Flushing Meadows this fortnight, although Tuesday's play finishing at 3:34am on Wednesday was the product of unusual circumstances.All three preceding quarter-finals on Arthur Ashe Stadium - Aryna Sabalenka beating Linda Noskova and Jessica Pegula overcoming Emma Navarro, with Tiafoe's win sandwiched in the middle - went the full distance.Data shows matches are becoming longer - so what is the solution?Starting the US Open night sessions earlier is the most common proposal.That is met by a resistance from television executives and the practicality of New York life, with many fans unlikely to arrive at Flushing Meadows much before 7pm.There is a more extreme suggestion - cutting back on the best-of-five sets format at the Slams.That idea gained further traction after Andrew Abdo - Tennis Australia's recently-appointed chief executive - suggested the Australian Open could look to reduce men's matches to three sets in the future.Abdo's comments provoked a backlash, with Tiafoe among those defending the traditional way. "Do I love five-setters? Absolutely not," Tiafoe said. "But it's tennis, man. I grew up watching so many incredible five-setters. "Novak-Rafa, Federer-Rafa, epic five-setters that go on for hours and hours. That's the history of the game."More on this story

articles.title: Five dead and dozens injured in coach crash in Swiss Alps
articles.summary: The tourist coach was carrying dozens of Dutch passengers when it overturned in the south-eastern Swiss Alps.
articles.body: Five people have died and dozens are injured after a tourist coach crashed in the south-eastern Swiss Alps, police say.The Dutch tour bus hit a safety barrier in a roadworks area, left the road and overturned between Susch and Zernez in the Graubünden region late on Thursday afternoon.Swiss police said on Friday that the deceased had not yet been identified. They added that the other 40 people on board the coach - whose injuries ranged from serious to minor - had been transported to hospitals by rescue helicopters and ambulance crews.The coach reportedly left the Netherlands on Monday and was on a day trip to Switzerland from Austria when the crash happened.Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said his thoughts were everyone involved, and King Willem-Alexander and Queen Máxima said their hearts went out to everyone affected by "this great tragedy".Swiss President Guy Parmelin posted on X that he was "deeply shocked" by the incident and offered his "sincere condolences" to the families of the victims.

articles.title: Son charged with murdering parents in own home
articles.summary: Yasin Leli, 46, is charged with two counts of murder after his parents, 80 and 78, were found stabbed.
articles.body: A man has been charged with murdering his parents in their own home. Ismail Ahmed Yeli, 80, and 78-year-old Fatma Leli were found stabbed to death in a house on Hardman Street in Blackburn on Monday, Lancashire Police said.Their family described the couple as "inseparable", adding they were "heartbroken" to have lost "the oldest and most cherished members of our family".Yasin Leli, 46, also of Hardman Street, has been charged with two counts of murder and is due to appear at Blackburn Magistrates Court later.Officers were called to the house at just after 08:20 BST and found the couple had died from multiple stab wounds.Lancashire Police said: "Our thoughts remain with their loved ones at this distressing time."The family thanked police for their "professionalism and compassion", as well as local councillors and the wider community and Masjid-e-Quwwatul mosque for their support.

articles.title: Neijuan
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neijuan
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49655176
Points: 29
# Comments: 10
articles.body:
NeijuanChinese内卷Hanyu PinyinnèijuǎnLiteral meaning"to curl inwards"TranscriptionsStandard MandarinHanyu PinyinnèijuǎnBopomofoㄋㄟˋ   ㄐㄩㄢˇIPA[nêɪ.tɕɥɛ̀n]Yue: CantoneseYale RomanizationnoihgyúnJyutpingnoi6gyun2IPA[nɔj˨kyn˧˥]
Look up neijuan in Wiktionary, the free dictionary.
Neijuan,[a] sometimes known by the English term involution, is a Chinese term that describes a condition in which a system, institution, or competitive process continues to intensify in effort, complexity, or participation without a corresponding increase in output, efficiency, or collective benefit.[1] Neijuan is the Chinese calque of the English word involution. Neijuan is written with two characters which mean 'inside' and 'curling/rolling'.[2]
Neijuan had been used to describe an uneven distribution of social, economic, and educational resources and ongoing economic malaise, especially in terms of higher education bodies and labor markets. On a macroeconomic level, neijuan has led to overproduction and diminishing returns for capital owners who engage in fierce price wars that aggravate deflationary pressures in a pure unregulated market.[1] When capital owners are driven by competition they must work increasingly more for little or no marginal gain despite falling prices for consumers so price fixing or 'price leadership' becomes impossible.[3] On a personal level, neijuan reflects a life of being overworked, stressed, anxious and feeling trapped, a lifestyle where many face the negative effects of living a very competitive life for nothing.[2]
Involution was developed as a sociological concept by American anthropologist Alexander Goldenweiser in his 1937 book Anthropology: An Introduction To Primitive Culture.[4] In this work, Goldenweiser identifies involution as a cultural process. That when a society reaches its final form it cannot evolve nor stabilize itself. Instead, it can only complicate its internal elements. Goldenweiser uses Māori decorative art as an example.[5] The development of art was done within the framework of already existing patterns. The final pieces were elaborate and complicated in appearance but fundamentally the same as existing art.
This term was later utilized by fellow American anthropologist Clifford Geertz, who popularized the term in his 1963 book Agricultural Involution: The Processes of Ecological Change in Indonesia.[6] In this work, Geertz analyzed the rice farming process in Indonesia following Dutch colonial rule. Geertz found that despite the complexity of the process, coupled with the increasing amount of labor being assigned to it, productivity remained stagnant. All these efforts to increase productivity yielded little results, while complicating the already existing processes and systems. For Geertz this was involution.
Geertz's concept was introduced into Chinese rural studies by the Indian sinologist Prasenjit Duara and the Chinese historian Philip Huang (黄宗智; Huang Chung-Chih), arousing some controversy in Chinese academic circles. Huang explained involution using the economic concept of diminishing returns in his book The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China (华北的小农经济与社会变迁), published in 2000, which deviated from Geertz's original explanation.[7]
Involution has been described as, 'a process in which increasing levels of individual effort and competition fail to produce proportional gains in productivity or outcomes, resulting instead in diminishing returns and intensified internal competition for capital owners.' As more participants in the market adopt similar strategies to secure limited opportunities, relative advantages among capitalists disappear, creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which greater input is required merely to maintain their same market position.[2] This lack of surplus value to spend on political control also hurts capital owners by preventing their natural capture of state power in a pure market at the expense of the consumer who funds their ownership of the persons and tools of government through patronage and relative advantage.
Since 2020, the word involution (neijuan) has become an internet slang word in mainland China, and by extension refers to a culture in which people are expected to keep ahead of others. It can also have other negative connotations including 'cut throat competition', and 'race to the bottom', depending on context. Xiang Biao, an anthropologist, describes involution as "a dead loop in which people constantly force themselves" and "a race that participants are not allowed to fail or exit".[8] Some other people[who?] describe it as a process in which people "gain a slight advantage by exploiting themselves and competing excessively within a group". Influenced by its popularity, the number of academic papers containing the word involution has increased, but the meaning has further deviated from the original sociological sense, leading to some criticism that the word is being abused.[9]
In contemporary China, the concept of neijuan has spread through media outlets like newspapers and social media platforms like Weibo. On Weibo, the number of page views of various topics related to neijuan has exceeded 1 billion, and in an election in 2020, neijuan was one of China's "top 10 buzzwords" of the year.[10] Neijuan has become so popular because it has a strong influence on the ways of living for youth and contemporary middle-class parents.
Involuted King refers to someone who works extremely hard, by fair means or foul, in order to cope with neijuan.
In September 2020, a picture of a university student from the elite Tsinghua University in Beijing working on his laptop while still riding his bike went viral on social media with more than 1 billion views.[11] The picture of the boy resonated with most millennials and generation Z which includes people born after the 1990s.[11]
This incident sparked others to post pictures of other hard-working students who were dubbed Involuted Kings. The liking and reposting of similar pictures made neijuan among China's top 10 buzzwords of the year.[11]
Neijuan in the IT industry[edit]
In 2021, the concept of university neijuan translated into China's competitive tech industry, which is the preferred destination for most graduates. With an increasing number of graduates with relevant educational qualifications, the job market is becoming very competitive. This leaves many to work in areas they are overqualified for, like becoming takeaway drivers.[12] In association with these views, these pictures were popularized.
Many graduates get involved in 996 working culture, like takeaway services, after they leave university.[13] Many takeaway drivers deliver food for Meituan , a delivery-service corporation with a competitive business culture.[13]
Beginning in 2024, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), in its theoretical journal Qiushi, has identified neijuan as a macroeconomic concern. In the context of macroeconomics, neijuan has been defined as "unhealthy competition in which economic actors seeking to maintain their position in a market, or competing for share of a limited market, constantly invest substantial resources and energy without generating any profit growth." With falling production costs and sales prices leading to concern over deflation, the CCP has sought to combat neijuan by guiding and regulating private businesses and standardizing nationwide market conditions.[14]
As a result of neijuan, most Chinese middle-class parents no longer see education as a conveyance of upward social mobility. Parents feel the need to overcompensate just to ensure their children won't fall back on the social ladder in the coming years. These intensified efforts are through active involvement and increased spending. Parental involvement is manifested in the following ways:
First, parents familiarize themselves with what is being taught at school, to ensure they can teach their children if needed. It has become a common occurrence for parents to buy three copies of books in subjects like mathematics, one book for the student, one for the parents at home and one to be left at work.
Second, compared to their Western counterparts, the struggle of choosing the best educational institutions starts as early as daycare and not pre-university. Parents are anxious because of increasing competition, and correspondingly start getting fully involved in their children's education from a very young age. As a consequence of neijuan, parents feel that nurturing competent applicants for elite universities requires them to follow an established order of doing things. Timing has also become a significant factor.
Third, parents now find themselves in positions where they must push their children very hard, and children have little to no say. Pressuring their children is a characteristic that many middle-class parents share. This behavior has popularized terms like jiwa ('chicken child'), tiger mom, and chicken blood,[b] referring to the ambitious and pushy parenting of contemporary Chinese parents.[13] A tiger mom is a controlling mother who does not allow her children any freedom. Examples of tiger mom behavior include making primary school children study subjects like chemistry and physics through after-school tutoring even though schools do not introduce these subjects until the third year of junior secondary school. One parent explained "it is not enough to compete just in terms of studies", having some sort of talent is now seen as a significant entry requirement to elite universities. As a result, some talents such as playing the piano and swimming are not as valuable as they once were, as shown in the lists below:
Music: Organ > harp > cello > violin > flute > saxophone > drums > piano
Sports: Equestrian > golf > ice hockey > fencing > baseball and American football > figure skating > tennis > soccer > taekwondo > badminton > swimming > running
Moreover, middle-class Chinese parents overcompensate for the cost spent on their children's education. In the 2010s and 2020s there has been a trend for parents to relocate to Haidian, a district in Beijing.[13] Haidian is well known for self-sacrificing and education-focused parents, because of the strong public institutions found in the area.[13] Schools in Haidian teach programming from a very young age; by the time children are in secondary school, they are already at an advanced level in programming languages like C++ and Python.[13] In other subjects such as mathematics, many schools in Haidian have their students start learning secondary school mathematics when they are only in the fifth or sixth grade, laying a foundation for future studies. Most parents want to move to cities with quality public schools like the city of Haidian, regardless of cost. To ensure their children can attend esteemed schools, parents pay high real estate prices. Meanwhile, the cost of after-school tutoring is extremely high. The price of an after-school class for junior secondary school students in Haidian can reach RMB 1,000 per hour.
In university, learning is more independent, and students are responsible for what and when they learn. Though university is thought of as a time to make new friends, explore new interests and understand oneself better, the reality is different in China.[16]
In China, the work–life balance of younger social elites is very different from their predecessors. Young people are "trapped" in hyper-competitive and unhealthy work environments, which have become the "new industry standard".[17] To ensure they stay relevant at work, employees follow the 996 work system. 996 is a new requirement for good-paying industries like finance and tech where employees work from 9 am to 9 pm for 6 days a week.[18] Under 996, employees work more than 60 hours a week, a number that is 1.5 times more than the legalized 44 hours a week as stated in article 36 of the Labour Contract Law of the People's Republic of China.[18] Although labor law requires workers to be paid 2.275 times their base salary if they work under the 996 schedule, there are reports that workers are rarely compensated.[18] To highlight their frustration, a number of programmers have created websites like 996.icu and posted a blacklist of companies that encourage an exploitative work culture.[18] Some of the most prominent companies are 58.com [zh], Youzan [zh], JD.com, Alibaba and TikTok's parent company ByteDance. However, neijuan has made entry into these jobs very difficult, and the workers' "greatest fear is perhaps losing what they already have".[19] Many workers, including takeaway drivers, feel like robots who work extremely hard but with no real purpose.[12]
The previous generation came of age during the opening up of China's economy, and experienced large social mobility and the creation of markets in many sectors. Xiang Biao points out that people from the previous generation had a more secure childhood and upward mobility.[20]  Now that markets in many sectors are largely saturated and social mobility has stagnated, Gen Z does not enjoy the same kind of opportunities.[20]
The culture that constitutes much of neijuan has engendered anti-capitalist sentiment from the overworked population. The former chief editor of Harper's Bazaar China, Su Mang, called neijuan "the gap between desire and indolence". Su has been lambasted as a "typical capitalist" and forced to apologize.[10] Jack Ma called 996 a "fortune earned through hard work",[21] and was labelled a "bloodsucking capitalist".[10]
As neijuan is associated with urban lifestyles, one response to it entails re-appreciation of the Chinese countryside as a mentally healthy setting. Linda Qian and Barclay Bram report that urban workers increasingly desire and attempt to migrate to rural areas to combat neijuan, where they often try to establish small-scale businesses.[22]
Tangping, a term that means 'lying flat' or 'giving up on the grind', has also gained a lot of traction. It has been interpreted as a kind of resistance to neijuan, as an exit from competition by renouncing pointless effort. Tangping spawned under stress from overwork and promised a form of resistance to the cycle of exploitation.[23]
The Chinese government's position on neijuan has been evolving. In the early-2020s, it was largely positive and encouraging, as it is perceived that people working hard will drive up the economy. Resistance to neijuan such as tangping has garnered concern from state media, and some media went as far as to openly condemn tangping.[10] Xu Fang from the University of California, Berkeley proposes that this is a part of the "stability maintenance" effort from the CCP; the government would rather people vent their emotions through online ranting than through a social movement.[10]
In the mid-2020s, the Chinese government took a more critical perspective of neijuan, in terms of excessive competition among manufacturers. This competition has led to significant gluts of various manufactured goods and cutthroat price wars.[24]
Tang ping – Chinese neologism, "lying flat"
Abilene paradox – False consensus due to communication failure
Crab mentality – Metaphor about spiteful attitude
Rat race – Metaphor for career pursuits and attainment
Kiasu – Hokkien word for 'fear of losing'
Karoshi – Sudden death from overwork
Occupational burnout – Type of occupational stress

articles.title: Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons
articles.summary: The revelations in Anthropic's threat intelligence report come after a former top researcher at the company warned of the risks of AI to humanity.
articles.body: Anthropic says it has identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons.The findings, made in the firm's recent threat intelligence report, is the latest in a growing series of warnings from AI researchers and industry insiders about the technology's potential risks to humanity.The warnings have prompted calls to action, with US Senator Bernie Sanders demanding a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".The company published its latest threat intelligence report, external on Thursday. Such reports have become a regular feature across the AI industry as firms seek to demonstrate how they identify and disrupt attempts to misuse their models.This includes Google, which wrote on Tuesday, external that a person had attempted to use its AI tool, Gemini, to obtain a "complete, step-by-step technical guide for synthesizing weaponised biological agents".Claude, Anthropic's AI model was also used by actors linked to a Russia-based cyber espionage campaign and by an Iranian propaganda institution, according to its report.The cases of concern detected over the past eight months ranged from fake dating apps and hotel Wifi scams, to surveillance built to identify dissidents.Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI firms of trying to replicate Claude's capabilities. The lengthy report lists cases in which suspected state-sponsored groups, criminals, spyware vendors, state propaganda institutions and politically motivated individuals misused its technology."Malicious use" of its Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus models was disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, it said.None of the misuse cases involved Claude Fable or the powerful Mythos-class models, with the exception of one instance of distillation - the process for training smaller AI models using larger, more expensive models.As well as detecting the use of its models for cyber and influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud and weapon development, Anthropic said it had blocked scientists who used its AI in ways that could support biological weapons development.The report highlighted "five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development".Biological misuse, it said, is "one of the most serious risks of frontier AI model". Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities "could have catastrophic consequences", Anthropic said."The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease," Anthropic said.Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, told the New York Times, external it was "an incredibly nuanced situation"."You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, 'Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,'" he said.The report also noted six cases where Claude was used "to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs, and other munitions, as well as the targeting and control systems that operate them".The report indicated that cybercriminals and state-backed hackers have increasingly used its technology to assist their operations.Hacking group ShinyHunters, as well as China-based labs, were among those named in the report.The report also said that a hacking group whose work is consistent with the Russia-based Midnight Blizzard allegedly used AI to build a system that automatically detected when its malware was flagged by security defences and rewrote code until it evaded detection.The California-based company said it had incorporated its findings into its processes "to better prevent, detect, and disrupt these activities in the future".Anthropic said it had shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners where appropriate.The report - the company's first this year - comes after a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.In an article published on 6 September, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called for the industry to implement "voluntary slowdowns" until safeguards are set."I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," Pachocki said, adding that OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, will continue its work on building safeguards, though broader interventions are required.The warning prompted an open letter to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling for a new multinational treaty for the safe development of AI and a call for governments to collaborate about what a treaty based on the development of superintelligence should look like.In the US, Democratic lawmaker Bernie Sanders has introduced legislation to ban AI  superintelligence and temporarily pause advanced AI development."When scientists tell you there is a chance, a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he said on Thursday on BBC's Newsnight.With additional reporting from Osmond Chia.

articles.title: Hall signs new contract with Newcastle until 2031
articles.summary: Newcastle United defender Lewis Hall signs a new contract with the club that runs until 2031.
articles.body: Newcastle United defender Lewis Hall has signed a new contract with the club that runs until 2031.The left-back, who has been the subject of interest from Manchester United, has agreed a two-year extension to his original deal.Hall said it was a "really proud moment" to extend his stay as a boyhood supporter of the club."It's an absolute pleasure to play for this club and to represent the supporters," he said. "I know how much it means to them."To be able to bring joy to their faces, it's a big thing for me. I obviously have a family connection with the club, which is incredibly important to us all. "One of the main reasons I play is to make my family proud, and I know how much it means to them to watch me playing for Newcastle United. "It's a really good place to be. It's really pleasing with how we've started the season, especially with the new gaffer [Matthias Jaissle] and coaching staff coming in, and I think we can go on to achieve really big things."Hall, 22, has made 106 appearances for Newcastle since joining the club from Chelsea in 2023.Jaissle said the defender is a "very important player for us and for what we are building here"."His mentality is exactly what you want in a young player," he said. "He wants to learn every day and he wants to be better in every match."Lewis covers ground in a way that few players can. He defends with maturity and intelligence, and his technical level means he can support the team higher up the pitch. "What excites me most is that I believe the best is still to come from Lewis. He has a lot of room to develop, and I am looking forward to working with him as he grows with us."This has been a busy summer at Newcastle - both in terms of ins and outs - but tying Hall down is a particularly significant move. It was just last month that Jaissle replied "no chance" when Manchester United legend Peter Schmeichel informed him that his former side were looking at Hall.This deal further strengthens the club's position.It also rewards Hall for his development since he arrived from Chelsea as a raw left-back three years ago.Hall has worked on the defensive side of his game and, on his day, proved he is capable of even keeping Barcelona star Lamine Yamal quiet from open play in the Champions League.He has been a real outlet going forward for Newcastle, too, and has already set up two goals this season.That should not come as a huge surprise.Of those full-backs to play a minimum of 900 minutes across the Premier League last season, Hall led the way for high-speed runs and underlapping runs per game. He also ranked in the top three for dribbles completed per match.It feels like there is a lot more to come from him as he looks to get back into the England squad after missing out on the World Cup.

articles.title: Man loses case to claw back $369,000 he spent on lavish gifts for ex-girlfriend
articles.summary: Singapore's High Court rules in the woman's favour, with the judge saying the man "willingly" showered her with gifts, even before they got together.
articles.body: A Singaporean man has lost a court case to claw back hundreds of thousands of dollars that he had lavished on his ex-girlfriend while they were together.The S$468,000 ($369,200; £273,260) that Chander Agarwal attempted to recover from Felicia Lee was money he had "willingly" spent on her, the Singapore High Court ruled.Agarwal "displayed a consistent pattern of showering [Lee] with lavish gifts" even before they got together and would reassure her that he did not expect repayment, Senior Judge Lee Seiu Kin said.Agarwal, the CEO of a logistics company, met Felicia Lee, a former flight attendant, during a flight in 2019. They were in a romantic relationship from September 2022 to December 2023, the court heard.Their relationship fell apart after Agarwal suspected Lee of having an affair. Agarwal, who launched the suit in March 2024, argued that Lee had "requested various interest-free loans" from him over the course of their relationship.He claimed that these included S$206,000 in credit card charges, S$129,000 for overseas trips, S$17,000 to engage a fengshui master for her apartment, and S$20,000 to pay for her life insurance premiums.Lee argued that these were "gifts made out of love and affection" and not loans.In agreeing with Lee, the judge noted that Agarwal's case lacked documentary evidence - for instance, he could not produce any proof that Lee had acknowledged receipt of the loans that she had allegedly requested."The evidence before me clearly shows that the claimant, smitten by the defendant, had showered her with expensive gifts during their relationship," the judge said."Unfortunately, when their relationship ended on a sour note, [Agarwal] became embittered and was determined to extract a price from her."The judge also noted that Agarwal was "clearly a man of ample means who has expensive tastes", in contrast to Lee "who was not in that league".In many text messages Lee had "expressed her awe when [Agarwal] suggested expensive gifts, and on occasion, her spontaneous reluctance to accept them", the judge noted.In concluding his written judgement, the judge cited English playwright William Congreve, who wrote in his tragedy satire The Mourning Bride: "Heav'n has no rage, like love to hatred turn'd, nor hell a fury, like a woman scorn'd.""This case shows that such emotion is not the sole province of one gender," he said.In early 2023, another Singaporean man had filed two lawsuits – in claims amounting to over S$3m - against a woman who rejected his romantic advances.K Kawshigan claimed that Nora Tan's rejection brought him emotional trauma and caused damage to his reputation. The Singapore courts struck out his suits. Tan later counter-sued Kawshigan to claim back expenses she said she had incurred while defending herself from his alleged harassment.

articles.title: CSS Curiosities of the Past
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://vale.rocks/posts/css-relics
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49654962
Points: 5
# Comments: 0
articles.body: The ebbs and flows of the web have gotten us to where we stand today. We simply wouldn’t have the web we do without the journey it has taken us to get here. However, some of the steps it has taken to get here have been interesting to say the least. CSS is how we style things on the web, but since its inception it has been made, on occasion, to wear a few more hats. It has taken on odd roles and picked up behaviours it probably ought not to have. Such is life. As I’ve detailed odd and context-specific HTML, this is a look at CSS largely outside the specifications. Browser-specific hacks, technology-scoped syntax, and engine-exclusive snippets forged from questionable circumstances, corporate complications, and esoteric implementations. Most browsers, correctly, would treat a property prefixed with an asterisk as invalid. However, Internet Explorer 7 and earlier would treat it as valid. It was so famous it garnered the name ‘star hack’ for the shape of the asterisk. Likewise, when prefixing a property with an underscore or hyphen, only Internet Explorer 6 would treat it as valid. There were many more similar hacks used, the vast majority of which are best documented at the eponymous browserhacks.com. The main gist is that some browsers would incorrectly parse properties, selectors, and values, and that could be used for gain in an era where browser behaviour was rather varied. Limiting CSS to apply only in certain browsers with conditional comments in CSS files, such as could be done in HTML documents, wasn’t possible.1 Therefore, this exploitation of questionable parsing of what is and isn’t valid was commonplace for targeting specific browsers. Internet Explorer 7 and earlier would treat almost any textual string prefixed by an exclamation mark as !important. Most commonly, people would make use of this by writing !ie to have a style only override specificity in Internet Explorer. As far as Internet Explorer was concerned, the arbitrary !banana and the specced !important were the same, while other browsers correctly only accepted the latter. There was another related bug in Internet Explorer 6 and lower where a style declared later in the same block would overwrite an !important value. For example, here the colour would be black rather than white, as it should be: There were so many ways in which you could identify what browser was in use on a document level via CSS. Some examples include: In Internet Explorer 6 and earlier you could write * html {}. For only Internet Explorer 7 you could use *:first-child+html {}. Browsers other than Internet Explorer 7 support html > /**/ body {}. Early versions of Firefox would apply styles within body:empty {} (even when the body had contents). This approach was often messy to use, as it meant writing multiple descending selectors to try to target elements in specific browsers only. Until version 8, Internet Explorer had a concept called hasLayout. An internal flag, it would designate whether an element was responsible for rendering itself (true) or if a parent element would be responsible for it (false).
