articles.title: Henry Zeffman: How Burnham got ready to govern with four key moments mapped out
articles.summary: As the prime minister looks ahead to autumn, Labour figures are asking whether his government represents continuity or change.
articles.body: Image source, PA MediaByHenry ZeffmanChief political correspondentAt the start of summer, in the pillared room in 10 Downing Street, Andy Burnham looked out at his new special advisers, the few dozen political officials tasked with driving hundreds of thousands of civil servants to deliver his government's agenda.Some had been with him in Manchester or Makerfield. Others had spent the past few months trying everything to prevent his hostile takeover of Sir Keir Starmer's government - and the new prime minister showed he was aware of it, going out of his way to praise those who had stayed on, for their efforts in the preceding years.At that meeting, Burnham's team mapped out four key moments in the coming months.First, the return to Parliament in September, when Burnham and other leading ministers would make their first statements to MPs. Second, Labour's annual conference at the end of September - Burnham's first as leader. Third, the Budget, taking place on 28 October. And fourth, the 10-year plan for Britain which Burnham intends to unveil in November.As MPs prepare to leave Parliament on Tuesday for almost a month and party conference season gets underway, the first phase of that route map is almost complete - enough for figures at all levels of the Labour Party to begin answering some questions about the shape of this new government.Most importantly, perhaps, how new actually is it? Does Burnham represent continuity or change?That question is especially relevant because those Labour MPs who pushed for Sir Keir to be replaced always fell into two broad camps: those who wanted a change of style and emphasis but continuity in policy, and those who wanted a major shift in policy. Both groups saw what they wanted in Burnham.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Andy Burnham speaks during his first Cabinet meeting since becoming prime ministerGoing by the words of the new prime minister himself, he represents a profound break with the past, and not only the immediate past. In his first speech as Labour leader in July, Burnham described his ascendancy as "the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years". That is the timeframe he has returned to again and again, signalling not just a desire to reverse issues he believes stem from the Thatcher era but also to break with aspects of the Labour governments since then, including his immediate predecessor's.Some in government are already quietly questioning, though, whether the ambition of that rhetoric can be squared with the early signals emerging from the Treasury under the new Chancellor John Healey.In interviews over recent weeks, and especially in his first major speech on Monday, Healey has said he will stick to Rachel Reeves's commitments not to increase the main rates of income tax, national insurance and VAT, as well as her rules on government borrowing.In the speech, he promised to "control public spending", and hailed Reeves for beginning to "recover Britain's fiscal discipline".It led to opposition parties labelling Healey a continuity chancellor. A similar critique is being voiced among some of his government colleagues.Most are more generous for now, arguing that Healey's first imperative - especially at a time of turmoil in the global bond markets - is reassurance, and that the Budget is the moment for him to show how he plans to substantiate Burnham's rhetoric. Even one official sympathetic on that point, though, asks: "Why did he do a big speech before he has something to say?"Those close to Healey argue that his emphasis this week on securing the economic growth which has eluded successive governments by spreading wealth around the country is a clear difference from Reeves. And finding ways to boost regional growth has been one of Healey's major causes since he was a junior minister at the Treasury more than 20 years ago - long before it was at the heart of Burnham's political personality.There is no question, though, that this week the minister who most starkly signalled change from the previous government was a man who coveted Healey's job - Ed Miliband, who was instead appointed foreign secretary.In announcing new sanctions on Israel over illegal settlements in the West Bank, Miliband explicitly cast the policy as a break from Sir Keir's approach, telling MPs: "We should have acted earlier, and it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation."On the other hand, acting alongside Canada and France in announcing the sanctions represented - in form if not substance  - continuity with the previous government, the three countries having moved together to recognise the state of Palestine a year ago.The sanctions announcement was received with near-universal warmth from Labour MPs, itself a marker of change from the Starmer government.It was also seen as a sign of the ability of Miliband in particular, but this government in general, to drive its agenda through the civil service machine. "There is a much clearer sense now from No 10 of what they want," one official who worked under Sir Keir as well as Burnham says. "Before there was a bit too much of 'let us know your ideas for what we should do', now it's 'this is what the PM wants, give us options to deliver it'."That is a culture shift which Burnham sought to drill into his cabinet at their weekly meeting on Tuesday, still only their third such meeting. According to one present, the prime minister said: "We need to be on the front foot. We need to be bolder. Let's get on and do things. It's about deeds not words."Image caption, Burnham has called for "growth in every postcode", and the establishment of No 10 North is a key part of that agendaPerhaps the most significant way in which Burnham is trying to make boldness easier for his ministers is by encouraging them to press ahead with policies when there is a risk they will face a serious legal challenge. The new attorney general, Ellie Reeves, has pared back rules introduced under Sir Keir which some ministers believed forced them to be over-cautious about legal risk, thereby slowing down or blocking new policies altogether.Louise Haigh, Burnham's deputy, has vowed to "strip out needless bureaucracy" from government more generally, citing an example of there being three public consultations between 2019 and 2023 on whether to microchip cats. "If we can't microchip cats without getting tied up in red tape, it should come as no surprise the public is losing faith that governments can get things done," she said.As Burnham moves into the next phase of his autumn, there is a recognition from some around him that he will need to produce some more significant policies to underpin his rhetoric. Those in government familiar with early work on fleshing out his commitment to "public control" of essential services insist the direction of travel is truly radical. Haigh is responsible for this, chairing a taskforce on how to reverse "over-privatisation" specifically of housing, water, energy and transport.Burnham may offer more details on these policies at Labour's conference, while he is likely to wait until after then to show his hand on whether he wants continuity or change when it comes to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's reforms to the legal immigration system - a much more divisive issue among Labour MPs.And whatever their differences on policy, Labour MPs are united on one thing. The fundamental reason they installed a new prime minister was because many of them believed that continuing on the same path meant losing the next general election. For them, a long-term improvement in Labour's poll ratings would be the most important change of them all.

articles.title: $10m on line at inaugural Ultimate Championship
articles.summary: The inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship begins on Friday. From the global stars competing to how it all works - here is everything you need to know.
articles.body: One trophy, no medals. Ten million dollars. A red carpet. A black infield. Noah Lyles as MC. Armand Duplantis singing before eyeing another world record.This athletics season was set to be the first since the pandemic which did not culminate in an Olympic Games or World Championships.To bridge that gap, the sport's governing body has devised a new competition.Introducing: The World Athletics Ultimate Championship.Across three days of competition in Budapest, live on the BBC from 11-13 September, the world's top athletes will compete for record prize money and a new title.A new event pitching the best against the best, with increased financial commitments. You may be thinking: 'Haven't we been here before?'Last year, Michael Johnson's inaugural Grand Slam Track league attempted to maintain focus on the sport following Paris 2024 while offering lucrative prize money, but ended after encountering serious financial issues.This innovative, biennial format is bankrolled by World Athletics - and president Sebastian Coe has said he hopes to use it as an "incubator for change" which will shape the future of the sport's established World Championships.So, how does the Ultimate Championship work, what do the athletes think, and is it needed? Here is everything you need to know.The sport has long grappled with the issue of retaining the attention and excitement it generates at the Olympics throughout those four-year cycles. Because of the disruption caused by the pandemic, and subsequent postponement of the Tokyo 2020 Games, each of the past five years have provided a pinnacle event which gathered the biggest stars in front of a global audience.For many top British athletes, a 2026 season centred around a Commonwealth Games and European Championship on home soil would probably have finished at the Diamond League Final.Coe and World Athletics have planned for three years to fill that perceived void."It is an attempt to just start experimenting a bit and innovating, with an event that will determine who really is the best of the best," Coe told BBC Sport."There's no guarantee we're going get everything right, and no guarantee that everything is going to work. In two years, we might look at a slightly different format. "I also want to be able to put some of the things we're doing into the World Championship format. We have a responsibility to try and engage new young audiences."The Ultimate features a condensed three-night schedule, held as three-hour sessions.It is reserved for reigning Olympic, world and Diamond League champions, plus athletes who have qualified by world ranking.However, a few star names who did not qualify have been granted exceptional invitations, including Great Britain's Josh Kerr and Norwegian rival Jakob Ingebrigtsen into the men's 1500m.There will be a total of 28 finals, including straight finals in all field events and both the 1500m and the 5,000m. The 800m and shorter distances will have semi-finals.Not every discipline has been included, however. World Athletics says those decisions were taken based on the popularity of each event and data it gathered on viewer behaviour, including sweat response and pulse rate.As a result, long distance events such as the 3,000m steeplechase and 10,000m, and field events such as the shot put and discus, have been left out.World Athletics is providing "the richest prize pot in the history of the sport" with a total of $10m (£7.4m) to be won.Each individual event winner will pocket $150,000 (£110,000) - more than double the offering at last year's World Championships - with $75,000 (£55,000) for the runner-up and $40,000 (£29,500) for third.Many of the sport's biggest names have voiced their support for athletics' new global event.Pole vault world record holder Duplantis was named as the inaugural 'Ultimate Star' last summer and has collaborated on the official anthem for the championship, Gold, which he has written and performed."It's super exciting. I think it was time to try something new and innovate within athletics," Duplantis said."It's tough for athletes when we have years without a championship. I think this fills the gap perfectly, you want to have some sort of climax to build towards."Kerr, set for a first race against rival Ingebrigtsen for two years, said the substantial increase in prize money showed how "serious" World Athletics are about the event. However, while the 2023 world champion agrees that a global championship was needed, he accepts there is "probably going to be some confusion from the outside world about what this is"."If that's what they're willing to put forward in prize money, it means that they're willing to put that effort into marketing and media," said Kerr."We're seeing progress. Obviously, $150,000 is a lot of money. It's not as much as other big sports, but they've earned that through years of pushing their marketing."But not everyone is convinced.Hurdles star Karsten Warholm has voiced his concern regarding the impact on the calendar, describing this year's late-season schedule as "chaos"."I think the Diamond League is a fantastic concept that should be cultivated. It will take a long time before people understand what an Ultimate Champion is," Warholm told Norwegian media outlet VG."It's pretty much the same athletes who participate but there could be two different winners at the Diamond League final and the Ultimate Championship."In terms of storytelling, it's going to be difficult. I don't think even athletics people are keeping up."There is also the matter of the excluded athletes and events.World triple jump champion Pedro Pichardo responded on social media to the decision to exclude his discipline: "I really don't understand what your problem is, and even less so making this decision without any explanation."This isn't track and field and it's not good for our sport."After ending her season with victory in the Diamond League Final, world shot put champion Chase Jackson told Citius Mag: "My body is saying 'yes' but my pockets are saying 'why the hell am I not at the Ultimate?' "How [do] you have track and field and just skip events? How does that make any sense?"

articles.title: Philippine rescuers board ferry 40 hours after blaze began
articles.summary: Thick, toxic fumes and extreme temperatures pose a challenge to rescuers who have boarded the ship.
articles.body: They finally got on at about 11:30 local time (03:30 GMT) on Friday, the coast guard said."The biggest challenge for us really is to penetrate the ship [as] there is still a visible, thick smoke," the coastguard's spokeswoman Noemie Cayabyab told the BBC earlier."No matter how we try to push through, high temperatures and toxic smoke remain a severe risk to our personnel," she told local media earlier.Smoke resulting from incomplete burning contains dense, lethal concentrations of carbon monoxide. Earlier, authorities reported that 86 were still unaccounted for, but as of Friday morning, the figure stood at 84 – two passengers whose names were on the ship's manifest did not go onboard, authorities say.Rescuers have widened their search area, Cayabyab says, adding that the coastguard has deployed one of its largest ships and done radio broadcasts to vessels in the area. The search teams are also accompanied by divers and nurses.A local diver in Coron told the BBC on Friday that he and his team were on standby to help out and awaiting instructions from the coast guard.The coast guard also conducted an aerial survey of waters near the disaster site. The plan is to resume firefighting efforts, first from the cargo hold of the ferry, which is the compartment where containers and or goods are stored, Cayabyab said. Earlier, the coastguard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that was where the fire started. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat had described the frantic cries on board the passenger-cargo vessel when the fire erupted on Wednesday evening.Roland Lerma recalled falling while scrambling to get off the burning boat."When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," the 30-year-old told the BBC.He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea. Lerma said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark."It was cold [in the sea] If the rescue had been delayed, I would definitely have died," he said.The ferry, which set off from Manila, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, in the province of Palawan, when it caught fire.The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry."Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.

articles.title: More than 100,000 watch 49ers shock Rams in Melbourne
articles.summary: San Francisco 49ers record dominant 27-7 victory over Super Bowl favourites Los Angeles Rams in front of a crowd of more than 100,000 at Melbourne Cricket Ground.
articles.body: San Francisco 49ers recorded a dominant 27-7 victory over Super Bowl favourites Los Angeles Rams in front of a crowd of more than 100,000 at Melbourne Cricket Ground.It was the NFL's first game in the Asia-Pacific region, and its longest-ever road trip for the first of a record nine international games in 2026.The 49ers arrived in Melbourne a week before the game, while the Rams opted to spend just over 24 hours in Australia.Sean McVay's side are Super Bowl favourites after acquiring defensive end Myles Garrett and welcoming one of the NFL's greatest defensive players, Aaron Donald, out of retirement."I love when they [the Rams] came out and they were booing. We were out here for a week. We enjoyed the city. I don't think you can fly 16 hours and be ready to play," 49ers receiver Deebo Samuel told Australia's Channel Seven.The game came to life in the second quarter as Kyren Williams ran in for a touchdown to give the Rams a four-point advantage following an earlier 49ers field goal.However, the 49ers hit back as Demarcus Robinson grabbed a touchdown before half-time.The momentum continued as receiver Mike Evans scored, followed by a touchdown from Samuel - and a second field goal sealed the win for the 49ers.Quarterback Brock Purdy completed 25 of 34 passes for 205 yards, including three touchdown passes.McVay added: "I make no excuses. Whether you want to say it's about travel, whatever. We just weren't good enough."I didn't coach good enough, and we'll look at it and we'll move forward."

articles.title: Astra for Coding: Why Are We Doing This Again?
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/9/7/astra-why/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49654229
Points: 334
# Comments: 242
articles.body:
written on September 07, 2026
I’m more and more convinced that all of AI engineering is
Neijuan (内卷, meaning curl inwards).  In
China it describes a system that demands ever more effort and competition
without improving output.  The way in which it sometimes shows up in the West is
the 996 nonsense.  The English term for Neijuan is “Involution”
Agricultural involution describes the intensification of farming that raises
productivity per square meter while leaving productivity per head unchanged.
That’s how I feel about AI right now.
Which brings me to GPT 6 Astra.  Astra is by all accounts an incredibly
impressive model.  There is really not much I can say against this.  It’s
amazing at computer use, understands images and complex topics, and it’s
relentless in its pursuit of completion.  It is absolutely impressive; these
types of models are going to change the world in one form or another.
But at least for the moment I don’t know how to work with it for actual software
engineering.  Since that got quite a bit of attention on Twitter, I figured I
might summarize my thoughts and just share what kind of code comes out of this
“Armin, you should run a software factory!” I’ve heard that a few times now, so I figured
I might celebrate the release of it by running a little software factory over
the weekend.  If everybody builds slop 3D games, then I should do something
useful with it.  My software factory was intentionally set up to let the model
decide the how of the workflow entirely.  It was free to manage its own context
and could maintain its own records in an agent-notes folder.  Then it spun off
subagents to work on stuff.  The goal?  What if we had a Python with virtual
threads and lexical scoping.  And well, I burned a
full reset’s worth of ChatGPT tokens on this which appears to be around 4 billion
tokens.  35 hours later, the factory has delivered absolutely nothing of value
and also not taught me anything about how to operate a better one.
But it produced a lot of code and input prompts, and so there is stuff I was able
to study.  And well, it shows behavior that I’m not used to with Sol and earlier
OpenAI models 1.  I have since encountered the same issues with regular
programming with Astra, so it’s not a result of just the factory.
I think I’m suspecting something is going “wrong” in the training process.  The
model is greatly rewarded for succeeding on long-horizon tasks, but presumably there
is very little punishing going on for “shitty code.”  The apparent result is
that Astra is amazing at producing 3D stuff
can keep going for a very long time, coming up with its own work in the process.
I had it do quite a bit of reverse engineering of my robot vacuum in ways that
were quite impressive.  So it’s definitely cool!
The first issue I have with Astra comes from the type of code that it uses for
tool calls.  Codex increasingly has been relying on “just bash” to do more and
more operations.  For a few versions now the original Codex harness just uses
sed and other tools to read files.  You just usually can’t see them because Codex
and hides them if it recognizes them.  But Astra … really loves Python?  That is
not much of a surprise because even older OpenAI models had a tendency to
sometimes use on-demand Python code to read and manipulate files at times, but
Astra does it really quite excessively for me.
Now here is an important disclaimer: this project is very meta here because I
on the CPython interpreter.  But I can assure you that I have seen this model
do weird Python things even in TypeScript code in Pi.  But I have the most
evidence of odd code from when I had the thing work over the weekend
with zero oversight from my slop factory.
That it writes Python is not interesting; the type of Python is interesting, and
I collected some outputs for you to gloss over.
Python string splicing to edit C code
In the Codex harness I found multiple cases where subagents resorted fully to
manual string manipulation with Python instead of using the patch tool.

The failure case here seems somewhat obvious: the model is trained for token
efficiency for tool calling which also looks like code, and sometimes it seems to
be taking that code into a place where it should not be: the codebase.
35 Hours on a Single Prompt
I’m not really sure what to say here, but the slop machine was running for 35
hours until I turned it off.  In that time it produced a net addition of 75k
lines of code and it did not stop.  In the 35 hours it burned around 1B tokens
for a total of around 1200 USD in raw API costs.  It managed to produce 79 commits,
and that comes to a cost of around 15.5 USD per commit, and the agents exchanged
I honestly do not need an agent to run for 35 hours on a single prompt.  It clearly
does not work or result in reasonable outputs.
So obviously: prompting it like this is stupid.  But when left unattended, it
will keep going, and earlier models did not do that.  Even Fable wasn’t as
crazy as that.  When you accidentally give it slightly too big of a task, it will
continue until it succeeds, even if it burns through an entire subscription.
And that’s more or less why right now I do not manage to trust this model much.
It has shown that it will commit slop, and it requires me to review it more as a
result.  Even if the failure rate is quite low, I would not want this.
Disposable Code vs Committed Code
In a world where code for tool calls is optimized for token efficiency and
“getting the job done”, I wonder if there is really enough signal going to the
training processes for “a human understands what is going on”.  I would say that
quite a lot of the code I get out of Astra is in my mind “objectively bad”.  But
it’s objectively bad by my human sense.  Maybe it’s objectively good for a
codebase that is entirely written by agents and only needs to be understood by
Which is why I’m honestly asking myself more and more why we are doing this.
These new models are absolutely amazing, for sure.  But I’m more and more
skeptical that the trajectory they are on still lends itself to present-day
software engineering processes.  The reason why I’m asking why we are doing
this is because I felt like we achieved a pretty good spot for
software engineering with those models, and that is the part of the AI economy
where it was possible to show a positive return.  But for how much more Fable
costs, for how much more Astra costs, I do not feel like the results are there.
In fact, with Astra and Fable I feel like not only are the costs astronomical,
but the models are also just not for me as a software engineer.  And presumably
that’s because these models increasingly are for other people.  For lawyers, 3D
artists, mathematicians, whoever uses computer use, etc.
And potentially as a byproduct of enabling all of this, you can now slop your
way to a one-shot 3D game over the weekend which looks impressive.  And probably
you can now run a software factory for as long as you don’t care about the code.
I’m sure I will get used to this, but man this stuff is weird.
Postscriptum: speaking of weird: how is it that these models, in a sandbox,
with supposedly no way to communicate with other agents, manage to find the same
public wikis as a scratch pad for agent communication?
Did they collude during training runs to remember resources on the internet
which might come in handy in the future?

articles.title: Hong Kong's Tiananmen activists sentenced to up to seven years in prison
articles.summary: Hong Kong used to be one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could gather to mark the 1989 crackdown.
articles.body: Three Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils commemorating Beijing's 1989 crackdown on Tiananmen Square protests have been handed prison sentences of up to seven years.Two of the defendants - Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41 - were convicted last month of inciting others to subvert state power, under the city's controversial national security law.A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, had pleaded guilty in January.For years, Hong Kong was one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could hold gatherings to mark the Tiananmen Square crackdown - a topic that is highly sensitive and heavily censored in mainland China.These gatherings were banned by Hong Kong's authorities in 2020, citing Covid-19 policies, but never resumed. That same year, the national security law, which makes illegal a wider range of dissenting acts, officially came into force.Authorities say the law is necessary to maintain stability, but critics argue it has eroded Hong Kong's autonomy and created a climate of fear.Lee, Chow and Ho were charged in 2021. They faced up to 10 years in prison after their conviction.On Friday, the court sentenced Lee to seven years in prison, while Chow was handed seven years and three months. Ho, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to five years in prison.As the court session started, Chow and Lee stood up and smiled at the public gallery, which was full of people. Ho wore a serious expression. After their sentences were handed down, Lee appeared to pray as he was led out of the dock, while Chow blew a kiss to those seated in the public gallery.According to a court summary in August, Lee and Chow had "incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power".Chow told the court in May the law itself was on trial.A key part of the trial concerned the group's slogan of "ending one-party dictatorship", which the court said had incited people to undermine the Chinese Communist Party.Lee's wife, Elizabeth Tang, told Reuters that it was a "sad day" for her."I cannot imagine that he has to spend another three years in jail, it is really unacceptable," she said, adding that Lee intended to appeal his sentence.Chow's mother Medina told a crowd outside the court not to be "overly saddened" about the verdict. "Do not lose heart. And above all, do not feel guilty," she said, Reuters reported.Speaking to the BBC before her arrest in 2022, Chow said she was "prepared to be arrested" and "willing to pay the price for fighting for democracy".The defendants were leaders of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, a group founded in May 1989 to support students holding pro-democracy rallies.Weeks later, the Chinese Communist Party sent troops and tanks to crush pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square. Estimates of the death toll range from a few hundred to many thousands.Over the next three decades, the Hong Kong Alliance called on authorities to accept responsibility for the crackdown, free dissidents and introduce democratic reform.The group also held yearly vigils commemorating the Tiananmen Square crackdown. Organisers said some of the gatherings attracted more than 100,000 people, though police had lower estimates of the turnout.On Friday, the court also handed a HK$1.5m fine ($191,000; £142,000) to the Hong Kong Alliance. "This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history," said Amnesty International's Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks. "The harsh sentences against peaceful Tiananmen vigil organisers expose the cruelty and insecurity of a government afraid of memory and the people," Human Rights Watch said in a statement.

articles.title: I was weeks from marrying a violent serial rapist - my loved ones saved my life
articles.summary: Amy, not her real name, has told the BBC how her family and friends sent crucial evidence to police which led to the arrest of rapist Christopher Malcolm.
articles.body: This article contains details, including depictions of violence, which some readers may find distressing.Without the interventions of her family and friends, Amy says she would have married the man who had physically and psychologically abused her for much of their relationship.Had the wedding gone ahead, she fears he would have eventually killed her.Christopher Malcolm, a serial rapist who was recently jailed for his crimes, inflicted life-changing injuries on his former fiancée - on one occasion she said he left her face "black and blue" just before she visited her terminally ill father for Father's Day.Amy, not her real name, told the BBC that staying in the relationship was often a means to calm the violence and survive. So long as Malcolm was free, she said she did not feel safe enough to report him to police.Her loved ones, meanwhile, grew increasingly worried. On several occasions they reported their concerns for Amy's welfare to Police Scotland's disclosure scheme for domestic abuse, external (known as Clare's Law in England and Wales), and handed police evidence including text messages and photos of her injuries.This ultimately helped officers build a strong enough case to arrest Malcolm, who was taken into custody in September 2024. Shortly afterwards, Amy gave a full report of the rapes, assaults and abuse she had been subjected to.She had been due to marry Malcolm four weeks later.Without Amy's knowledge, four people separately reported their concerns to police. Malcolm was arrested and released on bail after the first report, but evidence continued to mount and officers urged Amy to make her own statement."They were very explicit with me," she said. "They said 'if you don't make a statement we're going to find you in a ditch at the side of the road'."I remember that hitting me really, really hard because I'd never really had someone say something so candidly to me before. I was very aware that this was potentially a possibility at some point, if I continued."Amy, now aged 30, approached the BBC to tell her story as she believes her family, friends and the police officers involved in her case ultimately saved her life.In her case, she said, the system worked.Police Scotland said that in cases where abuse survivors are reluctant to make reports, officers will look for a whole range of evidence that is not dependent upon the survivor.This includes body-worn video, phone analysis, injury photographs, medical evidence and histories of previous incidents or evidence from previous partners. Such evidence can allow cases to proceed if there is a realistic chance of conviction.A spokesperson for the force said the information Amy's family and friends gave was "crucial" in painting a picture of Malcolm's offending.Following a trial involving 56 witnesses, Malcolm, 37, was convicted of crimes against four women in Lothian and Moray, including Amy, stretching as far back as 2008 when he was still a teenager.He recently lodged an appeal against his 16-year sentence.

articles.title: I watched as a hijacked plane flew over my home - moments later my wife was killed
articles.summary: A quarter of a century since the 9/11 attacks, Charles Wolf reflects on his wife's final moments.
articles.body: Charles first met Katherine in New York in 1988, when he was singing with a theatre group and she was a piano accompanist."We met quite accidentally outside the rehearsal hall and we fell in love with each other in about two minutes, and that was it," he said.Charles said he "hit the jackpot" when he met her, adding: "There was no parting us."Katherine took Charles back to the UK for a visit in 1989, as well as trips to parts of Wales that he admitted he "could not pronounce", including Machynlleth and Llanfairpwllgwyngyll."It was just the beginning," said Charles. "We had a wonderful, wonderful relationship."At 08:06 EDT, on September 11, 2001, Charles kissed Katherine goodbye from their New York City apartment for the last time.Exactly 40 minutes later, a jet smashed into the 97th floor of the tower - the very floor she had been working on, in a new job she had started less than a fortnight earlier."I knew instantly when it flew over my building - our apartment building - that it was a twin engine jet at full throttle," said Charles, a trained pilot."I knew it so well that I called the FBI and told them... 'That was no accident, that was deliberate'."A year later, when Charles met the FBI agent who took that call, he said the agent told him: "You were the first person to get us on to the fact that that was not an accident."Katherine had told her husband she was working in "building one". After the first plane hit, news reports described the Twin Towers as "north and south" - and Charles did not know which was which. But a mile from their home, he could see smoke billowing."I couldn't reach her on the phone. Little did I know she ceased to exist the instant that plane hit the building," he said.Charles "could only assume the worst" until he had confirmation from her employers three days later that nobody had managed to escape above the 91st floor of the north tower - six floors below Katherine's office."She didn't know it was going to happen and she never felt a thing," he said."In fact... all of her people right there, they were vapourised instantaneously."He added: "You never knew it was coming - couldn't, not at 450mph (724km/h)."It was not a blessing that I lost her. It was a blessing that she never knew it happened, and I am grateful for that."Not everybody got that. Some people had to make the decision to stay and burn to death or jump from the upper floors."Last weekend, more than 200 firefighters from across the UK climbed 110 floors - about 2,226 steps - wearing full [personal protective equipment (PPE) in Atlanta, Georgia to commemorate the 25th anniversary of 9/11. Each of the responders taking part represented one of the 343 firefighters who died while responding to the attacks. Carl Williams, station manager at Mid and West Wales Fire and Rescue Service, took part in the event along with eight of his colleagues, describing the experience as "quite humbling". "It was emotional at the end, a lot of people were finishing and crying," he said."To achieve that task of just doing the climb, let alone to try and understand the emotion behind it that people have lost their life. "Nobody expects to go to work and not come home that day."A documentary reflecting on 25 years since the 9/11 attacks, produced by Newyddion S4C, is available to watch now on YouTube, external.

articles.title: Rayner defends pause to local council overhaul
articles.summary: The cabinet minister tells the BBC she wanted to ensure the plans could survive potential legal actions.
articles.body: Angela Rayner has defended her decision to pause plans to redraw local council boundaries, saying she wanted to ensure they would survive legal challenge.The local government secretary also told the BBC she wanted to be "clear-eyed" about what the planned shake-up in 16 areas of England was likely to achieve.It comes after earlier this week she abandoned proposals in four other areas, in the face of legal threats from Reform and Conservative-led authorities.The surprise announcement on Monday has thrown the reorganisation plans into doubt, and drawn criticism from local leaders preparing for the changes.Councils in affected areas have been drawing up proposals and consulting with residents since the reorganisation was announced in late 2024, in a process that is already thought to have cost millions of pounds. Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Rayner conceded the decision to press pause had been "difficult" and she understood local authorities had put a "lot of time and effort" into their plans.But she added she wanted to have "all the information" about the proposals before going ahead with them, after her reappointment to her cabinet role under Andy Burnham, ten months after her resignation last year."I got the legal advice and I hadn't had the time to review and to go through all of that, and court cases were looming," she told the podcast."If I'm making a decision that is highly likely to be in legal challenge, I want to make sure I've dotted my i's and crossed my t's," she added.Rayner also said she wanted was "really clear-eyed on where we were going" with the plans, after Burnham had asked her to look again at the blueprints, which were announced by her predecessor Steve Reed.In her announcement on Monday, Rayner said she was withdrawing plans to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.Those proposals, announced in March, were already subject to legal challenges from Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk, and the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire, which were lodged over the summer.She also said she wanted to review plans for 16 other areas, including 14 announced by Reed days before Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister and reappointed her to her old role.Some councils affected by those plans, including Kent and Leicestershire, had threatened similar bids to challenge the lawfulness of the decision-making process.The government has argued that the plans, which will abolish remaining two-tier areas in England where county and district councils share responsibility for services, would make local government more effective and cost efficient.However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities.Others have also complained that the reorganisation could stymie or delay parallel efforts to merge councils into regional authorities led by mayors, which Burnham has cited as a key part of his economic plans.Elsewhere in her interview, Rayner said Labour under Sir Keir should have been quicker to recognise a Palestinian state, having promised to do so as a "contribution to a renewed peace process" at the last election.Starmer took the move in September last year, having spent much of the prior year  resisting pressure to do so from Labour MPs."It's always been Labour policy to recognise a Palestinian state, and it felt like we got there too late. It was something that should have been really clear," she said.She also denied that UK sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, announced on Tuesday, had been made to help Labour ahead of the forthcoming by-election in Holborn and St Pancras in central London.Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.Pointing to the fact that Western allies had also announced sanctions, she said: "The French and the Canadians are not going to be like 'oh well, we'll just signal something to help you with a local by-election in London'".Reflecting on her return to government, she said a "big difference" between Burnham and his predecessor in Downing Street was his inclination to tell "the story of why we're doing something" in government.She said both men shared "passion and the commitment" to deliver for Labour in office, but added: "Andy is probably more like me, in terms of [he] wears his heart on his sleeve". The interview with Angela Rayner will be broadcast on BBC2 at 12:30 BST on Friday 11 September, and 17:30 BST on Saturday 12 September.

articles.title: The man who bought an island, hired hitmen and throttled a theatregoer
articles.summary: Malcolm Potier is beginning his third spell in jail after attacking the woman at a Queen musical.
articles.body: The man who bought an island, hired hitmen and throttled a theatregoerImage source, FacebookImage caption, Malcolm Potier's dark past was unknown to the woman he strangled at the theatreTheatre-lover Kirsty O'Donnell was a regular visitor to the West End to enjoy musicals and plays.But her life took a dramatic and frightening turn during a performance of Queen musical We Will Rock You at the London Coliseum.She was throttled by the stranger sitting next to her – a disgraced ex-millionaire who had twice tried to have his former partner murdered.Malcolm Potier launched his violent attack on 51-year-old O'Donnell as she was singing along to Queen hits on 7 June 2023.Potier, 75, from Sarratt in Hertfordshire, was found guilty of non-fatal strangulation at Southwark Crown Court in July and jailed for two years on Thursday.The bizarre violent attack was the latest carried out by Potier, once a wealthy landowner who had outbid Sir Mick Jagger to buy a remote Scottish island.Image source, Sarah Jeynes/BBCImage caption, O'Donnell was sitting in the dress circle at the London Coliseum when she was attackedAmong the crowd at the West End's biggest theatre on the night of the attack were Sir Rod Stewart, former Strictly Come Dancing judge Bruno Tonioli and comedian Jimmy Carr.It was the show's press night, and Potier was sitting next to his partner, theatre critic Lizzie Loveridge, in the dress circle.In her subsequent review, having already taken aim at the production itself, Loveridge wrote: "The other problem at the Coliseum is the behaviour of the audience."Maybe worst of all are those sing along audience members who inflict their mediocre singing voice on the rest of us."What Loveridge's review failed to mention was that one of those people singing, O'Donnell, was throttled by Potier at about 21:45 BST.Loveridge had told her to "shut up", to which she replied: "That's a bit rude."Potier then told O'Donnell, "I'll show you what rude is" and pressed down on her neck for up to five seconds.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sir Brian May delivered a guest performance on the night on 7 June 2023"This has been particularly difficult because theatres, concerts and public events have always been an important part of my life," O'Donnell told the court.Any trouble confronting what had happened to her was worsened by what she found out about her attacker.O'Donnell was told the man she was to give evidence against had twice been jailed for trying to hire a hitman to kill his ex-partner, as well as her significant other."Because I chose to give evidence, I cannot know whether there may one day be consequences for doing so," she told the judge.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Potier outbid Sir Mick Jagger for the Scottish island of Gigha in 1989Potier's colourful past can be traced back to the 1980s, when he was building up a vast property empire.The chartered surveyor outbid Rolling Stones star Jagger for the idyllic Isle of Gigha, off Scotland's west coast, in 1989.It was the jewel in the crown of his growing investment portfolio, before Swiss bankers repossessed it just three years later.More from Beds, Herts and Bucks:Call for answers after student dies at boat party'Batman mansion' owner hits back in bats rowOyez! Town crier passes bell on after 23 yearsA few years later, he hit the headlines in Australia.Potier was in custody there, having snatched his young daughter from her mother and fled there.Police found he had entered the country on a false passport and sent him to a detention centre in Sydney.While there, he met a man who agreed to kill his child's mother and her boyfriend.It never happened. The man took the £4,500 Potier paid him and fled to Italy upon his release.The next would-be killer Potier inquired about turned out to be an undercover agent and he was jailed in Australia for six-and-a-half years in 2002.That did not stop him, however. While on remand ahead of his sentencing, Potier was again caught plotting to kill his ex-partner.Image caption, Potier, pictured in the late 1980s, made international headlines with his offendingPotier had urged his cellmate to carry out the hit, asking for it to begin with an apparent car accident.The instructions? "Must be accident... must die. No mistakes. No drugs."But his plot unravelled again, and Potier was sentenced to 12 years behind bars. He returned to the UK in 2015.Reflecting on her own courage in giving evidence, O'Donnell said: "I was dealing with someone who had previously demonstrated an extraordinary willingness to use extreme violence and involve others in carrying out those crimes."Despite knowing this, I was determined not to let fear dictate my actions. If anything, it strengthened my resolve."Potier is now beginning the third prison sentence of his turbulent life.As for the Isle of Gigha, that is now in the safe hands of its residents – who crowdfunded £4m to purchase it in 2002 and take control of their own destiny.Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below.Get in touchMore on this storyRelated internet links

articles.title: Brother of Muslim policeman killed in attacks 'disappointed' by calls for Mamdani to sit out memorial
articles.summary: Zeshan Hamdani speaks out after push back against New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is Muslim, attending 9/11 events.
articles.body: This year’s 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks has become embroiled in divisive politics. There are controversial calls for the city’s first Muslim Mayor to sit out the commemorative event, including from Rudy Giuliani who was New York’s mayor on the morning of 9/11.Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he will attend and his focus will be on the families who lost loved ones.Zeshan Hamdani lost his older brother Salman, a Muslim American New York police cadet, in the North Tower. He spoke to the BBC's Nada Tawfik over his thoughts on this anniversary.Video filmed and edited by Andrew Blum; produced by Pratiksha Ghildial

articles.title: Mexican student creates an acoustic fire extinguisher to put out fire in seconds
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://www.upsocl.com/en/16-year-old-mexican-student-creates-an-acoustic-fire-extinguisher-that-uses-sound-waves-to-put-out-fires-in-seconds/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49652237
Points: 220
# Comments: 79
articles.body:
Ángela Karime Venegas Hernández is 16 years old and has an idea no one else had.
She studies at CETIS 78 in Altamira, Tamaulipas, and one day decided to put out a candle without blowing, without water, without anything but sound. She assembled a device with a 12-volt battery, a frequency generator, and a speaker that emits 30 pulses per second. That vibration pushes oxygen away from the flames, and the fire simply goes out in five to eight seconds.
She tested it over and over, more than 100 times, until confirming that it also worked on wood, flammable liquids, cooking grease, and electronic equipment. It does not pollute, leave residue, or hurt the person using it. What began as a school experiment now has a name of its own, “Vortex Tech”, and is taking Ángela to represent Mexico at an international fair, where she will present her way of combating one of humanity’s oldest dangers to the world.
articles.author: rguiscard

articles.title: People long for simpler times, say Practical Magic reboot stars
articles.summary: Actresses Maisie Williams and Joey King feature in the upcoming sequel of the 1998 fantasy romcom.
articles.body: People long for simpler times, say Practical Magic reboot starsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are joining the cast of the sequel to portray the daughters of Sandra Bullock's character ByNaomi ClarkeBBC NewsbeatMix together a beloved film simmering for decades, a sprinkling of social media hype and a generous glug of star power and you just might conjure up the long-awaited sequel to Practical Magic. The 1998 fantasy romcom, starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as witchy sisters Sally and Gillian Owens, received mixed reviews from critics when it was first released.But it's put a spell on a new generation discovering it online, with some now regarding the film as a cult classic and autumn staple.The demand for a follow-up by this new wave of fans helped convince Bullock and Kidman to reprise their roles nearly 30 years on, they say. "You never get the opportunity to do something where people really are asking you, 'please do it'," says Bullock. "It's usually us going to them."Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are joining the cast this time round to play Sally's daughters, Kylie and Antonia. Kissing Booth star King tells BBC Newsbeat she feels this desire for nostalgic content, which has become one of the defining forces within entertainment in recent years, has been influenced by "the world moving so fast".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Practical Magic 2 sees the cast return to a world which is steeped in powerful ancestral magic"I think with technology moving at the speed that it is, we're really missing the times when we were less reachable," she says."If we couldn't figure out something, we'd stare out the window until it came to us, and I think we're nostalgic for a time like that."  She feels this can also be a strength of cinema as it can help "make memories" and "feelings" for people that they can revisit by rewatching. The upcoming release comes at a time when reboots, reunions and remakes are dominating film and TV lists.Game of Thrones star Williams agrees the drive for nostalgic content feels like a "symptom of people longing for simpler times", but says she is "very grateful" that they have made a sequel and not a remake. "I do believe in pushing the story forwards and I do believe in telling new stories," she says."And I do believe stories can come back around and they can still be meaningful."But I am not the biggest fan of the remake because I think it's a shame to withhold ourselves from telling a new story." Image source, Warner Bros. PicturesImage caption, The bond of sisterhood is at the heart of the 1998 film and continues into the sequelPractical Magic 2 sees the cast return to a world which is steeped in powerful ancestral magic with the characters once again confronting a family curse which condemns anyone who loves and is loved by an Owens woman to death.There are also nods to the original throughout, with bubbling family tension, dark romantic "witchcore" fashion and the iconic midnight margaritas.US acting stalwarts Dianne Wiest and Stockard Channing return to their roles for the follow-up, while Guardians of the Galaxy actor Lee Pace, Cobra Kai's Xolo Maridueña and House of the Dragon's Solly McLeod are new additions. Reviews so far have been mixed, with the Guardian describing it as a "nostalgia-bait return", external which is as "strange and messy as the first" but with "warm seasonal pleasures to be had".Meanwhile The Hollywood Reporter, external says the "slapdash" sequel "works better the less you look for any sense of logic, and the more you just lean into the transient joys of watching these actresses bounce off each other".Image source, Warner Bros. PicturesImage caption, Joey King says the idea of "being witchy" can be "empowering right now"Amid the scrutiny around the film, Williams admits joining the Practical Magic world was "a little bit overwhelming", but says the cast were "so supportive the whole time" and "welcomed us into the sisterhood".The bond of sisterhood is at the heart of the first film and continues in the sequel, but Bullock has recalled this was initially one of the criticisms of the original, external, with some branding it as "too witchy" with "too many women". With women's rights under pressure in some countries, Williams says it is a "challenging time" and she feels it's "so important in a time like this for women to be supporting one another"."We are in a time when young women are staying in education longer and women, before having children, are sometimes being paid more than their male counterparts, which I do find to be really exciting," she adds."But there's a lot of work to do."And this feeling of witches, symbiosis and power - I feel like there's something in that which can just push us forwards."Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.More on this story

articles.title: Setting up OpenCode with Ollama and sbx on Mac
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://tensorsandtokens.com/posts/opencode-ollama/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49652122
Points: 6
# Comments: 2
articles.body:
Software developmentHow to get started with running Ollama local models with Opencode and Docker Sandboxes.Viable local LLM development is here. With powerful models like Qwen 3.8 and Gemma4 we can now finally use these models to build out web applications. I'm using a Apple Macbook pro m5 48GB model. I think this is the sweet spot for local development as it allows you to run 30B models with a decent sized context.
Why I use Ollama. To be frank it's just easy. It has mlx now, so it's fast on Apple silicon. It has a pretty good model directory. It is also very stable and won't crash.
Why Opencode. Well, we need to start somewhere with this blog and opencode is a great harness.
There is one other tool that I use, docker sandboxes aka sbx. I use frontier models at work which require us to sandbox our harnesses. I also, like to run my local models in containers as they can just as easily mess up your computer with a unwanted hallucination.
brew trust docker/tap && brew install docker/tap/sbxInstall Opencode:
To install ollama, goto https://ollama.com/ and download and install the app.
For the models, we'll pull 2 models. First ensure ollama is running.
Qwen 3.8 27B mxfp8 (32GB): This is a great workhorse model that will do most of your long running work and can run undisturbed for multiple hours within opencode.
ollama pull qwen3.8:27b-mxfp8Gemma 4 31b mxfp8 (34GB): This is a great big dense model when you need something bigger.
ollama pull gemma4:31b-mxfp8Note: If you don't have the 48GB Apple, you can pull the standard models: qwen3.8:27b-mlx and gemma4:31b-mlx .
For this setup, it requires you to setup a sbx kit for every project. A kit is a way to customise the sandbox. Create the following folders and files:
displayName: Local Ollama for OpenCode
description: Configure OpenCode in Docker Sandboxes to use Ollama running on the Mac host.
Local Ollama runs on the host machine.
Deep file analysis / reasoning:
"name": "Qwen 3.8 27B MXFP8 [31 GB] [64K ctx]",
"name": "Gemma 4 31B MXFP8 [33 → ~50 GB] [256K ctx]",
For the qwen model, we've limited the context to 64k, this will ensure your system dose not lock up when it runs out of memory. We also need 3GB for the sandbox.
To run opencode, run the following:
sbx run opencode --kit ./sbx-kit/This will start Opencode with Qwen selected. Ensure you change down to "low" effort via /models command.
You should be good to go.
Note: You will need to login into Docker to run sbx. This feature is not really liked by the development community but there is no way around it.

articles.title: Google will buy half the electricity of a nuclear power plant
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c8r6y4me2g6o
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49652105
Points: 78
# Comments: 50
articles.body: Google picks Finland for its largest single investment in EuropeGetty ImagesGoogle will buy up to half the electricity produced by one of Finland's nuclear power plants as part of a record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in the country's AI infrastructure, the company announced.The US tech giant said the package would fund three new data centres, expand an existing site and support energy projects to power growing demand for AI services."This is Google's largest single investment in Europe and a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure," the company said on Wednesday."Google's decision is a clear testament to our strengths," Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement.As part of the deal, Google signed a 22-year contract with Finnish utility Fortum to buy up to 50% of the output from the Loviisa nuclear power plant.Earlier this week, TikTok announced a $1bn investment in Finland to build a new data centre in Kouvola, pointing to the country's "strong digital infrastructure, clean energy mix, robust data governance and skilled tech talent".    Finland has emerged as an attractive location for data centres because of its cool climate, plentiful low-carbon electricity and relatively uncongested power grid. The colder temperatures can reduce the energy needed to cool facilities packed with computer servers.Technology companies are racing to secure power supplies as the AI boom drives demand for vast networks of data centres.The Google investment is expected to support more than 37,000 jobs during construction and boost Finland's GDP by €3.6bn a year, according to Google. Construction is set to take place in 2027 and 2028."The value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment into spurring innovation, research and development," Orpo added. "Deepening our collaboration with Google will deliver lasting benefits for both parties."Google will build new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, while expanding its existing facility in Hamina, which it established after converting a former paper mill in 2009.The infrastructure will help support products such as its AI chatbot Gemini, alongside services including Search, Maps and YouTube.Google said the investments also covered "clean energy projects, and dedicated nature and community funds to support local biodiversity, education, research, and workforce development"."Google is proud to deepen our roots in Finland," said Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google."This investment underscores Google's commitment to grow our presence responsibly, pairing the expansion of our technical infrastructure with new energy capacity, grid enhancements, and energy affordability initiatives," she added.Earlier this year, Google's parent company Alphabet raised its global spending plans to as much as $205bn as it sought to expand computing capacity for AI services.The agreement with Fortum provides long-term financial certainty for the Loviisa plant, which currently generates about 10% of Finland's electricity.Fortum said Google's commitment would support an investment programme aimed at extending the life of the nuclear station and increasing its generating capacity.

articles.title: YuE2 · Frontier Music with Symbolic Planning
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://map-yue2.github.io/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49652028
Points: 39
# Comments: 27
articles.body:
Listen to a song, then explore the melody, rhythm, and chords in its symbolic plan.
Red notes follow the score recording.
A familiar song can take a different shape. Listen to changes in melody, lyrics, tempo, and arrangement.
A song takes shape through a conversation. Loading the editing story…
The listening selection, gathered across genres and languages.
YuE2 (best-of-8) reaches 6.9632 on SongBench, the highest observed mean among 15 evaluated settings on WildSongBench (192 prompts). Suno v5 scores 6.8721 in the same comparison.
Song quality and text alignment on WildSongBench. Bubble area shows AudioBox PQ; black outlines mark Pareto optima on the two plotted axes. Bo8 = best-of-8. How to read the indices.
Model architectureComposing in symbols, performing in audio.Vector PDF
An editable score becomes semantic music tokens, acoustic latents, and full-song audio. The model has approximately 3.59B parameters and 28 layers, and supports creation, covering, and editing. The AR and NAR experts share an attention computation while using separate normalization, projections, and MLPs.
Explore benchmark scores WildSongBench · 15 settings · 7 metrics
How to read these results
WildSongBench. 192 prompts and 15 system settings. The table reports automatic evaluation scores. Best-of-8 selects one of eight generations by musicality, prompt control, and lyric accuracy.
Figure 1. Song quality combines SongBench and SongEval; text alignment combines MuLan, AllMusicCaps, and prompt control. Both axes show normalized comparison indices. Bubble area represents AudioBox production quality.
MERT2 · Music representationsLearning the structure behind the sound.Vector PDF
MERT2 provides the music representations behind both analysis and generation. A ConvNeXt frontend and 24-layer Conformer learn to predict masked codes built from complementary MuQ and Qwen2-Audio features. Full-song adaptation supplies SheetSage2 with musical context; a separate causal branch becomes YuE2’s 25-Hz semantic tokenizer.
State of the art on MARBLE
MERT2-30s and MERT2-FS (full-song) achieve SOTA on 14 of 15 MARBLE metrics, leading across tagging, key, genre, and emotion recognition.
SOTA metricsMERT2-30s & MERT2-FS14 / 15
Genre accuracy · GTZANMERT2-30s · score × 10091.72
Key refined accuracy · GiantStepsMERT2-FS · score × 10067.05
Explore MERT2 benchmark scores MARBLE · 15 metrics · 2 encoders
SOTA counts use the best score across the two MERT2 encoders against the nine published baselines in this comparison. Both encoders have 632M parameters. MERT2-30s uses a 30-second training context; MERT2-FS uses 300 seconds. These are full-context representation benchmarks. MERT2 reports the best observed results across representations selected using test scores; each ROC-AUC / AP pair uses the same representation.
SheetSage2 · Audio to scoreHear a song. Read its composition.Vector PDF
SheetSage2 turns a recording into an editable lead sheet. A full-song MERT2-FS encoder, adapted with LoRA, feeds a six-layer autoregressive decoder. Task prompts select beats, sections, keys, chords, and melodies; a shared event timeline becomes ABC notation with vocal and instrumental melody voices. These scores supply symbolic training targets for YuE2.
Six transcription tasks, one model
SheetSage2 achieves SOTA on 10 of 13 benchmark metrics with one model for beat, downbeat, key, chord, structure, and melody transcription.
SOTA metricsOne model · six transcription tasks10 / 13
Vocal melody · RWC-PopPitch-class note F1 · score × 10082.51
Chord recognition · osu2017Maj/min · score × 10090.08
Explore SheetSage2 benchmark scores 6 tasks · 13 metrics
SOTA counts refer to the leading scores against SheetSage1, Madmom, and the task-specific systems in this comparison. Results use one model selected by validation loss. Melody F1 measures pitch-class notes; structure F1 measures section boundaries at the stated tolerance. On Chords1217, ChordFormer uses five-fold cross-validation, while SheetSage2 evaluates one fixed model on all 1,217 tracks.
Our models are trained primarily on CC0 music and synthetic data. Tokenwave.AI provides most of our synthetic training data under license. We are committed to the ethical and responsible use of data.
