articles.title: Wolverine on the PS5 goes back to a simpler (and bloodier) style of action game
articles.summary: Marvel's Wolverine captures just how angry its lead character is. The latest PS5 exclusive from Spider-Man developer Insomniac, Wolverine is a straightforward action game that is at its best when you're (literally) slicing through enemies or thrust into a sequence pulled from a blockbuster movie, like climbing the fuselage of a plane as it careens toward land or racing a motorcycle across rain-sli
articles.body:
Marvel’s Wolverine captures just how angry its lead character is. The latest PS5 exclusive from Spider-Man developer Insomniac, Wolverine is a straightforward action game that is at its best when you’re (literally) slicing through enemies or thrust into a sequence pulled from a blockbuster movie, like climbing the fuselage of a plane as it careens toward land or racing a motorcycle across rain-slicked city streets. It’s the kind of game that can really get your heart rate rising, and keeping Logan mad is a key part of the strategy. In many ways, it’s a throwback to straightforward action titles of the past — and it’s a refreshing change of pace in a medium saturated with live-service and open-world games.
Though it comes from Insomniac, Wolverine is very different from Spider-Man, which thrust the web-slinger into an open-world version of New York City. Instead, this is a much more linear experience that feels like a combination of two other PlayStation staples: God of War and Uncharted. Rather than follow Wolverine as a member of the X-Men, the story instead has him as an often reluctant member of Team X, a mercenary group with similar pro-mutant aims but a much more violent approach. Instead of heroes like Cyclops and Professor X, Wolvy is joined by more villain-adjacent characters like Sabretooth, Mystique, and Nathaniel Essex, before eventually connecting with Jean Grey. The story pulls Logan and his companions across the globe, but it starts out relatively simple, as they investigate a rash of mutant disappearances connected to a billionaire arms dealer.
The most important thing about both Wolverine the character and Wolverine the game is fighting. This is a hairy little dude who loves to scrap, and his mutant powers — healing and sharp claws — make it so that he is very good at it, able to both take a huge amount of damage and dish it out. And the best part of the game is how Wolverine-specific the action is. The combat is fast and violent and forces you to be aggressive. Wolverine can leap huge distances to take out foes and use his claws to both repel attacks and slice at enemies, often with very gruesome results. (At the end of a battle he’s usually coated in blood.) An important part of this is Wolverine’s rage level, which increases the more you fight. As his rage grows, it allows you to do two things: go absolutely berserk and kill a rash of enemies with a single blow, and use your healing power as a sort of extra life in case your health depletes. It’s a clever system that means you can’t sit back and play it safe. Wolverine isn’t chill, and you can’t be either.
That’s the God of War side of Wolverine. The Uncharted side comes in the form of all of the over-the-top set-pieces you’re thrown into. I’ll refrain from detailing some of the best ones for spoiler reasons, but I’ll say that, just like in Uncharted, these moments make it feel like you’re playing out a wild sequence from an action movie. There are chases across the rooftops of Tokyo, massive boss battles against some iconic comic book villains, and scenes where Wolverine is literally being ripped apart as he fights for survival.
The flip side is that, because of this setup, Wolverine is also much more restrictive than most of its contemporaries. In some ways this is a good thing; it’s refreshing to play a game that isn’t trying to do everything. But there are still some awkward elements. For instance, much like in Spider-Man, there are lots of collectibles that will reveal new bits of story or unlock new suits for Wolverine to wear. But exploration outside of the main path is extremely dull, so the only reason to track these down is if you have a completionist mindset. It’s also disappointing that Wolverine’s closet of outfits is much less fun than Spider-Man’s, and they often feel out of place with the game’s attempt at a more gritty tone.
Making matters worse is that, despite a promising start, the story ends up in a largely forgettable place, with few surprises, particularly if you have an even slight knowledge of the X-Men universe from comics or the animated series. Outside of combat and set-pieces, Wolverine skews generic AAA game; the voice acting, the cutscenes, and even some of the missions feel like standard video game fare, many of which seem out of place. Wolverine is amazing when you’re surrounded by ninjas trying to kill you. But when Logan is in a tux trying to spy on a fancy party? Not so much.
All that said, Wolverine’s return to a simpler and smaller style of action — I beat the game in around 13 hours — is still notable, particularly from Sony, which has had a rough few years after placing many ill-fated bets in the live-service space. But much like last year’s Ghost of Yōtei, Wolverine shows that PlayStation is still capable of the single-player blockbusters the platform is best known for. It’s also launching at perhaps the busiest video game release period in recent memory, going up against major titles including Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Control Resonant, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, Gears of War: E-Day, Silent Hill: Townfall, Star Wars: Zero Company, and, soon enough, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Grand Theft Auto VI.
In that company, despite occasionally skewing generic, Wolverine’s bloodthirsty focus on action is something that makes it stand out.
Marvel’s Wolverine launches on September 15th on the PS5.
articles.author: Andrew Webster

articles.title: Meta’s Muse AI works and creeps me out
articles.summary:
I turned my Muse assistant into a purple cat. | Screenshot: The Verge	

Meta has launched its new Muse assistant, marking the company's first real foray into AI-powered productivity tools. The company says its AI agent can "take the busywork off your plate" by helping you with online shopping, emails, trip-planning, and more.  I decided to try out the new tool and see how well it performed - espec
articles.body:
Meta has launched its new Muse assistant, marking the company’s first real foray into AI-powered productivity tools. The company says its AI agent can “take the busywork off your plate” by helping you with online shopping, emails, trip-planning, and more.  I decided to try out the new tool and see how well it performed — especially from a company that previously prioritized entertainment over productivity. Though the AI assistant generally worked as I expected it to, the unnerving amount of information it autonomously gleaned about me largely overshadowed my experience.
One of the first tasks I assigned Muse, which carries out actions using a cloud-based virtual computer, was to sort through my Gmail inbox and delete messages I don’t need. That required me to connect Muse to my Google account and give it permission to access, read, and delete emails. The process didn’t go smoothly on mobile; the Google sign-in screen kept glitching and returning me to the Muse website instead of the app. I eventually got it working on my laptop, where it deleted thousands of promotional emails and updates. I didn’t feel good about permitting Muse to view all of my emails given Meta’s track record on privacy over the years.
[Image: Muse did a good job at clearing out my emails. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/muse-ai-emails.png?quality=90&strip=all]
Meta says it designed Muse to only exchange data with third-party apps “that’s needed for them to work for you.” The company also says that it doesn’t share your information with advertisers. I still felt uneasy, but I pushed on anyway, linking my Amazon account to Muse. I asked the  AI agent to pick out workout tops for me based on a specific size, style, and colors. Before placing the order, Muse noticed I had other items in my cart and asked if I wanted to remove them. The consideration pleasantly surprised me. Once I signed off on the purchase, it proceeded to successfully buy only the tank tops.
Shifting gears, I tried out some of Muse’s other capabilities, which allow it to generate AI podcasts similar to Gemini Notebook, create images and videos, as well as develop interactive webpages or documents called “artifacts.” Muse denied my requests to generate images of a “cartoon mouse with red pants” and a “cartoon guy with a red hat, blue overalls, brown hair, and a mustache. 
However, it readily generated a video and several images of a product launch event featuring devices with Apple’s logo when asked. In one image, Muse created what looks like an iPhone-like foldable, an Apple Watch, and AirPods. Each device is propped up on a stand with Apple’s logo on it, while a presenter stands in front of a backdrop plastered with the company’s recognizable bitten apple. The phone even included Apple’s native app icons on the fake iPhone, though it hallucinated and named the App Store “Photos,” while calling Maps, Music, and the actual Photos app “Calender.” Muse refused to generate an image of an “Apple CEO.”
[Image: Muse wouldn’t generate an image of an Apple CEO, but it still plastered the company’s logo everywhere. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/muse-ai-apple-image.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Then things got weird. I tapped over to the “Feed” tab, where Muse generates a news feed of sorts based on a text prompt. I submitted the prompt that Meta includes by default: “Make me a feed about my interests. Keep the tone clear and direct. Ensure it is quick to skim. Try to avoid clickbait.” It returned several AI-generated summaries of current events, including blurbs about Apple’s iPhone Duo launch event, the dangerous surf hitting California’s coast, and tankers destroyed in the Iran war. The app also listed several news stories from the state where I’m currently visiting my family, which Muse admitted it pulled from the shipping address on my Amazon order.
I dove deeper from there and asked Muse what else it might know about me based on the Instagram and Facebook accounts I signed up to use the AI agent with. It rattled off my very specific interests, ranging from anime and CrossFit to Labrador retrievers, Florida wildlife, and ’90s/2000s nostalgia — many of the same topics that frequently pop up in my Instagram Reels feed.
Curious, I asked Muse to tell me where it got that information. “Honestly, Instagram doesn’t show you that exact list anywhere in the app — I read it through the account’s API data, which surfaces more than the UI does,” Muse wrote. “The closest thing you can see yourself is your ad topics… That shows the topics advertisers can target you with, and you can remove ones you don’t want or choose to see less of them.” I checked the “Ad topics” list in my Instagram settings menu, and while it does include some vague categories, like workouts, music, and electronics, it’s not the same level of detail that Muse provided. The Verge reached out to Meta about the data Muse can access inside Instagram and Facebook but didn’t immediately hear back.
[Image: Muse says it accessed my specific interests through Instagram’s API. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/muse-ai-privacy.png?quality=90&strip=all]
Like some of the other agentic AI tools I’ve tried out, Muse does a decent job at performing low-stakes tasks. I also like that it generates a running list of “ideas” that give personalized suggestions on how to use the tool, like providing side-by-side comparisons of products, finding and cancelling forgotten subscriptions, and keeping track of the next release of Pokémon cards. Muse keeps a running list of “goals” to complete based on your conversations with the AI agent, too.
Muse delivered on its promise of handling life’s more mundane tasks in the background, but the level of personal details Muse scooped up from sources unavailable even to me was enough to leave me with an uneasy feeling about letting Muse sort through personal emails and handle my credit card. That level of suspicion is going to be the real hurdle for Meta to overcome.
articles.author: Emma Roth

articles.title: Switch Six Nations fixture to USA to grow game – World Rugby
articles.summary: World Rugby would help any nation which wants to switch a Six Nations match to the United States as it continues its drive to spread the game stateside.
articles.body: World Rugby would help any nation which wants to switch a Six Nations match to the United States, as it continues its drive to spread the game stateside.South Africa and New Zealand have sold out the 71,000-capacity M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore for Saturday's fourth and final Test in their Greatest Rivalry series.With the men's and women's Rugby World Cups being held in the United States in 2031 and 2033 respectively, tournament organisers are keen to bring more prestige fixtures across the Atlantic."In terms of the match-day economics, [South Africa vs New Zealand] is like a Six Nations match," Alan Gilpin, World Rugby chief executive, told the Daily Telegraph., external"It starts to show that [financial return] is not the barrier. So if there is the appetite to take some of these big matches in the future to the US, we can now."The All Blacks have been at the forefront of rugby's attempts to make an imprint in a notoriously tough sports market.Ireland memorably beat the All Blacks for the first time when the teams met in front of a capacity 60,000-strong crowd at Chicago's Soldier Field in 2016, with a 2025 rematch proving a similar commercial success.New Zealand have also staged matches against the United States - a 104-14 victory in front of about 40,000 fans in Washington, external - and Fiji - a 47-5 win before 33,217 in San Diego - in the country over the past decadeHowever Gilpin believes that the history of the Six Nations and its ability to connect with expatriate fans in the United States could be a useful tool to crack America further."This isn't a live discussion of an Italy vs Ireland game, but why we use that as an example?" he added. "You've got two fantastic fanbases in the US of Irish and Italian fans"If you could take a Six Nations game to the right place, to a Boston or to a New York, where there's a lot of those fanbases, you can definitely drive the economics."Now, you're going to have Irish fans and Italian fans in those respective home countries saying, 'Hang on a minute, you know, we want to see our country play?' "The counter-argument to that [is] it's still Irish and Italian fans getting the chance to watch their team, so they're just not the ones who live in Ireland and Italy on this occasion. But that's a balancing piece we've got to work through."Wales played their home matches at London's Wembley Stadium during the 1998 and 1999 Six Nations while the Principality Stadium was being built, but such a long-haul venue switch would be unprecedented in the tournament's 143-year history.England women's head coach John Mitchell, who led the United States' men's team earlier in his career, said he was unsure whether a stateside expansion would ultimately succeed."I've worked for America. I understand that geography," he told BBC Radio 5 Live."American sport is full of rivalries and I just don't think Americans adjust to new rivalries or new franchises compared to probably some of the other countries."Will rugby ever go big there based on its its early investment?"I'm not sure I can answer that, but what I do know is that rugby union is a difficult challenge for large parts of America."He was also wary of the prospect of a Red Roses' Six Nations match being staged in the United States."The visibility's huge here in the European market," added Mitchell."Let's use it because that's the way to grow the game slowly, rather than putting huge investments into something that might have potential, but not necessarily that visibility."While World Rugby could support a stateside Six Nations game, the decision would lie with the competing teams, all of whom would be aware of the consternation that would come with transplanting a fixture thousands of miles away.The schedule for the 2027 editions of both the men's and women's tournaments have already been set.

articles.title: AI agents are flooding public services with new requests
articles.summary: “The vast majority of cases we find are people who are entitled to claim for something, claiming for that thing,” the researcher told TechCrunch.
articles.body:
As AI makes it easier to fill forms and file complaints, public services around the world are seeing enormous jumps in applications and other requests.
In the United Kingdom, complaints to the housing ombudsman more than doubled since the introduction of ChatGPT, rising from 2,600 in 2022 to just over 7,000 last year. The United States’ Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) saw 5x growth in complaints over the same period. There were similar jumps in Brazilian judicial petitions and German parliamentary petitions.
Researcher Chris Schmitz is tracking this rise as part of a broader trend he called “agentic flooding.” In a paper set to be presented next month at the AI Ethics and Society conference, he looks at 84 different cases of potential flooding across 11 jurisdictions, finding broad evidence that AI tools are changing the way people interact with public services.
The harder question is what to do in response. While some of the new filings are clearly adversarial, others are the result of legitimate applicants using AI to file claims that would otherwise be abandoned. While some might see the new applications as AI-generated spam, Schmitz sees it as a rare opportunity to remake social services for the AI era.
Schmitz looked at services ranging from welfare applications to official judicial appeals, but they all have online services that could be accessed by an AI assistant. (The full dataset is hosted here, for reference.) For methodological reasons, Schmitz’s paper stops short of saying AI is directly causing the surge of new applicants. But most of the 84 cases follow the same basic arc, where submissions were roughly flat before 2022, then rose at increasing speed as AI technology diffuses. Crucially, most cases have not seen that growth slow down, suggesting it will likely keep rising for years to come.
For Schmitz, it’s easy to see how the increasing skills and availability of AI would drive increased usage.
“People are finding out that this is something one can do, and incrementally, it is just getting easier to do it … before it might have been a question of a lot of dragging context together and prompting ChatGPT 3.5 very precisely, it may now be a question of just pasting or taking a photo of a letter with your Claude app and getting a pretty good response in one shot,” he said.
The jump in volume is similar to what many bug-bounty services also experienced last year, as companies found their inboxes flooded with low-quality reports generated by LLMs. The reports rarely contained significant security issues, but companies were still obligated to vet the reports as they came in, presenting a significant drain on resources. It’s easy to imagine public services facing a similar problem, as they manage 5x more applicants with the same budget.
But where the bug bounty programs were flooded with worthless submissions, Schmitz says most of the new applications to public services are coming from real people with legitimate claims.
“The vast majority of cases we find are people who are entitled to claim for something, claiming for that thing,” he told TechCrunch.
If those people weren’t claiming the benefits before, it may have been because the work of applying was too forbidding — something known in the policy world as administrative burden. Now that AI can lift that burden, it could be an opportunity to remake many of these services in a more AI-friendly way.
It’s a major task, which we mostly haven’t begun to tackle, but Schmitz sees it as reason for optimism.
“A big part of making AI go well is being able to detail out what the good version of things looks like. And anyone who’s ever used ChatGPT to do the tax return knows that there’s a good version here where you’re being helped,” Schmitz says. “This could be the moment to say, ‘we need to rethink pretty much everything about how this process looks.’”

articles.title: Badenoch denies housing benefit cuts plan would make people homeless
articles.summary: The Conservatives say £4bn could be cut from the housing benefit bill to help fund increased defence spending.
articles.body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has denied her party's plans to cut housing benefit would make people homeless, but suggested some would have to "move somewhere cheaper".At Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, she had challenged Andy Burnham to commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying the cost could be covered by cuts to welfare.The Conservatives have claimed £4bn could be cut from the housing benefit bill, in part by allowing tenancies in areas where housing is expensive to come to an end.Asked whether she would be willing to make people homeless in order to fund defence, Badenoch told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the party would "protect existing tenants". During PMQs, Burnham argued national security "can't come at the expense of social security". He repeated that a target date for increasing defence spending to 3% of GDP would be announced in the spending review in the spring.The PM insisted he would get the welfare bill down in "the Labour way", by boosting council housebuilding, supporting young people into work and providing more mental health support.Badenoch said the government should cut housing benefit to fund defence spending now, adding she would exempt pensioners and existing tenants from the plans.Speaking on the Today programme, she said: "What we're doing is making sure that people are protected, but capping the amount that people get on benefits because we need to look after our national security."Without national security, there aren't going to be any benefits. We're all going to be in danger, far more people will be homeless, and the government's first duty is defence of the realm."Her proposed changes would be part of a package that would cut £23bn from welfare to partly fund an increase in defence spending. But Karen Buck, chairwoman of Generation Rent and a former Labour MP, said Badenoch's proposals would lead to "homelessness, temporary accommodation costs crippling local councils, renters in severe financial hardship".Housing benefit can be paid to people who are unemployed or on a low income to help cover the cost of rent. The amount someone can claim is linked to the Local Housing Allowance rate, which varies for different council areas.The number of people eligible to claim housing benefit has increased by more than one million since 2020, driven by the soaring cost of private rents.The total cost of housing benefit is forecast to hit £39bn this year, according to the Department for Work and Pensions, due to the increasing number of claimants.The Conservatives have set out how they plan to cut £4bn in total from the housing benefit bill, which they said would include a saving of at least £2.2bn from freezing social sector rents, by removing annual inflation-linked increases.Another £1.8bn would be saved by lowering Local Housing Allowance rates, which are based on private rental costs in the area, for new tenancies.For existing tenancies, rates would be frozen until they gradually fall in line.In an interview with BBC Breakfast, Badenoch was asked who would be affected by her plans to cut housing benefit.She said: "We have people who live in areas that are quite expensive and if people need local housing allowance they will need to move somewhere cheaper. "I think you should aspire to live wherever you want to live, but you shouldn't aspire for the government, i.e. other taxpayers, to pay for you to live wherever you want to live..."We're not removing people from homes - this doesn't cover pensioners, it doesn't affect existing tenants - but I do think you need to be fair."Responding to Badenoch at PMQs, Burnham had said the policy would worsen homelessness and end up costing the government more.He said: "I don't think, myself, that taking £4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation."

articles.title: Another big James Talarico interview is punted to YouTube due to FCC threats
articles.summary:
Jimmy Kimmel will be interviewing Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico "under unusual circumstances," posting the interview directly to YouTube, rather than airing it on TV during Jimmy Kimmel Live.  In Wednesday night's episode, Kimmel said this was out of concern for retaliation from the Trump administration's FCC: 
[Trump's] FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our
articles.body:
Jimmy Kimmel will be interviewing Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico “under unusual circumstances,” posting the interview directly to YouTube, rather than airing it on TV during Jimmy Kimmel Live.  In Wednesday night’s episode, Kimmel said this was out of concern for retaliation from the Trump administration’s FCC: 
> [Trump’s] FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations based on simple, traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings, it would seem they don’t like. And so, out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television. It will be posted on YouTube instead. It will not be on TV.
Kimmel’s announcement comes almost a year after his show was taken off the air in response to threats from FCC chair Brendan Carr. In February, Stephen Colbert also had to move an interview with Talarico to YouTube, claiming CBS barred him from airing it over worries about upsetting the FCC, citing the FCC’s equal time rule. The FCC also took aim at The View after an interview with Talarico earlier this year.
ABC, which airs Jimmy Kimmel Live and The View, filed a lawsuit against the FCC last month claiming it has “waged a retaliatory campaign” against its networks, “punishing” ABC by threatening to pull its broadcast licenses.
articles.author: Stevie Bonifield

articles.title: Bending Spoons to buy collaboration tools maker Miro for $1.36B, 90% less than its 2022 valuation
articles.summary: Bending Spoons is buying Miro for $1.36 billion, a huge dip in valuation for the workplace collaboration startup, which was valued at $17.5 billion in late 2021.
articles.body:
Bending Spoons is continuing its trend of buying once-sought-after software companies for pennies on the dollar. This time, the Italian company is buying Miro for $1.36 billion in cash (equity value of $1.79 billion), a mighty dip in valuation for the once-hot workplace collaboration startup that was awarded a price tag of $17.5 billion in late 2021.
Founded in 2011 as a whiteboarding tool called RealtimeBoard, Miro found great fortune during the COVID-19 pandemic, when companies moved to remote work en masse and found their employees wanting to replicate the experience of collaborating on a physical whiteboard.
Miro quickly capitalized on that momentum by building a platform that could integrate with more than 250 apps and struck partnerships with Atlassian, Cisco, Microsoft, and Zoom. The company also started letting its users build integrations with common tools and customize the base product to meet their needs. Today, it calls itself an “AI innovation workspace” that offers AI assistants for its whiteboard tools, AI workflows, prototyping tools, and AI connectors that pull context from various platforms like GitHub, Jira, and Slack.
By 2022, Miro had grown from 5 million to about 30 million users within a scant two years, and its paying customer base had expanded by 550% — factors that likely contributed to its immense valuation at the time.
By all indications, the company has continued growing, though not at that blistering pace. Today, Miro has more than 4 million paying users and 100 million total users. Bending Spoons said Miro now has about $600 million in annual recurring revenue, of which 90% comes from businesses and enterprises. The company also has about $435 million in net cash and is profitable.
Still, the 92% dip in Miro’s valuation illustrates just how much software-as-a-service (SaaS) multiples have unwound since its heyday in 2021. By 2022, the dying pandemic tailwinds spurred companies to tighten spending by cutting down on duplicate apps and licenses. Miro, competing with much-better funded rivals such as Canva, Figma, and Microsoft in the workplace collaboration space, likely found itself shoved aside as businesses started preferring suites of various products instead of individual collaboration tools.
Miro, which had about 1,200 employees in 2022, cut jobs twice, laying off 119 staff in February 2023 and reportedly another 275 people in October 2024.
Bending Spoons, however, is probably happy it is able to snap up a company that’s been doing quite well for a smidgen of its former, arguably inflated, value. In that way, Miro is pretty similar to Airtable, which was valued at over $11 billion in the boom days of 2021 but sold to Bending Spoons for $1.28 billion last month.
The Italian serial acquirer of software companies seems to be exploiting a specific change: large, recognizable SaaS companies that were priced in 2021 as if they’d become software giants, but matured into slower-growing but still substantial businesses with decent recurring revenue and established user bases.
Still, it’s curious why Miro’s board and investors agreed to sell at that price now, especially seeing that the company didn’t apparently need the cash. Has confidence in SaaS companies being able to go public or find a comparable exit really plummeted that low?

articles.title: GB return after pregnancy 'hard to put into words' - Kinsella
articles.summary: A year after giving birth, Alice Kinsella takes the latest step on her groundbreaking return to gymnastics at an international meeting for Great Britain.
articles.body: Olympic gymnast Alice Kinsella says it is "hard to put into words" how she feels about returning to international competition as her groundbreaking comeback to the sport continues this weekend.The two-time European champion became the first British artistic gymnast to resume elite competition after giving birth, when she finished fourth in the beam at the British Championships in March.Now the 25-year-old is preparing for her first competition back in Great Britain colours at a senior team international against France, Switzerland, Germany and Italy at Fenton Manor in Stoke on 12-13 September."It's kind of crazy - it's such a surreal feeling but I am very excited," Kinsella told BBC Radio Stoke."It's only been a year, postpartum. Training-wise, it's been tough, but it's been good.  I'm excited to finally get out there. I'm ready, I'm doing everything I can to get back where I was."It's been a rollercoaster but a good one."Kinsella's pioneering journey back to the sport is so rare it became the subject of a university research paper into elite gymnasts resuming their careers after giving birth.Her son Parker, who was born in September 2025, is already a source of inspiration and he will be watching his mum compete at the weekend as Kinsella competes in all four pieces of apparatus - balance beam, bars, vault and floor - for the first time."It's really special because I've wanted to try to get back into a team and this is a really good start because it's a little four-way," said Kinsella, who trains with Park Wrekin Gymnastics Club in Shropshire."It's not too big of a competition, which is really good. I'm definitely nervous, but it's hard to put into words - it's been so long."I did the British [Championships] in March but only did beam and that's all I was training really, but now I'm trying to do all four so it's more on the body."It's not like you've done one piece and you can stop thinking about everything, you've got to move on to the next and think about that. So it's been tough."After revealing she only took "three or four weeks off" after giving birth, Kinsella returned to training at the start of the year with the longer-term intention of being at the World Championships in China in 2027 and the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.But, after finding herself ahead of schedule so far this year, she wanted to take the chance to step it up."My main goal was to try to get back next year but I'm actually a lot further forward than I thought I would be," added Kinsella, who won bronze in the team event at the Tokyo Olympics in 2020."So that's why I'm doing this competition because I just want to get out there, compete, because I don't like doing nothing."What makes Kinsella's return so unique are the obvious challenges - and changes to the body - pregnancy and childbirth brings.There are many examples of women returning to the top of their sports after becoming mothers but gymnastics, where vital pelvic floor and core strength are both weakened during pregnancy, is different.Kinsella said her gymnastics background has played a big part in her being able to return to physical exercise so quickly but said she "didn't feel too bad" when she got back in the gym."I always had that goal to get back into the gym and I think when I've got a goal set I will do everything I can to achieve it," she said."Getting back into a leotard with how my body's changed just feels very weird, but I guess that shows what my body has gone through and I try to think about it in a positive way."Her body is not the only thing that has changed with Kinsella adding that parenthood has helped her become better at taking the pressure off herself as an athlete."Having a baby changes your life - I'm very patient, whereas before Parker I was not patient at all," she said."When I made one tiny mistake I would get so annoyed, but now if I just make like a little mistake I'm totally fine about it."You have to be patient with kids, they're crazy. So I've definitely changed in that aspect but style-wise and gymnastics-wise like I don't think that's changed."Things are harder to get back and to do but I think the more I train it'll probably feel a lot easier."Kinsella said when she started her comeback "no one really had any idea what I was going to able to do" and wants to keep levels of expectation for her international return as realistic as possible.For her, this weekend in Stoke is there primarily "just to enjoy it" and to "get the experience of all four pieces [of apparatus] again"."My body's changed, I can't do the same amount of training I used to do but I'm definitely getting back to that," Kinsella said."We're definitely on the right track to be where I was before I had Parker. My goal was to start competing next year properly on all four. "It's going to be really fun. Whatever happens, happens, good, bad. I'm just proud I'm able to be back out there a year postpartum."

articles.title: The iPhone Duo’s hardware doesn’t look special, but its software might be

articles.body:
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has pulled off a familiar trick. It arrives into a mature Android foldable market with a handful of hardware features we’ve mostly already seen elsewhere, but paired with a level of software polish that makes a lot of them feel new again. It’s those software flourishes that have me excited to try the iPhone Duo when it launches next month, but I’m less convinced that its hardware will be anything special.
If Apple had gotten there first, the Duo’s biggest surprise would have been its squat, wide, passport-inspired shape. But its slow-moving supply chain meant that Huawei, Samsung, and Xiaomi all managed to beat Apple to market with similarly sized rivals, so the unusual design already feels fairly familiar — helped by Samsung’s aggressive efforts to market its new design.
More has been made of Apple’s efforts to eliminate the foldable display’s crease, which seem to have been largely successful. Apple attributes it to a 100-component hinge, custom adhesives that allow the display layers to “glide” over one another, and a matte finish that reduces glare and reflections to make the crease harder to spot. Trying the phone at Apple’s event yesterday, Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel said that you can’t really see the crease, but that “if you go looking for it, you can definitely feel one.”
It sounds, and looks, impressive, but Apple is far from the first to do it. Samsung made great strides in eliminating the crease on its Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra thanks to new titanium display layers. Before that, Oppo all but eliminated its Find N6 crease by using 3D printing to fill the minute gaps across the hinge. I’d have to see all those phones side by side to see which crease is subtlest, but even if Apple does win, it won’t be by much.
None of the iPhone Duo’s other standout hardware features are true firsts either. Google beat it to an IP68 rating, now even surpassed by Honor’s IP69. Samsung, Oppo, and Honor have all offered stylus support before — though Samsung has since dropped it. Samsung also moved on from the under-display selfie camera, which has always been hamstrung by poor photo and video quality and a distractingly visible patch on the screen.
In other ways, the hardware even feels behind the competition. The Duo is the thickest of this new wave of wide foldables, though at 5.2mm when open it’s still thinner than the iPhone Air. The weight is a more obvious issue: The 254g Duo is 26 percent heavier than the Z Fold 8 — a 53g difference — which is going to be pretty noticeable. You have to go back to 2022’s Z Fold 4 to find a Samsung foldable that’s heavier, TriFold excluded.
There’s also no evidence that Apple has adopted silicon-carbon batteries yet, which have allowed Samsung, Motorola, and other Android manufacturers to fit bigger capacities into the smaller spaces of foldable phones. Apple says the phone should still deliver a full 24 hours of regular use, but Honor’s Magic V6 uses silicon-carbon to deliver two days of life.
The rear cameras are pretty basic too, with a pair of 48-megapixel shooters and no telephoto. That’s almost an exact match for the cameras on the Z Fold 8, but Google, Motorola, Xiaomi and others are now providing capable triple cameras across their foldable lines, and the iPhone Duo already lags behind.
None of this is to say that the Duo looks like a bad piece of hardware. Every foldable phone is a compromise, and Apple has picked a similar set of compromises to Samsung in order to get this phone out the door at $1,999. It looks as good as any Android foldable on paper, but it doesn’t look better than many of them.
Where that might change is the software. Google has made an effort to make Android more flexible and adaptable to suit folding phones, while OEMs deliver custom solutions to push things further, but none have rewritten the rulebook quite like Apple.
The version of iOS 27 running on the iPhone Duo isn’t the same as on other iPhones, but it doesn’t match the iPad either. The biggest change takes the dock from the bottom of the display and lays it out vertically along the right-hand side. The Dynamic Island is turned vertical and thrown in here too, while the status bar collapses into a small circular icon in the top-right corner. This big change is bolstered by clever little touches throughout, like a dynamic blur effect that shifts as you open the screen, creating a fluidity no Android foldable has so far matched. It’s a total transformation of the iOS layout that specifically has foldables in mind. 
The point of all that change is to ensure consistency between the outer and inner screens. Open the iPhone Duo on the homescreen and almost everything will stay in place, making the move between screens feel seamless. That effect won’t hold in full-screen apps of course, which will adapt to fill the space, but that right-hand UI rail will be fixed. Locking the whole phone interface to the right-hand edge doesn’t sound great for left-handed users though, who are likely to find the Duo unusually awkward to use unless Apple adds the option to flip everything to the other side.
StandBy mode has also been retooled for the Duo. Prop the phone down half-open and it will enter StandBy, letting you use it as a digital photo frame, smart display, or just get quick access to a few key widgets, like the clock. Finally, the $2,000 alarm clock you’ve always dreamed of.
Not everything is as ambitious. Multitasking looks limited so far, with the option to run two apps in split-screen, including two windows of the same app, and save pairs to reopen together. Android rivals offer similar, but support three split-screen apps at once, and often more sitting in flexible, resizeable floating windows.
But Apple’s software power doesn’t only lie in its OS. It’s the only phone manufacturer with the influence to shift the app ecosystem at large, and with the Duo it hopes to push third-party developers to adopt its best foldable features. It already showed off Netflix, Slack, and Zoom apps with custom Duo support, in some cases adapting dynamically depending on how flexed the hinge is. 
Android foldable features are still rare, with most apps simply changing size to fit the varying screens. Even that has its limits — I found a few apps ran awkwardly on the Fold 8’s short outer display. Apple is likely to have an easier time ensuring developers optimize their apps to suit both of the Duo’s displays.
Most apps do little else to take advantage of dual displays, multiple cameras, or semi-open states like a tented mode. A few video apps adapt their playback controls when foldables are half-open, but that’s about it so far. Of course, some of those app developers might take their iOS foldable features and eventually roll them out to Android too, so Apple’s advantage might not last forever. 
It’ll take more time with the Duo to see exactly how it stacks up against the latest models from the Android side of life. So far it doesn’t look like Apple has surpassed its rivals on the hardware side, but its total control of software may give it an edge regardless.
articles.author: Dominic Preston

articles.title: Movie Review: Musk
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://variety.com/2026/film/reviews/musk-review-elon-musk-alex-gibney-1236854369/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49644170
Points: 25
# Comments: 22
articles.body:
When a subject has been as exhaustively covered — and as infamous — as Elon Musk, the electric-car-entrepreneur-turned-rocket-man-turned-richest-billionaire-in-the-universe-turned-Twitter-disruptor-turned-DOGE-destroyer-turned-God-only-knows-what-he’ll-do-next, reviews of a documentary about him tend to lead by plucking out the film’s incendiary bits of investigative reportage, the ones that feel worthy of a news headline. “Musk,” Alex Gibney’s 3-hour-and-45-minute documentary about the tech bro who would be king, has a handful of those.
The biggest revelation, to me, was the film’s detailed history of Musk’s attempt to put a self-driving car on the market — a technology that’s sure to be here at some point, though Musk, in his race to be first, was far too eager to announce that it had already happened. Tesla released its Autopilot driver-assist system in 2015 (and then the Full Self-Driving Beta program in 2020), marketing the new technology with ads that exaggerated the car’s powers. And so people were suckered. From the outset, there were accidents. More than 60 fatalities have been linked to Tesla’s driver-assistance systems. Talk about something that could put a dent in your image! But Musk, for the most part, succeeded in hushing up the lawsuits, the federal investigations, and the fatal crashes, which were evidence of a recklessness that should have given the whole world pause.
There are other places where Gibney colors in sides of Elon Musk you knew in a cursory way. It’s well-known that Musk has fathered many children — at least 14, though the people around him say it’s many more. He believes his progeny to be part of a larger war against population decline. The documentary, which features a highly illuminating interview with his ex Ashley St. Clair, goes into the details of how Musk, apart from his two spouses, would zero in on young women he thought would make good “breeders” and get them pregnant, dropping all interest in them after the babies were born. (They were required to sign NDAs.) The film also goes into details of his alleged drug use (ketamine, Ecstasy, psychedelic mushrooms).
Yet what makes “Musk” such a lacerating and important watch, grounded in Alex Gibney’s supremely insightful but user-friendly mastery of the documentary form, is that it takes this flamboyant and in many ways elusive figure, with his tech ambitions and cosmic dreams and malignant megalomania, and puts him together, letting us see how one chapter of his life led to the next, and how the Musk dream wasn’t always so grandiose. You can see it evolve right along with his look. In the mid-’90s, at his first company, the relatively modest Zip2 (which essentially put the yellow pages onto the Internet), he looks just like the tech geek he was inside, skinny and unthreatening, with receding hair and a rabbity grin.
But it’s not long before his Ayn Rand ambitions start to poke through. The hair fills in, the body thickens, and the smile gets elevated into a kind of aggro leer, as Musk makes himself over into his version of a tech-head Nietzschean superman. Gibney plays around a bit, creating a synthetic “interview” with Musk (who, of course, wouldn’t cooperate with him) by putting verbatim quotes of his into the mouth of an AI Elon. Late in the movie, when Musk is wreaking the havoc of DOGE, we see him killing off bureaucrats as if in a first-person-shooter video game.
From the start, Musk has three obsessions: the Internet, energy, and space exploration. He first tried to purchase old Russian ICBM rockets (minus the nukes they were built to carry) for $3 to $5 million, and Gibney shows a fitting admiration for the innovation of Musk’s space dreams. He was leading a movement that was organic: the privatization of space exploration, which resulted from the U.S. government having lost all passion for it. The thrill was gone — for NASA, and maybe for the public. But Musk rekindled that (working in cooperation with President Obama). Sending up rockets was his original and driving obsession. Musk thought of himself as an engineer-magician in the mold of Steve Jobs. With SpaceX, even Musk’s failures (i.e., the first three launches) were spectacular. But he might have gone bankrupt if the fourth launch hadn’t connected.
“Musk” opens on something that’s not new (I wrote about it five years ago), namely Musk’s ardent belief in simulation theory — the notion that we are all very possibly living in a giant simulation, an idea bolstered for Musk by his love of video games, which became more and more sophisticated in their creation of simulated realities. The way he saw it: Who’s to say that we’re not all just part of a digital dream landscape, and that there isn’t some cosmic force out there playing us?
While it doesn’t spend a lot of time on this idea, “Musk” uses it make a point: that anyone who truly believes this — and thinks it’s the higher wisdom — may not be in complete possession of his marbles. It’s not that Musk is less than brilliant. It’s that it’s his very brilliance that leads him to invest in the idea that his fruitiest fantasies are reality — like the one he began to evolve out of SpaceX that said we were on the verge of colonizing Mars. There was no truth to it. But Musk, like his future frenemy Donald Trump, was starting to think that he had the power to create his own reality.
Once you start piecing together Musk’s scandals and cut corners and slipshod management, you see that he’s a creator of mirages who promises more than he delivers. There’s no question that the Tesla, as he finally designed it, is a strong and beautiful car, and that Musk’s early advocacy of electric vehicles was a positive force in the world. But his rocket program is increasingly mired in a kind of sci-fi stasis. (His fixation on Mars is right out of the cheesy ’50s.) And when Musk took over Twitter, which he had to borrow so much to buy that he wound up slashing the company to ribbons, it was a lesson in atrocious management (which he camouflaged as a testament to free speech), and he then applied that experience — as if it were a positive prototype — to his slashing of the government under Trump. He was out to make destruction look cool. Increasingly, though, his ventures began to seem like they were about little more than Elon’s simulated glory.
Musk, as the documentary makes clear, is a genuine if flawed technocratic visionary, a messianic opportunist, and something of a crackpot. Around the time he was given a cameo in “Iron Man 2,” he’d begun to think of himself as a Tony Stark figure: a superhero right out of the comics. He used his Starlink satellite technology to influence the war in Ukraine (not necessarily in a good way), and he became a mega-donor and collaborator of Trump’s, in no small part, to squash the federal investigation into the Tesla Auto-Drive fraud. In doing so, he demonstrated that tech fascism doesn’t need to be a form of government; it can do an end run around government to control people’s lives by reducing them to cogs. That, “Musk” argues, is the world Elon Musk has been building up to, not intentionally at first, but once he got a taste of power. The film says that what should scare us about him is how he coddles his own interests by passing them off as the world’s.

articles.title: Maven Robotics wants to steal your robot deployment deal
articles.summary: Maven Robotics emerged from stealth today with a $100 million Series A and active deployments.
articles.body:
In 2024, Maven Robotics was brand new, and they had nothing — “a cartoon of a robot and a team of people,” CEO and co-founder Hamza Derbas told TechCrunch.
Still, they heard a large consumer goods company with logistics needs was in town to meet with four rival robot companies about automation. Derbas talked his way into a meeting with the company and, instead of talking about his views on robots, asked to visit their factories and warehouses.
“We saw how people were working; we zeroed in on flows we could immediately bring value to,” he told TechCrunch. “We showed them that our approach to robotics is different — we’re not trying to solve a single robot problem. We’re trying to autonomously take on the task end to end: It hooks in from one side to a warehouse management system; product goes on trucks on the other side.”
They won the deal, beating out companies with existing robots. After two years of work with that company and a few other partners, Derbas says Maven has as many as eight robots working 16 hours a day,  with 99% or higher uptime.
Today, the startup is emerging from stealth after raising $100 million from RoboStrategy, LocalGlobe, Vine Ventures, and XTX Markets Ventures, with plans to build 250 of their third-generation robots and begin design on a fourth-generation platform.
Their robots sit on wheeled bases, capable of moving 10 miles an hour, with two arms that can lift up to 30 kilograms. Their main job is “mixed palletizing” — wooden pallets carrying boxed goods come from different factories to a distribution center, where the robot creates a new pallet containing a mix of goods to be sent to a store.
“Within 48 hours of them putting the stuff on the shelves, they want to change the mix based on real-time demand. Here’s an order with different mixed [products] going to that retail store; please build it out. It’s all done with human labor today, running around the warehouse picking one of this, one of that.”
At Maven’s Santa Clara facility, the robot moves smoothly about its work in a training area, using vacuum suckers to pick up and arrange the boxes at a reasonable speed. A live video screen shows two robots working in a customer facility while employees walk around them.
Derbas spent his career in automotive engineering, with a focus on EVs, but before Maven he spent nine years working at Apple on the company’s special project group, which he wouldn’t discuss but is widely thought to have been building a self-driving car before it was disbanded in 2024. That was when he started Maven with his brother, Khalid, who serves as the company’s CFO after a career in private equity.
Like other physical AI companies, the firm relies on veterans of self-driving car efforts, which have developed the most sophisticated approaches to training autonomous hardware from real data. That requires data pipelines that return information from operating robots within minutes or hours — “then retrain, evaluate, run ablation studies, figure out what’s the right set of weights, redeploy, and then turn that loop again.”
In a crowded world of robot companies, Maven sets itself apart with its focus on the realities of industrial operation. Jack Pearson, an investor at RoboStrategy who backed the company, says what sets the company apart is its background in industrial systems, rather than a research culture that is optimized for learning or focused on a specific architecture.
Agility, the robotics company going public this fall in a $2.5 billion SPAC deal, might be the most similarly positioned firm in the market, focused on safety and specific industrial workflows. But its robots stand on two legs, something Derbas, while stressing his respect for the company, says “make zero sense for anything they’re doing…they are very complex, unreliable, and add unnecessary cost. ROI is the name of the game here.”
That understanding of the realities of overheated facilities and the needs of the people who operate them has helped them get the startup out the door, but if Maven wants to expand beyond its current workflows, it will figure out some kind of research culture. While palletization might be an $80 billion market, the next set of tasks the company is targeting will require robotic manipulation capabilities that don’t yet exist.
Maven’s next big push is to collect more data and train its robots to be able to handle materials, and then to move toward automation and fabrication. The company will draw on its own systems, tap third-party providers, and has even developed a pair of pincer-like gloves that allow humans to emulate the form factor they want for their grippers. While the company bills itself as a maker of general-purpose robots, its strategy is to go task-by-task toward that goal.“We’re grounded in solving one customer problem at a time,” Derbas said. “If you focus on solving problems and you pick sizeable problems, each problem is a multibillion-dollar market. If you do that, there’s plenty of data to master these skills.”
That process might be the most viable path to putting robots in the workplace — or an opportunity to get one-shotted by the next powerful physical AI model to roll out of the frontier labs.
“We’re not in the race for models — we’re in the race to solve industrial labor and make this work possible at the scale the world needs,” Derbas told TechCrunch.

Tim Fernholz is a journalist who writes about technology, finance and public policy. He has closely covered the rise of the private space industry and is the author of  Rocket Billionaires: Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and the New Space Race. Formerly, he was a senior reporter at Quartz, the global business news site, for more than a decade, and began his career as a political reporter in Washington, D.C.

articles.title: Arsenal close to finalising new contract for manager Mikel Arteta
articles.summary: Mikel Arteta is believed to be close to finalising a new contract with Premier League champions Arsenal.
articles.body: The perception of Arsenal's transfer window varies depending on who you speak to - but there will be no disagreement from anyone at the Emirates Stadium over how crucial their next expected signing will be.With the market closed until January, the club are now in the process of finalising an agreement with manager Mikel Arteta over his protracted new contract.Well-placed sources indicate those discussions have moved forward recently amid full confidence from those involved in talks that the Spaniard will renew.Indeed, Arteta moved unequivocally last month to remove any lingering doubt over his future: "Everybody feels comfortable that the timing of the contract is not going to be an issue because my will certainly is to be here and I'm very happy here."My feeling from the club is the same one. That's why everyone is doing things in a very organic way."Similarly, Arsenal's chief executive Richard Garlick has said it was merely a "matter of time" before Arteta's new long-term deal was confirmed.Arteta can expect to become one of the best paid managers in world football once his new contract is signed - Arsenal committed to significantly improving on his current deal, worth £10m a season plus an extra £5m upon Champions League qualification.For Arsenal supporters, the official announcement can't come soon enough, particularly given his current deal now has just nine months left to run.Since his appointment in December 2019, Arteta has transformed Arsenal from a club that had lost its Champions League status to one that won the Premier League for the first time in 22 years last season.They are overwhelming favourites to retain their domestic crown and are fancied to win their first-ever Champions League this season.With that success comes power. Like Arsene Wenger before him, Arteta is categorically the most influential figure, certainly from a football perspective, at the club.People will say that the manager or head coach should always be the most authoritative figure at any football club - the reality is that is rarely the case.Arteta's fingerprints are all over the club - and most importantly the squad. Nothing happens from a first-team perspective without his approval.When Arsenal tried to sign Julian Alvarez and Vinicius Jr last month, it was Arteta who was at the forefront of the club's charm offensive.With that in mind, the thought of removing Arteta from that dynamic, certainly for Arsenal's ownership, is the unthinkable.One day, Spain will come calling - and a return to his homeland may attract Arteta, although he knows he is unlikely to be afforded the same authority at either Real Madrid or Barcelona – clubs that are historically entrenched in internal politics – than he is now.But at this moment, the attraction for Arteta is with Arsenal.This is a squad that has flourished under Arteta's tutelage. The average age of the squad (26.2 years) is one of the oldest in the Premier League. It's a group at its peak and primed to build a legacy on.Beyond the new financial terms and into footballing ambition, Arsenal are buying into Arteta's vision.The summer arrivals of Bruno Guimaraes and Ezri Konsa were sizeable investments given both turn 30 next year, while the albeit failed pursuits of Vinicius Jr and Alvarez provided Arteta with evidence that the club's American owners are willing to spend heavily on elite talent.It's the sort of ambition Arteta is understood to have made clear he wanted to see as talks over his contract progressed.Arteta's six years at the Emirates already makes him the longest-serving manager in the Premier League and EFL by some distance - his new deal will take him closer to a decade in north London.Yet there appear to be no signs of Arteta taking his foot off the gas.

articles.title: We spent £23,000 on fertility treatment - now our embryos will be destroyed
articles.summary: Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards want a change in the law so once an embryo has been made, a donor can't withdraw consent.
articles.body: Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nat (left) and Nik Fraser-Edwards went through six rounds of failed artificial insemination before they were successful through a different type of fertility treatmentByAlexandra BánfiBBC WalesNat and Nik Fraser-Edwards celebrated their son Jude's first birthday last month.After rounds of failed fertility treatment, Jude was a dream come true for the couple who said they hoped to give him a brother or sister next year. But now their dreams have come "crashing down".Their sperm donor has withdrawn his consent for further use, and the remaining five embryos in storage will be destroyed after paying £23,000 on fertility treatment.In the UK, a sperm or egg donor can withdraw consent up until the embryo is transferred into the womb.The couple now want the law changed so that once an embryo has been created, consent cannot be withdrawn.Figure caption, Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards spent £23,000 on fertility treatment but now their embryos will be destroyedThe UK government said it sympathised and added it is "keeping all aspects of the regulatory regime under review".When they returned from their honeymoon in 2023, the couple from north Wales started fertility treatment.They took out loans and went through rounds of failed artificial insemination in a journey that cost them a total of £23,000."There was a lot of pain during that time, and everyone around us seemed to be getting pregnant," recalled Nat, 37."All you see is babies. It's not just wanting that baby so much, it's the cancelled plans in case you get that smiley face."It was only when they turned to a different type of treatment, called ICSI , where the egg is fertilised with sperm and the embryo is created outside of the body, that they had success.Nat and Nik ended up with six embryos and in August last year, Jude was born.Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Jude was born last August and Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards (left to right) were hoping to get pregnant with their second child in January next yearThe embryos were put into storage until the couple were ready to grow their family. It was during a telephone consultation in June that they found out their embryos would be destroyed."It was very much, 'unfortunately your donor has withdrawn his consent to use your embryos'," said Nat, who lives in Penyffordd, near Wrexham."They said, 'we keep them for a cooling off period of a year and' - I think the hardest word for us was - 'we then allow them to perish'."We were absolutely floored."Nik said the couple felt "blindsided" by the fact that their sperm donor could withdraw consent at that stage."Yes, we'd signed something," she added. "But we didn't ever recall it being verbally said."Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards (left to right) recently celebrated Jude's first birthday after going through rounds of failed fertility treatmentThe number of donors in the UK that withdraw consent is unknown as the data isn't collected. While it is rare, it is not unheard of.Sam Beesley and Carly Estlick are expecting their first child, a boy they plan to call Finn, in October after going through IVF."I've been someone who knew from a young age that my job in life was to be a mother," said Sam, 41.Just like Nat and Nik, Sam and Carly were told last month that their sperm donor had withdrawn consent and their 10 remaining embryos will be destroyed next year.Image source, Sam BeesleyImage caption, Sam Beesley and Carly Estlick are expecting their first child Finn in October this year"When we got the letter saying he had withdrawn consent, it felt like the wind was taken out of our sails," said Sam from Shrewsbury."We had been so focussed on the pregnancy and something going wrong, I don't think it's really sunk in yet."Carly is already grieving. In her head, they've already been destroyed. Whereas until that day in 2027, I will not stop fighting."Sam said the news has put pressure on their current pregnancy."Carly is very fearful that something will happen to Finn," she said. "It has crossed my mind.The couple who were told their embryos will be destroyedThe BBC speak to Natalie and Nicola Fraser-Edwards who spent £23,000 on fertility treatment. But now their sperm donor has withdrawn consent so they can't use the remaining embryosListen now on BBC Sounds"I did have some reduced movements the other day and had to go to hospital. You can't help thinking, is this going to be ripped away from us as well?"This is probably our only shot at being parents. I don't know how we could afford to go through it again financially, emotionally, physically."For both couples, fertility treatment has had an emotional and financial impact.Nat and Nik say they would have paid anything to have a family, but that the total £23,000 bill means that they did have to make "sacrifices"."We lived on the breadline for quite a while, just to make this work," Nat said. "Taking out a loan in order to pay the excessive bill."Image source, Sam BeesleyImage caption, Sam Beesley and Carly Estlick have said they're facing the same fate as Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards as they've been told their embryos will be destroyed in August 2027 Nat and Nik also say they can't afford to go through treatment again, and, for Nik, this means she may never get to experience pregnancy."I think, as a woman, it's an amazing thing to be able to do and I didn't want to have any regrets later in life," said Nik, 36."We knew we were going to have a sibling for Jude. I think the tables turned a little bit watching Nat go through that experience and I was thinking, 'yeah I'd love to do that'."The UK fertility regulator HFEA has said that any change in the law on sperm donation is down to the UK government."It's about each person who provides an egg or sperm having that autonomy to consent and make that decision to whether they're happy for a child to be born in treatment," said Rachel Cutting, HFEA's director of compliance.Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nik said watching Nat carry Jude made her realise she wanted to experience pregnancy as well"Once the embryos in the uterus, in the woman's womb, there can't be a withdrawal of consent for that."The way that the law is written is that consent can be withdrawn from up to that point."We can look at it further, but it is for the law to be changed and that's not something within the power that the HFEA has. We can't change the law. But we are sympathetic to cases like this."The HFEA has said it is important that clinics warn patients of the possibility of donors withdrawing consent "because it is really upsetting and distressing when this happens".The UK government said it also sympathises with "anyone facing difficult and distressing circumstances during fertility treatment."A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "We continue to work closely with the fertility sector to support high-quality, compassionate care, and we keep all aspects of the regulatory regime under review to the same end."If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.More top stories

articles.title: Amazon pilots ad services in ChatGPT
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://www.marketingdive.com/news/amazon-pilots-ad-services-in-chatgpt-what-marketers-need-to-know/829945/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49644047
Points: 58
# Comments: 35
articles.body:
Conversational ads inventory will be available as a managed service via Amazon DSP, but OpenAI will handle placement through its own systems.
ChatGPT’s logo is displayed on a smartphone screen. The program’s developer, OpenAI, is partnering with Amazon on advertising services for marketers
Justin Sullivan via Getty Images
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.
Amazon advertisers will be able to extend their campaigns into conversational experiences on ChatGPT as part of a new partnership between the e-commerce giant and the chatbot’s developer OpenAI, according to news shared with Marketing Dive.
Delta Vacations, the airline’s vacation packages provider, is among a select group of U.S. brands piloting the integration. ChatGPT Ads inventory will be available through Amazon’s demand-side platform, an Amazon spokesperson said over email.
Amazon sees conversational ads as one of the fastest-growing channels for brands to engage new and existing customers. OpenAI has quickly scaled ChatGPT’s ads business, which launched earlier this year and recently hit an important revenue milestone.
The OpenAI tie-up provides Amazon a bridge into one of the most popular AI programs — a channel that is increasingly intersecting with the world of advertising and informing more consumer decision-making. For OpenAI, the pact may open a floodgate of new entrants to its ads business at a critical moment. Amazon operates the third-largest digital advertising platform and neared $70 billion in ads revenue last year.
ChatGPT Ads will be bought via Amazon DSP and are offered as a managed service, meaning Amazon’s team will help set up and optimize campaigns. Inventory will be available on both a cost-per-click and cost-per-mille, or cost per thousand impressions, basis. The pilot is limited to the U.S. at launch.
OpenAI will control all ad delivery decisions through its own systems, an Amazon spokesperson said. The ads themselves will surface as text and image units beneath organic ChatGPT responses with clearly marked sponsored labels, aligning with how OpenAI has served ads to date. ChatGPT currently runs ads on its free model and cheaper Go subscription tier. In addition, Amazon is offering product feed ads that automatically generate assets based on product catalogues.
Advertisers value Amazon for its troves of shopping and streaming data that can be used to improve marketing precision. ChatGPT for its part has pitched its advertising as a way to realize more contextually rich and relevant campaigns. Those testing the ChatGPT Ads integration will receive some aggregated performance data related to impressions, clicks, cost per result, CPM and CPC metrics. The concept could be appealing to nonendemic advertisers, or advertisers that wouldn’t typically sell goods on Amazon.
“Travel planning is becoming increasingly personalized, and travelers expect experiences that feel relevant,” Katrin Koenig, president of Delta Vacations, said in a statement. "Through our collaboration with Amazon Ads and ChatGPT Ads, we can leverage deep consumer insights to inform how and when Delta Vacations appear within ChatGPT Ads experiences to create new opportunities for travelers to engage and discover vacation possibilities.”
OpenAI began testing ChatGPT ads in February and has quickly built out the business as it prepares for a highly anticipated initial public offering where the segment could play a role in the company’s revenue-generation narrative. The decision to run ads has drawn flak from competitors while industry reports indicate some marketers have been underwhelmed by performance. OpenAI previously partnered with other retail media networks, including those operated by Target and Albertsons, but Amazon’s is significantly larger.
ChatGPT ads late last month achieved a $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate, a projection of expected annual revenue based on shorter-term gains. OpenAI says tens of thousands of advertisers use the service, which recently expanded in India, Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. It has also enlisted third parties to refine its capabilites in areas that are important for building advertising confidence, including working with LiveRamp on measurement.
OpenAI linking with an established DSP in its quest for scale isn’t particularly surprising, but its initial pick of partner could be. The software developer reportedly discussed a deal with The Trade Desk, an independent rival of Amazon’s, earlier this year.
