articles.title: Top four seeds in historic semi-final line-up
articles.summary: For the first time since 1975, the top four seeds in the women's US Open singles draw have reached the semi-finals.
articles.body: "Oh, wow".That was Coco Gauff's surprised reaction when she learned she was part of a US Open semi-final line-up the like of which has not been seen in more than half a century.For the first time since 1975, the top four seeds in the women's singles draw have reached the semi-finals at the New York major.Now, 51 years later, the stars have aligned once again with Aryna Sabalenka, Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula and Gauff all surviving three-set thrillers to create a semi-final line-up for the ages."How amazing - it doesn't get much better than that does it?" former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live."It has felt fantastic the whole tournament - I just feel like I've been more enthused about looking forward to the match-ups this Grand Slam than any I can remember."It is the first time the top-four ranked players have reached the women's semi-finals at any Grand Slam since Wimbledon in 2009, and it hints at a shift away from the unpredictable landscape that has characterised the women's game in recent years.Since the start of 2020, there have been 13 different Grand Slam women's singles champions - compared to just seven on the men's side."I just feel like there's lots of really big names now, big personalities going up against each other and it's really exciting," Croft said."We've been blessed with the amount of intriguing matches we've had. You're seeing these warriors out on court."Top seed and two-time defending champion Sabalenka will face American Pegula in Thursday's first semi-final (00:00 BST, Friday), while Rybakina - who will replace Sabalenka as the new world number one on Monday - takes on fourth seed Gauff afterwards.While Sabalenka is bidding to become the first woman since Serena Williams in 2014 to win three successive US Open titles, Pegula is the only player remaining in the women's draw still chasing a maiden Grand Slam.The pair need no introduction to each other, having faced each other 13 times.That includes the past two US Open tournaments, when Sabalenka denied Pegula a first major title in the 2024 final and fought back to win in last year's semi-finals."It's fun to look at it like a rivalry. I think that's what motivates me," said Pegula."I know that she's definitely pushed me to become a better player, so I always respect and appreciate that aspect of our rivalry."Pegula, who has got the better of Sabalenka on four occasions on the WTA Tour, said beating the four-time major winner at Grand Slam level is a "hurdle" she must overcome.Sabalenka, meanwhile, said she was "super excited" to face Pegula, who arrived in New York in better form after reaching the final in both Washington and Cincinnati."I'm loving playing against her because it's a battle, because it's a fight, and I love being under pressure and going through tough challenges," said Sabalenka, who is into her first semi-final since falling to Pegula at June's Berlin Open.Pegula added of Sabalenka: "I know she hasn't maybe had the best results this summer, but I know that she has a lot of confidence playing here at this tournament, and she's going for a three-peat."By reaching the semi-finals, second seed Rybakina will become the new world number one on Monday - ending Sabalenka's 99-week reign at the top.But the second seed has described the top ranking as "just a number" and stressed that her focus remains focused on winning her third Grand Slam title."It's never quite the same if you become world number one having lost a Grand Slam final or semi-final just beforehand, so she will be trying to cap off an absolutely perfect couple of weeks by winning the title," tennis correspondent Russell Fuller said on BBC Radio 5 Live.Standing in her way, however, is Gauff, who will have the home crowd's backing on Arthur Ashe Stadium.The 22-year-old American, who won the Flushing Meadows title in 2023 but suffered fourth-round exits in the following two years, said she has a different perspective to this year's tournament."Sometimes you're just so focused on the now, now, now, because you want it now, and obviously you want to take advantage of your opportunities," she said."In the grand scheme of things, [I'm] definitely sitting here in a different mindset and perspective than I was last year."It inspires me a little bit more to keep working, as I see how much I have improved in a year."Gauff leads the head-to-head 2-1, but Australian Open champion Rybakina fought back from a set down to triumph in last month's Canadian Open semi-finals."I'm going to have some aces hit on me and some winners hit on me, but I'm going to keep fighting and give it my all. That's all I can do," Gauff said.

articles.title: Thanks to Siri Recaps, your Apple Watch is always listening
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://www.techradar.com/health-fitness/smartwatches/thanks-to-siri-recaps-your-apple-watch-is-always-listening-as-you-go-about-your-day-but-apple-may-be-risking-a-meta-glasses-style-backlash
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49641401
Points: 129
# Comments: 100
articles.body:
The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 have landed, along with a revolutionary folding iPhone at this year's Apple event, but despite major advancements under the hood, the feature that is standing out to me is a software-based one.Siri Recaps is a new Audio Intelligence feature that turns your Apple Watch into an always-listening device. The idea is that Siri Recaps, which lives on the Siri app, uses the Apple Watch's sensors to provide a summary of your day, including conversations that have taken place. It can be toggled with a schedule, or at the top of the Smart Stack.It's a little like the Amazon Bee, which is a microphone attached to a smart band, which is used to capture and summarize conversations. While I can see this feature as being useful for people who attend lots of meetings (having a virtual assistant taking minutes in the background all day long could be very useful), there are understandably privacy concerns here.We're told the Recaps feature doesn't record or store audio and it can't show a transcript. Instead, it processes events live as they take place, using Siri AI to turn that raw data into actionable notes, never written into permanent storage. Below is a screenshot from Apple's presentation:
(Image credit: Meta / Ray-Ban)I'm thinking, of course, about Meta, and its smart glasses being banned in some public spaces and generally disparaged with names like 'pervert glasses'. Smart glasses have obviously garnered a real stigma thanks to people drilling out the LED recording light and using them to discreetly record inappropriately and without consent for clout, content, or their own personal use.This has created a general feeling of malaise around wearables equipped with discreet cameras and microphones in general. Like Meta Glasses, the Live Rewind and Siri Recaps features have accessibility potential for those hard of hearing, but they're going to make most people uncomfortable.Watch: Audio Intelligence features being announcedApple is keen to evidence its trustworthiness, with on-device AI and Private Cloud Compute and an insistence that it doesn't record or log audio and transcripts. However, if people think they're being discreetly recorded without their permission, it's possible Apple Watch wearers could experience their own slice of the abuse hurled at Meta Glasses wearers.I wrote earlier this year that wearable tech has to separate itself from surveillance capitalism if it wishes to be cool again. It seems Apple has taken a step in the other direction.Update: Apple has published an article on its website, specifically about Audio Intelligence, and much has been made about how Audio Intelligence protects user privacy and is used responsibly. You can read the full article here.In short, Apple says audio is not recorded or stored because "there is no recording to share, forward, or produce if requested by any party, because no recording exists". Instead, audio data is processed by Siri live, and raw audio "is never accessible".Your data is not accessible to Apple either, thanks to Private Cloud Compute, and "independent security experts can verify this promise at any time". Siri Recaps auto-delete after seven days too. Apple is serious about getting users to trust this feature.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Matt is TechRadar's expert on all things fitness, wellness and wearable tech. A former staffer at Men's Health, he holds a Master's Degree in journalism from Cardiff and has written for brands like Runner's World, Women's Health, Men's Fitness, LiveScience and Fit&Well on everything fitness tech, exercise, nutrition and mental wellbeing.Matt's a keen runner, ex-kickboxer, not averse to the odd yoga flow, and insists everyone should stretch every morning. When he’s not training or writing about health and fitness, he can be found reading doorstop-thick fantasy books with lots of fictional maps in them.

articles.title: Primark finally set to launch home deliveries
articles.summary: The retailer launches the service four years after making its first foray into internet shopping.
articles.body: Primark has said it plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain, four years after it made its first foray into e-commerce.The retailer did not say when it expects to launch the service, but it has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.The company said there was "opportunity for profitable growth" through home deliveries, which could help boost trade after Primark reported subdued sales following the recent hot weather.Analysts said the decision to offer home delivery after years of resistance - including through the pandemic - indicated that Primark was facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.Primark did not sell goods online until 2022, when it launched a click-and-collect service which meant shoppers still had to travel to pick up their purchases. Associated British Foods (ABF), which owns Primark, said the fashion chain would "continue to grow click and collect and... will in the future offer home delivery in Great Britain".ABF predicts Primark's UK sales will grow by about 1% in the fourth quarter of the year. But like-for-like sales - a key metric in the retail industry, which strips out the impact of store openings and closures - are expected to be "broadly flat" in the UK, and fall 3% across its global operations.It said sales of autumn/winter clothing started later than normal due to the hot weather in the summer, but "trading was stronger when the weather cooled towards the end of the quarter".The fast-fashion chain is struggling to compete with brands such as Shein and Boohoo, as well as alternative platforms such as TikTok Shop and Vinted, and in July said it was lowering prices on hundreds of clothing items. Retail analyst Julie Palmer said that "Primark has been playing catch up for years" and launching home deliveries "is as much about defence as growth".She told BBC News that "the real test" for the brand is whether it can make home deliveries profitable at the low prices customers have come to expect from fast fashion chains."Shein and Vinted have already reset customer expectations on convenience," she said, adding that a "slick and effective returns policy" will also be key.ABF is planning to spin off Primark from its food business next year. Retail analyst Natalie Berg said Primark was "more than fashionably late to the e-commerce party".She said the brand will need to absorb additional costs of returns, which tend to be higher than in-store purchases as customers cannot try clothes on before buying them."Not even the pandemic could convince them to launch online, so the fact that Primark is making such a U-turn tells us just how much the retail landscape has evolved," she said.Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said that thanks to greater competition among delivery firms such as InPost and Relay, "it's become a lot cheaper in the past few years to send items by post, compared to the old days when Royal Mail dominated the market", he added.Retailers across the UK are grappling with higher costs for labour and energy.On Thursday, John Lewis - which operates the department stores and Waitrose supermarkets - reported that its half-year losses had widened to £124m from £88m a year earlier.Chairman Jason Tarry said the results reflected the partnership's "continued investment in our transformation, a more challenging trading environment and the increased costs of doing business".Sales in the department store arm of the business fell 2%, as it said consumers were holding back on discretionary spending. Waitrose sales were up 4%, but profits slipped slightly which the company said was due to a decision to lower prices and also reflected "the extra cost of running our operations through the heatwaves".

articles.title: The variable aperture isn’t the cool part of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera
articles.summary:
The iPhone 18 Pro’s triple camera setup with a variable aperture in the main (bottom) camera. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge	

Apple always makes a big show of the latest cameras in its phones, and the major talking point of the iPhone 18 Pro is about the new variable aperture. Both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have an adjustable mechanical iris in their main camera modules to let m
articles.body:
Apple always makes a big show of the latest cameras in its phones, and the major talking point of the iPhone 18 Pro is about the new variable aperture. Both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have an adjustable mechanical iris in their main camera modules to let more or less light into the sensor, allowing users to shoot at f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. You can, of course, let the camera select your aperture automatically, but the manual aperture control comes along with other new pro controls allowing you to dial in shutter speeds, manual white balance, and even manual focusing.
As a whole, this is a wealth of new controls for an iPhone camera. You’d normally have to install a third-party camera app like Halide to do some of this, and now it’s all just baked into the 18 Pro’s native camera app. (It’s almost as if Apple poached a key person directly from Halide.) But I’d temper any expectations over the variable aperture being the standout feature. It’s going to be mid, at best.
Why? Because smartphone sensors are still pretty dang tiny, and most subjects are in reasonable focus until you get really close. And stopping down to f/4 is unlikely to blow you away with much sharper results like it does in full-size cameras or any special qualities aside from some sunstar effects in very particular lighting scenarios. In fact, due to lens diffraction, your photos might be less sharp at f/4 than f/1.8 or f/2.8. What you’re most likely to benefit from by stopping down the lens is more depth of field with close-up subjects, getting more people in focus during big group shots with plenty of light (where people aren’t all lined up together), and more flexibility in shooting video in overly bright situations (like direct sunlight). That might prove useful for those particular situations, but they’re likely to be few and far between.
And smartphone sensors are small enough to already have plenty in focus at mid-range and further distances, even when shot wide open. It’s probably why other brands like Samsung and Xiaomi have experimented with variable apertures but quietly ditched them. 
I think the real star feature of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera is its f/1.48 maximum aperture. Fuck stopping down, man. People love bokeh. 
Last year’s Pro iPhone cameras had an f/1.7 aperture, and now being at f/1.48, the 18 Pro camera should work better in low-light as well as have a slightly shallower depth of field. Will f/1.48 be a huge difference in bokeh from f/1.7? Probably not. It’s likely to have depth of field that’s just a smidge shallower — but that’s the look that people often like.
I speak from experience here, as I usually shoot on full-frame cameras and one of my go-to lenses is a 50mm with an f/1.2 maximum aperture. A lens that fast, with depth of field that shallow gives a unique look that’s easy to overuse, but it almost never fails that people swoon when I take their portrait using that lens — with that blurry, “dreamy” blur isolating them from the background. The f/1.48 of the iPhone 18 Pro is obviously not going to compare to an f/1.2 on full-frame, but f/1.2 and similarly wide apertures on big sensors is the look that people often want to emulate. It’s the whole reason Portrait Modes on smartphones came into being in the first place.
The iPhone 18 Pro is likely to have a very good camera just like most top-flight smartphones have very good cameras. The added controls are exciting and fun, even if I don’t always want to be bothered with manual controls when taking quick snapshots. It’ll be nice to have them right at your fingertips without having to install a more specialized app. Just don’t be surprised if you start ignoring that aperture setting after some initial tinkering in the new phone honeymoon phase. But even long after that, f/1.48 will be the gift that should keep on giving.
articles.author: Antonio G. Di Benedetto

articles.title: Royal family rift after popular TV news presenter chosen to succeed Ugandan king
articles.summary: King Oyo's family say he left a will naming his young son as heir to the Tooro kingdom.
articles.body: "My brother did leave behind an heir to the throne, and that was very clearly stated," she said, accusing those behind the announcement on Wednesday night of creating "confusion and turmoil" while the family was still grieving.Meanwhile the late king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, has said royal guards have been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed, restricting the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing the situation as "house arrest".She appealed to the army's leadership and President Yoweri Museveni to allow the family to mourn and bury Oyo in peace on Saturday."I appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."Thousands of mourners are expected to attend the burial at the royal tombs near the palace in Fort Portal in western Uganda.His body was returned to Uganda from the US on Friday, and preparations for the funeral are under way.Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. Its monarch has no formal political authority but remains an important cultural figure in western Uganda.Uganda abolished its traditional kingdoms in 1967, but they were restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.The existence of Oyo's son was first publicly revealed in the days after the king's death by President Museveni, who said he had been told about the young boy by the queen mother.No other details have officially been disclosed, and he had not previously been presented as Oyo's heir.The disagreement has exposed the complicated way in which succession works in Tooro.Unlike Britain's monarchy, where the crown passes according to an established line of succession, Tooro's monarch is chosen from the Babiito, the royal dynastic clan.At a press conference in ​the kingdom's capital of Fort Portal, the royal clan's succession committee announced Kijanangoma, Oyo's cousin and a news presenter ​at the state-run broadcaster UBC, as monarch.The clan elders said they had the customary authority to choose a suitable prince to become "the Omukama" - the local title for the king of Tooro.The succession panel said it had carried out "due diligence, consultation and adequate consideration" before selecting Kijanangoma, with 19 members signing the resolution. Kijanangoma is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of former Tooro king George David Rukidi III.Another royal, UK-based Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, was initially considered for the throne but declined, citing other responsibilities, according to the succession committee.It is not yet clear when the enthronement will take place, but the committee said it would be conducted in accordance with the traditions and customs of the Tooro kingdom.

articles.title: Apple's new boss starts with big gamble on £1,999 first folding iPhone
articles.summary: Apple showed off at an event the first major design change to the iPhone in almost 20 years.
articles.body: Apple has launched its most expensive iPhone ever - a foldable handheld that costs at least £1,999 and marks the first major iPhone design change in almost 20 years.The iPhone Duo is a gamble by new boss John Ternus, who took over from long-time chief executive Tim Cook this month. Apple is entering the foldable phone market comparatively late, following the likes of South Korea's Samsung and China's Huawei. Ternus told an audience at Apple's California headquarters: "Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together". Apple's model, he claimed "redefine[s] the experience of using a foldable phone".In the US, prices start at $1,999, but can go up to $3,200. It has taken eight years to develop, something Ternus was directly involved in after spending many years as a top executive inside Apple's hardware division.When unfolded, it looks like a small iPad and a wider iPhone when it is folded.Ternus said: "It's entirely new and at the same time remarkably familiar. A similar size to your passport, it feels familiar to hold and comfortable to use with one hand."But the product is facing established competitors. "The real fight is China, where Huawei owns nearly 80% of foldables," said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president for data and analytics, devices at IDC EMEA.Ben Wood, chief analyst at technology research firm FDM CCS Insight, said it was likely Ternus's promotion was timed specifically "to coincide with what will be arguably one of the biggest iPhone launches for many years"."Nothing happens by accident at Apple," he said.Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at Creative Strategies who attended the Wednesday presentation, said the spotlight on Ternus made it feel "almost like he was a product himself". Altering the design of the iPhone may address some criticism that Apple has yet to land a major product hit or truly exciting innovation since the first iPhone came out in 2007."The foldable risks becoming a premium-priced ornament in the portfolio, imparting badge value but not meaningful growth," said Dipanjan Chatterjee, an analyst at Forrester.Previously, the highest starting price of the newest iPhone was $900 (£664).Apple also revealed on Wednesday the new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, which in the US start at $1,199 and $1,299 respectively. Chatterjee said the foldable iPhone could go the way of Apple's Vision Pro headset, which the company priced at $3,699 and has not been a hit with buyers.Or, he said, it could be the company's next Apple Watch which, while not as popular as the iPhone, is bought by millions of people each year.The way people have become accustomed to the way the iPhone operates is another potential hurdle to Apple seeing big sales of the new design."Foldables are interesting devices," Milanesi noted. "A lot of people are intrigued by it, but the software and the learning curve that you have from moving from a traditional phone to a foldable is real."Wood noted that the current market for foldable smartphones from the likes of Samsung and Huawei make up only 2% of smartphone sales. Even with Apple's version likely driving interest and demand, sales are only expected to reach 4% of the total market in the next decade, according to data and analytics firm FDM CCM Insight.The iPhone has been Apple's top-selling product and accounts for more than half of the company's sales each year.In recent quarters, the company has boasted that the iPhone is more in-demand than ever, with the most recent version of the device becoming its most successful product launch.The company also revealed more about the coming relaunch of its audio and chat assistant Siri, which it now calls Siri AI.Starting with the iPhone 18, the bot will now be able to go across information on a person's phone, like messages and emails, to find information, answer queries and take action on a person's behalf.Some Siri AI features will also be available on the new Apple Watch, including the ability to take notes of conversations and transcribe them, should a wearer enable that feature.Ternus referred to new AI-enabled capabilities on the iPhone as an "intelligent personal hub", and admitted that Apple would be making use of "the most private details of your daily life".He insisted that all of it will remain private, with the AI features often running "on device", meaning not through third-party companies. And when a third-party is required for a function, Ternus said it will remain private in a remote server, or cloud."Others see that data as something to collect and store," Ternus said. "Here, not even Apple can access what's yours."

articles.title: 'My cancer spread while I waited months for surgery': The cost of England's cancer wait times
articles.summary: Cancer care has got worse since the government announced plans to speed up waiting times and save more lives, BBC analysis shows.
articles.body: Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year.The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up waiting nearly five months, by which time the cancer had spread, making his surgery more complex."I was so frustrated and angry and couldn't understand why they would leave me like that," says Alan.On two occasions, scans were cancelled because machines had broken and for weeks he heard little or nothing from the hospital about when he would eventually have the urgent surgery.Alan is one of thousands each month in England who are not being treated within the target timeframe.Earlier this year, the government's National Cancer Plan, along with the NHS Planning Guidance, set out that 80% of patients in England would start treatment within 62 days from urgent GP referral by March 2027. This was to reach 85% by March 2029.But in the months since the government announced this ambition, performance has got worse, according to NHS England data, not better.Now, 71.2% of patients start cancer treatment within the 62 day timeframe. Previously it was 71.9%.Radiotherapy UK analysis, shared exclusively with the BBC, suggests more than 2,800 extra patients would need to start treatment every month - a near 15% increase on current numbers - to achieve the March 2027 target.That is likely to grow as referrals keep rising across nearly every cancer type.Price says thousands of patients "are going to die unnecessarily, just because the government can't get their act together to treat people on time".  For every month a cancer patient waits before starting treatment, their chance of survival falls by around 10%, on average.By the time Alan had his operation, the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes and the nodule "had grown at an alarming rate", according to the lung specialist.He has since been told the cancer has cleared awaiting his one-year review, but the operation has left him in debilitating pain. "I used to play golf and get out and about. Now I can't do any of the things I love," says Alan.Roughly 54,000 more patients will need to start treatment within 62 days before 2029 for the government to hit its goal.One NHS trust that is gaining traction on its waiting list numbers is Salisbury, but it is still not hitting targets.  Staff say there is no single fix, just a relentless focus on getting the basics right; making sure patients know about their appointments and turn up, keeping IT systems working, recruiting the right people, making sure surgical lists are full and expanding capacity.Much of the visible progress has come through skin and prostate cancer, two of the most common cancers in the country.But staff in Salisbury also say missed appointments, whether down to late letters, illness, transport problems or anxiety, are a constant drain on a system already stretched thin.Emilia Scutt, cancer manager in Salisbury, says that efforts to reduce missed appointments have really helped their numbers."We know cancer can be terrifying so we are a bit like a dog with the bone, backing up patients and supporting them wherever we can."Trusts with the sharpest declines in performance - including Buckinghamshire Healthcare, Bolton NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust, East Cheshire, and Torbay and South Devon - told the BBC they face pressures across the board. Rising demand, workforce shortages and diagnostic bottlenecks have all played a part.Some pointed to industrial action and staff sickness, others to reliance on outside diagnostic providers or major changes to how their systems work. All say they are investing in extra capacity, working through backlogs and redesigning pathways, and are already seeing early signs of improvement."If government is serious about delivering on the ambitions of the National Cancer Plan for England, it must match ambition with urgency," said Steve Haines of Macmillan Cancer Support.He said that "visible progress" was needed on a promise to set up a National Cancer Board to oversee progress on improving waiting times and treatment.A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson says "cancer waiting times are moving in the right direction will all three cancer standards better than a year ago".They concede that "there is more to do," and that the plan "will help people get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner."Additional reporting Daniel Wainwright and Jess Carr

articles.title: The Trump phone just got a $250 price hike
articles.summary:
It’s going to take a lot more gold coins to buy the Trump Phone now. | Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge	

Bad news if you didn't lock in a Trump phone at launch: It now costs $749, a $250 increase on its price at launch. The T1 Phone itself hasn't changed.
Trump Mobile didn't announce the price increase, instead quietly changing its website overnight. This wasn't a total surprise though,
articles.body:
Bad news if you didn’t lock in a Trump phone at launch: It now costs $749, a $250 increase on its price at launch. The T1 Phone itself hasn’t changed.
Trump Mobile didn’t announce the price increase, instead quietly changing its website overnight. This wasn’t a total surprise though, especially given the phone ships with an unexpectedly generous 512GB of storage and 12GB of RAM. When I spoke to two Trump Mobile executives earlier this year, they called the $499 launch pricing “introductory,” and a few months later, the website itself was changed to reflect that, calling it a “promotional price.” That wording is now gone.
When I reviewed the Trump phone in July, I wasn’t especially impressed, even at $499. At $749 there is absolutely no reason recommend it. You could buy an iPhone 17E or Galaxy S26 FE and have $50 left over to buy a gold case; $50 more would net you an older flagship like the iPhone 16 or Pixel 10. Any one of these phones would blow the T1 Phone out of the water.
To my surprise, my Trump phone has received some support since it launched. There’s been exactly one software update, moving it from Android’s February 2026 security patch to the May 2026 version. It’s still running Android 15 though, which is now two years old.
While the Trump phone officially started shipping in May, almost a year after it was announced, it remains unclear just how many customers have received their phones. A report from the BBC last month found that at least some buyers still say their phones never arrived.
articles.author: Dominic Preston

articles.title: RNLI reviews security after volunteers targeted online
articles.summary: Volunteers were targeted online after it assisted in the rescue of people crossing the Channel on Sunday.
articles.body: The RNLI is reviewing its security procedures to ensure the safety of its members after protests in Dover and Portsmouth which saw its members targeted. As part of this, volunteers have been told to consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing in some circumstances while representing the charity. It comes after the charity helped carry around 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight, to Eastney, in Langstone Harbour, where roads were blocked by protesters. Following this, some crew members had their photos and names shared on social media, in posts accusing them of treason. RNLI chief executive Peter Sparkes called the abuse "wholly unacceptable in a civilised society".As a charity, the RNLI relies on donations from the public to fund its work.  Many lifeboat stations have shops attached to them, not just to raise money, but also to raise the profile of the organisation.  Volunteers have been told they are "empowered to make decisions to keep yourself, your team or crew safe" and "go home or close for the day if you need to".For it to tell its volunteers they should feel empowered to shut shops or even lifeboat stations if they do not feel safe shows how seriously it is taking potential issues. Sussex Police are looking to establish whether any criminal offences have been committed.  The Home Office said that platforms should enforce their own terms of service over this matter, and "take swift action against discriminatory content". In a statement to the BBC, a Home Office spokesperson said: "Directing abuse at people who risk their lives in the service of others is appalling." They added: "Where content is shared to intimidate, harass or incite violence against someone, that can cross into criminality," adding the Home Office would work "with platforms and law enforcement to ensure appropriate action is taken".Speaking to BBC Breakfast about the new safety guidance for RNLI volunteers, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "My concern is about people calling them traitors and accusing them of treason, that is quite wrong. "It is the government's job to stop the boats. They should not be attacking volunteers."In a message sent to volunteers, Sparkes said its participation in the rescue on Sunday had been requested by HM Coastguard. "This was the first time we have been involved in a Channel crossing incident of this magnitude this far west," he said. Initially crews from Bembridge and Yarmouth stations were involved, later being joined by crews from four more stations after "large numbers of protesters were in and near the water in Portsmouth". During the incident, the RNLI said it also helped to ensure the safety of anti-migrant protesters in the sea off Portsmouth.BBC Verify spoke to Neil, one of the volunteers who was called a "traitor" and whose image was shared online. "We were there, purely for the safety of the protesters in the water," he said."It would be nice for those people who called me a traitor to know that I'm not a traitor." Speaking to BBC Newsnight, RNLI vice-president Sir Robin Knox-Johnston encouraged people abusing lifeboat crews to "have some sense about this". Sir Robin, a legendary sailor who was the first man to sail solo non-stop around the world, said: "The people who are abusing the volunteers - I wonder how abusive they'd be if they suddenly got a stitch when they're out swimming? "They'd be screaming for the RNLI to rescue them and the RNLI would do it."In his message to volunteers, Peter Sparkes said "at times of increased media activity like this it is only natural that members of the public, supporters, family and friends may have questions about our lifesaving work in the Channel". "When our crews are tasked by HM Coastguard, we will go to the aid of those who need our assistance, including those crossing one of the world's busiest shipping lanes in small, overcrowded and unseaworthy boats," he said. "When called upon, we rescue people - men, women, and children - in distress."He said the RNLI would then pass over responsibility for the people it rescued to the ambulance service, HM Coastguard, police or Border Force. Figures from the RNLI show only a tiny fraction of its lifeboat launches involved assisting people "in distress in the Channel", with the majority of small boats intercepted by Border Force.  Sparkes encouraged crew members to take measures to ensure they feel safe in their roles. He said volunteers could do things like "choosing not to wear RNLI branded clothing when representing our charity in public places" or "removing yourself from a conversation with a member of public if you feel uncomfortable".  He also encouraged RNLI members to visibly wear ID identifying themselves while on site, and to challenge anyone not wearing an ID - especially if they are acting suspiciously or trying to gain access to the building.

articles.title: Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 update adds VRR support in TV mode
articles.summary:
Nintendo always promised that the Switch 2 would support variable refresh rate (VRR) when docked, but the console launched without this key feature. A new 23.0.0 firmware update now adds VRR support to the Switch 2 when it's docked and in TV mode.
VRR adjusts a display's refresh rate to match a game's frame rate, smoothing out gameplay and reducing screen tearing. It will be particularly useful fo
articles.body:
Nintendo always promised that the Switch 2 would support variable refresh rate (VRR) when docked, but the console launched without this key feature. A new 23.0.0 firmware update now adds VRR support to the Switch 2 when it’s docked and in TV mode.
VRR adjusts a display’s refresh rate to match a game’s frame rate, smoothing out gameplay and reducing screen tearing. It will be particularly useful for games on the Switch 2 that have an unstable frame rate, and it’s a feature that the PS5 and Xbox Series S / X all support.
The latest Switch 2 firmware also includes a new toggle for handheld boost mode in quick settings, as well as an update to the Mii editor that lets you enable music for some nostalgic Wii, 3DS, or Wii U Mii creation. Nintendo has also added the ability to perform a full system transfer from one Switch 2 console to another, just in time for a Zelda-themed Switch 2 next month.
articles.author: Tom Warren

articles.title: What algorithm did Windows XP use to choose your initial user picture?
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20260909-00/?p=112683
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49640646
Points: 306
# Comments: 148
articles.body:
I noted some time ago that  Windows XP chose your initial picture at random from among the pictures in the %ALLUSERSPROFILE%\Application Data\Microsoft\User Account Pictures\Default Pictures directory. But it seems people want to know more.
Has anyone attempted to figure out the RNG for how Windows XP determines what profile picture is used on first account creation?
— Xeno (@XenoPanther) December 11, 2025
The random number generator is our friend RtlRandomEx, using the current value of GetTickCount() as the initial seed.
The function uses a one-pass random selection algorithm. I can immediately think of two benefits of this decision. First, compared to the naïve two-pass algorithm of counting up all the items, then randomly picking a number from 1 to n, and then iterating a second time to find the item at that index, it’s more efficient because it reduces the amount of calls into the file system, which is where the bottleneck is. Furthermore, the one-pass algorithm avoids complications if the number of files in the directory changes while the code is running.
The one-pass algorithm is a special case of  reservoir sampling, where k is 1. This special case permits a tailored algorithm that is much simpler.
if (uniform_random(min: 1, max: count) == count) {
The way this algorithm works is by observing that in a collection of n items, the last item has a 1/n chance of being randomly selected. If it isn’t selected, then you need to select randomly from the first n − 1 items, which you can solve recursively.
Playing the recursion forward, you start with the base case which is that if you have a list of 1 item, then your only choice is to chose that item. Otherwise, if you have a list of n items, first choose an item randomly from the first n − 1, and then switch to the nth item with a 1/n probability.
As a final safety check, the code stops after sampling 100 pictures. This avoids pathological behavior if somebody puts a million files in the Default Pictures directory.
Raymond has been involved in the evolution of Windows for more than 30 years. In 2003, he began a Web site known as The Old New Thing which has grown in popularity far beyond his wildest imagination, a development which still gives him the heebie-jeebies. The Web site spawned a book, coincidentally also titled The Old New Thing (Addison Wesley 2007). He occasionally appears on the Windows Dev Docs Twitter account to tell stories which convey no useful information.

articles.title: How history points to another Solheim Cup thriller
articles.summary: With no more than one point separating the teams at the past three Solheim Cups played in Europe there is every reason to expect that this week's contest will be just as exciting, writes Iain Carter.
articles.body: How history points to another Solheim Cup thrillerImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Charley Hull, who was the youngest Solheim Cup player aged 17 in 2013, is making her eighth appearance for EuropeRecent history suggests this week's Solheim Cup will be another epic clash to follow hot on the heels of Great Britain and Ireland's dramatic victory over the United States in the Walker Cup.The extraordinary climax at Lahinch last Sunday, where GB&I won with the last putt of the match, evoked memories of the past three Solheim Cups staged in Europe.Three years ago in Spain the contest ended in a dramatic 14-14 tie to allow a delirious European team to hold on to the trophy, having initially wrestled it from American hands with a single-point victory at Gleneagles in 2019.Then it was Suzann Pettersen's gut wrenching and ultimately successful putt on the final green at the Scottish course that decided the outcome.And the previous Solheim Cup held on continental soil was a 2015 single point away win that capped an astonishing comeback by the United States in Germany.So the past three matches in Europe have had no more than a point in them and the home team and the US are tied on aggregate at 42 points apiece."I think it just shows how important each game is," said British number one Lottie Woad, who makes her debut for Europe this week."Even if you're a couple down early, you can get it back and even just getting a half point could be vital. So I think you've just got to have that mentality that any half point or point helps."Woad's compatriot and potential partner Charley Hull believes it can be tougher playing at home. "We get big crowds in both places, but obviously, it's a little more pressure over here when it's a home Solheim Cup," she said."You've just got to deal with it, just stay focused, and be in the zone."Europe's quartet of debutantsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lottie Woad is the top European player in the world rankingsWoad is among four rookies in the European team joining fellow Englishwoman Mimi Rhodes, France's Nastasia Nadaud and the big hitting Spaniard Julia Lopez Ramirez."I can't wait for them to tee it up," said European captain Anna Nordqvist.  "It's always easy to try to describe to the rookies what it's like playing in the Solheim, but it's something that you need to experience."And you have to get your own feel for it. But I can't wait for them to feel what it's like stepping up on that first tee."Players prepare for the intimidation of packed crowds in a huge grandstand around three sides of the opening tee, but of more significance will be the play as matches reach their climax down the closing stretch of holes.And that will be amplified further if it is again close in the closing singles matches on Sunday. "Obviously it's elevated," said 2025 US Open winner Maja Stark."But you're still just playing golf and you're trying to do your best and you're trying to beat one person. There's not much more you can do."You can't rely on team-mates on Sunday afternoon. You have got to go back and remember what's important for me now."The three-day contest starts on Friday with four foursomes - alternate shot - matches, with four fourball matches to follow. That format is replicated on Saturday before the 12 singles matches on Sunday.Form means little at SolheimImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Solheim Cup will begin with foursome matches on FridayAmerican captain Angela Stanford is bullish about her line-up's ability to handle the unique pressure of the Solheim Cup. "I think they're very mentally tough," she said."They don't let things bother them. They let things kind of roll off their back if something doesn't go the way they planned and they seem really focused."Ironically none of the 24 players are bringing stellar individual form into this match, not even Nelly Korda, the world number one who claimed her fourth title of the year by winning the US Women's Open in June.Korda has had only two top-10s since that major triumph at the start of the summer and finished in a lowly share of 50th place at the recent FM Championship.Since Korda's US Open victory there have been no LPGA wins for any of the Solheim players.For Europe only Celine Boutier and Woad have claimed titles this season and American Lauren Coughlin is the sole other tour winner in 2026 on show.But that backdrop will be forgotten when it comes to head-to-head matchplay. As the Walker Cup showed it goes to a rarified level when put into the team environment."You can lose or win any match regardless of rankings or how you're playing at the moment," said Linn Grant, Stark's Swedish compatriot who has missed the cut in five of her past six events."When everyone shows up on Friday, you're just going to bring your best game."It's so different playing matchplay in this setting. It's kind of like just everyone's best game just shows up normally which makes it a lot more fun to play as well."Bernardus' key holesSolheim Cup11-13 SeptemberBernardus Golf Club, NetherlandsThey are competing on a testing course at Bernardus Golf near Hertogenbosch in the Netherlands, which hosted the Dutch Open on the DP World Tour from 2021-23. It has a Surrey heathland feel, that can play like a seaside links in certain areas.But that fast running aspect has been compromised by the storms that lashed the layout on Wednesday. "I think it's a great course for matchplay," said Stark."There are a lot of bunkers that you don't really want to be in. You can have a lot of really long irons into par-four holes as well."The par threes are also likely to generate plenty of drama, especially the 15th where matches will reach a crucial stage. "It is my favourite hole both visually and strategically," says Bernardus club professional Roel Verdonschot."It is built for drama. Players must decide whether to take the risk and attack the pin for a short birdie opportunity or play towards the middle of the green and accept a longer putt."The tee is sheltered, so the wind can be difficult to feel, even though it is still influencing the shot."And any match that goes the distance will involve an exceptionally tough 389-yard par-four closing hole. There is water from the left of the tee, while bunkers await players attempting to play safely towards the right.And the green is tiny with a deep run-off to the left and water to the right. "The 18th is the most difficult playing hole at Bernardus," said Verdonschot."You face a tee shot that you cannot afford to miss left, but you do not want to miss right either. If a close match reaches the 18th, there is a very good chance of drama."Which is completely in keeping with Solheim Cup matches, especially those staged in Europe.

articles.title: Xbox picks up Kojima’s Physint after PlayStation dropped it
articles.summary:
Xbox will now publish Physint, an upcoming game from Metal Gear creator Hideo Kojima, after PlayStation decided to cancel it. 
The unexpected swap came in a flurry of announcements from PlayStation, Xbox, Kojima Productions, and Kojima himself. Sony, which published both of Kojima Productions' previous Death Stranding games, framed it as a "difficult decision to step away from collaborating with K
articles.body:
Xbox will now publish Physint, an upcoming game from Metal Gear creator Hideo Kojima, after PlayStation decided to cancel it. 
The unexpected swap came in a flurry of announcements from PlayStation, Xbox, Kojima Productions, and Kojima himself. Sony, which published both of Kojima Productions’ previous Death Stranding games, framed it as a “difficult decision to step away from collaborating with Kojima Productions,” but insisted their “relationship remains strong.”
Kojima put things more bluntly on his personal X account, claiming that Sony gave the studio an unexpected cancellation notice in June, and that it has spent the last three months “searching tirelessly” for a new publishing partner. He called Xbox “a partner with whom we share a common vision for the future.” It might have helped that the two companies are already working together, with Xbox lined up to publish the studio’s next game, OD.
“Creators have choices about where and how they bring their ideas to life,” said Xbox CEO Asha Sharma in a statement. “We’re honored that Kojima-san has chosen Xbox to work with Kojima Productions on Physint. His ambition to challenge conventions reflects the kind of creativity we want to support at Xbox.” Securing a title of Physint’s stature reflects the priorities Sharma laid out in a memo to Xbox staff this summer, promising a focus on “our strongest franchises and biggest new ideas.”
The Xbox announcement also notes that the relationship between the two companies will “extend beyond games,” with plans in the works across film and television, though no further details were given. Kojima Productions first announced plans for TV and film projects back in 2021, so far resulting in two upcoming Death Stranding adaptations: an animated spinoff called Mosquito and a live action adaptation from the director of Pig.
Kojima calls Physint a “genre-defining action-espionage title,” prompting hopes that it will serve as a spiritual successor to his Metal Gear series, though it’s not expected to launch until at least 2030. OD also has no release date, but should arrive sooner — the horror title was announced in 2022, and a first trailer dropped this time last year.
articles.author: Dominic Preston

articles.title: Group entered hotel where Pakistani cricketers mistaken for migrants were staying
articles.summary: Protesters congregated at a Portsmouth hotel after false rumours that a coach of migrants had arrived.
articles.body: A group of people reached the hotel floor where members of the Pakistan under-19 cricket team were staying after protesters wrongly believed they were migrants, the Pakistan Cricket Board has said.About 30 to 40 people congregated at the Marriot Hotel in Cosham, Portsmouth, on Tuesday evening after false rumours circulated that a coach carrying migrants had arrived.Sumair Syed, chief operating officer of the Pakistan Cricket Board, said the team reported people "knocking on their doors" during the incident, but the players "behaved responsibly and didn't escalate the situation".Hampshire Police said officers found no offences had been committed, and the crowd dispersed by about 21:00 BST.The team went on to play a scheduled match the following day, Syed said.He described the incident as "unfortunate" but said he was in contact with the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB), which had "assured us that every possible measure should be taken for the security of the escort"."This is the responsibility of the whole sport to ensure the safety, security and well-being of the visiting team," he said. "They are on it and we are hopeful that nothing of such sort will happen in the future."

articles.title: Spurs should be awarded 2016-17 title - Pochettino
articles.summary: Mauricio Pochettino believes Chelsea should be stripped of the Premier League title for 2016-17, when his Tottenham team finished runners-up.
articles.body: Mauricio Pochettino believes Chelsea should be stripped of the Premier League title for 2016-17, when his Tottenham team finished runners-up.Chelsea were fined £10.75m in March after being charged by the Premier League for historical breaches of competition rules.The club also had a six-point deduction "set aside" on appeal. Antonio Conte's Chelsea team finished seven points clear of Pochettino's Spurs in 2016-17.Chelsea owners Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital self-reported 74 breaches of Football Association rules when they purchased the club in 2022.The Blues admitted making £47m in secret payments to unregistered agents and third-parties over transfers between 2011 and 2018.Pochettino, who managed Spurs from 2014 to 2019, said: "We should win one title, one Premier League. We should have been awarded it."[Chelsea] were punished, they admitted, so that's it? The title should be for the team that was second."It's true that we didn't compete with the same rules. It's completely fair to say that we didn't compete before the start of the season with the same card."The current USA coach led Tottenham to the 2019 Champions League final during his five years in charge of Spurs.They did not win a trophy during his time there, with his best Premier League finish being that second place to Chelsea in 2017."Maybe with the same rules, if we apply the same things, maybe we could've signed some players that would have made the team better or scored more goals," added the Argentine, who later became Chelsea boss for the 2023-24 season."It's not me complaining - it's the truth. If they admitted they broke the rules, the Premier League title was for the second-best team."I'm not scared to say the truth. The Chelsea fans will be upset with me because I'm saying this, but if we were at Tottenham and broke the rules I'd admit the same."After reporting the potential rule breaches, Chelsea said that it "treated these matters with the utmost seriousness, providing full cooperation to all relevant regulators".A subsequent investigation by the Premier League found that payments by third parties associated with Chelsea were made to players, unregistered agents and other third parties, which were not disclosed to the regulatory authorities at the time.The Premier League's report named a number of transfers related to those payments between 2011 and 2018, including those of Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o, Willian, Ramires, David Luiz, Andre Schurrle and Nemanja Matic.There was no suggestion of any wrongdoing on the part of those players. Hazard, Willian, Matic and David Luiz all played for the Blues in 2016-17.The Premier League assessed a series of recalculations of the club's historical financial submissions, taking into account the previously undisclosed payments, and concluded that Chelsea would not have breached its profitability and sustainability rules had the payments been registered at the time.It therefore deemed that a points deduction would not be an appropriate punishment.The £10m fine would have been £20m, but was reduced by 50% on account of Chelsea's proactive self-reporting and co-operation with the process.The additional £750,000 fine in March was for the registration of academy players between 2019 and 2022, for which Chelsea were also given an immediate nine-month academy transfer ban.

articles.title: BBC drops Drag Race UK after eight series
articles.summary: Future series will no longer be broadcast on BBC Three as the show moves to a streaming platform owned by its production company.
articles.body: RuPaul's Drag Race UK is leaving the BBC after eight series, the broadcaster has confirmed.A spokesperson for the broadcaster said it was facing "very difficult choices" in the face of "significant financial pressures".The show is currently broadcast on BBC Three and iPlayer. Future series - as well as its spin-off vs The World - will be broadcast on Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.At its peak, the UK version of the international drag competition averaged at around 1.5 million viewers per episode.A spokesperson for the BBC said it was "proud [...] of this groundbreaking show" and thanked "RuPaul, World of Wonder and everyone involved, both on and off screen".Started in 2019, Drag Race UK brought British drag into mainstream entertainment in the UK, and has made household names of drag performers such as La Voix, Danny Beard, and Tia Kofi.The show sees drag queens compete in a series of challenges to impress judges RuPaul, Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Alan Carr, and often features big name celebrity guest judges.It has become a staple of LGBTQ+ culture and has been praised for its portrayal of the distinct style of British drag.The corporation is currently rolling out plans to make £500m of savings, with director-general Matt Brittin previously telling staff "the scale of savings requires tough choices".A BBC spokesperson said: "As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly."Announcing the news on Instagram, Wow Presents Plus said a "new era" of Drag Race UK was on the way.A new series, Drag Race UK All Stars, which sees previous fan favourites return to compete again, will premiere in Autumn 2027 exclusively on Wow Presents Plus. BBC News understands the current series of Drag Race UK, which launched in September 2026, will continue to air as normal on BBC Three and appear on iPlayer, and all existing series will continue to be available once the move is complete.Tia Kofi, the winner of RuPaul's Drag Race UK vs The World series 2 in 2024, stated that the programme has, until now, provided a platform for performers who otherwise lack mainstream representation.The performer told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday that cutting the show also means a "marginalised" audience now has nowhere to go."I think the mistake is that they seem to be dropping programmes that they consider to be for more niche audiences, which I just don't think makes a lot of logical sense because the niche audiences are the ones who are very much staying on and watching these things," the Drag Queen and singer said."But particularly when it comes to programs like Drag Race UK or the cancellation of I Kissed a Boy and I Kissed a Girl, or the Rap Game UK on the BBC as well, the more marginalised audiences have limited representation in mainstream media."[They] offer people a platform when they wouldn't have that. There aren't really those alternatives for drag performers in the UK."The BBC does represent the LGBQT+ community through storylines in shows including Mr Loverman, Rob & Rylan's Grand Tour, Amandaland, EastEnders, What It Feels Like For a Girl, The Dickie Show, Vigil, Smoggie Queens, Such Brave Girls and Juice.The corporation declined to comment on whether future series of other international versions of the show, including Drag Race Canada and Drag Race Down Under, would continue to air.Earlier this year, the BBC announced it was dropping LGBTQ+ dating show I Kissed a Boy - which made history as the UK's first gay dating show - and I Kissed a Girl.Jordan Burrow, a contestant on series two of I Kissed a Boy, said the decision was an example of "where we're at within the queer community".The corporation said at the time that it was "exceptionally proud" of the shows but they had to make "difficult choices in light of our funding challenges".

articles.title: The first drink-driving conviction may have happened in London
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://www.ianvisits.co.uk/articles/the-worlds-first-drink-driving-conviction-may-have-happened-in-london-92107/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49639730
Points: 3
# Comments: 0
articles.body:
On 10th September 1897, a London taxi driver became the first person in Britain — and quite possibly the world — to be convicted of drink-driving.
At the time, there were no breathalysers, no legal blood-alcohol limit and the vehicle involved in the historic incident wasn’t even petrol-powered. It was an early type of electric taxi.
Bersey electric cab on display in the Science Museum (c) ianVisits
The driver was 25-year-old George Smith, who was driving one of the new Bersey electric cabs. According to news reports at the time, he was driving along New Bond Street around midnight when his cab began swerving across the road, mounted the pavement, and crashed into 165 New Bond Street.
The site of the drunken driver’s accident (c) ianVisits
He was arrested by Police Constable Russell and taken to nearby Vine Street Police Station, where a police surgeon certified that he was drunk.
The following day, he appeared at Marlborough Street Police Court, where he admitted that he had consumed “two or three glasses of beer”. Unsurprisingly, Smith pleaded guilty to being drunk while in charge of his cab and was fined 20 shillings, which would have been the equivalent of about a week’s wages at the time.
The magistrate warned Smith that drivers of the new machines needed to be particularly careful. Police, he observed, had developed ways of stopping a runaway horse, but stopping a runaway motor car was another matter entirely.
A law written before the motor car
Although Smith’s case was a motoring first, Britain already had legislation dealing with drunken people in charge of carriages.
Section 12 of the Licensing Act 1872 made it an offence to be drunk while in charge of a “carriage, horse, cattle, or steam engine” on a highway or in another public place. The maximum penalty was 40 shillings, or up to a month in prison.
When horseless carriages appeared a couple of decades later, the existing legislation for horsey carriages was used to deal with them as well. But with motoring becoming more popular the previous year, the Locomotives on Highways Act 1896 swept away some of the most restrictive rules introduced for motor cars.
And the speed limit was raised to an eye-watering 14mph, but even so, it would not be until 1904 that driving licences and vehicle registration numbers were introduced.
Smith was therefore convicted of drink-driving several years before Britain even required him to have a driving licence.
Another curious aspect of the story involves one of London’s earliest electric taxis.
The Bersey electric cab had entered service just a few weeks earlier. Designed by electrical engineer Walter Bersey, the battery-powered vehicles quickly earned the nickname “Hummingbirds” because of the unusual sound of the electric motors. With a top speed of 9mph, they could travel roughly 30 miles between battery changes. The batteries weren’t recharged in the cab, but swapped at the depot for charged ones, speeding up how quickly they could get back on the road.
The Hummingbirds themselves weren’t around for long. Their heavy batteries contributed to tyre wear and mechanical problems, while operating and maintaining the vehicles proved expensive. Just a couple of years after being introduced, the company closed down.
From police judgement to breathalysers
At the time, there wasn’t an official test available to determine how much alcohol a motorist had consumed. Police instead relied on how someone behaved, spoke and walked, together with later medical examination and witness evidence.
Early devices for measuring alcohol in a driver’s breath were developed in the first half of the 20th century, leading to much more practical breath-testing equipment in the 1950s. It wasn’t until the Road Safety Act 1967 that the first blood-alcohol limit for motorists was introduced, and police were allowed to use roadside breath tests.
In the meantime, the corner of New Bond Street and Grafton Street should have a blue plaque marking the ignoble spot where the first drink-driving conviction took place.

articles.title: Volvo XC40 PHEV is back with a new look, better sensors, and Gemini AI
articles.summary: It's been about three years since Volvo discontinued its plug-in hybrid XC40. The mild hybrid version remains on sale in the US and elsewhere, alongside the electric EX40. Today, Volvo announced it was bringing back the PHEV version and giving it a major facelift. When it arrives at dealerships early next year, the new XC40 will have updated exterior styling, a gut-renovated interior featuring Goo
articles.body:
It’s been about three years since Volvo discontinued its plug-in hybrid XC40. The mild hybrid version remains on sale in the US and elsewhere, alongside the electric EX40. Today, Volvo announced it was bringing back the PHEV version and giving it a major facelift. When it arrives at dealerships early next year, the new XC40 will have updated exterior styling, a gut-renovated interior featuring Google’s Gemini AI assistant, an enlarged infotainment screen, and a new sensor-and-software safety suite.
As a hybrid, the XC40 serves as a bridge for customers who want better gas mileage but aren’t ready for the pure EV lifestyle. Volvo itself needs that bridge, after backing down from its pledge to sell only EVs by 2030. That said, the automaker didn’t divulge any details about the powertrain, engine options, electric motor, range, or battery capacity for the XC40 — so we’ll have to wait and see whether this SUV can sufficiently compete in an increasingly cutthroat hybrid market.
On the surface, we’ve got a new take on Volvo’s signature “Thor’s Hammer” LED headlights, as well as an updated front grille, bumper, hood and front wings. Same goes for the rear: new lighting, new bumper, and an upgraded tailgate. Additionally, the XC40 is getting a trio of diamond-cut wheel options, available in 18-, 19-, and 20-inch sizes.
But the interior is where the meat of Volvo’s improvements comes through. The screen has been bumped up to a higher resolution and a larger, 11.2-inch size. It will run Volvo’s latest user interface, which the automaker designed for faster navigation with fewer taps. Google’s Gemini serves as the voice assistant, using its big AI brain to plan routes, find specific locations and detours, and manage messages. The XC40 rounds it out with an improved wireless phone charger and smart storage solutions.
What about safety? This is a Volvo after all, the automaker most committed to safety (at least according to its well-cultivated reputation). Don’t worry, the XC40 ups the ante in that department with a new software and sensor platform that’s designed to provide real-time collision avoidance, automated emergency steering, and automatic emergency braking.
The sensor upgrade includes new front and corner radars, a new front camera, new rear corner radars, 12 new ultrasonic sensors, and new parking cameras. Cloaked in this new sensor suite, the XC40 is getting a host of new safety capabilities, including new door opening alerts that warn occupants before dooring passing cyclists, lane change assist and smoother lane following support on long drives, and an optional 3D/360-degree camera to simplify low-speed maneuvering and parking.
The ultimate goal is to build a better XC40 — one that’s safer and more capable, which hopefully translates to better sales numbers and a long, continuous shelf life for Volvo’s tiny SUV.
“By enhancing the XC40’s design, technology and safety features, we’ve created the best version of the XC40 yet,” says Akhil Krishnan, Interim Lead for the 30 and 40 Series at Volvo Cars, in a statement. “This already popular model is now set to continue being one of our best-selling cars for years to come.”

articles.title: I think I hate the internet
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://strategictree.bearblog.dev/i-think-i-hate-the-internet/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49639104
Points: 43
# Comments: 16
articles.body:
I’ve just finished reading Careless People by Sarah Wynn-Williams and was equally parts shocked and unsurprised by the events she witnessed at Facebook / Meta.
It’s a terrifying, breathless, and gripping read, and pretty much eviscerates Meta and everything it has professed to stand for since about 2012.
I’ve not had a Facebook account for years now, and it’s coming up to a year since I removed my Instagram and WhatsApp accounts too. My Facebook account was the first to go, and looking through my old emails I can see I requested deletion in 2018.
I can’t put my finger on the exact reason I binned it, but I suspect it was because it had become increasingly filled with posts and content from people I’d grown distant from since school, college, and university. As well as those people, it was filling with news, groups, promoted adverts and posts, and other general crap. I guess overall it felt low value and just another of those vast online troves of personal data waiting to be monetised.
I kept Instagram and WhatsApp for a lot longer; these were only deleted by me last year. For instagram my reasons were much of the same as with Facebook, but with the added toxicity of Meta and their misdeeds to add fuel to the fire. Brexit, Trump, Myanmar, child suicides, alt-right, and just a whole lot of hate speech, propaganda, fake news, and of course AI slop.
WhatsApp was the final Meta service to leave, but I figured that I only maintained contact with a pretty close circle of friends, most of whom I could always text (SMS) or iMessage.
Have I missed any of these platforms? Honestly, no. I definitely recall being concerned that I’d be out of touch with friends and acquaintances, or that I’d miss some hilarious meme or news that was popular, or that I’d not be able to keep others up to date with what I was doing in my personal life.
Ultimately though, all that’s happened is I spend far less time consuming low value content, and more time doing other things that interest me. I also make a more conscious effort to meet regularly (in person) with my close friends; an admittedly smaller group of people, but a group that I think I have more rewarding friendships with.
Sorry for the lengthy preamble but I think this all underpins what has been going through my mind after reading Careless People. The internet is all about connectivity (duh), and most social networks have sought to justify their existence with lofty and worthy sounding goals like “connecting people across the world”, and “giving everyone the tools to build new relationships and friendships with people that matter”…blah blah blah.
Sarah Wynn-Williams certainly believed all this too. In her book she describes her idealism and enthusiasm for Facebook especially in her first few years working there. She truly believed that this company was going to “do good”. But even a cursory glance at Facebook’s backstory shows how it was never borne out of these ethical or morally guided desires, it was a way to rate how attractive the classmates at Harvard were. Facebook is an empire of shit built upon a foundation of misogyny and judgemental behaviour.
Mark was never a genius. He was a good coder who got into Harvard, acted like a dick, stumbled upon a half decent idea, and a whole bunch of dumb luck and privilege later ends up with one of the most valuable companies of all time.
And this is what so many of these tech bros and Silicon Valley startups are like. The “move fast and break things” mantra. The exploitative hyper-capitalist mentality. They have all corrupted the internet and now we can see it happening again with AI slop.
The internet was about connection, but the way I see it, it’s become a great way for bad actors to defraud vulnerable people. For racists to find other racists and amplify their unsavoury views. For paedophiles for groom children with anonymity. For governments to manipulate with ease. For companies to advertise with incredibly accurate and exploitative advertising campaigns. The list just goes on and on.
I work in IT, so I feel kind of stuck in this industry and I increasingly feel a revulsion for everything it stands for. I struggle to see the value in the internet and in IT in general. Social networks have become an evil for global societies and I think the negative impacts have far outweighed any positives.
What is the internet now to me? In many ways it’s something that I have to tolerate to do many things that functioned fine before. I have to use an app to pay for parking. I need to create an online account to pay for a family swim at the local leisure centre. I have to submit an online form to book a slot at the local recycling centre. I need an app to check my bank and credit card balances. And to allow this experience to be bearable I have to service and finance a £600 phone, pay a monthly contract and subscription to Apple, I then have to install an adblocker because otherwise sites are just unusable. I have to navigate endless authentication prompts and MFA codes, and generate unique passwords for everything and store them in a password manager. I have to charge a phone daily and apply a screen protector and a case to ensure this delicate glass and metal object doesn’t smash to pieces and remove my access to my own digital life I’m forced to maintain. And this phone itself needs maintenance and demands my attention all the fucking time; I have to turn off notifications, and ensure the apps are up to date, and make sure the iOS version is updated too, and I need to opt out of marketing emails, and ensure I don’t click on a phishing email, and I need to keep my spam filter in check, and run a VPN to maintain a basic level of privacy, and on and on and on…
It’s exhausting, and I’m just gobsmacked that within living memory none of this really existed. I’m a 90s child and I vividly remember being out of the house on days out without a smartphone or even a feature phone. How insane does this feel now? Can you imagine leaving the house without a phone? But I have this yearning for a simpler time and I guess this is what happens as you get older. Maybe it’s all rose tinted glasses I’m wearing but I just look at the internet and every day I think “I fucking hate you. I actually hate everything you’ve done to me and everyone else”.
The internet has stolen innocence, wonder and serendipity out of society.
I’ve been turning my iPhone into a dumb phone so we shall see how that goes. But here I am now, writing a blog post on a tiny iPhone keyboard for some reason. Why didn’t I just get a pen and paper? Does anyone need to read this?
The internet needs to piss off, and I mean just back the fuck up. It never needed to be this enmeshed in everyone’s lives. I want to go live in a cottage in the countryside and literally not have an internet connection.
