articles.title: Apple Watch’s new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening
articles.summary: Apple says its new watches won’t save raw audio, but features that can transcribe recent speech and summarize ambient conversations raise new questions about consent, privacy, and how people behave when they know they could always be recorded.
articles.body:
Apple is trying to get consumers to accept, and even welcome, a new reality: Your tech is always listening.
At Wednesday’s Surprise and Shine event, where the company introduced its new hardware lineup, the real surprise turned out not to be the foldable iPhone, but how the privacy-sensitive tech giant has decided its watches will now be able to process live audio and transcribe what was said.
Does this mean you’re always being recorded if the person you’re interacting with is wearing an Apple Watch? Not exactly — though it may make some people uncomfortable regardless.
It also raises the question of whether consumers actually want this technology, or if Apple forged ahead in this area because it was afraid that another company, such as OpenAI, would soon introduce a competitive AI device of its own.
Today, a number of startups are acting on the belief that AI-powered transcription is a key consumer use case for AI. So far, this has often involved transcribing meeting notes or recording lectures or interviews. Some companies, like the AI pendant Friend and Amazon’s Bee, ventured into other areas, too, with always-available AI companions that can help you remember your day by passively taking notes.
Apple decided to go a slightly different route. With its new watches’ “Audio Intelligence,” “Live Rewind,” and “Siri Recap” features, the company is straddling the line between accessibility and utility on one side and what starts to feel like invasive technology on the other.
On its own, Audio Intelligence seems to be a useful feature for the deaf or hard of hearing, as it can alert Apple Watch wearers to sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, babies crying, and more, using on-device AI. This can work even when the wearer’s iPhone is not with them and, in some cases, could provide life-saving assistance, such as when a fire alarm or carbon-monoxide detector goes off. It’s doubtful anyone would take issue with this type of audio AI.
However, Live Rewind and Siri Recap move out of the assistive tech space and into a murkier area.
While Apple’s data protections may make these features more palatable to some, there’s still the possibility that normalizing listening technology may not be the best move for a privacy-conscious company. This is especially true given the broader consumer backlash against surveillance technology like Flock cameras, AI data centers, and AI apps in general.
For starters, the Live Rewind AI feature lets you go back in time 15 seconds and transcribe what was just said by double-pressing the watch’s Digital Crown. This transcription can then be saved to Apple’s new stand-alone Siri app so you can revisit the information later.
Apple suggests this could be used to remember things like a “book recommendation, a colleague’s brilliant idea, or something you didn’t hear the first time,” but it also means that you can essentially catch anyone saying something they didn’t necessarily mean to have recorded and make a note of it.
This has implications around consent, not only from an ethical standpoint but from a legal one as well. AI device maker Plaud, for instance, advises customers to obtain legally required consent before recording. Amazon Bee’s terms of service remind users that they’re solely responsible for complying with the law around minors’ data privacy, not Amazon.
Since Apple isn’t saving audio, it’s unclear how the court system might handle these new, text-only transcripts. It’s possible the notes could be introduced as evidence in court, but their lack of audio could make them harder to authenticate or verify. Plus, the evidentiary rules around their use will also likely vary by state.
Beyond the legal issues, the idea that someone can always record from their watch has cultural implications.
Already, recording devices have impacted the way people behave in real life, studies have shown, as has social media and data surveillance culture. Knowing you could be recorded at any time has a dampening effect on how you interact with others and engage in self-expression.
However, recording a photo or video still requires a fairly obvious move on the recorder’s part: You have to hold up your phone and face it toward the action. Snapping up a bit of audio to turn into a transcript just by pressing the watch’s Digital Crown is arguably a much subtler gesture, even though it comes with an audible chime and full-screen animation of a microphone, Apple says.
Another new Apple Watch feature, “Siri Recap,” uses ambient listening to “take high-level notes” of your conversations, which can be reviewed in the Siri iOS app. These notes will automatically generate a title, summary, and key points based on what was recorded and summarized by AI. They will not be exact transcripts.
Apple suggests this could make sense for recording meeting takeaways or key info from a parent-teacher conference, for instance.
The company also tried to assure users that it has approached these listening features with respect for user privacy.
Apple notes that Siri Recap doesn’t default to always being on like some other AI wearables are. Instead, you can choose when it’s enabled, like only at work or only during the day. Plus, you can turn the feature off and on at any time from the Control Center.
Notably, Apple points out that it does not create or store audio recordings and that the raw audio isn’t accessible, even to Apple. It also doesn’t identify or attribute the speakers, and it protects the generated transcripts and recaps with end-to-end encryption.
Whether that’s enough for consumers not to feel like the feature is creepy is another matter. Either Apple has found the right balance between utility and privacy, or it’s about to see some consumer backlash.

articles.title: Benn 'dragged down to pits of hell' by weight cut
articles.summary: Conor Benn says making the welterweight limit for his world-title challenge against Ryan Garcia has felt like being "dragged down to the pits of hell" but insists he is healthy and will make weight.
articles.body: Conor Benn says making the welterweight limit for his world title challenge against Ryan Garcia has felt like being "dragged down to the pits of hell" but insists he is healthy and will make weight.Benn, 29, faces WBC champion Garcia at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Saturday in the first world title fight of his 10-year professional career.The Briton must weigh no more than 10st 7lb (67kg) when he steps on the scales in on Friday, having not made the welterweight limit for more than four years."It's been extremely difficult," Benn told BBC Sport."It feels like I've been dragged down to the pits of hell, had a fight with Satan and God brought me back to life."Making weight has been the hardest thing I've done. I haven't made weight for four and a half years so it's going to be hard."But I won't moan when I'm getting paid a fortune to headline in Vegas for a world title. I know what I signed up for."Benn last made the welterweight limit when stopping Chris van Heerden in two rounds in April 2022.He stepped up to 11st 6lb (73kg) for two lucrative contests with Chris Eubank Jr last year, suffering the first defeat of his professional career in April 2025 before avenging the loss on points seven months later.Benn's appearance in pictures and videos posted on social media during fight week has prompted concern among some observers over the effects of dropping back to welterweight.Former world champion Carl Froch and Benn's former opponent Chris Algieri are among those to have questioned whether the weight cut could leave him depleted.It is particularly pertinent given the contrasting styles on Saturday. Benn is an aggressive, front-foot fighter who likes to apply pressure, while American Garcia, 28, possesses fast hands and is renowned for a dangerous counter left hook.But Benn dismissed concerns over his condition."I'm healthy," he said, adding that he expects to rehydrate significantly and enter the ring at around 12st 7lb (80kg) - two stones heavier than the welterweight limit.Even if he fulfils a lifelong ambition by winning a maiden world title and following in his father Nigel's footsteps, Benn intends to vacate the belt "straight away" and move back up to middleweight or potentially as high as super-middleweight."I love challenges and that's what life is about, otherwise it's boring," he added.For all the difficulty presented by the weight cut, there was little outward sign of Benn being weighed down by the occasion.He was relaxed and in good spirits as he made time for the travelling British media at the UFC's Meta Apex, with father and British boxing great Nigel Benn by his side.The former two-weight world champion has been a prominent presence throughout fight week, despite previously suggesting he would take a step back from his son's career.One man Conor Benn is yet to see, however, is his opponent.Garcia did not appear for a scheduled face-off at Mandalay Bay on Tuesday, with Benn told beforehand that the champion would not be attending.Benn turned up regardless and jokingly squared up to his 62-year-old father instead.He described Garcia as a "strange geezer" and said the no-show had done the champion "no favours"."I'm not bothered, I've dealt with worse," Conor Benn added. "If he turns up or not, it makes no difference to me."Irrespective of how hard the weight cut is or anything else, we owe it to the public to give the fans what they want. It's a lack of discipline and professionalism."

articles.title: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations
articles.summary: The investigation, which follows a broadcast by Channel 4 News, is being folded into the inquiry that has been under way into other donations.
articles.body: The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform UK over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.An undercover reporter recorded two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled £500,000.The police investigation by the Met's Special Enquiry Team is being folded into an inquiry that has been under way into other donations to the party.A Reform UK spokesman said the party "denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation". "We won't be commenting further while a live investigation is under way."A Met spokesperson said it had received "a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party", after the film by Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations was shown on Thursday evening. In its statement, the Met Police said: "All allegations under investigation relate to potential offences under the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000.""Detectives continue to liaise closely with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as enquiries progress."The police spokesperson said detectives were seeking to obtain footage relating to the broadcast.An Electoral Commission spokesperson said the Channel 4 News report included "serious allegations of wrongdoing", adding: "It is right that these are properly and thoroughly investigated by the police. "In parallel, we are also considering all relevant information and regulatory steps."The film overshadowed the party's conference in Birmingham and led to the party losing two key figures - Dan Jukes, chief of staff to the leader Nigel Farage, and James Orr, head of policy.In the news report, an undercover investigator posing as the son of an American donor is recorded raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.Electoral law states that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.Jukes appears to suggest that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.Elsewhere, James Orr, the party's head of policy suggests that the father could pay for opinion polling to support one of Reform's campaigns.Farage and Jukes were also filmed at a lunch in Clacton where it is suggested the US donor, who was being played by an actor, gives £500,000 to Reform through his son.Farage told the BBC he "frankly wasn't listening" to the discussion about the potential donation. Channel 4 News has said the payment was never made. He dismissed the comments made by his aide in the film as "loose pub talk including a couple of boasts that simply were not true".Jukes has denied "any wrongdoing" and said he had "stepped back from politics in order to clear my name".Last week, Orr told Sky News he would cooperate with the party's internal investigation "fully".The Met had already been investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.The probe is examining donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Nigel Farage ally, George Cottrell.It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, which received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.A Verbatim Investigations spokesperson said: "Verbatim will cooperate with the police's investigation."Labour Party Chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him."Reform's failure to take responsibility for their actions shows just how unfit they are for office."The Liberal Democrat's Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said: "Every Reform MP urgently needs to state whether they or their campaigns have benefited from any foreign money."Zack Polanski, leader of the Green Party in England and Wales, said: "Nigel Farage and Lee Anderson hoped they could pin all this on two of their most senior advisors, but they have more questions to answer about how much they knew."

In this episode, Justin, Sumi and Marianna discuss America twenty five years on from 9/11 and to what extent it still shapes the United States, despite millions of Americans today having no lived experience of the attacks.
We also look at the politics, as families who lost loved ones in the attacks have petitioned New York mayor Zohran Mamdani not to attend the 25th anniversary ceremony. More than 100,000 people have signed the petition, objecting to specific members of the mayor’s team.  Is this the biggest test yet of Mamdani’s standing in New York City?
Peter Bergen, a national security analyst for CNN who produced the first television interview with Osama Bin Laden in 1997 joins us to give his reflections, and details how the interview came about. His latest book, All the Presidents' Wars, charts the quarter century of conflict that followed the attacks. He is also donating an archive of 150,000 documents on the rise of al-Qaeda to Georgetown University.
He reflects on the legacy of 9/11 and argues that America, not Bin Laden, created the quagmire that came after. And he explains why the alleged mastermind of the attacks, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, is still awaiting trial at Guantanamo Bay, more than 20 years after his arrest.

articles.title: Factoring RSA 260
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://cognition.com/blog/factoring-rsa-260
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49633534
Points: 98
# Comments: 11
articles.body:
By Eric Lu09.09.26Over the past few weeks, the Cognition research team and I have been optimizing our job scheduler to better use disaggregated compute. As a proof of concept, and because I’ve enjoyed factoring numbers as a hobby for the past ten years or so, I drove a bevy of Devins to obtain a factorization of RSA-260. In order to do this, my Devins built the world's highest-performance GPU lattice siever, which enables factoring numbers at 10x lower cost than the previous public state of the art. Here is the factorization:22112825529529666435281085255026230927612089502470015394413748319128822941402001986512729726569746599085900330031400051170742204560859276357953757185954298838958709229238491006703034124620545784566413664540684214361293017694020846391065875914794251435144458199
× 5028695206842569864686141618253083416610081090075366674776775706538324961364412200138116378509733307971876652984898985905923678379RSA-260 (a 260 digit number) sets a new record for the largest publicly solved RSA Factoring Challenge problem, which benchmarks the feasibility of breaking the RSA cryptosystem. The previous record, RSA-250, was set in February 2020. For reference, state-of-the-art RSA public keys contain 2048 bit (~617 digit) factoring problems, while 1024-bit (~309 digit) RSA was deprecated in 2013.Below I’ll give some details about how this was accomplished, but here are two important takeaways:Hyperscalers or frontier AI labs could likely factor RSA-1024 numbers at a cost on the order of $30 million per number — and, with a bit more optimization, likely substantially less. On the other hand, RSA-2048 remains roughly a billion times harder than RSA-1024 and does not appear to be meaningfully affected by this work.Devin is a sufficiently powerful software engineer to solve a challenging problem at the intersection of computational number theory and GPU performance engineering. My role was primarily to set priorities, establish benchmarks, and recognize when work was going off-track. Devin otherwise autonomously handled measurements, cluster operations, and optimization end-to-end. This substituted for what would likely have been a multi-month effort by a team of highly specialized domain experts.In conclusion, the barrier to entry for cryptanalytic work, other computational mathematics more broadly, and likely most large-scale scientific computing research, is far lower than it used to be. Exciting work beckons anywhere programming can be used to solve a research problem; I encourage all to be ambitious and explore what autonomous software engineering agents can do when applied to these fields!How did this happen?Contrary to some circulating claims, I did not factor RSA-260 by guessing and checking 130-digit prime numbers by hand. Cognition also has not yet built a multi-thousand-qubit quantum computer. RSA-260 was factored by a new implementation of the general number field sieve (GNFS) for GPUs, prepared and run using Devin. GNFS is the most efficient algorithm known for (most) numbers above roughly 100 digits in size and was used in previous record-breaking RSA number factorizations.The implementation was a significantly modified CADO-NFS. I report essentially no algorithmic advancements — implementing lattice sieving and sparse linear system solving on GPUs required only “good old performance engineering” to take advantage of the preposterous memory systems of the GPU.Cost estimatesIn total, I estimate that this factorization cost about 4,900 GPU-days, or 13.5 GPU-years, which is about $400k at current market prices. In more detail, modern GNFS implementations consist of a few stages run sequentially: polynomial selection, lattice sieving, and linear system solving. The time breakdown was:643 GPU-days in polynomial selection (this is anomalously high basically due to operator incompetence)3,813 GPU-days sieving467 GPU-days linear system solving (of which about 7% failed to make progress due to crashes or preemption by more important work)I did this as a side project using a single-digit percentage of our cluster, in the course of optimizing our job scheduler to improve allocations to use disaggregated compute. What does this mean for larger RSA instances?RSA-1024 is equivalent to 309 digits; according to standard GNFS scaling this is merely 78x more computation than RSA-260. I estimate the cost of factoring RSA-1024 at market GPU prices to be roughly $30M, which can trade off against wall clock time. I know for a fact that the current implementation remains significantly suboptimal; I would not be surprised if moderate further work could reduce the cost of factoring RSA-1024 by another multiple of 2.Of course, the fact that RSA-1024 is insecure is not news. There was speculation that the NSA might have the capability to do RSA-1024 economically as early as the mid-2000s (see e.g. TWIRL or the Bernstein matrix machine). Instead, as we describe below, the main developments are (1) a potentially lower cost (in dollars and time) for the factorization, (2) potentially more parties capable of performing the factorizations (you just need enough GPUs rather than making specialized hardware), and (3) the relative ease with which non-cryptographers can now work on speeding up factoring.Finally, I emphasize that the efficiency gains have little impact on the feasibility of factoring RSA-2048-sized numbers with GNFS.Factoring on spare computeThe factorization ran at no marginal cost on spare or fragmented compute that couldn’t be used for other purposes. Why does this compute exist?The clusters we use for LLM training and inference contain NVL72 racks, each nominally comprising 18 computers interconnected by fast NVLink. LLM workloads use groups of computers within single racks in order to take advantage of this fast interconnect. The job scheduler must solve a constrained optimization problem to pack workloads into racks. In this global allocation, some racks may end up with an idle node or two; sometimes jobs request spare nodes to accommodate failover, or jobs might need even numbers of computers on a rack that has only 17. For us, these inefficiencies amount to a single-digit percentage of overall compute.To make use of this spare compute, as a first step, I rigged our job scheduler to fill single-node jobs around other workloads at bottom priority. However, we also lacked a consistent source of readily preemptible single-node workloads. Naturally, at this point I thought of lattice sieving, which is a perfect fit for this situation.Lattice sieving is embarrassingly parallel over billions of small work units, can make progress using single nodes at a time, and is safe to preempt instantly. It is also the most computationally expensive part of GNFS, so getting sieving done is a lot of progress toward a factorization. However, all prior public GNFS factorization records used only CPUs for lattice sieving; indeed, due to challenges of efficiently implementing lattice sieving on GPUs, for a long time it was not clear that GPU lattice sieving could be more cost-effective overall.In short, all that I was missing was a sufficiently high-performance GPU lattice siever that could accept the parameters needed to factor RSA-260. So, what did I do? Ask Devin.Using Devin to optimize GNFSAt August 13th 0:11:58 Pacific time I aimed Devin at producing a drop-in replacement for las, the CPU lattice siever of CADO-NFS. Here is the prompt I used:CADO-NFS is FOSS software for performing GNFS. I'd like you to develop a fast GPU lattice siever. This has historically been difficult with present techniques because optimizations for CPU lattice sieving employ a lot of conditional branching and complex memory access patterns, and the intersection of GPU kernel-writing experts and number field theory experts is quite small. However, the higher total memory bandwidth available in a GPU promises a higher performance ceiling. And that intersection now contains you.You have Modal access keys available that I authorize you to use to spin up a single GPU box for performance testing. Obtain the CUDA toolchain etc. and build locally; use GPU only for performance testing and shut it down between measurements.The resultant GPU lattice siever should be a drop-in replacement for the siever step of CADO-NFS. Iterate until you exceed the performance of the CPU lattice siever.Two hours later I added that glas (GPU las, of course) should be able to handle the parameters used for RSA-250. Then I went to bed. I woke up to find that, after another 7 hours of iteration, Devin had succeeded.Over the subsequent week I drove Devin to optimize lattice sieving, then the rest of the GNFS pipeline. First, I will give a high-level description of our GNFS optimizations, and then I will describe the optimization workflow.GNFS optimizations (high-level)At a high level, GNFS consists of a number of stages run sequentially: polynomial selection, lattice sieving, and linear system solving.Polynomial selection fixes the number field over which the algorithm is run. The choice of polynomial controls a constant-factor speedup on the lattice sieving step. It’s therefore typically worth spending a fixed fraction (~5%) of overall sieving compute finding a “good” polynomial. There was little technical innovation here; we adapted CADO’s stage-1 polynomial selection to GPUs (resulting in gps1), using also some kernel equipment from msieve’s well-optimized stage-1 polynomial selection. Polynomial selection is more or less embarrassingly parallel.The bulk of the GNFS computational effort is in lattice sieving. The goal of lattice sieving is to produce lots (8.3 billion in our case) of sparse linear relations over GF(2), where here (suppressing some details) the vector entries represent the parities of prime exponents in the prime factorization of a smooth number. Lattice sieving is also embarrassingly parallel over work items called “special q”s, but each work item requires performing a large number of read/writes at (for our purposes) pseudorandom locations in a large array; handling this was the primary technical challenge in optimizing sieving.Ultimately, we pack these relations into a large matrix over GF(2) and use linear system solving to find a linear dependence. At this scale, linear system solving is typically distributed and requires a lot of communication bandwidth; this is available in spades over Infiniband and NVLink. The block Wiedemann algorithm permits relaxing the communication constraint somewhat, and the particular implementation in CADO-NFS is also susceptible to optimization and running on GPUs, which we undertook. Solutions can be processed into congruences of squares modulo N, which yields the factorization.Overall, Devin substantially modified almost every piece, including modifying a couple of interfaces:A GPU-adapted version of CADO-NFS’s stage-1 polyselect, with components from msieveA GPU-optimized lattice siever based on lasAn optimized CADO head to handle the workunit volumeParallelized and optimized dup/purge and fused merge/replay programsA new GPU-optimized block Wiedemann implementationGPU-accelerated sqrtAssociated run scriptsThe only untouched programs in the CADO-NFS pipeline were: cado-nfs.py itself, polyselect_ropt (stage-2 polynomial selection), makefb, and dup1. We even had to optimize fake_rels to get reasonable performance for synthetic inputs of the needed sizes.N.B. I understand these components only in the same way a mid-level car hobbyist might understand car components: their approximate role in the overall system, their effects on performance, some tradeoffs of making changes, and what good operation and usage looks like — but not the underlying physics, nor how to fabricate the component from raw materials. That’s to say that I do not understand much of the underlying mathematics. I can tell you that polynomial selection provides a constant factor on lattice sieving yield; I cannot tell you how the polynomial is used in the siever. In this field I am far from an expert!The optimization workflowI drove several parallel Devins. Across the 3-week duration of the project, I had an average of 3 and a maximum of 18 concurrent Devin sessions running. These were roughly of two types:iteratively optimizing an individual component — designing and running experiments, interpreting results, selecting target improvements, implementing them, and repeatingmanaging end-to-end factorization runs on the cluster — exercising the whole pipeline and supporting scripts, revealing the most important inefficiencies (errors, utilization, performance) for further optimizationIn particular, Devin handled substantial portions of:choosing and tuning parameters for sieving and linear system solving (though using benchmarking equipment that I had to help bootstrap)generating/optimizing polynomial selections (again, with varying degrees of difficulty)running the iterative optimization loopdebugging (naturally)setting up and optimizing the processing scriptsorchestrating large-scale computation on the clusterI interacted with this optimization loop once every couple of hours, alternating with talking to other Devin sessions for my regular work.Devin Cloud was especially convenient for this workflow: sessions are persistent and independent from my computer, parallelization is straightforward, sandboxing prevents interference between independent workstreams, and sessions can run autonomously for weeks. We already knew that Devin was effective at GPU programming, experimentation, and cluster management for ML-relevant workloads, but lattice sieving and GNFS are fairly different; I found Devin’s ability to generalize here quite impressive.Running up the scaling ladderThis workflow permitted an incredible rate of progress that I (and even Devin itself) could barely keep up with. For the first five days we ran up a scaling ladder. But I cannot claim that Devin iterated autonomously on the entire end-to-end pipeline. It is interesting to consider what he needed me for.Somehow, the answer seems to be: still a lot. In retrospect, Devin claims that I sent 82,702 words (502,887 characters) in 3,328 messages across 192 sessions out of 233 used for factoring (totaling 14,450 ACUs). Of these, Devins themselves started 101 child sessions, and 36 received no intervention from me at all.Devin needed me for executive function, talking through and sanity-checking what it was doing, to wit:setting a hierarchy of goals and keeping Devin properly scopedrecognizing when Devin was doing something unproductive and redirecting (“you don’t need to take that measurement”)recognizing repeated inefficiencies in Devin’s workflows (“you can amortize this setup work”)pointing out untried directions (“make sure the GPU never blocks on the CPU”, “can you use NVLink SHARP here?”)organizing experimental frameworks and results (“do measurements this way and find previous results here, don’t cook up new incomparable approaches every time”)catching when Devin prematurely gave up on a directionWhile in retrospect I appear to have supplied a couple of specific technical insights, my biggest contribution was probably to handhold the creation of a unified set of measured results, benchmarks, and performance estimators, which evidently were not otherwise going to self-assemble. This enabled Devin to more easily run and understand measurements, and me to understand the extent of progress and where more improvements were needed.Taking a step back, I also want to emphasize that this effort would not have been possible without CADO-NFS. CADO-NFS is an advanced, robust, open source implementation of GNFS that was used in many previous records and also by the factoring hobbyist community. It provided all the relevant techniques, the pipeline stages and their interfaces, and a reference CPU implementation. Using those, I could have the Devin swarm optimize programs roughly independently and compare the outputs with the originals. Like in many other cases, I believe that the human-engineered decomposition of the problem was essential to enabling the agents to make progress.In fact, I noticed that the further the codebase got from upstream CADO-NFS, the more confused the agents became. This could be attributed to accumulating complexity, but I wonder whether CADO-NFS’s presence in pre-training is also relevant here.This concludes the technical part of the blog post (except for the appendix, which has far more details).Assorted reflectionsWhat has happened here is strange to me. My name is on the result, but it’s not clear to me how to apportion credit among myself, Devin, the hardware, and the world at large.For programming tasks, I think of current models and agents somewhat like a sewing machine or a loom. I push it along in some way; it evidently could not happen without me, but neither am I throwing the shuttle by hand. It is hard to say exactly what my role was, although I am confident that it was not nothing. In some glib sense, doing this with Devin was not that different from what would have happened otherwise: I interacted with a physical system much larger than me whose precise workings are obscure to me, energy was dissipated, and the factors resulted.On the other hand, something clearly new is happening. About three weeks elapsed from first prompt to RSA-260 factors found. The rate evinces a capability overhang whose extent we are only beginning to explore. I think we should not shy away from this exploration. In particular, if a problem can be solved via “just programming”, it seems worthwhile to attempt this immediately.In the past few days, we’ve also seen some impressive claimed results in mathematics, including a claimed solution to one of the Millennium Prize Problems. I share some concerns about a loss of human understanding. I did not learn as much about NFS or GPU programming as I could have expected to had I done this on my own, though likely more than I would have if I were not using Devin at all. It seems important to figure out how to globally allocate resources to maintain human understanding even when technology enables or incentivizes us to forgo this. At the same time, these tools may allow us to choose where deeper understanding is most valuable, explore further than any individual could previously reach, and expand the set of people who can make meaningful contributions. I see this work as an example in both directions.AcknowledgmentsThanks to Alex Lombardi for mathematical consultation and much editing.Thanks to my employer Cognition; this would not have been possible without Cognition compute. articles.title: Everything Apple announced at its fall iPhone event, from the foldable iPhone Duo to an always-listening Apple Watch
articles.summary: The main event was the tech giant's highly anticipated first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo.
articles.body:
Apple on Wednesday unveiled its latest iPhones and Apple Watches at its first fall event under newly appointed CEO John Ternus. The main event was the tech giant’s highly anticipated first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. Apple also announced its iPhone 18 Pro lineup, along with new AirPods, and more.
We’ve compiled all of the announcements from today’s “Surprise and Shine” event.
Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, features a 7.6-inch Retina display when unfolded, while its outer display measures 5.4 inches. The company said that the new device was “inspired by the versatility of iPad.” The inner display features an “underdisplay” camera that gives users an all-screen feel.
Apple says the iPhone Duo delivers up to 31 hours of video playback on its inner display and up to 44 hours on its outer display.
The phone features a 48-megapixel fusion main camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera with 2x optical zoom. As with other foldable phones, users can take rear-camera selfies and look at previews on the outer display.
The Duo’s hinge is made from Grade 5 aluminum and comprises more than 100 specially engineered components designed to ensure smooth opening and closing.
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage and is available in two colors. Preorders for Apple’s new foldable open October 16, with the device hitting stores on October 23.
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max
The new iPhone 18 Pro lineup retains the same design as its predecessors, but its biggest upgrade comes in the form of enhanced cameras.
The new Pro series camera features a 48-megapixel sensor with a variable aperture controlled by six thin blades. This system is expected to improve low-light photography while also increasing shooting speed. The camera software also introduces new Pro controls, including white balance, shutter speed, aperture, and a histogram. In addition, new “Photographic Styles” offer greater customization with texture and grain controls.
The new camera can record 4K video in Dolby HDR Vision and apply cinematic effects after shooting the footage.
The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299, which is $100 more than last year’s models. Preorders will open Saturday, with both devices officially available on September 18.
Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4
A new “Sound Recognition” feature can listen for sounds such as sirens, alarms, doorbells, and a baby crying, providing helpful alerts for people who are hard of hearing. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 aren’t getting a major hardware makeover, but they are getting some significant software updates.
Apple is taking aim at the growing wave of AI-powered wearables with new “Audio Intelligence” features that can rewind moments and help users remember details from their everyday conversations.
The smartwatches are introducing a “Live Rewind” feature that shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, and a “Siri Recap” feature that’s designed to help you remember key moments from daily conversations, like takeaways from a team meeting or a parent-teacher conference.
The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 costs $499. Preorders open today, with availability in stores beginning September 18.
The latest generation of Apple’s wireless earbuds, the AirPods 5 introduces several upgrades, including improved audio quality, stronger active noise cancellation, and expanded Siri and Apple Intelligence features.
Apple says AirPods 5 can reduce background noise by 50% more than the previous generation. They also feature volume control on the stem, which was previously only available on Apple’s more expensive AirPods Pro.
Transparency mode on AirPods 5 has also been improved to allow users to hear nearby voices and ambient sounds more naturally.
The AirPods 5 offer up to five hours of listening with active noise cancellation on a single charge. The charging case brings total listening time up to 22 hours.
AirPods 5 start at $129, while the version with a Wireless Charging Case costs $149. Preorders begin today, with the earbuds set to arrive on September 18.
Apple announced a redesigned Apple Health app that takes advantage of Apple Intelligence to make better sense of your health data.
The updates introduce a new Insights tab with a summary of the most timely health information, along with personalized guidance, assessments, a new “Readiness” score, and a calculation of your “Health Age.” The updates also introduce a new Longevity tab that uses metrics from your Apple Watch and iPhone to assess your overall health across factors such as sleep, movement, heart health, and more.
The revamped Health app rolls out later this year, starting in U.S. English.

articles.title: There are new shiny iPhones, so Apple is making you pay more for older models
articles.summary: Apple is raising the price of its existing iPhone models by $100, including iPhone 16, iPhone 17, and iPhone Air.
articles.body:
Apple, at its Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, unveiled its new iPhone 18 and its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo. But amid all the attention on Apple’s newest and most expensive devices, there’s another change: Apple is raising the price of its existing iPhone models by $100.
Starting today, customers will notice a price hike for existing models on Apple’s online store, including starting prices for iPhone 16 at $799, iPhone 17e at $699, iPhone 17 at $899, and iPhone Air at $1,099.
The price increases are even steeper in some international markets. In India, for example, prices have reportedly risen by around 20.5%. The company also discontinued the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max.
The strategy is an unusual one for Apple. Traditionally, the arrival of a new generation of iPhones means older models become cheaper.
However, the price hike wasn’t entirely unexpected. Speculation had been building that Apple could raise prices as it introduced its next-generation iPhones. One of the biggest pressures is a global shortage of memory and storage chips. Demand for those components has surged as AI companies and cloud providers build out increasingly massive data centers.
In a June interview with The Wall Street Journal, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that rising component costs could eventually force the company to rethink its pricing strategy. He said Apple could no longer fully absorb the rising costs of memory and storage chips.
About a week after those comments, the company raised prices across its Mac and iPad lineups.
Another reason Apple may consider increasing iPhone prices is to remain competitive with rising prices from rivals like Samsung and Google. Additionally, Apple might feel that its new Upgrade program, which allows customers to spread the cost of an iPhone through manageable monthly payments, could cushion the impact of a price hike, making it less noticeable to consumers.

articles.title: Verge staffers react to the iPhone Duo: What we love and don’t love
articles.summary: Apple has just announced its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo. The new phone has a 5.4-inch outer screen and a 7.6-inch inner screen, two back cameras, Touch ID for authentication, an IP68 rating, and all sorts of slick software tricks to make iOS feel more at home on the new device. Preorders start on October 16th ahead of availability on October 23rd, and it starts at $1,999 for 256GB of st
articles.body:
Apple has just announced its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo. The new phone has a 5.4-inch outer screen and a 7.6-inch inner screen, two back cameras, Touch ID for authentication, an IP68 rating, and all sorts of slick software tricks to make iOS feel more at home on the new device. Preorders start on October 16th ahead of availability on October 23rd, and it starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage.
It’s a huge announcement for Apple, and we have many feelings about it. Here’s our gut reactions to the phone. And let us know in the comments what you think!
The Duo name is good
I think iPhone Duo is the perfect name for Apple’s foldable. Two screens, Duo. Two back cameras, Duo. (I imagine a future version will get three, but right now we have two.) Duo is a concise three letters, putting it in line with other memorable Apple monikers like Air, Pro, Max, and Neo. Though somewhere at Microsoft, I am sure someone is fuming. —Jay Peters, senior reporter
I’ve never wanted a new iPhone more. As an iPad Mini stan, it is the ideal device for me. The size, the form factor, the multitasking possibilities. But I won’t be buying it. It’s just too expensive. [Ed. note: The phone starts at $1,999.] —Jennifer Tuohy, senior reviewer
The Apple Pencil support makes the Duo an iPad Mini killer and the perfect on-the-go sketchbook for digital artists. —Kevin McShane, editorial director, audio & video
It’s the opposite of what I need and I’m mad that I want it
A folding phone sounds great, and I dig the form factor of the iPhone Duo. As my eyes get worse, I want a bigger phone, but I don’t want to carry a bigger phone. But if I’m real with myself, I don’t need to spend more time looking at my screen, and I don’t want to downgrade my camera system either. I am a bad photographer who has fast-moving kids and puppies, and I’m not willing to give up the telephoto lens on my 17 Pro. Maybe I’ll get some reading glasses. —Nathan Edwards, senior reviews editor
If Apple takes foldables beyond niche, the new 1.4:1 aspect ratio (a far superior ratio!) might change how content creators operate. Seriously, that is a far more reasonable aspect ratio, especially for portraits, and, strangely, it might be the thing that I’m most excited about with the Duo. —Marina Galperina, senior tech editor
Apple is selling me on the passport shape
I wasn’t a big fan of the short and stout foldable look when I saw Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, but it’s starting to grow on me. The iPhone Duo looks like it’s comfortable to hold in one hand (which could mean no more dropping my phone on my face while lying down), and its thin profile makes it look pleasant to carry around in a purse. —Emma Roth, news writer
Love the bigger size, but can’t stop thinking about a crease
I find myself using my iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPad more and more for watching TV shows and movies, so having a portable screen that unfolds to something larger is so enticing to me. But I can’t stop worrying about a visible, distracting crease as I fold and unfold it over months of use. I know my eyes (and brain) will attempt to focus on it no matter how slight it is. Maybe the crease will be completely indistinguishable even after over a year, but a minimum of $2,000 is too much for me to take a chance. —John Higgins, senior reviewer, TVs and audio
Apple and Samsung had the same idea
The Duo is similar to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 in more ways than just its passport-ish size and shape. Both phones have prioritized solid core performance but use more basic rear camera setups that distinguish them firmly from the companies’ Pro and Ultra models. They’re a close match in price, too, with the Duo only $100 more. That leaves space in the market for Android manufacturers like Xiaomi to come in with higher-specced foldables that place more of an emphasis on photography, battery life, and pro features, leaving Apple and Samsung to make the mainstream play. —Dominic Preston, news editor
articles.author: Verge Staff

articles.title: Apple’s new iPhone camera mode promises to prove your photo isn’t AI
articles.summary:
Apple is launching a new way to prove that the picture you took isn't manipulated by AI. A new feature, called "Reference Image," will arrive with the iPhone 18 Pro lineup later this month and is supposed to use the device's new camera sensor to "sign every pixel it sees."
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will only authenticate photos when placed into Reference mode. Once the camera captures signed s
articles.body:
Apple is launching a new way to prove that the picture you took isn’t manipulated by AI. A new feature, called “Reference Image,” will arrive with the iPhone 18 Pro lineup later this month and is supposed to use the device’s new camera sensor to “sign every pixel it sees.”
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will only authenticate photos when placed into Reference mode. Once the camera captures signed sensor data, Apple says its Private Cloud Compute will develop it “into an unalterable reference image” that can be viewed in the Photos app. You’ll be able to compare the reference image with other versions of the photo to see if any edits were made.
[Image: You can compare the Reference Image to other versions of the photo. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/reference-image.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
As AI-generated images and videos become more realistic, several new standards have emerged to label images not created by a human, such as SynthID, C2PA, and Meta’s Content Seal. Apple is putting a twist on these methods by building authentication directly into its hardware.
Apple is letting developers access a Reference Image API across iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, which could eventually allow users to inspect these digitally-signed photos in third-party apps. The company says the iPhone 18 Pro lineup won’t come with its Reference Image feature at launch in the European Union, but says users in the region will still be able to “develop and view” them in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27.

articles.body:
We’ve just gotten our hands on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max at Apple Park following the company’s “Surprise and shine” presentation.
The new phones look quite similar to the previous iPhone 17 Pro lineup, keeping the same general design, aluminum body, and screen sizes. The 18 Pro lineup comes in four colors — black, silver, “glacier” (which is blue), and burgundy — and they now have color-matched glass on the back that blends in more seamlessly with the body.
Another major new feature is the variable-aperture lens for the main camera and new “pro” controls to help give you more options when taking photos. Apple has also added pro controls to the native camera app; at last our national nightmare is over. You can set the aperture to adjust automatically or use one of four selectable stops: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0. There are also manual controls for shutter speed, white balance, and focus — the latter comes with peaking in the preview to help determine what’s in focus, which is a nice touch. The Dynamic Island is also smaller, and Apple says you can now use it to look at three Live Activities at once. I can confirm, yes, this works.
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will be available to preorder starting September 12th ahead of a September 18th release date. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299.

articles.title: Gay should open for England in South Africa - Cook
articles.summary: England batter Emilio Gay has done enough to lock in an opener's spot for their winter tour of South Africa, according to Sir Alastair Cook.
articles.body: Former England captain Michael Vaughan said Gay "played nicely" but might reflect on an missed opportunity to reach three figures for the first time after he dragged on a delivery from Razaullah Khan."Emilio Gay found his balance early. He had it hard at the start and then he found his flow," Vaughan said."He'll be really disappointed to get out for 60. He'll be desperate to get his first Test match century and I thought it was on today. "That extra little bit of pace from Razaullah and a little lack of concentration at the end of the day has cost him."England seamer Josh Tongue said Gay's rigorous preparation has helped him develop the necessary powers of concentration for Test cricket."The one thing I've seen in Emilio is he trains really hard in the nets. He'll bat for ages, putting a lot of hard work in, and it's shown on the pitch," added Tongue."Even last week at Lord's, he had two quite horrible dismissals, but I felt today he batted unbelievable on a tricky pitch."He was obviously really disappointed with how he got out. It's not a nice feeling, chopping on, but he's put the team in a really good position for tomorrow."

articles.title: The hinge for Apple’s new foldable phone was built with AI
articles.summary: Apple says it used AI and 3D printing in the manufacturing process for its long-awaited foldable phone.
articles.body:
12:21 PM PDT · September 9, 2026
Duo, Apple’s long-awaited foldable phone announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, contains a number of surprises, including a critical hinge that was designed and built with the help of AI and 3D printing.
The new phone represents Apple’s first entry into the foldable phone genre — a category of devices that has seen significant consumer enthusiasm but whose form factors haven’t always lived up to the hype. As you might expect from a product that, by design, undergoes twice as much wear as a traditional device, most foldables suffer significant degradation and don’t have the durability of other smartphones.
Apple claims that it has integrated innovative protections into the Duo’s design to keep the phone from falling prey to the typical wear and tear associated with foldables. That includes the hinge, according to Johny Srouji, the company’s chief hardware officer.
“During manufacturing, we use AI algorithms to precisely match each individual hinge with its best-fit housing to ensure perfect alignment, and a confocal laser progressively scans the topology of every single unit and 3D prints up to 25 micro layers of a custom photopolymer to eliminate residual waviness,” Srouji said during Wednesday’s event.
Srouji also shared that Apple gave the foldable phone “a custom nano-texture finish that significantly reduces glare and reflections,” as well as a multilayer lamination strategy designed to increase the device’s durability. Of course, it remains to be seen whether those protections will be enough to keep the Duo in peak physical condition in the long run.

articles.title: 'An injustice' or 'righting a wrong': British Jews debate sanctions move
articles.summary: The UK's decision to sanction trade with illegal settlements has prompted a range of opinion among the British Jewish community.
articles.body: From his home in the occupied West Bank settlement of Efrat, British-Israeli Rabbi Leo Dee wrote an open letter to Andy Burnham on Wednesday, accusing him of deciding "to single out Jewish Israelis like me for economic punishment".The rabbi's British-born wife Lucy, and their daughters Maia and Rina, were killed by Palestinians in the occupied West Bank in 2023. They were shot dead as they drove through the Jordan Valley."I am enraged at the injustice of the situation," he told the BBC, claiming the government's decision to place sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements, and not the Palestinian authority, was hypocritical.He said Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband was "living in a different universe", and argued that the main group who would face hardship as a result were the hundreds of Palestinians who were employed in them.Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the occupied West Bank by settlers since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.Miliband said the sanctions, announced after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes, were necessary to safeguard the possibility of a two-state solution - and to ensure the UK "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".Rabbi Dee said he believed that, apart from a small group of "hooligan settlers" who could not be controlled and whom most people do not support, many others wanted a different outcome."Ninety-nine percent actually want to work closer with Palestinians" and have peaceful relations with them, he said, just as he did "before the 7 October attacks".Another British rabbi was also in the West Bank as the UK government made its announcement - and takes a different view.Rabbi Jonathan Wittenberg was in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, visiting the family of Awdeh Hathaleen, a prominent Palestinian activist and English teacher who was shot and killed by an Israeli settler last year.The Emeritus Rabbi of the New North London synagogue told the BBC he wanted to show that what was happening to Palestinians there mattered to him and his community.Rabbi Wittenberg said he had "seen with my own eyes several times in the West Bank, the intimidation and threats towards Palestinians - and this needs to be called out"."It's terrible for Israel and for Israel's future, it's not what Judaism teaches and it's deeply wrong", he added.Supported by other Rabbis in the liberal and progressive UK Jewish communities, Rabbi Wittenberg believes that it is possible to support Israel, be concerned for the safety of British Jews, and that it is right for the UK government to take action to protect Israelis and Palestinians.However, he also said he was "extremely sad that it's come to this" and that he shared the "concerns of the Jewish community leadership that people will use this for antisemitism and for demonising Israel even further".Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, who represents the Orthodox community, previously  said the sanctions marked a "truly dark day" and placed British Jews at greater risk of attacks.In Golders Green - where ambulances run by a Jewish medical charity were set on fire and two visibly Jewish men were stabbed in what police called a terror attack earlier this year - there was concern the government's actions against Israel would increase attacks against British Jews."It's so tricky because, in principle, I agree with opposing these new settlements," Michael Cohen, who works for a Jewish charity, told the BBC.But he added: "The timing of it, I think, was completely... just self interest for the Labour Party, signalling before a by-election, before the party conference."He said the practical impact of the move would be "almost zero".One woman, who runs a jewellery shop that was was twice cordoned off due to incidents in Golders Green, was very critical of the sanctions and said she would "make it my mission" to continue to buy Israeli goods whenever she could."We have to [support] our own because no one else is going to", Deborah Miller told the BBC.At the end of the week, Jewish congregations will celebrate Rosh Hashana, the Jewish New Year.Police are already increasing security around Jewish areas to protect communities who have faced multiple attacks this year and are fearful of more.The number of antisemitic incidents recorded across the UK since the start of the year is up by a fifth compared to last year, figures show.The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026.The Crime Survey for England and Wales, external, estimates that only 44% of hate crime incidents between April 2022 and March 2025 came to the attention of the police.

articles.title: Failures 'contributed to' death of Sir Richard Branson's wife
articles.summary: Lady Joan Branson died after suffering a cardiac arrest at the private Lister Hospital in Chelsea last year.
articles.body: A private hospital's failure to provide preventative medication contributed to the death of Lady Joan Branson, an inquest has concluded.The 80-year-old, who was married to Sir Richard Branson, died on 24 November last year after suffering a cardiac arrest at the private Lister Hospital in Chelsea, west London.Senior coroner Professor Fiona Wilcox told Westminster Coroner's Court on Wednesday that Lady Joan did not receive prophylactic anticoagulants at the hospital despite a "very high risk of developing deep vein thrombosis"."I do find her death would have likely been prevented and the lack of anticoagulation did cause or contribute to her death probably," she said.The coroner's court heard that Lady Joan was admitted to the hospital on 17 November after a fall weeks earlier on Necker Island, a British Virgin Island owned by her billionaire husband.She died after suffering a pulmonary embolism, a sudden, dangerous blockage in a lung artery, resulting from deep vein thrombosis.Haematologist Dr George Adams told the inquest that Lady Joan was "extremely high risk" for blood clots and the "biggest risk factor by far was her immobility and her fracture".From her hospital admission to her death, Glasgow-born Lady Joan did not receive any prophylactic anticoagulation, which is used to stop blood clots from forming.The hospital's admitting doctor, Dr Basir Kunduzi, did not complete a bleeding risk assessment on the day of her admission, the inquest heard.Dr Kunduzi said Lady Joan's death led him to "reflect on my role as a doctor" and the importance of "good communication between team members".Giving her conclusion, Professor Wilcox said it was "not a case of neglect" and there "wasn't an absence of treatment".After her death, Sir Richard described his wife as the "shining star around which our family's universe has always orbited".Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

articles.title: Tate brothers to remain in US jail as they fight extradition to UK
articles.summary: A federal judge denied them bail, saying the dual US-UK citizens' wealth and frequent international travel "constitute quintessential flight risks".
articles.body: Andrew and Tristan Tate have lost their bid to be released from a Florida jail as they fight potential extradition to the UK to face charges of rape and trafficking.A federal judge in Miami denied them bail, saying the dual US-UK citizens' wealth and frequent international travel "constitute quintessential flight risks".The brothers have been held in US custody since their July arrest, after the UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) unveiled new charges against them. The UK has until 16 September to submit a full extradition request.They will "continue to defend themselves against the allegations" and "engage with the appropriate legal processes in each jurisdiction", their lawyers said.The two are facing a total of 59 charges in the UK, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child.CPS originally brought 21 charges, but added 38 more in July for alleged actions spanning between 2010 and 2017.US authorities took the men into custody in July after the UK announced the new charges.Last weekend, Romanian prosecutors officially indicted the polarising social media influencers with a range of trafficking and sex offences. The former kickboxers had primarily been based in Romania since 2017, drawing a large audience - primarily young men - through controversial messages about women and images of a luxury lifestyle. Self-proclaimed "misogynist" Andrew Tate first rose to fame after a 2016 appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother.The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025.Several prominent US politicians, including Florida's Republican Governor Ron DeSantis, objected to the Tate brothers' arrival in the US.The brothers have denied all charges and allegations.Wednesday's decision means the brothers will remain jailed during what could be a lengthy extradition process.US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis ruled that, while the Tates "may not in fact possess what extravagant holdings they portray themselves as possessing online, the record reflects that they possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction".The judge said that their lack of ties to the US and their strong foreign connections "demonstrate a risk of flight that has not been overcome".The Tates' lawyers have argued they should be released on bail pending their extradition proceeding, saying the brothers were not a flight risk and did not pose a danger to the community.The lawyers have also argued that they had complied with the terms of their release while facing charges earlier in the UK and Romania.At a hearing on the question of their potential release in August, Andrew Tate said he had "never committed the crimes I'm accused of."Tristan Tate described his detention conditions as small and hot, with little access to sunlight and exercise, adding that he had lost 14 pounds (6.4kg)."It's beginning to grate on me because I can't partake in helping with my defence," he said, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. The British Embassy had asked the judge to keep the Tates in custody as the UK sought extradition, writing in court filings that the brothers were "flight risks" and claiming they "would interfere with witnesses if released".

articles.title: Apple Watch’s new feature listens to your chats and recaps them
articles.summary: The Siri Recap feature is similar to other note-taking apps like Granola.
articles.body:
At its Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, Apple launched a meeting notetaker for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, one of a series of new audio intelligence features that can listen to sounds through your Apple Watch.
The feature, called Siri Recap, uses ambient listening to take high-level notes of your conversations, according to the company. Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title, summary, and key points from the conversation, which can then be reviewed in the Siri app.
Apple said that you can choose to keep this feature always on, set up a schedule, or turn off completely.
The notetaker wasn’t the only audio-focused feature introduced for the Watch during the event. Apple’s new audio intelligence features also include Shazam, which can identify songs instantly. This means Apple has finally caught up to Google’s Now Playing feature. The Watch can recognize loud sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, or a baby crying and notify users.
Apple also introduced a feature called Live Rewind, which lets users recap 15 seconds of conversation when they double-press the Digital Crown.
Apple emphasized that the features don’t store recordings and that raw audio is inaccessible. The Siri Recap feature doesn’t identify speakers either. Users can access Live Rewind recaps, which are end-to-end encrypted. Despite these guardrails, an always-listening feature will likely raise privacy concerns because Siri Recap may still capture sensitive information in its summaries.
Besides some of the privacy features, Siri Recap sounds similar to other notetakers like Granola and Circleback, which also have Apple Watch apps.

Ivan covers global consumer tech developments at TechCrunch. He is based out of India and has previously worked at publications including Huffington Post and The Next Web.

The Apple Watch Series 12 once again starts at $399 for the aluminum case option in space gray, black, light gold, and dark bronze aluminum. The natural or radiant gold titaniu
articles.body:
After Apple wrapped up its “Surprise and shine” event today, we were able to get a look at the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
[Image: Ceramic is back, baby. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/series12ceramic2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Both of the new watches launch September 18th, with preorders available starting today.
The Apple Watch Series 12 once again starts at $399 for the aluminum case option in space gray, black, light gold, and dark bronze aluminum. The natural or radiant gold titanium version costs $699, and the night blue or pearl white ceramic costs $899. Apple says this year’s watch offers up to 24 hours of “everyday” battery life, and now offers up to 10 hours of battery during outdoor workouts and supports faster charging with up to 12 hours’ worth recharged in just 15 minutes.
The ceramic Series 12 sure does look and feel nice in person. The night blue version is very fetching, but the stark pearl white is also très chic on the wrist. The new dark bronze did look a lot darker in person, however. Like how the dark green Series 7 looked a bit less green and more blackish green, there’s a similar vibe with the bronze.
[Image: See what I mean about the bronze color? https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/darkbronze.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The Series 12 runs on a new S11 chip that powers a few new Audio Intelligence Siri AI features, including Sound Recognition, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It also got some health upgrades, including new optical and electrical heart sensors with support for continuous background heart rate sensing that takes readings every five seconds. There’s also a new Health Age feature that compares your health metrics to your chronological age, and a Readiness feature that gives you a score for how to handle the day ahead based on your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score. The Readiness feature will be limited to the Series 12 and Ultra 4, however, because it requires the new heart rate sensor array.
[Image: You can see the difference between the sensor array on the Ultra 4 and the Ultra 3 (right). https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/sensorultra4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Speaking of the array, this is the first major update on this front in a while. You can definitely see the difference side by side. Notably, the Apple reps on hand pointed out that the new Series 12 and Ultra 4 have a “32-petal design,” whereas the older watches had a two-petal design. This refers to the spoke-like lines coming out of the electrode. It should theoretically enable much more accurate readings. You can also see that the optical sensors themselves are situated much closer together. This is to help minimize light leakage.
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 also includes the new S11 chip and Audio Intelligence features. It starts at $799 and comes in natural and black titanium, along with a premium Apple Watch Hermès version. Apple says the Ultra 4 offers up to 50 hours of battery life.
articles.author: Victoria Song

articles.title: Here’s how the new iPhone 18 Pro stacks up to the last-gen models
articles.summary:
Apple's release cadence for the latest iPhones is unusual. It'll start with the 18 Pro models, then with the foldable iPhone Duo releasing in October for $1,999. It hasn't confirmed when its base iPhone 18 model will launch. So this post is focused just on the new the 18 Pro and the 18 Pro Max.
Both phones are launching on September 18th, with preorders opening Saturday, September 12th. The 6.3-in
articles.body:
Apple’s release cadence for the latest iPhones is unusual. It’ll start with the 18 Pro models, then with the foldable iPhone Duo releasing in October for $1,999. It hasn’t confirmed when its base iPhone 18 model will launch. So this post is focused just on the new the 18 Pro and the 18 Pro Max.
Both phones are launching on September 18th, with preorders opening Saturday, September 12th. The 6.3-inch iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, which is $100 more than last year’s phone. The 6.9-inch iPhone 18 Pro Max goes up to $1,299, another $100 jump.
With the iPhone 18 Pro being Apple’s 2026 flagship phone, it makes sense to compare it to its two predecessors to see how things have evolved. The biggest differences between the two sizes of this year’s Pro phone are the same as always: the physical dimensions, the battery size, and the size and resolution of the screen. The specs are otherwise identical. But compared to previous Pros, the most meaningful updates come with the cameras, performance, and speed for chewing through AI-related tasks.
By holding off on unveiling its base iPhone 18 until a later date, Apple is making deciding on a new phone this fall a little easier — that is, if you’re someone who typically buys the pricey Pro variant. Whether you’re ready to upgrade or not, we’ve got the specs below to make it simple to compare the specs of the most popular high-end phones of 2026.

articles.title: Hands-on with the foldable iPhone Duo
articles.summary:
The first foldable iPhone is finally here, and following its announcement, we got the chance to try the phone for ourselves. We've long been told that Apple would make a foldable iPhone once the tech was good enough - has it been worth the wait?
It definitely feels like something different. The inner screen has a decidedly matte finish that handled even some glare from the windows above the hands-
articles.body:
The first foldable iPhone is finally here, and following its announcement, we got the chance to try the phone for ourselves. We’ve long been told that Apple would make a foldable iPhone once the tech was good enough — has it been worth the wait?
It definitely feels like something different. The inner screen has a decidedly matte finish that handled even some glare from the windows above the hands-on area well. The folding mechanism is smooth, and even IP68 rated, and the crease is almost impossible to find with my finger. The 5.4-inch outer screen looks petite by modern slab phone standards.
The real show happens when you open and close the phone — rather than just switching one screen off and lighting the other one up, there’s a gradual transition that happens, and it looks as if the contents of the screen come into focus as it moves toward its final position. It’s a pretty nice touch.
I also saw the phone positioned in laptop mode with Netflix on the inner screen, displaying controls on the bottom half before fading them away. There’s also the usual tricks in tent mode, where you’ll get StandBy even if you don’t have the phone plugged in. I’m very curious to see what that does to battery life.
Rumors that a foldable iPhone was in the works have been circulating since at least 2017, with Samsung releasing its first foldable two years after that. Since then, almost every Android manufacturer has entered the market, including Google, Motorola, Huawei, Xiaomi, Oppo, and more. 
Over the last decade, Apple has been variously reported to be developing traditional book-style folding iPhones, smaller flip phone variants, and even larger foldable iPads, before it eventually settled on its final form factor. While early rumors suggested it would be like having two iPhone Airs side by side, the 1.4:1 aspect ratio is squatter, closer to a passport book when closed. That makes the 7.6-inch internal screen wider and better suited for watching videos in landscape than other foldables, but great for reading long scrolling pages or multitasking in portrait.
The dual main camera setup shoots 48-megapixel photos and includes a 2x optical zoom. It’s largely the same as the iPhone 18 Pro but lacks the variable aperture.
articles.author: Allison Johnson

articles.title: Harvey hits $15.5B valuation, months after reaching $11B
articles.summary: The legal AI startup and VC darling has nearly doubled its valuation in nine months.
articles.body:
11:34 AM PDT · September 9, 2026
Harvey, the legal AI startup that VCs can’t get enough of, has raised another $550 million in funding, this time at a $15.5 billion valuation, the company announced on Wednesday.
The round was co-led by Diffusion and Lightspeed Venture Partners and follows the previous $200 million round at an $11 billion valuation announced in March. And that was just a few months after an $8 billion valuation from a round in December.
With this latest infusion of capital, the company has raised more than $1.55 billion total and nearly doubled its valuation in about nine months. Like Databricks, the company didn’t name the round, though it has completed at least eight priced rounds since 2023 (five of them since 2025), PitchBook estimates. Since a couple of those were considered extension rounds, this one could be considered a Series F.
The fresh cash comes a couple of weeks after Harvey announced its first in-house model, Harvey Tenet, built from open-weight model Kimi K3 and post-trained with legal data with the help of inference provider Fireworks (which also helped Cursor train its homegrown model). In addition to offering a model, Harvey is encouraging its customers to adopt and post-train their own open-weight models. So Harvey is quickly becoming an example of how an entire industry — law — can both heavily use AI and not rely on proprietary frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.

articles.title: Man charged with assisting Russian intelligence service
articles.summary: Joshua Cammidge will appear in court on Thursday accused of two offences under the National Security Act.
articles.body: A 31-year-old British man has been charged under the National Security Act over alleged contact with Russia's military intelligence agency.Joshua Cammidge, from Swindon, allegedly received instructions from an individual believed to be linked to the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said.He has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.He is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday.Cammidge was arrested at an address in Swindon on Friday by Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London officers, supported by officers from Wiltshire Police.He was taken to a London police station and searches were carried out at a different address in Swindon, the Metropolitan Police said.He was further arrested and detained under the National Security Act on Saturday.The force said he has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service contrary to Section 3 of the National Security Act 203 and preparatory conduct contrary to Section 18 of the National Security Act 2023.Frank Ferguson, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings."We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial."It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."Security Minister Dan Jarvis said: "The police have taken action against a potential threat, and I thank them for the vital work they do every day to keep us safe."Whilst it would be inappropriate to comment further on the specifics of this case, I know people will be concerned about recent incidents across Europe, intended to sow fear, create disruption and undermine support for Ukraine. They will not succeed."
