articles.title: Fury says he is looking for new opponent, calls out Usyk
articles.summary: Tyson Fury has sparked more speculation his all-British heavyweight fight with Anthony Joshua is on the verge of collapse by suggesting he needs a new opponent for November.
articles.body: Tyson Fury claims he is looking for a new opponent for November and has called out Oleksandr Usyk despite being contracted to fight Anthony Joshua next.The all-British heavyweight showdown is being targeted for November, with both Joshua and Fury signing individual contracts for the contest.But the issue of where the fight takes place has caused a delay in an official announcement with organisers pushing to stage it in the US rather than Joshua's preferred location of Wembley Stadium.In an expletive-laden video posted on Instagram, Fury claimed Joshua was backing out of the fight."This will only lead me to a fight with Oleksandr Usyk," he said."Oleksandr you're his [Joshua's] trainer and his sensei and you know he is weak minded... and that he would never fight the Gypsy King which you have had the guts to do twice."You got the decisions last time, fair play to you. "Good luck to you, let's do it again. Let's run it back in November. The ball is now in your court... do you want to fight me this year, 2026, or are you calling it quits? "Let me know because I am now looking for a new opponent."Fury has twice lost to Usyk, with the two-time undisputed heavyweight champion now working with Joshua as part of his training and coaching team.Sela, Queensberry and Matchroom declined to comment on whether talks had broken down when contacted by BBC Sport.Saudi Arabian promoter Sela is fronting the bill for the prospective Joshua-Fury fight, with both men signing separate contracts with the company.Joshua's contract stipulates it must take place in the UK, leading to his promoter Eddie Hearn renegotiating details in that deal.But after London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan made a public plea for the fight to happen at Wembley, Hearn said talks about staging it in the UK had "re-opened".Sela and broadcaster Netflix are understood to favour New York's Madison Square Garden.BBC Sport understands Sela has contacted the London mayor's office in recent weeks about bringing the long-awaited contest to the national stadium, but have not progressed talks further since last week.Hearn had said he hoped an announcement could happen in the coming week, but that now seems unlikely given the latest developments. A bout at Wembley may need to happen in the early hours - which would draw in a larger television audience in the US.Khan says his team would back such a proposal."A message to the promoters - we want to host it in London. Talk to us, we're really keen to have it," Khan told BBC Sport on Thursday."I'm hoping the promoters understand that not only will you get 100,000 people watching this bout live, you'll get millions watching it across the globe, where both boxers are cheered on by their loyal fans."

articles.title: Smaller rugby ball for women makes it 'harder to do my job'
articles.summary: A smaller ball is being trialled in women's international rugby union for September and October's WXV Global Series - and it is dividing opinion.
articles.body: England will play Australia, Canada and New Zealand in the next three weeks and, like all the world's top women's players, they have some new equipment: a smaller ball.During September and October's WXV Global Series, World Rugby is trialling a size 4.5 ball - about 3% smaller than the size five used in the men's game, but the same weight.Their introduction has not been without controversy and for England hooker May Campbell, responsible for throwing the ball in at the line-out, told BBC Sport it can go "a bit skew-whiff".One of England's kickers, Helena Rowland, has found a much bigger margin for error with the smaller ball, saying: "If you get it slightly wrong, the difference is massive."The fly-half says England players have noticed passes "dying", falling to the floor earlier than expected, "which they wouldn't have done previously".Not all feedback has been negative. Wales wing Lisa Neumann is a fan, saying "it's changed the game" for her passing because of improved grip on the ball.The thinking behind the trial is that the smaller ball will suit women's physiology and improve their skillset. In other sports, like basketball, women use a smaller ball, and in athletics sprint hurdles are lower for females.But Rowland says she has never felt "hindered" by playing with the same size ball as in men's rugby.Players with a specific skillset may find the change harder than others. Hookers must throw in at a line-out, scrum-halves are the most frequent passers and fly-halves the most regular kickers.Rowland explained: "We've learned for however long how to kick with a size five."So I've had 13-odd years of doing that and training my routine and trying to nail that and get as much consistency as I can."So it's about, I suppose, trying to pack all those years of training and all those kicks into a four- or five-week block to get used to it, to then go out on to the world stage."Rowland added that she has not "necessarily seen any positives", saying: "I know some of the girls have said that from an offload perspective, it's maybe made them more confident."But for me, it hasn't. I don't think there's enough of a change in the ball for me to be able to be running around with it in one hand and offloading left, right and centre."I haven't necessarily found any of the positive impacts. I've just found it a bit harder to do my job."A World Rugby spokesperson said everyone involved in the WXV Global Series, including players, coaches and match officials, would have their views taken into account "with equal value" through surveys.One area of concern for the England players is the ball changing shape.Campbell says they "played around" with how much the ball was blown up, adding: "In previous weeks it was actually a bit fatter, and then this week it definitely feels smaller."Rowland agrees, saying: "There needs to be a bit more done in terms of how the balls are made. We had some new balls today versus the ones we've had for the last three weeks [and the difference] is massive."If you've been training with an old ball that's fat to then go into a game and it's a completely different shape, actually that makes a massive difference as well, which I think is something that you don't necessarily find so much in the size five."The ball has already been trialled in the Under-18s and Under-20s Women's Six Nations as well as the HSBC Sevens Series.Rowland says she would "love to see the data on if it actually has made a difference".It seems a fair request, and is one that BBC Sport put to World Rugby, but we did not receive any data.A spokesperson said: "The balls haven't been used in the international XVs environment yet so there isn't directly comparable data to share with players either directly or via their unions."Once we've built up a large enough data set of player responses, match official responses and game data, we'll publish the results, so it'll be available to players, unions, the International Rugby Players Association, coaches, match officials, the media and everyone else."Some players are frustrated as they feel they have become guinea pigs on the global stage. To compound that frustration, they will then return to their clubs where the league season will be played with a size five ball once again.BBC Sport asked World Rugby when the trial period is likely to conclude, and were told: "We'll be able to assess our position on women's 15s once the international window has started. "This will allow for completion of the WXV tournaments and full analysis in early 2027. The evidence to date suggests that further exposure produces greater results."While it looks like players and coaches will get to see the data in early 2027, any wider outcomes or decisions might take longer.

articles.title: Indonesia volcano eruption leaves 270,000 stranded as airports extend closure
articles.summary: Anak Krakatau, which lies about 150km from the capital Jakarta, began erupting late on Friday.
articles.body: Snaking queues formed at the departure halls in Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.Finna, who was supposed to fly home to Jakarta from Malang, a city in East Java, on Sunday morning, described the frezny at the airport as flights got repeatedly rescheduled."It was very crowded because passengers from the morning flights had piled up, while those scheduled for later departures still didn't know what would happen," the 46-year-old told BBC Indonesian. "We were all glued to the flight information screens."Not wanting to deal with the uncertainty, Finna eventually spent the night on two intercity trains before arriving in Jakarta at 03:00 on Monday."Everyone seems to be racking their brains [figuring alternative transportation options]", said Jo Shaw, who was visiting Indonesia with members of her conservation charity Save the Rhino International. Shaw's team had axed their plans to camp out at Java's Ujung Kulon National Park after authorities raised its alert level for the Anak Krakatau volcano."Being stranded in an airport hotel is a relatively minor inconvenience to be resolved in a few days hopefully," Shaw said, adding that she was more concerned about the teams working on the ground with the rhinos under such environmental conditions.A newly wed Malaysian couple who had just spent a week in Bali said they were told that the next flight back to Kuala Lumpur wouldn't be until 11 September."What are we going to do here for another five days? We only prepared enough money for our honeymoon and [were supposed] to go home yesterday," Amir Hamzah told Malaysia's national news agency Bernama."We thought we would just sleep at the airport for a few hours and then take the morning flight home [on Monday]. We never thought we would end up being stuck here for days," the 29-year-old said.On Monday, Indonesia's Geological Agency warned that "the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high".Volcanic ash reached as high as 6,000m on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000m on the Sumatra side and in some parts of Java's westernmost province Banten, the meteorological agency BMKG said.Anak Krakatau sits on the Sunda Strait about midway between the islands of Java and Sumatra.The most recent eruption occurred at 20:23 on Sunday, according to the agency."We ‌cannot ascertain when this ‌will end due to the dynamic weather," Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said in relation to the temporary closures of the affected airports.Dudy said on Sunday that authorities across the airports have been conducting tests every 30 minutes "to anticipate whether the ash spread is widening or subsiding".Authorities have warned against approaching or engaging in activities within a 3km radius from the active crater, while ships passing through the Sunda Strait have also been prohibited from entering an exclusion zone of 3km radius from it.Authorities have also confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano.Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.The volcano collapsed in December 2018 triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java.Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high.The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand.Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes.With reporting by Farida Susanty in Jakarta and Koh Ewe in Singapore

articles.title: Cost of living on many minds ahead of Manx election
articles.summary: Residents, businesses and charities are focused on the economy ahead of the general election.
articles.body: Image source, Manx ScenesImage caption, Growing the economy has been billed as a top priority for the majority of candidatesResidents, businesses, and charities say they are feeling the pinch of rising costs, with many describing the economy as a key priority ahead of the Isle of Man general election.Several independent shops in Ramsey said custom was down and running costs had become harder to manage, while the island's foodbank said demand for support had doubled in two years.The Isle of Man Chamber of Commerce warned the Island faced "a very hard five years" ahead, citing a shrinking tax base and the recent loss of many high‑earning jobs.Candidates have been urged to explain how they will fund their plans, support businesses, and reduce the pressures on working families.Residents in Douglas said rising prices were affecting everyday life, with several describing the cost of living as their biggest concern ahead of the election.Sharon Cox, from Douglas, said life was "not affordable.. especially for older people and vulnerable people". Prices were rising "not just by pennies", but by "25 or 30 pence" each time she visited the shops, she added. Image caption, Sharon Cox said daily life on the Isle of Man had become unaffordableMum-of-one Caitlin Gibson said she was living with her mum and struggled to save anything while caring for her young daughter. She said: "I can't really afford to move out. I can't afford to save anything, so everything I earn, which is very little in the first place, is going on my baby."Another Douglas resident, Andrew Cairns, said rising fuel and energy costs were having "a massive impact". Image caption, Andrew Cairns said he could notice prices rising month on month"Petrol is going up, electric, gas. You've only got to go in a shop a month apart and you can see the prices rising," he added.He said it was something on his mind ahead of election, adding there was "a lot we can do to cut down our costs".A number of businesses described the last few years as some of the hardest they had faced.Image caption, Tania Dolores has run a shoe and accessory store in Ramsey for more than 10 yearsTania Dolores, from Tania Dolores Shoes and Accessories, said: "Every day is a struggle. We are not making what we used to make." She said her takings were "exactly the same amount of money as ten years ago", but that her bills were "much higher".Amy Salter, from the Brunch cafe, said the cost of supplies and energy had changed how the family business operated.When the business opened three years ago, it was "a lot easier than it is now", she said, adding that even small price rises in stock were having a big impact. Image caption, Linda Murphy wanted candidates to be looking out for small businessesLinda Murphy, from Oma Sustainable Living, said footfall dropped sharply after government services were removed from the Post Office earlier this year.She said she wanted to see in charge "somebody who understands and is looking out for small businesses, somebody who understands the value of the community, the high street and what it benefits".'Not earning enough'Chairman of the Isle of Man Foodbank David Gawne said the third sector was also seeing the impact, and said the charity had become "something of a barometer" for the island's economic pressures."Two years ago, we were giving out 200 parcels a month. We're now giving out 400 parcels a month and we're pushing that boundary now," he said.He explained that 80% of people it supported were working full time, but "not earning enough now to be able to support themselves or support their family". Gawne said many families were living on a financial knife-edge."A lot of people are just one payday away from relying on the food bank… that is a reality for a lot of people."He called for the next administration to prioritise the economy.Image caption, Claire Watterson said the next House of Keys needed to be ready for a tough five yearsBusiness lobby group the Isle of Man Chamber of Commerce said the island was entering "a very hard five years" of economic challenges, warning that pressures on public finances and the loss of high‑earning jobs had created a difficult environment for both households and businesses.She said that after decades of economic growth, the latest statistics released by government showed the economy had declined by 7.4% in the two years to March 2024.And she added that in the last year, a thousand jobs had been lost in the export sector, which included financial, insurance, and manufacturing sectors.She described the figures as "incredibly concerning", with the true impact of artificial intelligence on the workplace yet to be quantified.Watterson called for an election focus on national issues rather than local."What we are voting for in September is our national government… how we are going to grow the Isle of Man economy and set us apart on an international stage," she said.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover on the Isle of ManMore like thisRelated internet links

articles.title: Switzerland's Federal Government Is Replacing Microsoft on 3k Computers
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://itsfoss.com/news/switzerland-replace-microssoft-pilot/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49594251
Points: 178
# Comments: 125
articles.body:
Switzerland's federal government has launched a pilot program to replace Microsoft 365 with open source alternatives across 3,000 workstations. That's about 7% of the federal workforce. The target is to complete the migration by end of 2027. This move follows a successful proof-of-concept and a new digital sovereignty law. A separate fast-track military migration is also already underway.The great migration goes into the pilot phaseThe Federal Chancellery is investing CHF 9 million in an open-source workplace rollout for 3,000 federal employees.On September 3, 2026, the Federal Council published results of "PoC BOSS", a feasibility proof-of-concept involving 172 federal employees who tested the openDesk suite, a German open-source collaboration platform.During the proof-of-concept phase, core office tasks like document processing and email received positive assessments, while large-scale video conferencing still showed technical limitations.Based on the 'success' of the PoC phase with 172 employees, the pilot is now launched for 3,000 employees. Do note that during the pilot phase, the new system runs in parallel with Microsoft 365 rather than replacing it outright. That's okay, I think. Migration of such kind should be gradual rather than sudden.If the pilot is successful, we might expect the migration to continue on all the 54,000 workstations owned by the federal administrations. That's my guess.Why?According to Matthias Stürmer, professor at the Bern University of Applied Sciences (BFH), Microsoft’s supremacy in public institutions poses three problems that are driving this migration.First is the risk of foreign access. US cloud legislation could expose Swiss government data to foreign authorities.Second is the risk to service continuity, as dependency on a single foreign vendor creates operational risk.The third risk is the escalating costs as proprietary licensing fees are rising with no Swiss leverage.Swiss Army is already moving fasterSwitzerland's military cybersecurity unit, Cyber Command, is not waiting for the civilian pilot. It is already poised to replace Microsoft 365 entirely with openDesk by October 2026.It is pretty much the same reason. Military doesn't want foreign governments accessing sensitive Swiss data.Part of a bigger planBack in 2024, the EMBAG Law came into effect. It requires all Swiss federal agencies to publish government-developed software as open source by default. The law also aims to promote digital sovereignty and encourage innovation and collaboration within the public sector.Then in December 2025, the Federal Council designated digital sovereignty as a primary focus theme. It defines digital sovereignty as "the federal government being able to fulfil its essential mission without depending on an external supplier or country."Which is essentially moving away from big tech companies from the USA. Neighboring France and Germany have also been trying similar moves. Let's hope that the great Swiss migration succeeds and sets an example for other countries who may speed up their own plan of moving away from Microsoft.By the way, Microsoft has deep pockets, so they are also investing over CHF 325 million to expand AI and cloud infrastructure in Switzerland, partly to reduce the sovereignty argument.Let's see how things move from here, but so far, it is looking positive for us open source supporters.Source: RTS

articles.title: New videos of man at centre of 9/11 lawsuit reveal links to extremists and Saudi state
articles.summary: The footage and other evidence the FBI failed to share undermine Omar al-Bayoumi's 25 years of denials.
articles.body: The man at the heart of a $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought by 9/11 families had extensive links to Saudi government officials and went paintballing with one of al-Qaeda's future leaders, video obtained by the BBC reveals.The footage, which the FBI had within days of the 2001 attacks, stands in stark contrast to Omar al-Bayoumi's 25 years of denials that he was an extremist and a Saudi spy.Bayoumi, who claimed to be a student when he was in the United States, is seen in one clip embracing Anwar al-Awlaki, who would go on to lead al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. In another, Bayoumi and Awlaki are paintballing near San Diego with an official from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Islamic Affairs.The videos form part of the 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia and have never been shown publicly before.The lawsuit argues Saudi Arabia was complicit in the attacks and that Bayoumi aided two of the 19 hijackers who flew planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon - with another crashing in Pennsylvania.Bayoumi was arrested in the UK by the Metropolitan Police days after the attacks and the videos were found among his possessions, along with other crucial evidence.This included a diagram of a plane with a flight descent equation written alongside.Multiple FBI agents received copies of the diagram, but it was never shared with the British interrogators, even though it had been couriered to the police station where Bayoumi was being held in custody.The diagram was also kept from some FBI agents investigating Bayoumi, as well as from the 9/11 Commission - the independent inquiry into the largest mass murder in US history, in which nearly 3,000 people were killed. Bayoumi was never prosecuted.He and the Saudi government did not respond to the BBC's requests for comment, but both have always denied any involvement in, or prior knowledge of, the attacks. The FBI declined to comment.After a judge ruled the lawsuit could go ahead in 2018, thousands of documents, as well as videos and photographs, have been released to the court and also declassified through an executive order made by former President Joe Biden.BBC Panorama and Radio 4 have examined these documents, and spoken to dozens of special agents and investigators, to trace the evidence the FBI gathered about Bayoumi and Saudi Arabia's alleged involvement in 9/11 - and to understand why it was never fully pursued over 25 years.Our investigation also found:The plane diagram was sent to the FBI's New York office and was analysed, according to an FBI source. But a US Department of Justice (DOJ) official told the BBC he was never shown a proposal to prosecute Bayoumi based on the evidence, even though "we've convicted people for less"FBI agents in San Diego, where Bayoumi had lived in the US, repeatedly requested copies of evidence but never received most of itThe San Diego and Los Angeles FBI offices were both blocked from interviewing Bayoumi's Saudi government contactsStaff on the 9/11 Commission objected to the conclusion that Bayoumi was "unlikely" to have been involved with extremists, prompting the report to attribute this to "our investigators who have dealt directly with him"Omar al-Bayoumi arrived in San Diego from Saudi Arabia in 1994. He claimed to be studying English, but court records show that within a few years he had, in effect, abandoned his studies. He was more usually found organising religious events, often with a camcorder pressed to his eye.One video Bayoumi filmed, from 1997 or early 1998, shows men, including Anwar al-Awlaki, paintballing. Filmed near San Diego, the group engages in urban combat scenes and target practice, many wearing military fatigues.At one point, some of the men charge into battle, shouting "Allahu Akbar". A visiting Saudi sheikh is with the group and Bayoumi can also be heard addressing Anwar al-Awlaki with the honorific "Sheikh Anwar".The following morning, in Birmingham, officers began the meticulous process of logging and bagging up evidence in his properties - a cache of many thousands of pages of documents, hundreds of photographs, flight ticket stubs, phone cards, and carrier bags and boxes containing at least 80 videotapes.Within hours of the search starting, several items of documentary evidence - categorised as the highest priority at the direction of the FBI - were taken by police directly to Paddington Green, where the FBI had stationed an agent.This evidence included a phone book containing more than two dozen names of Saudi government officials in the US and Saudi Arabia; flight simulator software; tickets and travel documents; and the yellow lined page of a notebook with the sketch of a plane, which an officer had marked: "contains handwritten notes mathematical calculations re height of planes".Eighteen years later, the FBI would hand the notebook page to the court in the 9/11 families' lawsuit, following a subpoena. The page was made public in 2022."It's the mathematical calculation of the crash," Jodi Westbrook Flowers, a member of the 9/11 families' legal team, told the BBC. "When we figured out what it was, we knew that it was the smoking gun that we'd been looking for."The equation, written in Omar al-Bayoumi's handwriting, indicates the height and distance required for a pilot to guide an aeroplane to a given object on the ground. Underneath it is a small drawing of a plane and a series of numbers.Last year, the federal judge in the families' lawsuit found the notebook page, on the face of it, "connects Bayoumi with knowledge of the 9/11 Attacks".In 2021, when questioned about it in court, Bayoumi said he had the diagram because he liked finding equations and could not remember when he had written it.By the evening of 22 September 2001, copies of the plane diagram were in London in the hands of both the FBI and UK counter-terror police - and just metres from the custody suite where Omar al-Bayoumi was being questioned. Records show they passed through at least three further FBI agents in the following two days.But here, the mystery begins. The FBI briefed the Met officers to question Bayoumi about the other high-priority exhibits, but the detectives in the custody suite were never given, or briefed about, the plane diagram.Many FBI agents have told us the immediate aftermath of 9/11 was a round-the-clock frenzy. But it is hard to understand how a piece of evidence of this importance, in a case being handled with considerable urgency, was not put into the hands of the interviewing detectives.The FBI declined to respond to our questions. The Metropolitan Police told us it could not comment because of the ongoing legal case.On the day he would need to be charged or released, the Met detectives joined a conference call with several senior officials from the US Department of Justice and FBI.Panorama and Radio 4 have spoken to two participants at the meeting. One recalls the British detectives setting out the evidence they believed met the threshold for the Americans to extradite Bayoumi to face charges in the US.The response from the DOJ officials was that no extradition would be sought because there was insufficient evidence.On 28 September 2001, Bayoumi was released.But, at that point, the FBI had not shipped all of the evidence found in Birmingham back to the US, let alone exhaustively analysed it.One memorandum from the FBI's legal attache in London, sent two weeks later, noted there were a "number of videos, floppy disks and documentation still to be viewed".After Omar al-Bayoumi's release, agents continued analysing the evidence against him.The BBC understands the plane diagram was couriered from London for analysis at the New York Field Office, which was in overall charge of the 9/11 investigation.But we have not been able to trace any records of this analysis or its conclusions. A 2021 Presidential order required the FBI to declassify files relating to its 9/11 investigations, including into Bayoumi.However, of the files released, the FBI has only produced one document referring to the diagram, despite its evidential significance, and this was only created 11 years after the diagram's initial discovery in 2001.The diagram seems to have fallen into a black hole.It was not passed on to San Diego, where Bayoumi had lived in the USA and where the FBI Field Office was also investigating him.In fact, San Diego - where agents were interviewing his associates, searching his mosque, analysing his telephone records and bank statements - received almost none of the large volume of evidence seized by the Met Police in Birmingham. Rick Lambert, who ran the FBI's investigation there, told the BBC his office made repeated requests to New York to send copies of all the evidence. "Their position was, we're in charge of the case; we'll send it to you when we're finished analysing."Lambert said New York did not comply his office's requests. "I believe there is the potential that had we received that evidence and analysed it, that we would have been able to put the pieces of the puzzle together much more quickly."Documents show that, in spring 2002, the San Diego office was ultimately able to get copies of a handful of videos by obtaining them not from New York, but from the FBI liaison in London.Jeffrey Breinholt, then the deputy director of counter-terrorism at the Department of Justice who oversaw prosecutors working on terrorism charges after 9/11, told the BBC that Bayoumi's name had come up "as one of the hot possibilities for charges".But he said the New York Attorney's Office never sent charges to him or his colleagues for approval. If they had, the plane diagram would have been significant evidence against Bayoumi, he said. "We've convicted people for less."The paintballing video, Breinholt told us, is another "very telling bit of evidence" with the presence of Anwar al-Awlaki being "pretty damn significant"."As a manager who reviewed a lot of proposed terrorism cases over the years, I can tell you that that would have jumped out. I think it would be a material support charge against Bayoumi."There were no charges brought against Bayoumi.Agents who tried to investigate Omar al-Bayoumi encountered other roadblocks.In October 2001 in San Diego, Lambert and colleagues wanted to interview a number of Saudi officials in the US - many connected to the Ministry of Islamic Affairs - who they suspected had co-ordinated the help Bayoumi gave to two of the hijackers, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar.Because diplomats have a special protected status, the agents needed permission from FBI headquarters and the State Department."The answer came back, 'no, you're not going to do that'," Lambert, who is now a consultant for the 9/11 families in their lawsuit, told us.Agents in Los Angeles experienced a similar outcome the following year, when they applied to interview a Saudi religious diplomat Bayoumi had met immediately after his first encounter with Hazmi and Mihdhar in the city."We hit a roadblock so hard, I think we all had airbag burns," said Steve Moore, who oversaw the FBI's 9/11 investigation in LA. Moore says his team made repeated requests to interview the official, but permission never came.Like the FBI, the State Department declined to comment.In October 2003, the 9/11 Commission - set up by Congress to provide a "full and complete" account of the attacks - interviewed Omar al-Bayoumi in Riyadh. He had returned to Saudi Arabia in the months after his release by British police.The interview was conducted, in the presence of Saudi secret police, by the Commission's executive director Philip Zelikow, a former advisor to President George W Bush, along with a senior staffer and an agent from FBI headquarters.The Commission's notes from the time record that Bayoumi was given a remarkable degree of reassurance during the interview. He "was told that no-one believes he knowingly helped the hijackers carry out their terrorist mission".Bayoumi indignantly said he was a peace-lover who had become "a victim of the victims". During the interview, the delegation broke away for a multi-course dinner hosted by the Mabahith, the secret police, without Bayoumi.After the interview concluded, the Mabahith told the American delegation they "would like to see him cleared". The Americans responded that no exoneration would be possible before their report was published.When the 9/11 Commission Report was published in July 2004, Bayoumi was, in effect, cleared. It described him as "obliging and gregarious" and stated there was no evidence he had extremist views.But some staff on the Commission were not convinced of Bayoumi's innocence, and thought it likely he knew Hazmi and Mihdhar were al Qaeda operatives.The BBC can reveal that those staff objected to a line in the report concluding that he was "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists".In the end, a compromise was agreed, and this conclusion was attributed to "our investigators who have dealt directly with him and studied his background".The line was written based on the four and a half hours the Commission delegation had spent with Bayoumi, which included the interruption for dinner.The Commission never saw the plane diagram, the paintballing video, written evidence of Bayoumi's alleged extremism, or much of the rest of the evidence the Met Police had seized.Philip Zelikow did not answer the specific questions we asked him. He told the BBC the 9/11 Commission's findings had been subject to two government reviews, in 2015 and 2021, and the Commission had been "open about our suspicions and uncertainties. We were careful about whom to accuse of complicity in mass murder."The Department of Justice told us it was unable to comment on matters and decisions from 25 years ago, involving staff who no longer worked there.The head of the FBI's 9/11 investigation, Mary Galligan, has previously stated the Commission had "access to everything".We tried to contact Omar al-Bayoumi through the Saudi government, but he did not respond. He has previously denied knowing Hazmi and Mihdhar were hijackers, that he was a Saudi spy, and that he had any involvement in 9/11.The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia did not respond to our request for comment. It has previously said any allegation that Saudi Arabia or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.

articles.title: Chemo hair loss doesn't define me - it's a symbol that I'm strong
articles.summary: The beauty and resilience of women living with cancer is celebrated though photography.
articles.body: Chemo hair loss doesn't define me - it's a symbol that I'm strongImage source, Caroline SikkenkImage caption, Rhiannon is one of 11 Welsh women who have been photographed for The Pink Ribbon Foundation's BOLD campaignUpdated 7 September 2026 06:15 BSTWhen Rhiannon Thomas lost her hair during chemotherapy just weeks after having a mastectomy, her confidence was at an all time low. But being photographed for a campaign that celebrates the resilience of women living with breast cancer helped her find an inner strength she never knew she had. "For the first time I feel I look pretty, I look confident and strong," said the 36-year-old mum."It's surprising the strength you find when you go through such a hard time."Image source, Rhiannon ThomasImage caption, Rhiannon Thomas recently completed her chemotherapyRhiannon, a mother to two daughters aged 14 and nine, was diagnosed with breast cancer after finding a lump while in the shower in November 2025. "I had an absolute breakdown," said the teaching assistant."Like, how do you tell your children? I was so scared to just tell them."Since then she's had a mastectomy, chemotherapy and is currently having radiotherapy. When her hair began falling out during chemotherapy she decided to shave her head, but wanted to make it as positive an experience as possible for her children. She encouraged her youngest to play at being a hairdresser and do whatever she wanted with a scissors before getting the shaver out. "I was like, 'just cut whatever you want because it's going anyway'," said Rhiannon."I wanted to make something hard joyful for my children and for myself because I didn't want them to see me upset, and my daughter loved it."Image source, Rhiannon ThomasImage caption, When Rhiannon was diagnosed with breast cancer her first thought was her childrenFootage captured on her phone shows the family laughing at home in Abertridwr, near Caerphilly, as her daughter got creative with the scissors.But afterwards, in private moments, the radical change to her appearance was hard."I remember looking in the mirror and like just crying because it's just you know we don't recognise yourself," she said.Rhiannon was brought to tears recalling the look on her parents' faces when they first saw her after her head had been shaved. She took to wearing a head wrap whenever she left the house. Image source, Caroline SikkenkImage caption, Sam Gronow-Walters says she is proud of her portraitsAll this sounds very familiar to mental health nurse and mother-of-two Sam Gronow-Walters.The 44-year-old has also lost her hair though breast cancer treatment. Her cancer is incurable. She was first diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer, external five years ago, which was successfully treated with intravenous chemotherapy, a lumpectomy and radiotherapy, followed by oral chemotherapy.But seven months later she found another lump and tests showed it had returned.A mastectomy followed and she was told she was cancer-free. In 2024, she was told it had spread to her lung. Last July, tests showed it had spread to her liver and lymph nodes."You've got to keep going," said Sam from St Athan in the Vale of Glamorgan."You've just got to do whatever you can because I want to see my kids grow up."Image source, Caroline SikkenkImage caption, Sam was diagnosed with breast cancer five years agoLike Rhiannon, when she felt she had no option other than to shave her head, Sam's thoughts were immediately how to make it easier on her children, a daughter aged 20 and a son aged 13.  Her son requested she have her head shaved with a bit left at the front in homage to Brazilian footballer Ronaldo's memorable hairdo at  the 2002 World Cup - and she obliged."To me that that's quite a happy memory, so he'll see that even when I'm poorly I can still have fun, can still smile and I can still make my children happy and laugh," she said. Again, she was concerned about the impact her new appearance would have on her children."I used to ask my son when I took him to school, 'do you mind if I don't wear a hat?'" recalled Sam."He was like, 'why would I care?'."Image source, Sam Gronow-WaltersImage caption, Sam agreed to have her hair styled like Brazilian footballer Ronaldo's memorable hairdo in the 2002 World Cup finals Rhiannon and Sam first met after signing up to be part of breast cancer charity Pink Ribbon Foundation's BOLD Wales campaign.The project celebrates the courage and confidence of women who have lost their hair through breast cancer. Alongside nine other Welsh women they spent a day in Cardiff being photographed by Dutch photographer Caroline Sikkenk. The photos will be displayed at London's Piccadilly Lights next month.Image source, Sam Gronow-WaltersImage caption, Sam says her husband and children help her stay positiveBoth women had been nervous about being photographed but said the experience couldn't have been more joyful."It was like we'd all known each other before meeting that day, and we still keep in touch now," said Sam.Rhiannon had never spoken to another woman who had lost her hair during cancer treatment."I just felt really safe and not judged," she said.Figure caption, The beauty and resilience of women living with cancer is celebrated though photographySeeing the photos for the first time was emotional for both. "I was like, 'oh wow'," said Rhiannon, who was proud of the courage it had taken to be photographed at such a vulnerable time. Sam barely recognised herself."I was like, 'wow, that's not me'," she said."I was quite proud to show them to my family to say, 'oh, this is me'."Image caption, Rhiannon, Sam and the other women who took part in the campaign have stayed in touch after the photoshootBOLD began in 2022, when Lisa Allen from The Pink Ribbon Foundation met  photographer Caroline Sikkenk at a breast cancer conference.Caroline had spent years photographing women who had experienced hair loss through illness."What struck us about her photographs was that these women weren't being shown as patients," said Lisa. "They were strong, beautiful and completely themselves."The first BOLD shoot took place in 2023."What we hadn't anticipated was that we would create a community," said Lisa.She said the impact often began before a photograph has been taken."We set up a WhatsApp group beforehand, so by the time the women arrive they already feel they're going through it together."The friendships and support that grow around it last long after the photograph is taken."Image source, The Pink Ribbon FoundationImage caption, Lisa Allen from The Pink Ribbon Foundation, on the right pictured with Rhiannon, says a community has grown around the projectBoth women said taking part in the project had given them a new-found strength and sense of optimism."I feel like my confidence and my positivity just got stronger from the photoshoot," said Rhiannon."I walked out of there just so confident and I felt so free and like I don't have to hide."Gone are the head wraps and proudly showing her shaved head has become "the new normal".For Sam, the photoshoot helped her find self-acceptance."This is me now - I wouldn't have long hair again," she said. "Hair loss doesn't define who I am. It's just a symbol that I'm getting through this and I am strong."If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.More top stories

articles.title: More funding needed to boost construction jobs for young people, housing boss says
articles.summary: Recent analysis showed the construction sector needs an extra 2,200 workers a year to meet demand.
articles.body: Image caption, Cian Halliday, 26, became a joiner after being made redundant in recent yearsA long-term plan and additional funding is needed to create more placements for young people within the construction industry, according to one housing association boss.Iwan Trefor Jones, chief executive at Adra, said it was important that organisations worked together to make sure "that there are opportunities for young people".Adra had seen a rise in demand in its academy scheme, with one of their recent openings attracting 108 applicants for only six positions.The Welsh government said work was already under way "to boost construction skills" and new apprenticeships were set to launch later in the year. Recent analysis by the Federation of Master Builders showed that the construction sector was facing a shortfall of labour and needed an additional 2,200 workers a year in order to meet demand.Steven Walker, a construction manager with Williams Homes, said it was "really important" that more young people came into the construction industry."We have an ageing workforce across the country" he said. "It's really important that young people are being pushed through to be work ready... to be the next generation of construction workers."There was always room for more workers, he added."We can always create the space for young people to come and work on our construction sites."We buddy them up with an experienced worker, we show them the ropes, we give them the training, we look after them, we interview them regularly to see that they're OK and that they're looked after."Image caption, Steven Walker wants to see more young people getting into constructionHe mentioned schemes like Academi Adra give young people hands-on experience on the job."The classroom-based teaching is really important. It prepares them for the work... and then when they come to us, they'll actually put into practice what they've seen in the classroom.Jones said that it was vital there were enough opportunities in place."It's really important that organisations like Adra work in partnership with other organisations to make sure there are opportunities for young people."Image caption, Iwan Trefor Jones believes that a long-term plan is needed "to support the funding of placements in work, to support young people"Speaking at one of Adra's developments of over 58 social and affordable homes in Bangor, Jones said additional funding was needed to give more young people opportunities to get into the sector."There's a need for a long-term plan, but also a plan is nothing without the funding behind it," he said."We need some kind of assurance that there is a long-term plan to support the funding of placements in work, to support young people into employment and to support employers."The Academi Adra scheme was established in 2021 with the aim of providing young people with skills and experience in the workplace, offering courses in construction.Two-hundred-and-thirty participants have been supported since the launch of the scheme, with the most recent course having 108 applicants for only six positions. Elin Williams, who oversees the work of the Academi, said funding had been needed to offer more young people the chance to join similar schemes.She said: "We've been very lucky to be able to have some external grant funding to allow us to run some courses and pay for placement opportunities."We're calling for more funding for opportunities and projects like Academi Adra... We want to carry on to develop and expand to meet the rising demand that we're seeing."Image caption, Elin Williams is head of community services for AdraIn recent months, Welsh figures, external suggested the proportion of young people in Wales who are not in education, employment, or training (Neet) had risen sharply.They increased to 17% and returned to levels last seen around 2013, according to Welsh government figures.Cian Halliday, 26, a carpenter from Llanrug, had been made redundant during the Covid-19 pandemic, something he said had been "difficult, and a struggle"."Academi Adra were offering courses, and almost 16 weeks of work experience and at the end they decided to keep me on as a labourer. I did that for a year," he said."Then they offered me an apprenticeship and I chose to be a carpenter."He said that being made redundant had been very tough."It was difficult, and a struggle to find work, so I decided, the minute this opportunity came up, to start a new job."While looking for work, Cian said there had not been enough opportunities for young people like him."I was happy enough to change careers. I jumped at the opportunity and never looked back," he said.Image caption, Daniella Williams says the construction industry is "a great sector to get into"Daniella Williams, 35 also got into the construction industry after a period of not being in work following an illness."I used to work within the NHS. I had problems with my health and I had children, so left that job, and I really wanted to get into an office-based job," she said.Williams followed a course with Academi Adra to get into an administrative role."It's changed mine and my children's lives... I've been able to save, I've bought my own car, and it's given me so much more confidence," she said. "I've been able to achieve so much that I wasn't able to before, and it's inspired my children as well to go on and do bigger and better than myself."Williams said she was also passionate about helping inspire young girls to follow careers in the construction industry."'I work with schools... especially to get girls into construction."It's not just bricks and building, there are all kinds of different things. We work a lot with local companies, and it's a great sector to get into, I really enjoy it."'Significant growth'Local colleges had also seen a rise in demand.Aled Jones-Griffith, CEO of Grŵp Llandrillo Menai, said there had been a "significant growth" in the number of young people who had undertaken construction.He said: "Our enrolment has increased by 28% since 2025-26 to a record 461 learners this year. "To meet this demand, we have invested significantly in redeveloping our workshops, recruiting additional staff and buying additional course resources. "However moving forwards, we need additional funding to maintain this high level of provision and effectively minimise Neets in our community."'It's about health, jobs and opportunity'With the rise in demand for homes to be built, CHC said that opportunities needed to be made to end the "housing emergency".Clarissa Corbisiero, deputy chief executive at CHC, said: "Investing in our homes is the best investment we can make in Wales' economic health."In building 20,000 new social homes over the next four years, housing associations can deliver over 14,000 jobs per year during construction."By aligning our housing goals with a bold construction skills strategy, we can turn a national emergency into a wave of opportunity for every community."Ending the housing emergency is more than bricks and mortar - it's about health, jobs and opportunity."The Welsh government said: "We are committed to developing a Welsh skills system fit for the future. Work is already under way to boost construction skills with Level 2 apprenticeships in bricklaying, site carpentry, scaffolding and building maintenance set to launch later this year. "Construction will also be included in new VCSE qualifications from September 2027."A skills audit is currently under way to provide a clear, cross government view of current and future workforce needs across Wales. "A future Skills Summit is being held this October that will bring together employers, educators, training providers and policymakers to help shape reforms to vocational skills training in Wales."More top stories

articles.title: How long could you manage on £3 of food a day?
articles.summary: It wants people to experience what it is like for people facing food insecurity.
articles.body: Food prices remain a concern and there are fears they could rise following this summer's extreme weather, which resulted in poor crop yield, and as further climate changes are predicted.A government spokesperson said it is determined to turn the tide on poverty, using schemes including a £1bn Crisis and Resilience Fund to help councils tackle food poverty."Our recent statistics show that effort is beginning to make a difference - household incomes have risen 5% in real terms, food bank usage has fallen and food insecurity is down," the spokesperson added."To ease cost-of-living pressures we have brought forward a wide range of measures including raising the National Minimum Wage, suspending tariffs on everyday staples, leading to lower prices at the till."Hannah Worsley, project manager for Norwich Food Bank, said people who had already made changes to their lifestyle since the cost-of-living crisis began were still struggling to make ends meet.She said: "Several years ago, the problem people were facing was a one-off thing, like losing a job, which was then resolved and people would be back on their feet able to cope again."Now, we're seeing people who've made cuts maybe eating less or not using certain facilities like their cooker or their washing machine and it's still not enough to live on."She hopes the £3-a-day challenge will help people empathise with people who face a daily struggle to afford food.Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below.

articles.title: Show HN: Engrim – A universal, local-first SQLite memory engine for AI CLIs
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://github.com/timgordontg/engrim
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49594008
Points: 42
# Comments: 10
articles.body:
The Universal Cross-Model & Cross-Agent Episodic Memory Store. A local-first, project-scoped SQLite memory engine that allows developers to freely switch between models and environments (Google Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor MCP, Windsurf) on the SAME project without losing architectural decisions, user constraints, or project state. 1. The Core Value Proposition "Why pay for 200,000 tokens of forgotten noise on every turn? The models are disposable utilities; your project's decisions are not." As context windows scale to 1M+ tokens, developers face attention dilution: reasoning degrades, cost multiplies with every conversational turn, and clearing context causes total amnesia. engrim replaces attention dilution with 4,000 characters of curated episodic working memory: Switzerland of AI Memory: Decouples project intelligence from any single AI vendor or proprietary cloud silo. Switch from Gemini 3.8 in Antigravity to Claude 3.7 Sonnet in Claude Code to GPT-4o in Cursor mid-project — your agents pick up right where the others left off. Save Button for Autonomous Coding: Externalize decisions, constraints, and state as you work. Clear your agent session freely (/clear) and watch context reload intact. Smart, Hot Context Loading: Combines SQLite FTS5 (bm25 keyword search) with static vector embeddings (model2vec) in a zero-latency hybrid reciprocal-rank fusion engine. 2. Empirical Proof (The 105-Session Case Study) Tested across 105 continuous sessions on a 50,000-line algorithmic trading system. Zero regressions across 186 unit tests, zero context amnesia across model switches. In production testing on an active algorithmic trading codebase running real capital: Over 153,000 tokens of work across days of architecture, parameter tuning, and debugging was consolidated into an active memory pack under 1,000 tokens (<1% of the context window). That is a 99%+ cut in reloaded context cost on every session restart. Seamlessly switched between Google Antigravity CLI, Claude Code, and Cursor MCP on identical repos with zero model drift or architectural regression. subgraph Agents ["Supported Agent Environments"] AGY["Google Antigravity
(PreInvocation & Stop Hooks)"] CLAUDE["Claude Code
(SessionStart & Stop Hooks)"] CURSOR["Cursor / Windsurf
(Model Context Protocol stdio)"] subgraph CoreEngine ["engrim Core Engine (v1.3.0)"] ADAPTERS["Adapters & Hooks
(agy, claude, mcp)"] ROUTER["Hybrid Retrieval & Minder
(bm25 lexical + vector cosine)"] subgraph Storage ["Local-First SQLite Store (~/.engrim/memory.db)"] FTS5["FTS5 Full-Text Search
(porter stemmer, triggers)"] LOG["Flight Recorder Log
(turns + action lines)"] AGY <-->|"hook / CLI"| ADAPTERS CLAUDE <-->|"hook / CLI"| ADAPTERS Run engrim setup without arguments. It automatically detects installed environments on your machine and configures them all: If ~/.gemini exists $\rightarrow$ wires Antigravity lifecycle hooks, skill, and MCP server. If ~/.claude exists $\rightarrow$ wires Claude Code SessionStart, Stop, status line, and CLAUDE.md. If ~/.cursor exists $\rightarrow$ generates and merges Cursor MCP configuration. Configures ~/.gemini/config/hooks.json to execute engrim hook --agent agy --event boot on PreInvocation and engrim hook --agent agy --event stop on Stop. Deploys the canonical Antigravity skill to ~/.gemini/config/skills/engrim/SKILL.md. Registers the MCP server in ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/mcp_config.json and ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json. Wires SessionStart, SessionEnd, Stop, and UserPromptSubmit hooks in ~/.claude/settings.json. Configures live ambient status line in Claude Code's status bar. Appends memory usage notes to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Adds engrim to ~/.cursor/mcp.json running engrim serve --mcp. Add engrim to your ~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json: Configures every supported environment in one command. (Use --dry-run with any setup command to inspect changes without modifying disk). When multiple agents collaborate on a single codebase, provenance matters. engrim records the origin of every memory entry with the origin_agent field: Allowed values: antigravity, claude-code, cursor, cli, or user. Automatically populated based on the active hook, MCP client, or CLI session. Subtly surfaced in engrim context and engrim list: 🧠 engrim · memory restored for this project — you don't have to re-explain · /workspace 18 of 54 curated records loaded (~3850 chars) · the rest one `recall` away - #961 [DECISION] (via Antigravity): Inverted stop loss matrix for high volatility (risk, execution) - #942 [DECISION] (via Claude Code): Switched primary database from MongoDB to PostgreSQL (db, schema) - #910 [DECISION] (via Cursor): Standardized on Pydantic v2 schemas across API boundaries (api, types) Existing databases are non-destructively migrated on first access via ALTER TABLE memories ADD COLUMN origin_agent TEXT. 6. Hardened Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server Launch the zero-dependency, JSON-RPC 2.0 stdio MCP server: stdout is strictly reserved for JSON-RPC messages, redirecting all diagnostic logs to stderr. (query: str, project: str = "auto", k: int = 5, type: str = None) Hybrid (keyword + semantic) search over project memory. (type: str, summary: str, detail: str = None, tags: list[str] = []) Write a durable memory record persisted across sessions. (project: str = "auto", budget: int = 4000) Retrieve the session-boot memory pack within a character budget. Check uncaptured decisions from transcript logs before clearing. engrim add -t decision -s "..." [--origin-agent agy] Insert memory record (types: decision, fact, feedback, state, user, reference). Ranked hybrid recall for the project (--log searches raw turns). engrim hook --agent agy --event boot Agent lifecycle hook runner for Antigravity and Claude Code. Start stdio MCP server for agent integrations. "Safe to clear" coverage check: scans logs for uncurated decisions. List recent memories for the current project. engrim supersede --id 12 --status superseded Mark a record superseded without erasing history. Mirror markdown memories into the store (idempotent seed-once). Capture as you work: Whenever a major decision or architectural rule is made, run engrim add or invoke engrim_add via your agent. Use resume-pointer: Before ending a session or clearing, add a record tagged resume-pointer describing the immediate next task. The newest pointer is pinned under [▶ RESUME HERE] at the top of the next session's boot pack. Verify with engrim review: Check that all recent decisions are captured. Clear freely (/clear): The session window is wiped clean; engrim automatically re-injects the active memory pack on the next prompt or invocation. 100% Local & Offline: All memory records and logs reside in a local SQLite file (~/.engrim/memory.db). No telemetry, no cloud sync, no tracking. Model Storage: Uses model2vec for local static embeddings (~30ms load time, no GPU required, runs on CPU). Can run pure-lexical (ENGRIM_EMBED=off) for zero extra dependencies. POSIX File Permissions: Databases are created with restricted owner-only permissions (0600). Git Protection: *.db is gitignored by default; your memories never accidentally commit to version control. MIT © 2026 Tim Gordon.

articles.title: TiVo to charge money for skipping commercials in your own recordings
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://cordcuttersnews.com/tivo-plans-to-end-free-automatic-commercial-skipping-in-november-tests-paid-premium-replacement-service/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49593971
Points: 89
# Comments: 46
articles.body:
TiVo has begun notifying customers of a significant change to one of its longest-standing and most popular DVR features. Starting November 2, 2026, the current version of SkipMode that allows users to jump over commercial breaks with a single button press on the remote will no longer be available. The company is instead preparing to test a new paid add-on called Premium Auto Commercial Skip.
SkipMode has been a core part of the TiVo experience for years. After a supported show finished recording, the service added markers that let viewers leap from the end of one program segment directly to the start of the next, bypassing the ads in between. On newer TiVo Experience 4 devices, users could even set the feature to automatic so commercials were skipped without any remote interaction. The feature was limited to popular prime-time programming on major networks, typically appearing a short time after a show aired.
Under the new plan, that one-button and automatic functionality will disappear from the standard service. Viewers will still be able to skip commercials the traditional way by using the 30-second skip button or the fast-forward control on their remotes. Those manual methods have existed on TiVo boxes for more than two decades and do not rely on the company’s commercial-detection data.
In November, TiVo will offer a 30-day free trial of the new Premium Auto Commercial Skip service. After the trial ends, customers who want to keep the automatic or one-button skip capability will need to add it to their accounts for an extra monthly fee. The company has not yet published the price. Additional details about how the service works, which devices and recordings it will support, and exact pricing are scheduled to be sent to customers before the November 2 cutoff.
No immediate action is required from subscribers. Existing recordings that already carry SkipMode markers will continue to function as they do today until the change takes effect. After that date, new recordings will no longer receive the free skip data.
The shift comes as TiVo’s parent company, Xperi, has moved away from manufacturing new DVR hardware and focused more on its smart-TV operating system and advertising technology. Automatic commercial skipping has long been a selling point that distinguished TiVo from cable-operator boxes and competing DVRs. Making the most convenient version of that feature an optional paid add-on represents a notable change in the company’s relationship with its remaining DVR customers.
Many longtime users have relied on SkipMode as a primary reason to keep their boxes and service subscriptions active even as live-TV viewing has declined. The new structure will force those customers to decide whether the convenience of automatic ad skipping is worth an additional monthly charge or whether they will return to manually fast-forwarding through commercials.
TiVo has said it will provide more information in the coming weeks so households can evaluate the trial and the eventual paid option before the current free feature disappears. Until then, the familiar Skip button on TiVo remotes will continue to work as it has.

articles.title: How significant are AfD's historic gains for Germany and the rest of Europe?
articles.summary: The BBC's Europe editor Katya Adler sees the far-right win in Saxony-Anhalt state ringing alarm bells for the EU and traditional parties.
articles.body: "Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany".This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunning victory of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in local elections in Germany on Sunday. Is that an exaggeration?Saxony-Anhalt is one of the smallest of massive Germany's 16 regions. It boasts a mere 1.7 million out of 59 million eligible voters nationwide. How significant can its political sentiments be, especially since the AfD narrowly failed to win an outright majority?The answer: Very significant.First and foremost, at home in Germany.The vote may have been regional but it impacts at national level. The AfD landslide piles even more pressure on the already beleaguered centrist coalition government in Berlin. It may prove to be the nail in the political coffin of Germany's deeply unpopular conservative Chancellor, Friedrich Merz. He had promised to slash the AfD's popularity.These political woes will further weaken and distract Germany, the EU's most powerful player, at a time of continental crisis - as Europe struggles to contain Russian aggression, US President Donald Trump's tariff tantrums and the economic threat from China.The Saxony-Anhalt result also provokes soul-searching throughout Germany, where the Nazi past still looms large. This is the first outstanding electoral landslide for a hard-right nationalist party - giving it a real shot at governing, in this case, at regional level - since the fall of the Third Reich in 1945.The German authorities have labelled the AfD, in part, anti-democratic and a number of regional factions of the party, including Saxony-Anhalt, far-right extremist.The AfD is well-known to be particularly popular in east Germany but it is now also polling as the biggest political party nationwide.Germany's political mainstream has failed voters, it would seem. What does Europe's biggest single economy, its most populous nation not counting Russia, do now?Tiny Saxony-Anhalt is causing waves outside Germany, too.None other than the US president swiftly posted the Saxony-Anhalt exit poll on his Truth Social platform on Sunday.The AfD's anti-immigration, anti-woke, "Germany for Germans" message chimes closely with Donald Trump's Maga [Make America Great Again] missive. Along with a number of other nationalist parties in Europe, the AfD borrows heavily from the Trump playbook - undermining mainstream media, questioning the neutrality of judges and promising to "make Germany great again".Interesting to note though - the US president is rarely name-checked on the campaign trail in Europe. Politicians are keenly aware just how unpopular he is amongst voters.Hot on Donald Trump's social media heels on Sunday night was the influential Russian businessman Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund. He declared the AfD result "historic", Germany's national government "discredited" and the German chancellor "humiliated", comparing Friedrich Merz to the UK's not-long-gone Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, who felt forced to resign this summer.Also watching the Saxony-Anhalt election closely was the European Union. The next 12 months is bumper election season across the EU. Ballots are expected in key nations France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Brussels fears more "extreme" parties, left but particularly right of the political spectrum, may benefit across the board.The leader of Spain's nationalist Vox party, Santiago Abascal, posted on X on Sunday that the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt was " a great hope for Germany and for Europe".By contrast, France's Europe Minister, Benjamin Haddad, an ally of centrist President Emmanuel Macron, warned "this is a serious moment in Europe, seeing the far-right win in a regional election in Germany".Neither the AfD, nor other European parties labelled "extreme right" or "hard right", accept the label. They also differ from one another in tone and party programme. France's National Rally under Marine Le Pen kicked the AfD out of its grouping in the European Parliament two years ago, for being too "radical". What the parties do tend to share, however, is an anti-immigration platform and strong nationalist messaging. And that really worries the EU.Whether it is a rallying cry for "Germany First" or "Italy First" or "France for the French!", the concern in Brussels is that the rise of nationalist parties strains European cohesion at a time when outside events demand it more than ever.Nationalist parties like the AfD or Italy's League Party tend to be deeply Eurosceptic, but Brussels says Europe needs to stand united to counter Donald Trump's bullying, for example, or to effectively protect European business against China's goods dumping.Europe's defence establishment also warns that fractures in European sanctions against Russia or countries going tepid on Nato membership (as you see in Marine Le Pen's National Rally for example, or Germany's AfD) just emboldens Moscow.Security chiefs say nations must stick together to stop Russia in Ukraine, otherwise the Kremlin will be tempted to attack inside Nato, such as the Baltic states.The thing is, Europe's voters are very aware of these outside threats and the impact they have at home. They worry about the impact of wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, about crumbling health services at home and dwindling economic security for themselves and their families. Uncontrolled immigration and safety on the streets are huge concerns, too.And this is where the significance of the Saxony-Anhalt vote shines bright - a flashing red warning to traditional political parties, but also to institutions across Europe like the judiciary and security services. Those the AfD dismisses as the self-interested "Establishment".Voters on this continent feel lost and let down by parties they have supported over and again for decades. Looking right or left now at election time does not mean they have all suddenly become extremist.The AfD campaign slogan in Saxony-Anhalt was an upbeat "Anything is Possible!" - plus a promise to make Germans feel proud of their country again. Till now untried and untested in government, people seem increasingly willing to give them a go.

articles.title: Australians will be able to switch off social media algorithms under planned legislation
articles.summary: Firms like Meta, Google and TikTok should face "substantial" penalties if they don't give the option, minister says.
articles.body: Australians would be able to switch off social media algorithms under draft legislation to be proposed this week.Communications Minister Anika Wells, who last year helmed the government's world-first social media ban for under-16s, said the digital duty of care laws would ensure "some basic safety protections on an industry that hasn't had to observe it".If tech firms such as Meta, Google and TikTok did not give the option to turn off algorithms, they should face "substantial" penalties, she said.Some members of the opposition have criticised the proposal, with Liberal Party leader Angus Taylor saying he was "highly sceptical" and arguing the move could amount to censorship.The government will be taking "expert advice" on whether users would have to opt in or out of the algorithms feeding them content online, Wells said.This means that, as with its social media ban, the government is looking to bring in legislation before fully hammering out the specifics of how it would work."We want to give Australians more choice over what they see on their social media feeds," Wells told the ABC on Monday."We know that a lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility that they get out of it, seeing local businesses in their suburb."A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm. But we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place and they should respect that choice."Big tech is not a protected species and they should offer their customers basic safety standards."But she admitted that so far no tech firm had been fined for not enforcing the social media ban, despite research consistently showing that the vast majority of under 16s who were on platforms before the ban was introduced last December, still use them.Some members of the opposition have said they support the idea in principle, but others argue it is an attempt to curtail freedom of speech. Taylor told News24 he feared this was "an attempt by the government to censor social media" and that Labor should first try to plug holes in the social media ban.Speaking to Channel Nine's Today show, Wells said: "This isn't about censorship. This is about identifying risks or making big tech identify the risks on their own platform and making big tech mitigate against those risks on their platform."Last week, high-profile consent advocate Chanel Contos gave a speech at Australia's National Press Club calling on the government to seek an opt-in for algorithmic social media feeds, making it harder for tech firms to find a way round any reforms.She argued algorithms were fuelling the prevalence of sexual violence in Australia and exposing young people to misogynistic "manosphere" material.The draft legislation is expected to be introduced in the coming days.  As well as addressing algorithms, it is also expected to put an onus on platforms to stop harmful content, such as illegal pornography and videos promoting disordered eating, from being shared.

articles.title: Keep Our Servers Running
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://blog.archive.org/2026/09/01/keep-our-servers-running-your-recurring-donation-goes-3x-this-september/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49593563
Points: 956
# Comments: 247
articles.body:
“Universal access to all human knowledge is within our grasp. Our job is to put the best our world has to offer within the reach of our children.”
—Brewster Kahle, Internet Archive Digital Librarian
Every time you search the Wayback Machine or explore a collection at the Internet Archive, you are accessing a global library built to put knowledge within reach of curious learners around the world.
The mission of “Universal Access to All Knowledge” is a commitment that goes beyond book scanners and web crawlers. It requires servers, storage, power, cooling, and the people who build and maintain our systems. Our infrastructure is the backbone of our digital library.
The Internet Archive has always been completely free for everyone, everywhere. We don’t charge for access, sell user data, or run ads. Rather than contracting out our core technology to corporations, we build and maintain our own systems.
That independence helps us preserve and provide public access to 210 petabytes of knowledge. However, it also means we are responsible for keeping that infrastructure running—and our needs are growing rapidly.
This September, you can help us meet that challenge and make your support go three times as far.
When you start a recurring donation of $25 or more in September, your initial gift will be matched 2:1.
That means your $25 monthly donation unlocks an additional $50 in matching support, resulting in $75 of giving on your behalf. A $50 monthly gift becomes $150. A $100 monthly gift becomes $300.
Recurring gifts provide the dependable support we need to keep our infrastructure running year after year. In fact, the Internet Archive is powered by donations averaging about $25.
When you join the Monthly Giving Circle, you aren’t simply maintaining servers. You ensure that books are readable and websites are accessible. You are preserving the best we have to offer for generations to come.
Join the Internet Archive Monthly Giving Circle this September with a recurring gift of $25 or more, and your initial gift will be tripled through the 2:1 match.
