articles.title: Man About the House star Richard O'Sullivan dies aged 82
articles.summary: His biggest roles included Robin Tripp in 70s TV sitcoms Man About the House and Robin's Nest.
articles.body: Actor Richard O'Sullivan, whose roles included Robin Tripp in 1970s TV sitcoms Man About the House and Robin's Nest, has died aged 82.He was also known for starring in Doctor at Large, Dick Turpin, and the 1980s sitcom Me and My Girl, alongside Tim Brooke-Taylor, Joanne Ridley and Joan Sanderson.O'Sullivan died surrounded by close family at Brinsworth House, the Royal Variety Charity's care home, in west London where he had lived for 23 years.In a statement, Giles Cooper of the Royal Variety Charity said: "Richard O'Sullivan was a master of effortless charm and impeccable comic timing, bringing pure warmth, wit, and unforgettable joy to millions of living rooms as a true giant of British television."Cooper added Sullivan would be "sorely missed by us all at the Royal Variety Charity". The actor's son James O'Sullivan said in his own statement: "My dad was as funny and charming in real life as he appeared on our TV screens over the years. "Although much of his career happened before I was born, I was fortunate enough to be able to enjoy and witness his incredible talents on the countless re-runs of his shows that made him the respected and loved actor that he was."He thanked the staff at Brinsworth House for their "love, kindness and care". Man About the House co-starred Paula Wilcox, Sally Thomsett, Yootha Joyce and Brian Murphy in six series on ITV. It was about a man sharing a London flat with two single women - quite a daring storyline for that era. In Me and My Girl, he played a widow living with his adolescent daughter. Born in London in 1944, O'Sullivan started his career as a child actor in the 50s and 60s, playing uncredited roles in dramas in 1953.He went on to appear, external in the Children's Film Foundation's first serial production Raiders of the River, and in 1956 he was in Sir Peter Hall's production of Love's Labour's Lost at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre Stratford.He also appeared in 1961 film Spare the Rod, a social commentary drama about a teacher working in a tough, deprived area, starring Max Bygraves and Donald Pleasance. O'Sullivan played a difficult and defiant student in his final year.After gaining steady work in dramatic roles, including 1963's Cleopatra, as Pharoah Ptolemy XIII, which starred Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton, he moved towards comedy, in shows such as The Ronnie Barker Playhouse, in 1968, and The Galton and Simpson Comedy the following year. Ray Galton and Alan Simpson went on to create the sitcoms Hancock's Half Hour and Steptoe and Son.  O'Sullivan was also in two films with Sir Cliff Richard in the 1960s – The Young Ones in 1961 and Wonderful Life in 1964. By 1973, he took his starring role in Man About the House, which was a big success, not least because of its daring plot about a man living with two single women. "The issue was not the living arrangement itself, but what it implied,"  British Comedy Classics said, external of the series."A man sharing a flat with two unmarried women would be read as sexual, and that risked the show being rejected or framed as inappropriate for prime-time viewing."In order to bypass any potential disapproval from their landlords, George and Mildred Roper, who also got their own spin-off TV series, the two women claim their flatmate Robin is gay. Robin keeps up the pretence for their landlords, which created the comedy and made it acceptable watching for a pre-watershed 70s audience. Between 1979 and 1982 he took on the more dramatic titlular role of 18th Century highwayman Dick Turpin, in ITV's series. But by the 80s he returned to sitcoms with Me and My Girl, which ran from 1984 to 1988, and Trouble in Mind in 1991, about a married psychiatrist who is having something of a mid-life crisis. After this his career became much quieter, with an appearance in Noel's House Party and a starring role in a 1996 film called Holed, about a golfing match.In his statement, James O'Sullivan concluded: "Always kind-spirited, good humoured, a doting grandfather and a wonderful dad – I will miss him dearly."

articles.title: Dog 'grounded' after rescue from roof of house
articles.summary: Sweetie was on the roof of a two-storey house after climbing through a first-floor bedroom window.
articles.body: Image source, Falmouth Community Fire StationImage caption, Sweetie was rescued from his adventure on a neighbour's roofByJulia GregorySouth WestThe owner of a dog that was rescued after getting stuck on the roof of their house said she was "incredibly grateful to those who saved him".Emma Seager said Sweetie the rescue dog from Macedonia "likes to get out and about so we have had to modify the house a lot, but we didn't ever dream he'd be able to open a window and scramble up the roof". He was rescued on 19 August by Falmouth Community Firefighters who used a 13.5m (44.3ft) ladder to return him to solid ground and the family now has to lock windows firmly before going out.Seager said: "He's kept us on our toes for the three years he's been with us... we're only too aware it could have had a very different ending." Image source, Falmouth Community Fire StationImage caption, Sweetie became stranded on the top of the roof The dog that got stuck on the roofBBC Radio Cornwall - 1 September 2026She added: "Sweetie is back on solid ground - for now - but we still expect more shenanigans from him."Seager said she was "incredibly grateful to those who saved him" and said the much loved pet was "charming and full of character, we love him to bits". Jon Walker, from Falmouth Community Fire Station, said the dog was on the apex of a two-storey house and had got there through a first floor bedroom window which opened onto a pitch of the roof.He said the team had to avoid frightening the dog to ensure it was brought down to the ground safely during the rescue.Image source, Falmouth Community Fire StationImage caption, Sweetie has been grounded after his rescueHe said: "The dog had been up there for an hour or two, but had no way of getting down. It was fairly traumatised."They used a ladder that takes four crew to handle to get Sweetie back to the ground.Walker said Sweetie jumped into her rescuer's arms and was brought back to ground level.He said: "It is a rarity and we get far fewer cats than people would believe."Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.More on this storyRelated internet links

articles.title: This NAS company wants to run your local smart home
articles.summary:
Ugreen’s HomeAgent H100 Pro hub combines local storage, on-device AI, and a new voice assistant, Uliya, to run your smart home. | Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge	

Ugreen, known for its phone power banks, chargers, and NAS storage solutions, is moving into the smart home - in a big way. This week at the IFA tech show, the company launched its HomeAgent smart home platform that combine
articles.body:
Ugreen, known for its phone power banks, chargers, and NAS storage solutions, is moving into the smart home — in a big way. This week at the IFA tech show, the company launched its HomeAgent smart home platform that combines security camera storage, on-device AI, and smart home control in one system, managed by a voice assistant called Uliya, with the promise that everything runs locally.  
At the core of Ugreen’s HomeAgent system is a hub that acts as the brain of your smart home, running a local-first AI (with some caveats) that you can interact with using natural language via Uliya. There are three hub configurations to choose from, each of which stores all data locally and processes video footage on-device, keeping it local and private and without monthly subscription fees. Albeit likely at a higher upfront cost.
[Image: Ugreen’s MasterAgent MA100 hub is a NAS and smart home hub in one. Powered by a Nvidia Jetson Thor T5000 platform, it has up to 2,070 TFLOPS of AI performance. It will probably cost a fortune. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/LR6B5610.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
The big pitch is that your data never needs to leave your home, addressing two key smart-home concerns: privacy and recurring subscriptions. Ugreen says its powerful AI runs on the hub, providing features like cross-camera tracking, smart alerts for people, vehicles, pets, and packages, and live status questions such as “where is my pet now?”
There’s also AI-powered video search and text descriptions of events, along with natural language voice control of smart home devices and automations. Along with local storage of your camera footage, the system can store personal files, including music, movies, and photos, just like a NAS. 
All this comes without monthly storage fees for video footage that are common with popular cloud-based solutions, such as Amazon’s Ring and Alexa and Google’s Nest cameras and Gemini for Home.
Full retail pricing hasn’t been announced. The system will launch on Kickstarter in October with discounted early-bird pricing.
The idea of combining your digital home and life on a single hub that uses local AI to store, manage, and run everything is fast gaining traction. Companies like SwitchBot, Reolink, and Aqara have made moves in this space, and this week at IFA, Anker launched a similar product called the Eufy MindBase.
Both systems use the Matter smart home standard to incorporate smart home devices from different brands. I visited Ugreen’s booth at IFA and got a hands-on demo, where I controlled Nanoleaf lights alongside smart blinds with voice commands to Uliya via the HomeAgent hub. 
[Image: The Ugreen smart speaker runs its own voice assistant, Uliya. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/LR6B5615.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
The HomeAgent hub is a Matter controller and will support third-party devices using Wi-Fi, Zigbee, Thread, Bluetooth, NFC, ONVIF/RTSP, and PoE. Ugreen says it will publish a device compatibility list, which is currently fairly small and includes devices from Aqara, ThirdReality, SwitchBot, and Eve. In theory, any Matter device should work, but the first phase supports only lights, switches, sensors, and curtains — and the company advises sticking with products it has approved.
Ugreen is also launching a smart speaker to run Uliya, along with a line of security cameras: the SynCare Indoor Cam ID500 Pro, the SynCare POE Cam OD600 Pro, and a battery-powered SynCare Cam OD800 Pro. A unique integration is with Ugreen’s new E Ink Spectra-powered digital photo frame that can display your photos stored on the hub, which again need never go into the cloud.
The three versions of the HomeAgent hub offer increasing levels of compute for more advanced processing and broader AI-powered features:
The HomeAgent HA100 can execute simple, basic rule-based automation and control using specific voice commands; the HomeAgent HA100 Pro adds semantic and context-aware understanding; and the MasterAgent MA100 version brings the highest level of local compute power via an NVIDIA Jetson Thor T5000 platform.
While everything can run locally on the HomeAgent, features such as push notifications and remote viewing of your security camera footage require internet access. There is also an option to use the cloud for the Uliya voice assistant.
Keeping all your data inside your home, while still enjoying the benefits AI can bring to managing your smart home and digital life, is a compelling idea. Whether Ugreen’s Home Agent succeeds will depend on how well it integrates with what you already own and how easy it is to set up and use.
Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge
articles.author: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy

articles.title: 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Harry Kane to break down how he did it
articles.summary: Harry Kane was the highest goalscorer in Europe last season, yet he plays like a midfielder. We ask him to break down his game.
articles.body: 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did itImage caption, Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and countryByFootball tactics correspondentAs Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face."Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.Figure caption, How dropping deep helps Kane scoreThe season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.Image caption, Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game - including as deep as his own box"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says."European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.Image gallery 1Skip image galleryImage caption, Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strengthSlide 1 of 4, A play-by-play photo gallery of Harry Kane's impressive dribble from in his own half against Borussia Dortmund in this season's Super Cup win. , Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strengthEarlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do."I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."Image caption, In the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random. Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it."I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark."If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into."It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two."When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."Watch Gamechangers: Harry KaneShowing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head."The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s."I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz."I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring."By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."Image gallery 2Skip image galleryImage caption, The Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.Slide 1 of 3, Screengrab from the build-up to Harry Kane's goal against Eintracht Frankfurt in the 2025-2026 season. , The Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge. Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable."These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind."Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me."I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here."As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away."Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."Image gallery 3Skip image galleryImage caption, Karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defendersSlide 1 of 3, Screengrab from the build-up to Lennart Karl goal against Club Brugge in the 2025-2026 season. , Karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defendersWith the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.More on this story

articles.title: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views
articles.summary: After renewed strikes this week, does either side have an exit strategy?
articles.body: Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DCThe problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic objectives are in Iran. The White House is persistently re-evaluating what it is willing to live with from a political standpoint.It was assumed the military component would be enough for a quick victory and that has not had the desired effect.What we are seeing is different levers - both military and economic - that the US is trying to pull at.Right now, the administration appears satisfied with some form of stasis. I think they are satisfied with maintaining the blockade and with allowing some periodic targeting against Iran's capability to upset the shipping lane in the strait.US officials are hopeful that the new sanctions will be enough to compel the Iranian regime to come to the negotiating table in a weaker position.US forces have seemingly been able to facilitate a sufficient trickle through the Strait of Hormuz in recent days to avert an oil-price shock or a global economic collapse. But those were not the US objectives when starting the war.My sense is that Iran is likely to demand a high price to get to a resolution, which is likely to remain politically untenable for the Trump administration.Dr Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, Associate Fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, LondonI do not think the latest strikes really alter Iranian calculations on the war. I think Tehran is preparing for an increased squeeze on its economy, and a continuation of the on and off attacks which we have seen over the past couple of months. Their intent will be to respond to these attacks in a proportionate manner in order not to spiral a larger conflict.On the economic side, obviously this is likely to hurt the Iranian economy which has already been affected by the war and has had underlying structural issues anyway, as we know from the December and January demonstrations in Iran.But I do not feel like there is the sense from the Iranian side that the economic squeeze is going to alter the Iranian calculation any time soon, including on any negotiations.That does not mean Iran is not looking for an off ramp, but I think what we are seeing is that it is waiting for the US to go back to the MoU, or to at least offer some sort of concession. Tehran does not want to cave in to US pressure or alter its own approach in response to sanctions or additional attacks.Nicholas Hopton, Distinguished Fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank in London and former UK ambassador to IranThe latest spike in military action is not going to produce Iran's capitulation - it is just the latest twist. Economic pressure is also unlikely to work because China, Russia and many other countries which trade with Iran are not going to support unilateral US sanctions.Iran can continue to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz - they have a thumb on the jugular of the global economy.What is the White House's exit strategy? Well, the US has already found it. If Trump was able to put a sustained effort into negotiating the deal outlined in June's MoU, that is the off-ramp.Not only would a deal give the US a kind of victory because it would weaken the hardliners in the Islamic Republic, but also reassure everyone that Iran is not going to get a nuclear weapon.There is a silver bullet in the MoU which is the lifting of all US sanctions on Iran.What lifting those sanctions would do over time is weaken Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC). Economic engagement between the outside world and Iran in a new way would gradually force radical political and social change - so you end up with an Islamic regime, but of a very different nature.Of course, that would not be straightforward to achieve, because of extensive IRGC penetration of the Iranian economy. But it should work, if given enough time and if the US and its partners exercised strategic patience which, sadly, is in short supply at this point.For the time being, I think we're going to carry on with a messy, inconclusive situation that is bad for everyone.

articles.title: Show HN: TERMy – A fast terminal assistant that does not use LLMs
articles.summary:
I love research and development, you may have heard of me because of PJON (Padded Jittering Operative Network). It is a network protocol I started developing in 2010, which was recently implemented in silicon by the ETH Zurich university thanks to the research of Pius Sieber.
I am excited to share with you TERMy, a terminal assistant built on top of the NPC-Forge framework. Unlike everything else
articles.body:
I love research and development, you may have heard of me because of PJON (Padded Jittering Operative Network). It is a network protocol I started developing in 2010, which was recently implemented in silicon by the ETH Zurich university thanks to the research of Pius Sieber.
I had a chance to focus for 2 months on my personal projects since early July, during the strange times of AI price hikes and the end of subsidized tokenmaxing. I was curious to see if I could develop from scratch a terminal assistant capable of handling simple natural language requests. I have a bad memory and got used to ask to copilot "activate the virtual environment" or similar trivial operations spending a non negligible sum every month. I started thinking, maybe I can do something to make my workflow more efficient? Do I really need trillions of parameters to accomplish those tasks?
I started an open-ended research on the feasibility of implementing a generative model at home and training it from scratch on the computer I used to play Kerbal Space Program in the early 2010s "upgraded" with 16GB of RAM, NVIDIA GTX 1050 Ti (4GB VRAM) and a i7-4790K (4.0GHz 8 cores) CPU. In my experiments I tend to look for minimalism, so I imposed myself a constrained environment to be forced to work towards an elegant and efficient solution.
I first developed a framework to train and evaluate transformers, which I implemented from scratch in Python. I have started with something very similar to NanoGPT with 100-200M parameters, then I added flash attention, and all the expected optimizations, I even tried novel architectures like Mamba. The results were generally unsatisfactory, creepy if not outright scary, like the following:
Enter your prompt (or leave blank for empty start):
He's not a member of the world. He can't believe anything anymore.
All of those animals are looking like excrements, but every mouth is not a bad one.
They look alike, all of which are really terrible.
They get their own life, and each is a sign that they're not.
They're all right, they say.
They're just some different things they can make.
They were better not. Some of them've got their rights.
Some of them have to go.
But we're not looking for the future on how many.
The last two of them are all in the universe.
(the word excrements was used instead of an expletive composed of 4 letters that I am not willing to publish in here)
All my tests produced models that were prone to enter in loops repeating the same sentence, and even if trained on QA they were rarely able to consistently answer questions, specially if technical. I trained models on a collection of royalty free books from the Project Gutemberg, a lot of open-source software, and various datasets available on Huggingface.
I quickly understood that this approach was not feasible; a proper run would have required at least a month of training non-stop. I was amazed by how my models looked alive and magical, but I was also ashamed because they were incredibly wasteful and effectively useless.
I pivoted to ollama and open-weight models and developed howto, yet another terminal harness that uses a pre-prompt to force the model to answer only with terminal commands. Results were generally unsatisfactory because of the time required to get a response. Models like ornith:9b, mistral:7b or cogito:14b can get the job done sometimes, but they are not fast and reliable enough for general use, specially if you have only 4GB of VRAM.
Then I remembered about the blockchain craze, when everyone wanted to fit a blockchain somewhere and sell it as the next big thing.  I didn't want to waste my time and money like all those people did in the previous hype cycle, so I started building a terminal assistant from scratch with a new set of constraints:
The first things I needed was a set of conventions to rely on, so I drafted the NDF 0.0 (NPC-Forge Dataset Format which specifies the dataset format of NPC-Forge. The following object contains category, input sentences, textual response, thinking traces, permission gating and tool calls to be executed in a format compatible with VS code.
"explanation": "Lists the files in the current directory.",
"goal": "Display current directory contents",
I am really in love with this, it is a self-contained atom of knowledge that can be easily edited and shared. It is very simple to expand the capabilities of conversational agents if you adhere to this convention; let's say I want my terminal assistant to learn about docker commands, I can just write down a list of objects in dataset_docker.json, drop the file in the dataset  directory, and the NPC will instantly learn them as Neo learnt Jujitsu in The Matrix.
The next problem to solve was, how to handle questions like "create file test.txt"? I needed to parse the "variable" in there and understand the true meaning of the request, so I came up with this:
"command": "echo '' > '<||file||>' && termy_set_context 'active_file' '<||file||>'",
"explanation": "Writes <||string||> in file <||file||>.",
"Ok, I am asked to create the file <||file||>."
Each tag like <||vocab_create||> represents a concept, in this case the action of creation, which is represented by multiple sinonyms:
One or more tags can be expected at the same position and each tag can be required or optional. The "variables" or named entities are extracted according to their type and a related regular expression:
I must thank my great friend Kevin to help me thinking this out.
Looking at the permission key I concluded that, enforcing the use of "permission": "ask" for all potentially destructive commands, the tool became inherently safe to use; obviously potential for human error remained, such as a bug in the implementation or in the dataset, but risks were strongly mitigated.
I wrote FlintParser and FlintNPC classes to make use of the data format described above, implement a NLU (Natural Language Understanding) pipeline, and all the required features for the terminal assistant to work in around 1000 lines of code. I wrote those classes in identical, cross-compliant implementations for both Python, for local OS environments, and JavaScript, running client-side inside any browser tab or Node.js instance.
The most difficult part was to determine what to do and in which order. I have worked a lot on a compiler for my own programming language BIPLAN and while developing that I had the honour to learn that the first thing you need to do when translating code is to remove noise and then work your way out trying the least expensive paths first.
So that's the pipeline I implemented:
Strip expletives, interjections, encouraging, discouraging and thanking words (remove noise)
IDF (Inverse Document Frequency) to identify rare words.
BOW (Bag Of Words) to accommodate word inversions.
IDF weighted Levenshtein to safely handle typos.
For the first time after almost 2 months throwing spaghetti at the wall and hope they stuck, I felt again the joy of working on something comprehensible and predictable. I finally had a reliable terminal assistant working on my computer!
I decided to call it TERMy:
How this compares to established NLU frameworks? Rasa and NLP.js are heavy and rely on machine learning classifiers and training pipelines, ChatScript is massive with a notoriously steep learning curve. NPC-Forge strips all that away, requiring zero training, specifying a powerful and flexible data format, and featuring a surprisingly capable parser small enough to run on a micro-controller.
Let's connect it to Copilot
I have developed TERMy and connected it to Copilot to handle a subset of the prompts I was before sending to Claude! It is not an LLM but it gets the job done and it is instantaneous! I suspect this is the first time most of us see a deterministic agent using a harness, although, I believe, this will be the prevalent topic in the near future:
It is ironic to think that Copilot's recent price hikes are what finally pushed me to dedicate time to this software. Maybe it's just the lifecycle of corporate SaaS? In any case, I believe that harnesses like Copilot and Pi should rely on deterministic NPCs like TERMy and route to a heavy LLM only as a last resort. Continuing to waste compute and electricity on trivial tasks is expensive and irresponsible.
NPC-Forge is a framework, a server and a CLI that provides the following functionalities:
With NPC-Forge now everyone can quickly build an NPC and share it with the community, those NPCs run on the CPU in any Linux machine, like the RPI Zero, responding in milliseconds. Imagine, now even your AC meter or your router can serve a conversational agent for free. This approach is also more democratic, your NPC will happily say something uncomfortable if you program it to do so, much better than corporate alignment filters and guardrails shaping public opinion, culture and language.
I ask for a bit of leniency: this is my first Python project, made in two months of passionate development. I am fully aware the code is not yet production-ready. I bet many Linux graybeards will curse me until the end of time because of the chain of commands TERMy sometimes emits; a lot of work must be done on the dataset and the source code to achieve safety and production readiness.
Consider that this is an early release to showcase what we may use in a not very distant future. If the shared effort of the community is focused on NPC-Forge and TERMy, I think they may provide us with more freedom and help us save money, electricity and time. If you liked this read and you agree with me, consider contributing to the project. Happy tinkering!

articles.title: Mum says 'no fat left to trim' on household costs amid 42% rise in water bills
articles.summary: Water companies were given the green light to increase bills for customers earlier this month.
articles.body: Victoria, from Cardiff, who is a single parent, said she spent "almost every single spare penny" on her household bills and there was "nothing left to waste", other than a Netflix subscription she had bought for her children.She has a water meter, meaning suppliers charge a customer for the precise amount consumed rather than using an estimated flat rate."We turn the taps off when brushing our teeth, use the excess water on the plants after washing the dishes."We don't throw it away," she said.Victoria has introduced a shower timer to save water which has been "quite difficult" to enforce."My kids want to stand there under the shower for hours," she said."They've got a limited amount of time and then the hot tap goes on in the kitchen, which means they get showered with cold water."Robert and Bernadette Guy, from Cardiff, said they were "absolutely shocked" to discover that their Welsh Water bill was set to rise by about £400 this year to £1,400 annually.They decided to install a water meter which had proven more cost-effective - bringing their annual bill down to £600.But Robert said this meant they were "having to think a bit more carefully" about their water usage."I've got a lot of pint glasses and every time I wash my hands in the sink, I put a pint glass below, and we line them up on on the windowsill before putting them on the garden. "The other day I had seven pints of water which would have gone down the drain."Robert said they were planning to buy a "dedicated bucket" to collect the water in the future."We've got a large garden and the thought of saying we can't afford to water it just felt awful," said Bernadette.Bernadette said she was "absolutely astounded" to find out the cost of paying for their water, as it used to be just a "little add-on" to their monthly bills.They said they felt it was also unfair to ask customers to take responsibility for years of under-investment into the ageing infrastructure."When I put the light switch on, I don't care how that electricity gets to my light bulb, I just want it to work," said Robert."I think that goes for a lot of people. We just want it to work when we want it and to work as cheaply as possible."Prof Ian Walker, head of psychology at Swansea University, said people could be "constrained by automatic habits" when it comes to water usage.He said: "You might think, 'I should take shorter showers', but once you get in there, you go into auto-pilot and take the same time regardless."One of the best things you could ask people to do is don't have showers and don't wash your clothes. But that's not going to happen either."He suggested an easier approach was to lock-in water savings measures, such as getting a low-flow shower."You do that once as a deliberate choice, but then you never think about it again."Welsh Water said it recognised that household budgets remain under pressure and understand that any increase in bills is difficult for customers. "The additional income will support our investment of more than £4bn between 2025 and 2030 to maintain and improve essential services, including work to reduce pollution, improve water quality, reduce leakage and upgrade vital infrastructure," a spokesperson said."The revenue we receive from customer bills is our sole source of funding for maintaining services and upgrading our infrastructure."Without profit-driven pressures, any financial surpluses are reinvested for the benefit of our customers, to improve services, support vulnerable households and address environmental challenges."We urge any customer who is worried about paying their bill to contact us. Our social tariffs and wider support schemes can make bills more affordable for eligible households."

articles.title: The Raspberry Pi Interactive Timeline · 2006–2026
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://raspberry.tips/en/raspberrypi-infos/raspberry-pi-history-timeline
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49562062
Points: 18
# Comments: 8
articles.body:
From a university prototype tackling falling computer science applications to a $35 computer that crashes servers.
The idea is born in Cambridge
At the University of Cambridge, Eben Upton notices that fewer and fewer young people are applying to study computer science — and that the applicants lack the hands-on tinkering experience of the home-computer generation. The first Atmel-based prototypes are built: still a long way from the later Pi, but the mission is already set — a computer so cheap that every kid can experiment with one.
Source: Raspberry Pi Foundation ↗
The Raspberry Pi Foundation is founded
Together with allies from academia and industry — including Broadcom colleagues and Cambridge lecturers — Eben Upton founds the Raspberry Pi Foundation. In May 2009 it is registered as a charity (UK charity no. 1129409). Its stated goal: promoting computer science education for young people.
Source: UK Charity Commission ↗
25 beta boards — 10 of them auctioned on eBay
The first 25 final beta boards are manufactured. In early 2012 the Foundation auctions ten of them off on eBay in a well-publicised campaign — individual boards fetch four-figure sums and fund the final polish before launch. The auctions give the upcoming $35 computer its first taste of international fame.
Source: Wikipedia (launch history) ↗
Launch: Raspberry Pi Model B for $35
The original Raspberry Pi Model B from 2012 (photo: Jwrodgers, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0)
On leap day 2012, the first Raspberry Pi goes on sale. The rush for the $35 computer with its 700 MHz ARM chip and 256 MB of RAM takes down the servers of both distributors, Farnell and RS Components, within minutes — the Foundation itself has to switch its website to a static page. The plan had been a small production run for British school kids; it turned into the beginning of the best-selling British computer of all time.
Source: raspberrypi.com (launch retrospective) ↗
Raspbian becomes the recommended operating system
Raspbian — a Debian build optimised for the Pi’s hardware, started as a community project by Mike Thompson and Peter Green — becomes the officially recommended system. It marks the start of the Debian lineage that the Pi’s operating system follows to this day.
“Made in the UK”: production moves to Wales
Manufacturing moves from China to the Sony factory in Pencoed, Wales — and most Raspberry Pis still roll off the line there today. For an electronics product in this price class, bringing production back to Europe was unheard of in 2012.
Model B gets 512 MB of RAM
At no extra cost, the Foundation doubles the Model B’s memory from 256 to 512 MB. It is the first example of a pattern that stays with the Pi for years: more performance for the same price.
Camera, Compute Module, Pi 2 and 3 — and a $5 computer at the newsstand.
Model A: the $25 variant
The stripped-down Model A (256 MB RAM, one USB port, no Ethernet) reaches Europe. Drawing only a third of the Model B’s power, it becomes the first choice for battery-powered projects and robotics.
The first Camera Module (5 MP)
The first Camera Module from 2013 (photo: Sven.petersen, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)
For $25, the Pi gets its first official accessory board: a 5-megapixel camera for the CSI port. Time-lapses, birdhouse cams and surveillance projects quickly make the camera the most-used Pi accessory of all.
Set up the Pi camera: our guide
1.75 million sold — 1 million made in Wales
Eighteen months after launch, the Foundation reports 1.75 million Pis sold, one million of them built at the Sony plant in Pencoed. The tinkerer’s computer is definitively no longer a niche product.
Compute Module: the Pi goes industrial
The Pi in SODIMM format kicks off the industrial line: companies can now build Pi technology straight into their own products. Along the way, the education project becomes an embedded supplier — today, industrial and embedded customers account for over two-thirds of sales.
CM4 vs CM5: our comparison
Model B+: 40 GPIO pins and microSD become standard
The B+ locks in the layout that still applies today: 40-pin GPIO header, microSD slot, four USB ports and the familiar mounting holes. Thanks to that decision, practically every HAT expansion board of the past ten years fits every modern Pi.
Raspberry Pi 2: quad-core and 1 GB of RAM
Four cores instead of one, 1 GB of RAM, same price: according to the Foundation, the Pi 2 is “six times faster” than its predecessor. For the first time the Pi actually feels usable as a desktop machine — and Microsoft announces Windows 10 IoT Core for the Pi in parallel.
5 million: the best-selling British computer
With five million units sold, the Raspberry Pi overtakes the legendary ZX Spectrum and becomes the best-selling British computer of all time — three years after launch.
The official 7-inch touch display
After years of development (including an EMC certification odyssey), the first official display arrives: 7 inches, 800×480, touch — the starting signal for countless Pi-based smart home panels, kiosk systems and car dashboards.
Pi Zero: the $5 computer on a magazine cover
The Pi Zero undercuts every price barrier — and the Foundation sticks it onto the cover of its own MagPi magazine as a free gift. A full Linux computer at the newsstand: the issue sells out within hours.
Astro Pi: two Raspberry Pis fly to the ISS
Two specially hardened Pis with Sense HATs launch to the International Space Station alongside ESA astronaut Tim Peake. Ever since, tens of thousands of school kids have run their own code in orbit every year — still one of Europe’s biggest STEM education programmes.
Pi 3: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth move in
Right on time for the fourth birthday (another leap day!), the Pi 3 arrives — for the first time with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on board and a 64-bit-capable quad-core. The dongle sprawl on the USB ports comes to an end, and the Pi finally becomes the standard building block for the connected home.
10 million Raspberry Pis sold
Four and a half years after launch, ten million Pis have been sold — Eben Upton had originally expected 10,000 in total. The first official starter kit is released to mark the milestone.
Zero W: wireless for the smallest Pi
For its fifth birthday, the Zero gets Wi-Fi and Bluetooth — for $10. IoT projects, smart cameras and retro handhelds no longer need a USB adapter.
Pi 3 B+: a speedy polish on Pi Day
More clock speed (1.4 GHz), Gigabit Ethernet (attached via USB), dual-band Wi-Fi and PoE readiness: the B+ is the most mature version of the Pi 3 generation — fittingly released on Pi Day, 14 March.
Pi 3 A+: the last Model A
The A line gets its send-off: full Pi 3 performance in the compact A format for $25. No successor has appeared to this day — anyone building small has reached for the Zero ever since.
The Pi matures into a desktop-class machine, gets its own chips — and survives the chip shortage.
Pi 4: USB 3, dual 4K and your choice of RAM
The Pi 4 brings USB 3.0, true Gigabit Ethernet, two 4K HDMI outputs — and for the first time a choice of RAM (1, 2 or 4 GB, later 8). The $35 entry price stays, but from now on the Pi is also a serious desktop and server machine. One sore point: the first revision has a USB-C charging flaw that acts up with “smart” cables.
Still worth buying a Pi 4? Our comparison
Raspbian becomes Raspberry Pi OS — and the Pi 4 gets 8 GB
Along with the 8 GB variant of the Pi 4, the Foundation renames its operating system: Raspbian becomes Raspberry Pi OS, and the 64-bit beta launches in parallel. The new name positions the system as an official product — the Debian base stays.
Compute Module 4: farewell to the SODIMM format
The CM4 switches to compact board-to-board connectors and brings PCIe into the Pi world for the first time — officially only for industrial customers, though. The community builds anyway: NAS boards, routers and the first NVMe experiments all emerge on a CM4 basis.
CM4 vs CM5 in detail
Pi 400: the computer inside a keyboard
In the middle of the homeschooling year, the Pi 400 appears: a complete computer in a keyboard case for $70 — a deliberate bow to the home computers of the ’80s whose spirit once inspired the Foundation.
Pico & RP2040: the first in-house chip
With the $4 Pico microcontroller, Raspberry Pi steps into Arduino territory — and with the self-developed RP2040 becomes a chipmaker for the first time. The step from board builder to silicon designer shapes everything that comes after.
Zero 2 W: quad-core in the Zero format
The Zero 2 W packs a quad-core into the unchanged Zero footprint — made possible by a custom system-in-package (RP3A0). For $15, even more demanding software now runs on the smallest Pi.
What the Zero can do today
Chip shortage: the Pi becomes scarce
The global semiconductor crisis hits the Pi with full force: boards are sold out for months, scalpers charge absurd prices, and the Foundation officially prioritises industrial customers. Things only ease up in mid-2023 — a dent that briefly gives the competition (Orange Pi & co.) a boost.
Pico W: Wi-Fi for six dollars
The Pico goes wireless: for $6, the microcontroller becomes a fully-fledged IoT platform. Sensors that beam their readings straight into your Wi-Fi now cost less than a lunch.
Raspberry Pi 5 with the in-house RP1 I/O chip
The Pi 5 brings the second in-house design: the RP1 chip handles all of the I/O. For the first time, PCIe is officially accessible — the foundation of the NVMe boom that finally turns the Pi into a server and desktop machine. On top of that come a power button and a real-time clock, two of the most-requested features ever.
Pi 5 vs Pi 4 compared
Boot from an NVMe drive
Raspberry Pi OS “Bookworm”: Wayland becomes the default
With its Debian 12 base (“Bookworm”), Raspberry Pi OS switches the desktop to Wayland — as one of the first major Linux systems to do so. The move brings smoother graphics, but also breaks a few old tool workflows.
From charity project to publicly listed company — and local AI becomes the new core topic.
Raspberry Pi Connect: official remote access
With Connect, there is finally an official way to control your Pi remotely — desktop and shell in the browser, without port forwarding or VPN fiddling. For beginners, one of the biggest hurdles of headless operation simply disappears.
AI Kit: the gateway to local AI
Together with Hailo, Raspberry Pi releases a 13 TOPS AI accelerator as an M.2 HAT for $70. Real-time object detection now runs locally on the Pi 5 — no cloud required. The starting shot for the AI product line.
Our hands-on AI Kit test with Frigate
IPO on the London Stock Exchange
Raspberry Pi Holdings plc goes public on the London Stock Exchange. The charitable Foundation remains the majority shareholder — the education legacy and the commercial arm have been formally separated ever since. Among other things, the IPO funds the company’s own chip development.
Pico 2 & RP2350 — now with RISC-V too
The second in-house microcontroller chip, the RP2350, offers freely selectable RISC-V cores alongside its ARM cores for the first time — a remarkable statement in favour of the open processor architecture. The Pico 2 stays at $5.
AI Camera: AI right inside the camera sensor
The AI Camera with Sony’s IMX500 runs neural networks directly in the sensor — the Pi receives ready-made detection results instead of raw images. AI image processing now works even on a Zero.
AI HAT+: up to 26 TOPS on the Pi 5
The AI HAT+ integrates the Hailo accelerator directly onto the board — with 26 TOPS in the top variant. Analysing video from several cameras at once becomes an everyday job on the Pi 5.
Touch Display 2: the 7-incher goes modern
Nine years after the first touch display comes its successor: 720×1280, five-finger touch, slimmer design — at the unchanged $60 price. The standard panel for smart home hubs finally gets a contemporary resolution.
Pi 5 technology in the industrial format: the CM5 brings PCIe, USB 3 and up to 16 GB of RAM to the embedded world — pin-compatible with the CM4, which makes switching easy for manufacturers.
CM4 vs CM5: worth the upgrade?
Pi 500 and the first official monitor
The Pi 500 puts Pi 5 technology into the keyboard case, flanked by the first official Raspberry Pi monitor (15.6″, Full HD, $100). Together they form, for the first time, a complete desktop setup from a single source.
Pi 5 with 16 GB of RAM
For $120, the Pi 5 is now available with 16 GB — four times as much as the former flagship Pi 4. The target audience: local AI models, larger container setups and everyone who seriously uses the Pi as a desktop.
Local AI on the 16 GB Pi
68 million Raspberry Pis sold
The first annual report after the IPO puts total sales at 68 million units. For perspective: the Foundation’s original goal was 10,000 units for British schools.
Source: Raspberry Pi Holdings, Annual Report 2024 ↗
Pi 500+: mechanical keyboard and NVMe out of the box
The most expensive Pi product to date: for $200, the Pi 500+ combines 16 GB of RAM, a 256 GB NVMe SSD and a mechanical RGB keyboard. Raspberry Pi is openly aiming for the desk now — no longer just the workbench.
Our take on the Pi 500+
The new major release based on Debian 13 (“Trixie”) brings a reworked desktop with a modular Control Centre and a fresh look. The Debian lineage that began with Raspbian in 2012 enters its fourteenth year.
The most important beginner’s tool is rewritten from scratch: Imager 2.0 modernises the path from blank SD card to running system — including a reworked interface and better preconfiguration.
RAM price crisis: the end of the “ever cheaper” era
Exploding memory prices force Raspberry Pi into broad price increases for the first time — and into a 1 GB Pi 5 for $45. Another round of increases follows in February 2026. The story of the ever-cheaper Pi, told since 2012, ends here.
Our analysis of the price shock
AI HAT+ 2: generative AI on the Pi
The second generation of the AI accelerator targets generative models: language models and image generators now run locally on the Pi 5 — right in line with the trend of running AI assistants like OpenClaw entirely at home.
Install OpenClaw on your Pi
The curious 3GB Pi 4
Not an April Fools’ joke: with 4 GB chips scarce and expensive, the Pi 4 appears in a 3 GB variant for $83.75 — a child of the RAM crisis and probably the most unusual model in Pi history. At the same time, prices for further models rise once again.
What the 3GB Pi 4 means for buyers
Touch Display 2 in 10 inches
The Touch Display 2 gets a big brother: 10 inches for $80. Smart home dashboards and kiosk applications finally get an official tablet-sized panel.
50 events, each backed by a primary source · Last updated: August 2026 · raspberry.tips

articles.title: 'Layer upon layer of miracles' to find tunnel survivors, Nepal rescue adviser tells BBC
articles.summary: From searching for a buried tunnel entrance to blowing up rocks the size of cars, rescuers had to surmount multiple challenges to reach survivors.
articles.body: 'Layer upon layer of miracles' to find tunnel survivors, Nepal rescue adviser tells BBCFigure caption, Watch: Moment workers are rescued from Nepal tunnelByTessa WongAsia Digital ReporterA tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border."It's like layer upon layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given the multiple challenges that they faced.The first hurdle was to locate the entrance to the tunnel, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people."I've never known a rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging.They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors."We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said.Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to use explosives to clear the way, something they would "normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," Dix said. He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel.At the same time, they discovered it was still full of water. Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water.Image source, Nepalese Prime Minister's OfficeImage caption, Rescuers found a substantial amount of water in the tunnel as they dug through itFinally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel.The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," Dix explained.In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices.According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay". Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive.But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over.Rescuers heading to 'Goldilocks zone'Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain.Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood did not reach the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded".The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers."Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," Dix said. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends."But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time. "It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before."Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life".This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located. "We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."Image source, Nepalese Prime Minister's OfficeImage caption, Rescuers had to pull the survivors through a tiny passageway created at the top of the rubble in the tunnel

articles.title: How 'unique' Bellingham is thriving in Mourinho's system
articles.summary: Jude Bellingham looks fit and ready to build on his World Cup form as he aims to rediscover his best at Real Madrid under Jose Mourinho.
articles.body: Jude Bellingham has started the new season looking like a player with something to prove.The 23-year-old's two goals and three assists have helped Real Madrid to an impressive start under new boss Jose Mourinho, with three wins from as many games.Bellingham's performances, and the freedom he has been given in his new role, has attracted a lot of attention.By playing higher up the pitch, he looks more free, more influential and closer to the role in which he first made such an impact at the Bernabeu in his debut 2023-24 season, where he scored 23 goals as his side won La Liga and the Champions League.Bellingham's last two campaigns were less consistent, with his displays and attacking influence affected not only by a deeper role, but by recurring injuries. He had a long-standing shoulder problem that required surgery in 2025 and a hamstring issue that kept him out for 10 matches in 2026.Now, however, he appears to be at peak fitness, ready to build on his impressive World Cup form for England and showcase the full extent of his talent.Since returning this summer to take charge of the club for a second spell, Mourinho has made an important adjustment in reducing the defensive workload that previously meant Bellingham had to cover huge areas of the pitch."We've organised the team differently," he said after Real Madrid's 4-0 La Liga win over Malaga."Bellingham sometimes defended like a second left-back last season. I told him I do not want to see that anymore. I made a deal with him."The Portuguese manager has used Bellingham primarily as a number 10 in a 4-2-3-1 system, operating behind French striker Kylian Mbappe and with the freedom to move across the attacking line.That gives the England midfielder a clearer role. Rather than constantly moving between midfield, defence and attack, he can spend more time in the areas where he is most dangerous."For me, this is his position, with his connection with the forwards, he can score goals," added Mourinho."He has to play close to the goal. Playing at number six or number eight, we're losing his closeness to the goal. I like this Jude."It has meant Bellingham can receive the ball between the lines, carry it forward, combine with the forwards and make late runs into the penalty area.Just as importantly, he is being given greater freedom to decide when to move.Bellingham has explained the difference himself in an interview with Real Madrid TV."I feel more free to decide when to drop back, when to stay up or when to get into the box," he said. "I think this is the best position for me."Mourinho still expects him to press and recover possession, but the difference is where that work begins. Instead of dropping deep towards his own penalty area, Bellingham can now use his energy to press opponents higher up the pitch.When Madrid win the ball, he is already closer to the forwards. That allows him to connect midfield with attack and provide another player who can combine with Mbappe and Vinicius Jr.It also explains why Mourinho has been keen to stress Madrid's attacking players must work together rather than operate as individuals."The team dynamic is about 11, not 2+9," he said.The midfielder also described working with Mourinho as a "dream", having previously only met the former Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham manager once before his appointment.There is clearly an early understanding and respect between the two.Mourinho has repeatedly spoken about Bellingham's importance to his plans, describing him as a "unique and super important player" with qualities that include physical, mental and tactical. He also suggested Bellingham should be one of the players in the running for the Ballon d'Or."He is a unique kind of player and extremely important for the team," said Mourinho."His mental strength, tactical ability, the way he recovers the ball, the way he pressures, the way he plays up front, I am very happy."For Mourinho, that versatility is part of what makes Bellingham so valuable. He can press, recover possession, score, contribute in the air and drive the team forward.The Real boss has also pointed to Thomas Tuchel's use of Bellingham at the World Cup as an example of how to get the best out of him.Bellingham was one of England's standout players, finishing with seven goals and an assist in his eight appearances, and his attacking qualities were allowed to flourish.That experience also appears to have given the player a confidence boost, particularly as he rejoined Madrid later than most of his team-mates and had less time to prepare for the new campaign. Although Real's three league wins - scoring 10 goals and conceding two - are only a small sample, and the demands will increase as the season progresses amid Champions League football, the early signs are very positive.For Bellingham, whose huge strength has always been his ability to affect almost every part of a game, Mourinho's system has given him more control over where that influence is used.After a difficult couple of seasons following the high standards he set in his first year, the England midfielder is enjoying his football again."I'm having a lot of fun, I'm really enjoying my football, and that's why I'm performing well," he told club media.If he continues in this vein with Mourinho's continued support, it could turn out to be his best season yet.

articles.title: 100 influencers invited to US Open spark debate on 'tennis etiquette'
articles.summary: The behaviour of influencers and content creators has become a major talking point at this year's US Open amid incidents of matches being disrupted.
articles.body: Lights. Camera. Quiet please...When it comes to etiquette in tennis, there are a fair few unwritten rules.Apologising after winning a point from a net cord. Honesty around line calls, double bounces and double-hits. Post-match handshakes. As for the spectators, it is common courtesy not to disturb the players during points.Around 100 influencers and content creators have been granted accreditation for the tournament in New York - double the amount from last year.Their presence has led to debate over how to balance bringing tennis to a new, different audience while respecting the game's etiquette."I definitely think it's cool to have a new demographic and I definitely think it helps grow the sport," world number four Coco Gauff said."But if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans."I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport. That's all."During two-time champion Naomi Osaka's first-round match on Arthur Ashe Stadium, one group held a photo shoot in their hospitality suite while play was going on.The group turned on a portable ring light while Osaka was serving, leading to a reprimand from the umpire.When Osaka returned on Thursday, the umpire had to remind the crowd several times to be quiet."Today the umpire told everyone to be quiet more than I've ever heard an umpire tell a crowd to be quiet," Osaka said."I tell people I normally just focus on the match and the court, but there was a moment where there was people shouting and you could hear it quite clearly."I think it bothered my opponent, too."In one video, which has gone viral, a group can be seen speaking loudly as they film themselves during Osaka's first-round match on Tuesday, which led to the chair umpire calling for them to stop."I think obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport," Osaka said."I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette."It could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like my first-round match."Overall, I think there are huge positives. You want people to continue to grow the sport. "I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."Arthur Ashe is the biggest tennis stadium in the world, and matches are often accompanied by a buzz of noise from conversations around the arena.Some players love it. Some do not.Men's seventh seed Daniil Medvedev, who has had a tricky relationship with the New York crowds in the past, believes whatever brings more eyes to tennis can only be a good thing."I think the more we try to raise awareness about tennis, the better it is, the more popular the sport is," the Russian said."The more the sport grows, the better it is. I trust USTA [tournament organisers the United States Tennis Association] with what they are doing. "I think [there is] a lot more upside than downside, so go for it."American 11th seed Frances Tiafoe praised the diversity of the crowd in New York."I think the Open is great because you get all types of people that want to come and watch tennis," he said."All different walks of life, different types of people, different type of occupations. Personally, I love that."I have no problem with anybody doing anything, coming to watch the tennis."American world number three Jessica Pegula, however, said some of the behaviour had been "disrespectful"."I can appreciate the influencers coming and showcasing the US Open experience," Pegula said."But I do think that it's tough when you see videos when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights."People are down there trying to perform. It's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful."I think it's become a little too much this year. "I can appreciate one side of it, but I think when you have the other side literally interrupting matches, it gets a little tough."The US Open introduced a policy of free fan movement in 2024, meaning fans no longer have to wait to take their seats during changeovers.A year later, the tournament was expanded to 15 days. The week before the singles draw is now marketed as a 'Fan Week', showcasing the revamped mixed doubles competition and exhibition matches between players past and present.It is all part of what tournament chief executive Craig Tiley hopes will become "the tennis Disneyland".Tiley, asked about influencers being accredited in a pre-tournament news conference, said: "We need to find ways of reaching new audiences, reaching people in a way that they connect with media today."The creation of the creator credential has been a key part of that because it's enabled us to talk to people in a way that they're listening. That's been a big focus."Since the incident in Osaka's first match, there has been increased messaging on screens around the ground reminding people to "refrain from any activity that could disrupt the game, including noise levels, flash photography and ring lights".The USTA said in a statement it "is always striving to grow tennis in this country and bring new audiences into the sport"."We want all of our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend, but we also need to ensure they do not interfere with the action and competition on the court," it added."We are continually looking for ways to ensure fans in the stands know what is permitted and what is prohibited."

articles.title: Volkswagen board approves plan to cut another 50,000 jobs
articles.summary: The group - which includes Audi, Porsche, Skoda as well as the VW brand - plans to cut a total of 100,000 posts by 2030.
articles.body: The board of German car giant Volkswagen has approved a plan to cut another 50,000 jobs as part of the biggest restructuring in the group's almost nine-decade history. It brings the total number of roles the carmaker plans to shed by 2030 to 100,000, after announcing in March that it would cut 50,000 roles.The group - which includes Audi, Porsche, Skoda as well as the VW brand - is also considering the future of four of its German plants.The move is a "strong signal" for the future of the firm, which is "taking responsibility for our entire workforce", VW's chief executive Oliver Blume said in a statement on Thursday.Blume said in July that the firm was looking to make the additional cuts.Shares in the company were up by around 7% in Frankfurt on Friday morning.The Golf-maker has been hit by a drop in profits due to falling sales and fierce competition, especially from Chinese brands.The firm also said that by 2035 it would cut the number of models it produces by 50% and reduce the complexity of its offering by 75%.VW will also prioritise the "most compelling vehicles" and make more of each model, which will help lower costs, it said.A "fundamental adjustment of the global workforce capability is necessary" to safeguard the competitiveness of the company, which faces shifting demand and technological change.It added "a group-wide workforce adjustment of approximately 50,000 positions - including management roles - will be necessary."The company is also weighing options for operations in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Neckarsulm, where it has said production capacity exceeds demand."Alternative uses for these plants are being assessed," it said.As of 2025, VW employed more than 660,000 people worldwide. Its brands also include Seat, Bentley and Lamborghini.Christianne Benner - the president of Europe's largest industrial union IG Metall and deputy chair of VW's Supervisory Board - said the carmaker had "fought hard for good solutions" to address a "crisis situation".VW's profits have fallen sharply in recent years, hit by falling sales in China, which was once one of its biggest markets.Sales have also fallen in the US, partly due to the impact of tariffs on car imports that were introduced by President Donald Trump's administration.Chinese carmakers have been expanding aggressively as they roll out new technologies while benefiting from lower production costs than their rivals.In recent years, firms such as BYD have seen their sales rise sharply in markets including the UK, European Union and South East Asia.

When the Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD launches later this year in 512GB and 1TB capacities it will be one of the slimmest you can buy. At its thickest point in the middle it measures just 3.8mm, but that tapers to only 1mm at the edges thanks to high-densit
articles.body:
Following the lead of companies like Xteink, Lexar is the latest to sacrifice a USB-C port in the pursuit of slimming down its hardware.
When the Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD launches later this year in 512GB and 1TB capacities it will be one of the slimmest you can buy. At its thickest point in the middle it measures just 3.8mm, but that tapers to only 1mm at the edges thanks to high-density NAND stacking and a “custom ultra-thin PCB architecture” inside. But performance remains solid with read speeds up to 1,050MB/s and write speeds maxing out at 1,000MB/s. That’s fast enough to record 4K Apple ProRes video at up to 120fps when connected to a compatible iPhone.
The downside is that without a standard USB-C port, you’ll need to rely on — and make sure not to lose — Lexar’s proprietary SnapLink cable that magnetically attaches to a pogo-pin connector on the side of the drive. The company doesn’t specify the strength of the magnets, but this approach also means there’s an increased risk of the cable being accidentally knocked off during a file transfer. And if you are using the Muse to record videos through your phone, you’ll need to slip it into an included magnetic sleeve in order to mount it to the back of your device, adding quite a bit of thickness in the process.
articles.author: Andrew Liszewski

articles.title: Aqara goes all in on smart lighting
articles.summary:
After showing off several smart home firsts at CES, Aqara has returned to IFA with a major lineup of smart lighting compatible with both Zigbee and Thread. One of these new devices is the Floor Lamp T1, which trades the look of a typical lamp for an LED-equipped pole attached to a base.
