articles.title: They were raised on Drag Race UK - but can they snatch the crown?
articles.summary: A new wave of queens raised on the hit reality show are among the 12 contestants set to compete for the series eight crown.
articles.body: They were raised on Drag Race UK - but can they snatch the crown?Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Mocha says Drag Race inspired her to get into drag ByNaomi ClarkeBBC NewsbeatA new batch of queens from across the UK are set to battle it out in the hope of hearing RuPaul's magical words: "Condragulations, you're a winner, baby". The UK edition of Drag Race has been putting hopeful contestants through their paces for seven years - plenty of time for a new wave of talent raised on the hit reality show to emerge. Now "Generation Ru" are ready to compete for the crown and £25,000 cash prize.Series eight contestant Mocha, 26, tells BBC Newsbeat she considers herself part of this new cohort.  "My drag has always been inspired by Drag Race because that's why I started," the Essex-born queen says. "I think watching Drag Race made me realise that all of these things that I grew up wanting to do - like be a fashion designer, be a singer, like be a dancer, do makeup - it's actually all these things combined and I can be all of them at once." Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Flesh is fighting for the crown after her best friend Bones took the title last seasonMocha, who describes herself as a "fashion clown" and musical theatre lover, says it has taken her nearly a decade to get to this stage but feels it is the "right time".And while watching the show has influenced her style and given her a something to work towards, she says the process isn't for those who just want to get on TV."Drag is hard and you've got to love it, you've got to have a passion for it," she says. "Drag Race is the extra-special prize you get at the end, but it's not the main goal in that way." London-based queen and fellow contestant Flesh agrees she is "100% Generation Ru"."I found drag through queens who had featured in the American franchise," the 26-year-old says. "And from the first season of the UK franchise I was hooked, I was a fan."It has always really been my blueprint.“She has also developed her "supermodel of Soho" style alongside her best friend Bones, the reigning Drag Race UK Superstar.Flesh says she was "so happy" for her drag sister when she won, but it also made her "terrified" to compete this year as she focused on proving herself. Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Naya Thorn says the expense of preparing for the show almost led her to drop-outAlmost 100 queens have lip-synced their way through Drag Race UK's challenges, but there are fans who worry whether the British scene can support more series of the annual show.Series eight's youngest contestant, Naya Thorn, who was 23 when she was chosen for the show, feels there are new queens cropping up all over the UK.But she admits the show would benefit if more "seasoned and colourful characters" from across the scene got involved.However, she says, cost-of-living pressures are putting a strain on queens trying to make it.Naya, from Dudley, West Midlands, says the expense of preparing for the show almost led her to drop-out, and she wouldn't have been TV-ready without her support network at home."It really upsets me that there's a lot of people that would do well on the show and should have that platform that feel like they can't go on because of how expensive it seems to be getting," she says. "But I am here to prove to everyone, you don't need that much money." Image source, BC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Series eight contestant Paris Baby feels the new season will usher in a "drag renaissance"Flesh, who has been running a drag show for the past five years, says she has also seen turnout at live performances drop, and feels soaring costs have likely impacted that. She thinks the TV show still appeals as it provides "the joy and the power of drag from the comfort of your own home", but says this comes at a price to performers."Expectations remain at a Drag Race level and our income and opportunities in the real world do not reflect that," she says. The Soho-based queen also says social media has become a "double-edged sword".Although it's vital to advertise live shows, "the more you show... the less inclined people are to go", she says.Flesh adds: "If the public aren't willing to support drag outside of the Drag Race vehicle" then "we won't be able to sustain Drag Race".The queens this year will be hoping to spark more interest into the show and drag, including Paris Baby, who describes herself as "UK's British Bajan Barbie".She has been hailing the new series as the "drag renaissance" as she feels it was a "really strong" year and hopes it will be "very well received" internationally."Hopefully we can bring a little 'je ne sais quoi' and reignite the interest in drag," she says.RuPaul's Drag Race UK series eight launches at 22:00 BST on BBC Three and is available to watch on BBC iPlayer.Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.More on this story

articles.title: Hohem’s tiny steadycam has a removable action cam
articles.summary: Hohem is trying something new with its Eyepic handheld stabilized camera to differentiate it from existing offerings from companies like DJI and Insta360. At its core, the camera is functionally similar to devices like the Osmo Pocket 4 and Insta360 Luna Ultra with a rotating preview screen and a small camera module stabilized by a three-axis gimbal. But the Eyepic borrows an idea popularized by r
articles.body:
Hohem is trying something new with its Eyepic handheld stabilized camera to differentiate it from existing offerings from companies like DJI and Insta360. At its core, the camera is functionally similar to devices like the Osmo Pocket 4 and Insta360 Luna Ultra with a rotating preview screen and a small camera module stabilized by a three-axis gimbal. But the Eyepic borrows an idea popularized by recent action cams by letting you detach the magnetic camera module and use it as a tiny standalone camera you can mount or wear.
The Eyepic captures 4K video at up to 60fps in a vertical or horizontal orientation that can be changed by rotating the 2.51-inch touchscreen display on its grip, which also includes a joystick for manually adjusting framing and a lever for changing the zoom level. Details on battery life, built-in storage, tracking capabilities, and pricing haven’t been shared yet.
[Image: The Eyepic comes with accessories for clipping the camera module to clothing like hats or wearing it using a magnetic lanyard. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/hohem2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
To capture more dynamic hands-free footage, the Eyepic camera can be used on its own clipped to clothing, worn using an included lanyard, or magnetically attached to compatible surfaces. The tiny action cam lacks a screen of its own but streams a live 1080p preview to the Eyepic’s touchscreen that can be used to preview framing or remotely adjust settings up to 32 feet away. The grip and gimbal aren’t water-friendly, but the action cam module is completely waterproof to a depth of just over 32 feet.

articles.title: How Sonos rebooted itself
articles.summary:
Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand. 
Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period,
articles.body:
Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand. 
Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period, and then took the permanent role just about a year ago. As you’ll hear him say, he thinks Sonos is fully out of that period now, and on to its next chapter with a huge product and platform launch called Sonos 27.
I mean, come on, you all listen to the show. That is all the most Decoder bait imaginable. I have been dying to have Tom on the show to talk about how the board decided to move on from previous CEO Patrick Spence, how he diagnosed the issues inside the company, and what decisions he made to fix them.
Those fixes involved a lot of big changes: to the company’s structure, its product lineup, and how it thinks about itself and what its product fundamentally is. That’s that new platform, Sonos 27, which you’ll hear Tom call a new foundation for the company that makes every Sonos product work better as part of a system. 
There’s a lot here, including how AI assistants can work across the system, the idea of having a mesh network of little computers in your home disguised as speakers, and of course, the testy relationship between Sonos and Google, which means Google’s Gemini assistant isn’t available on Sonos devices. 
Oh, and of course we got into the weeds about smart home standards, because I am a smart home nerd and simply cannot help myself. But to his credit, Tom was willing to nerd out with me, and I think this conversation is pretty fun because of it.
Okay: Sonos CEO Tom Conrad. Here we go.

Tell me about that gap. You came in, and you said this company thinks it’s a hardware company. That’s what your predecessor had been saying, but it went sideways in big, meaningful ways. Tell me about that moment and why you think it was the same conception even when you came in.

Like an ENTJ or whatever?

You’ve made some changes. It’s time for the Decoder questions. You have restructured the company. There have been a few rounds of layoffs. How big is Sonos today?
And how is that structured?
So the company that I stepped into was divided into business units. We had a team that was focused on home. We had a team that was focused on the professional opportunity, a team that was focused on home theater, and so on. While there’s something to be said for P&L responsibilities, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, there’s something to be said for that approach at a certain scale. I think that my appraisal was that we were sub-scale for the inefficiencies that creep in. We have the almost guaranteed duplication of effort across the silos.
What’s more, if you imagine that the product is really the system, the idea that your portables team sits far away from your home theater team, and sits far away from your plugged-in speakers team, is almost surely going to run counter to the kind of progress that you’re trying to motivate. We might, for an interval, be very focused on this part of the portfolio over here, and then we might be able to move to focusing on a different corner of the portfolio. You’re describing the shift from a divisional structure to a vastly more functional structure.
Everyone comes up, and there’s one big product meeting.
You obviously make a lot of software. I’ve described you as a software CEO. We’re at the turn, right? You came in, you restructured the company, you identified a new thesis for the company. Today you’re here to talk about all the new news. Do you think you’re through it? That brings me to the other Decoder question: how do you make decisions? What’s your framework?
Well, I don’t think you bring just one framework to every decision. So we talk about, for example, product decisions. As an idea moves through its lifecycle from its days as an early little sapling that you have to care and tend to, through final mass production for a hardware object, and out into the channels, I think how you think about [each of those] decisions is different.
So in the earliest days, I really tried to protect the creativity of the company and to not let the antibodies of doubt and critique erode an idea before it’s had a chance to express itself in a way that anybody could get excited about. And you ask the teams to bring a really thoughtful, detailed description of the puts and takes and the risks associated with it, and you use that to help you make your decisions.
But maybe on top of all of that, you just have to hire great people. I mean, you just do, and you have to put them on teams that are an appropriate size for the task at hand. I think it’s going to be very, very difficult for any CEO or any leadership team to make great decisions if the people who aren’t bringing the ideas themselves aren’t great. So I suppose it starts with the right people in the seats.
The reason I ask that question in that way is that, I think, the decision you made that is most emblematic to me of changing from a divisional structure with individual P&Ls to a more functional structure, and thinking about the platform as a whole, was the decision to kill a product that I believe was called Pinewood. It was a set-top box that was going to integrate all the streaming services. This was well reported by former Verge reporter Chris Welch, who’s now at Bloomberg.
The thing that really struck me about that was if you had a division that was focused on soundbars, the only place that division could go was to compete with Roku. Like so many things, these decisions do have more than one dimension that you evaluate. I think if we were, putatively, actually working on a set-top box at that moment, another thing that I might have wondered about was whether our desire to make this particular product came from our customer or did it come from some sort of internally sourced sense of business opportunity? Can I talk about it?
Yeah, let’s get into it. Sonos 27 and Sonos Fabric, what are these things? Explain to people what’s going on here.
So 100 percent hardware, 100 percent software. For 20 years, we’ve given all of our hardware objects names: Roam, Arc, Beam, Ace, Era. The Beam Ultra is the new soundbar, and I think it’s 7.1.2.

That might be an entirely different home theater podcast.

If you need a co-host, we should do it.
Look, I just judged the TV shootout, and Sony lost. It’s a big deal. There’s a lot going on in that world. 
Tell me about the idea of naming the operating system Sonos 27. It’s obviously the middle of 2026. It obviously tracks Apple’s naming scheme. This very much implies there’ll be a Sonos 28 one year from now, in August of 2027. 
It does. I think from the beginning we knew that we wanted to give it a name, and we knew that we wanted the name to be able to express this idea that Sonos does evolve. And for many, many years, that evolution was to the great benefit of our customers. We had lossless audio for Apple. We had high-fidelity audio for Spotify. We had AirPlay. We had Alexa. 
Through the years, we’ve just over and over and over again expanded the capability of the products that were already in our customers’ homes, and we didn’t have a way of talking about it at all. So we wanted to give it a name. We wanted people to understand that it improved over time.
So as we started thinking about, “Well, how do you really do that?” I mean, the first thing they came to was like, “Gosh, we already have ‘OS’ right in the name of the company.” So to try to brand some entirely new thing felt like a self-own, and so we pretty quickly reverted to this idea that the product is 100 percent hardware and 100 percent software. The product is Sonos, not Arc. Maybe the OS2 is called Sonos.
And then it’s like, “Well, what companion moniker can we give it to drive that idea home?” Obviously we talked about version numbers and any number of other things, but we decided that we’d like to take advantage of this. Once a year, we’ll stand up in front of our audience and tell them about how the platform is evolving, and using the year as a descriptor for that was a better mechanism than almost anything else that was available to us.
Those software cycles, yearly big releases… Apple is basically the only company that sticks to it. Even if it doesn’t do it, it announces all the features, and then they slowly dribble them out over the course of the year as they come into focus. 
Again, I have a lot of questions about the nature of software development in 2027, but the idea that there’s one monolithic release once a year — the industry’s gotten away from that. Is that your idea, or are you going to do something different?
No, no, no. Fortunately, the industry has gotten away from that, and our intention is to have a moment where we can tell the story of the operating system roadmap for the next six or 10 months. As you’ll see, even in this moment, the things that we’re announcing — many of them will be available in what we’re calling early access, which is the chance for us to put them out into the product as opt-ins for our customers. That way, we can do the perspective collecting, real-world data collecting sort of work. All of these products will continue to evolve through the year.
Frankly, I think as we go into the event, we will talk about all of this. I know that I’m going to get questions from customers and observers like, “What about this feature?” I think really the answer is just going to be like, “We know the stuff.” There’s very little that you can say, “Hey, someone should do this,” that isn’t on our list.
So to be able to say, “Look, part of what we’re communicating with the 27 of it all is that this stuff will come in 2027, and if it doesn’t, it’ll come in 2028 or beyond.”
One of the big ideas here is obviously that this is an operating system that addresses a bunch of hardware in your home. That thing mostly looks like speakers, but some of it is connected to your TVs. You’ve got command and control. You’ve got other assistants, which I want to talk about, and that operating system should gain more capabilities over time. 
What does the far version of that look like? Is it just that there will be an ambient assistant in your house that is addressing the fabric through MCP? Is it that you’ll interoperate with other speakers that might be in the house? What does the biggest vision of this look like?
I mean, I think in some ways you’ll have to stay tuned to see where we take this, but I’ll start with this: I think that every home deserves this infrastructure. I think sound is an incredible mood stabilizer, if you like. Take the audio track out of your favorite movie or television show, and so much of the life comes out of it. And I think having an out-loud audio experience in your home is something that everybody should enjoy. So part of the big picture is we want to spread this far and wide and make it accessible to everyone.
A running joke about the first generation of assistants is that they’ve ended up being for timers. I think you really do, when you’re building out this next generation of voice-centric experiences, have to look at not just what the technology can do, but also what the customer wants. And one of the new capabilities in Sonos 27 is our new voice assistant.
Our voice assistant is built on modern generative technology, but it’s really inspired by what people tell us that they like to see in the home. I’ll tell you, the killer app of the assistant is that they just want to be able to talk to it like a normal person, full stop. With the first-generation assistants, you just had to guess what to say every time, and even then maybe it took two or three attempts to get there. 
It’s such a game changer to be able to say, “Play that album I loved in college, the one with the Cocteau Twins singer. I think the song ended up as the theme song for that show. It was on Fox. It was about the curmudgeonly Doctor House… It’s ‘Teardrop’ by Massive Attack.”
I know. They took it off the [streaming version of House]. It’s sad.
It is. It is. So that’s job one, if you like. The first-generation assistants didn’t do it at all. Sonos Voice in the new OS is exceptional at this. So that’s meeting the customer where they are.
What else should they say? Well, they say a little bit about what I would call mood and ambiance. So lighting. Let’s bring lighting into the environment so that you can express a scene through both sound and light. 
My wife and I are constantly settling little bets in the kitchen: “What was this thing called? Who is that actor?” They do want comprehensive world knowledge. They want to get an answer to the kid’s homework assignment or whatever, and so these agents do need to be able to hand off to comprehensive frontier models to get perspectives on the world.
In some instances, those perspectives allow them to use the frontier model to manipulate the audio environment to play some music that people are talking about on TikTok and pick some stuff that sounds like the shoegaze music that I liked when I was in college. We can leverage the power of a frontier model to understand what’s being talked about on TikTok to sort that against my musical preferences, and deliver it.
I guess while we’re enumerating what I think a modern voice assistant has to do, it has to be fast, it has to be reliable, and it has to be responsible and affordable to run. I do think that customers want this as a fundamental capability of a product like Sonos, and we built an architecture that allows us to deliver it to every one of our customers as well.
There’s a lot of big Decoder, big Verge ideas in all of there, all the way down to where does the compute live? Where is the computer in your house supposed to be? You’re describing a lot of command and control. There’s integration with smart home stuff. I think it’s a Lutron partnership you have now.
But there’s an infinite number of smart light switches that might help you control your lighting. Your company is part of the Matter standard, but you don’t actually enable Matter on Sonos speakers. I think our reporting from the wonderful Jenn Tuohy, as our smart home reporter, has suggested that you don’t think it’s ready. 
This is a lot of stacked problems. I’m just going to read your press release to you. It says, “Sonos 27 MCP allows you to connect any outside AI assistant or agent to your system, including ChatGPT.”
Well, I’m a customer, and I’ll tell you that the one that I want to use is Gemini for Home, Google’s assistant, and that’s been broken on Sonos for ages because of an ongoing lawsuit. Is that fixed? Is Google on your list? Because there’s a lot of competitive dimension here.
So in many ways we have a strong relationship with Google to this day, despite the lawsuit. YouTube Music is one of the most-listened-to music services on the platform. We do have a long history of a first-generation Google Assistant on many of our products. We’d love to continue to work with them on all of these things, and those conversations continue.
I guess I’m just going to push on this idea of connecting any AI assistant or agent. There are two big ones. There’s Alexa, and there’s Google. You might be in third place. Siri exists. Those are the ones, right? Maybe there’s going to be a ChatGPT product in the future.
Well, listen. I want to tease apart two different things.
Let’s talk about command and control of the Sonos system through external agentic interfaces, just to use every buzzword. What I really mean is that we think there’s a lot of utility in showing up inside of ChatGPT on the web, on your phone, on the desktop in the same way that Slack or your calendar shows up in those environments.
So with Sonos 27 MCP, we’ll show up in the directory of connectable services in all of those environments: in Gemini, in Claude, in ChatGPT, in Grok. By connecting that tool into your experience, however you access it, you’ll be able to summon Sonos. So maybe you’re working on something, and you want some music to play; you can just tell Claude to make it play or just tell Gemini to make it play from the desktop or mobile surface that you’re sitting in front of.
That’s a pretty powerful building block as we see these OpenClaw-style agentic, proactive, asynchronous agents evolve. Now they have access to Sonos in a supportable way. There’s been a bunch of hack MCPs and CLIs for Sonos around, and a lot of reporting about how they’re among the most utilized examples for these things. We’re excited to officially support such a thing. As much as fun it is to see the mainstream use cases, I’m very excited to see what hobbyists are going to do with Sonos MCP.
So let’s now talk about on-device, though. So we’ve been working closely with Amazon for some time to bring Alexa Plus to our platform. That work continues. I’m excited about it. We don’t have anything to announce today, but we’ve had a long and really successful relationship with Amazon through the years. Panos was on the board with me for many of our years at Sonos.
By the way, just so people know, that’s Panos Panay, who now runs hardware and Alexa at Amazon.
That’s right, that’s right. He’s a friend of the show.
Yes. Panos and I are buds. 
But one thing we’ve demonstrated is something we call Sonos Custom Agents, which lets you take any of these inference engines — the Anthropic engine, the OpenAI engine, the Gemini engine, the Grok engine — and invoke it from Sonos. You’ll be able to give it a unique voice, give it a name, and give it a context that has it show up in a particular way.
So imagine that you’d like to have a personality that lives inside of Sonos, and it’s the John Cusack character from High Fidelity, an opinionated record store geek who is interested in subtly shading your perspectives in music, but also making recommendations. 
You’ll be able to go in and set up a custom agent in Sonos that says, “Let’s use OpenAI inference. Let’s use this voice I pick, and let’s give it this personality, and let’s have it live alongside an agent that’s powered by Anthropic inference that is going to give me advice on cooking. And let’s do another one that is only interested in connecting me with opportunities to see live music.” 
All of these tools will be able to show up inside of Sonos, invoked by the name you give it, like, “Hey, Sonos, connect me to the curator,” and talk to you only about that topic, have a point of view, and be able to access the Sonos context so that they can hand off from one to the other.
It’s super fun. It’s super creative. It lets our customers become participants in the Sonos platform. We’re just showing it off as a technology preview because there are still a lot of details to work out here, but it’s a lot of fun to play with in the lab.
Let me bring some of these ideas together. There’s the idea that there’s external command and control. I have an Echo Dot, and I say, “Turn on the Sonos,” and it just does that.
Then there’s the idea that there’s the assistant that lives on your device that is either the Sonos voice assistant or maybe you’re going to keep working with Amazon and Alexa+ being there. And then we’re going to make new custom ones out of building blocks that are enabled in lots of different ways.
When I asked where the computer is, this is, to me, the big question: where does all this ambient agentic AI actually live? Where does it have control? Is it going to happen locally? Are we sending everything to the cloud? 
Somewhere in your home, if you’re going to control lights, music, and everything else, there needs to be some logic happening in your home. There are a lot of standards to do that. Some of them are good, some of them are bad. Some of them have names that connect directly to the word fabric, like Thread.
There’s a lot going on here in terms of just the names and schemes of what could happen. Where do you see this view? Who is your competition here? 
Is it that Apple is going to launch a new HomePod with an AI-enabled Siri, and they already have a HomeKit, which is a pretty well-built and pretty popular smart home platform? Is it, “Well, OpenAI is going to have a hardware device, and maybe their first one’s going to be in the home, and you need to stave that off and make sure people are talking directly to you, and you have the customer relationship”?
That seems not only undeveloped, but even the foundations of how you build the products — like Matter and smart home standards — are messy and political in very specific ways. So how do you see the competition, victory, and success there? And then how do you solve just the capability gap that every other company has run into?
So one thing that I’m reminded of in this moment is that we, as an industry, have these platform shifts that unlock opportunities for companies who get lucky on timing. For example, the original dot-com era was really powered by Oracle and Sun Solaris boxes and data centers that you owned and operated yourself. We then went through a chapter where the infrastructure became Linux and open source for your data tier. 
Of course, we’ve had this huge long run of cloud infrastructure. I think that if you’re a company that builds your stack on Solaris and Oracle, it’s really that there’s an opportunity for a company to come along and build a stack on Linux and Postgres in that moment and suddenly find efficiencies that are very, very hard for you to claim.
I think something very similar is happening in voice assistants. When I hear you talk on the show about your experience with voice assistants that are going through the transition from first generation to second generation, it feels to me like so much of the challenge there is about how we drag along all of the committed relationships that we have for the internet-connected toaster, back massager, and all of the things that are connected into those existing historical ecosystems. 
Honestly, even in the world of AI, with just how much has changed in the last couple of years underneath the companies as they’re building out their answers here, it really feels to me like we are stepping into a moment where agentic tool use powered by protocols, like MCP, is going to disintermediate a lot of that stuff that you’re talking about.
I think that in the immediate term, we’re really excited about what we can do in the use cases that our customers are telling us they care about. Give me mood and audio in the home. We have great solutions for that today. And I think we can take advantage of this shift to a truly next-generation architecture without the baggage of a decade of internet-connected light switches from 17 different protocols with 17 different hubs in the closet.
Well, I mean, part of the opportunity there is that you don’t have a big voice assistant. I don’t think the current Sonos voice assistant is at the scale of Alexa or Google Assistant. I’m just guessing. They do have that problem. The light switches in my house, they’re in the walls. They’re going to be there. That Lutron hub is there. It’s not great. However, Lutron is the best one. 
It is. It is the best one.
There’s a box in my house, and there are a lot of those little weird little boxes in my house because I have a smart home, and all of those dependencies exist for those platforms for reasons. If you show up and say, “Use my voice assistant instead,” and it can’t operate all of the lights, well, I’m just going to fall back to Amazon, or I’m going to fall back to Google. They know it, and they know they can’t break those things. Panos and I have talked about it a lot, actually in the context of Alexa Plus. 
The promise of AI, at least from my very abstract vantage point, is, boy, I should not care about any of this. There’s a network in my house. There are lots of devices on that network. They have some access points on that network, and maybe they’re API-driven access points, maybe they’re MCP-driven. It should not matter. There’s just a bunch of devices in my network that you can control somehow, and this all-seeing robot that is going to replace every job in America should be able to traverse my network and turn on the lights without any help. That’s what it should do.
Some of the very first big vibe coding shockwaves were AI researchers, bleeding-edge AI researchers, being like, “I figured out how to control my shades. They walked through my network, and the shades go up and down now,” right? We’re not there at the consumer level. The promise is not there. I’m still here talking to you about Matter, Thread, HomeKit, and whether or not Google Assistant can control my Sonos Amp, which, by the way, it can’t, and that is my one ticket to you that I didn’t submit on Threads. 
That’s the promise, but the gap to that seems really, really huge. Are you able to close it? Is that the opportunity?
I think we’re just still in the Apple II days of the home automation space. So while there is, as you point out, this incredible, wild, heterogeneous world of different light switch controllers, I think when you talk to mainstream consumers about their homes, they’re not there yet. 
I do think that because of the profound technological step function of agentic control of these kinds of services and things like tool use, as the consumer catches up with the industry’s ambition to solve these problems, new technological solutions will emerge. I’m really excited about how we’re positioned to ride that transition and not be encumbered by the decade of early adopter internet-connected light switches.
What are you going to do about the light switches that are already in the walls?
I just don’t think that there’s enough of them to matter in the final answer. Of course, Lutron’s a great partner, and they do a great job with this.
They do. I mean, we have them. We’ve got all kinds of light switches. We mostly have Lutron ones. But that’s my question. The first natural customer for something like what you’re describing is somebody who is already using these products in some way. If you show up to my house and there’s no Matter support or whatever, I’m like, “Well, I can’t use it.”
Is it though, or is it more like the difference between the people that were adopting Creative Labs MP3 players before the iPod came along?
Was the iPod really for those people, or was it for people that had that problem but were nowhere near the people that had been early adopters? Or was the iPhone for people that were using Windows CE, or was it for people that were using flip phones who were ready for the transition? I think we’re making-
Is that the idea here “iPhone for smart home control” or “iPhone for audio in the home”?
The turn there that I think is really interesting is: who are you going to talk to? Where is the computer? What is the computer? You’re describing a situation where if you want music, you’re going to talk to Sonos. But you also have a general-purpose assistant like Claude or ChatGPT, and they can talk to Sonos, too.
It’s unclear to me — and it may be one of the most fascinating questions at this moment in tech — where the interface goes. Are we all going to have one chatbot that does everything, and all the demand is aggregated there, and OpenAI becomes more powerful than ever? Or are we going to have lots and lots of assistants that we address in lots and lots of different ways? 
It seems like your bet is Sonos will have a personality in your home, maybe multiple personalities in your home, and customers will address that, and all the other stuff will go somewhere else.
For 20 years, we’ve found a lot of success around the idea of embracing every dimension of the problem. Yes, there’s an app, but you’re welcome to engage with us through AirPlay or Spotify Connect. Yes, we have a voice assistant that lives side by side with Alexa. Yes, we have proprietary mesh, but it integrates with Bluetooth and even line-in. I think we bet that we’re of a size and scale that allows us to both be nimble and react to these changes, but also have enough horsepower to keep up technologically with what the best in the category are doing. So I think some of this just plays out on the field.
Just one last idea, since you said it a couple of times, this question about where the compute lives. I think one incredibly powerful opportunity for Sonos is that we do place compute in millions and millions of homes. People don’t think of them as computers often, but they are. They create a seamless experience that is really the integration of a set of cloud services and local services in a way that looks like just one surface area to the customer.
I think that the answer to your questions, “Does this live in the cloud? Does this live in the home? Does this live in a box?” is yes. I think we’re pretty uniquely situated to take advantage of an architecture where it’s not cloud-only, it’s not home-only, but it’s an integrated system that combines all of that together. And at the end of the day, that is what Sonos 27 is.
Just to make that really reductive, when I say “where is the computer” in the home context, what I mean is maybe in the ‘90s to early 2000s, there was a vision that we would all have home servers in our basements, and they would do all the logic of our home. They would have all the storage, and Microsoft would sell you a Windows home server in the basement and a Windows Media Center in the living room, and you and I probably both watched all of those Bill Gates keynotes at CES. 
None of that really ever came to pass. Instead, we put a lot of cheap computers near all the TVs, and they connected to cloud services, and they’re basically just running web browsers, as you well know. That is a very different version of what needed to happen and how the market played out.
In the smart home, I’ve got a bunch of automations in my house. When the garage is open, the lights turn on, and other stuff happens. At night, the doors all lock if they’re not locked. That logic has to live somewhere. My perspective on it is that it should live in my house. If the internet goes down, the lights should still turn on. 
This is not anything to do with big AI integrations or the new MCP way to address the Sonos system. Those are big ideas, and I’m just insistently dragging you back down into the dirt of: if the internet goes out, are the lights still going to turn on?
You don’t want to be the partner that puts in the internet-connected light switches that don’t work when the internet is down. 
But it’s not just the internet-connected light switches; it’s the logic of making it all work together.
I understand. Yeah, fair. Here’s what I’ll say about that. For 40 years now, we’ve been talking about technology for the home, starting with the personal computer, which is supposed to be the center of the technological household, but we didn’t really get that. We got laptops that people mostly use at work and use a bit at home.
Then we got mobile, and mobile is supposed to be the thing that you engage with when you leave your house on your way to work. Of course, the fundamental media of mobile is so addicting that it’s all-consuming. We use it at work, we use it at home — we use it all the time. But my observation about our use of it in the home is that nobody loves it. No spouse has ever said, “I wish my husband was on his phone more. I wish my kid used their iPad more,” and so we’re looking for ways to get beyond that.
To your point, the other compute that’s in the home, like I said, is the set-top box, which is largely just a web browser to a bunch of services that live in the cloud. I think it’s pretty interesting, actually, that in 17 million homes Sonos is an actual mesh of compute in your house with real horsepower, real memory, real CPU, real capability, a real operating system — all just waiting to be the container for some of the kinds of things you’re talking about. So it’s super interesting. We’ll figure it out over time.
I feel like you’re this close to being like, “And then the Teslas will be a data center.” There’s something there that is maybe the line. Actually, I want to talk about that. I actually want to push on that a little bit. 
The initial Sonos innovation 100 years ago, when the company started, was, “Oh, we can build a mesh network. We can do wireless audio at scale. We can synchronize the latency of all the speakers so it sounds like the same music playing at the same time.” This was a lot of big engineering back in the day. 
Still, I mean, candidly, still. A lot of what our software team does day in and day out is extend and maintain that infrastructure.
There are features you’re announcing here as part of Sonos Fabric that I think are interesting. If you have surrounds, you can just place them, and they’ll figure out that they’re surrounds and immediately start being the surround speakers in a home theater. 
There’s just a lot of potential, as you’re describing, in the notion that, “Oh, there’s a big network of small computers in my house that can come together and do things you would not expect.” Is your focus that they will always do audio things? Or is it the focus that they will have many more capabilities?
I think any thoughtful product leader is going to tell you the focus is an important part of success. I do feel like there’s so much interesting work for us to do around creating an audio system that sets the mood for your home that I don’t want us to take our eye off of that opportunity. We are doing some really exciting things in Sonos Fabric and Sonos 27 that we should talk about, that get to some of the work that you’re describing.
But certainly in the moments where you allow yourself to think about what the company is in five years and what it will be in 10 years, you can’t help but interrogate what the opportunity is for a mesh — a fabric of compute that lives in the home.
I want to end by talking about headphones really quickly. We just had the CEO of Bose on. She and I had a pretty searching conversation about what happens to the headphone market in the time of AI wearables. 
My fear, my anxiety, about audio is always that consumers will always pick convenience over quality. It’s just the history of the... I’ve got a set of AirPods on this desk, and they don’t sound great, but boy, are they convenient. And that’s just the way it goes. It has always been what the market has demanded: convenience over quality.
We’re going to enter a time when Apple puts cameras on AirPods, and you can talk to them with Siri. When Google and Samsung ship very similar products, there’s undoubtedly going to be a flood of AI hardware startups that want to put something in your ears or in your body in some way. 
You are in the headphone market. You’re talking a lot about AI; you’re talking a lot about Fabric. That seems like a cataclysm coming for headphones. The same way that the removal of the headphone jack was a cataclysm in the headphone market, this seems like the next one. 
How are you preparing for that? Do you think there’s going to be a range of voice assistants on headphones, or do you think what you would call the first-party vendors are going to just grab more and more of that share?
Before we jump to the hypotheticals about where headphones are, can I tell you a little bit about the new headphones?
All right. So one of the things that you get from entering a new market is the opportunity to build something and put it in customers’ homes and learn a lot about what matters and what doesn’t matter.
So we launched Sonos Ace two years ago. I think measured against any of the other premium over-the-ear noise-canceling headphones in the market, they’re a great product. They’ve got great reviews; they have great noise cancelling. They’re super comfortable, and they look great. We’re really proud of the product, but they weren’t thoughtfully integrated into the Sonos ecosystem. 
I mean, at launch you could swap to one of our soundbars, not even all of our soundbars. I think it was the most visible expression of the missed opportunity of that moment for the company to always remember that the products that we make are part of the Sonos system, not individual offerings.
So we ended up with a great pair of headphones, but honestly, I mean, you review them all the time; there are lots of great headphones. When we set out to take all the lessons that we learned from Ace to design Ace Ultra, at the very top of that list is that we have to do the hard thing. These headphones have to be able to show up in your home as a part of the system, and the model through which you invoke your headphones has to be completely seamless and delightful.
We built an entirely new hardware platform for Ace Ultra called Headphone Engine 2, and it unlocks this capability at the hardware level. And then in Sonos OS 27, we built virtualization so that any one of the speakers in your home can deliver the audio platform to that speaker but can also act as a proxy for your headphones, which don’t have the horsepower to run the full stack — it would kill battery life, et cetera.
Now with Ace Ultra, you’ll be able to link your headphones to your Sonos system, walk up to a speaker that’s playing, press a button on your headphones, and the music will jump from the speaker into your headphones. No Bluetooth, no phone. You’ll be able to walk around your whole house, enjoy the music, come to another speaker, press the button again, and it will jump to that speaker using some BLA location-sensing stuff that we’ve developed. It’s super magical. It’s the one job that we had and didn’t deliver on with Ace. We’re really excited to get it out into the market.
Analogous to that on the home theater side is, as you mentioned, that we’re making all of our portable speakers — Sonos Play, Sonos Move — capable of being rear channels for home theater. That sounds really easy. Maybe people will even be like, “Why wasn’t that always possible?” But to your point about the deep technology of it, the way that we achieve high-fidelity, low-latency surround experiences in the living room is by directly bonding our rear channel speakers and subwoofer to the soundbar on a proprietary network, not through your access point. So for a speaker to seamlessly hop between being part of your Sonos system as a music node and part of your Sonos system as a surround channel means that you have to do a real-time reconfiguration of that networking stack, and you have to know when to do it.
We’re using accelerometers in the product to actually know that you’ve picked it up and set it down in a new location. We’re using Sonos’ positioning system, which is ultrasonic signaling, to broadcast to the room, “Hey, is there a soundbar here?” Ultrasonic comes back saying, “I’m here.” They negotiate position, left and right, and distance, so that they can optimize the surround sound experience. You pick it up again, you take it back to the kitchen, and it’s a regular speaker again. All happens magically, no use of the app. It’s pretty cool.
Answer my question on headphones, though. This is my big worry. You’ve got really cool headphones. They have a feature that no one else can ship, and Apple’s going to say, “Look, our new AirPods have Siri AI in them.” 
You can just say, “Show me what I’m looking at,” and a picture will be taken automatically and something will happen. We’ll get over the privacy implications of that, but that’s a collapse of the headphone market.
Maybe. I mean, headphones come in all kinds of form factors today: over-ear, in-ear, cuffs, wireless, wired. So I do think it’s a market where people choose different form factors for different tasks. We’re really focused on this personal in-the-home listening — what do you do when the baby’s asleep? What do you do when you want to move the party from the kitchen to the den while you relax for the evening? We think that there’s a bunch of really interesting use cases there that other people aren’t paying attention to.
I think, broadly, over the course of the next couple of years, we’re going to get all kinds of adventurous wackadoodle consumer electronics that are connected to this new emerging AI universe. Most of them will be a swing and a miss. Of course, we’ve already seen some of those. So it’s a little hard to speculate, I think, about which of these things, if any, is going to have its iPod moment or its iPhone moment or whatever.
What do you think is going to happen?
I think we’re going to see a replay of what happened when the headphone jack got taken away. The headphone jack was an open interconnect. There was a really vibrant market for all kinds of headphones, and a bunch of those companies don’t exist anymore. The high-end wired headphones, for phones anyway, have mostly gone away, and you have a bunch of medium Bluetooth competitors, but the phone makers have largely taken that with first-party products. 
Now, you have your products at the high end competing with really high-end noise-canceling products from Bose and Sony and whoever, and that is the airplane set. The lack of the open interconnect has really killed the vibrancy of the low and middle end of the market.
Okay, well, there’s one big thing they can do to make sure the high end belongs to them, and it’s to integrate AI in very specific ways directly into their operating system. We’ll see how that plays out. There’s also a thing that’s different this time: there’s a vastly more energized European regulatory environment. Who knows how this will play out?
I can’t tell you, but all that stuff is a swirl, and you’re a headphone maker, and it seems like different headphone makers are taking different approaches to this.
The only counter that I might offer is that there’s a lot of talk about the walled garden of the Bluetooth advantages that the platform companies have. But I would say even without the European regulators, it’s notable that something like the Meta Glasses can have a reasonable, I think, commercially viable set of experiences that are principally powered by compute that lives on your phone and still deliver conversational AI that is mediated by a Bluetooth connection, admittedly behind some of the obstacles that you’re describing. But those obstacles aren’t so profound that clever companies aren’t figuring out how to work within those constraints.
I’m very curious to see how that plays out. It doesn’t seem like it’s in focus. Again, probably because, as you say, none of the products are in focus. No one knows what a hit product here looks like, so you might as well let a thousand flowers bloom and then radically constrict the market.
Tom, I’ve burned just a ton of your time. I think you can tell I could talk to you for ages and ages about all kinds of things.

We’re excited about the moment of co-creation that’s around the corner for us.
As we talked about at the top of the hour, Sonos 27 is absolutely a nod to the fact that we intend to keep doing this until the sun burns out. There’ll be Sonos 28 and 29 and 30 and beyond.

If your listeners have similar kinds of problems, we’ve got great people to help them, and we always like to hear from you. You can find me on social pretty easily.
Usually I end by inviting people back, but I’m saying we’ve got to fix it, and then we’re going to talk about what it took to fix it. That’s the plan.
Tom, this is great. Thank you so much, man.
This was super fun. Thank you.
Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

articles.title: Anthony Joshua's driver attempted overtake before fatal crash, trial hears
articles.summary: Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode is charged in Nigeria with offences including causing death by dangerous driving.
articles.body: Image caption, Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode, right, leaves court with his lawyer on ThursdayBySimi JolaosoAfrica correspondentReporting fromSagamuThe driver of a car carrying Anthony Joshua was attempting to overtake another vehicle when it crashed, killing two of the boxer's friends, a court in Nigeria has heard.Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode, 46, faces charges including causing death by dangerous driving and driving without a valid national driver's licence. He denies the charges.The court was told that the group - who had been travelling to visit Joshua's father in Ogun State, near Lagos in Nigeria, last December - were asleep when Kayode lost control of his Lexus SUV while he overtook a moving truck and collided with a parked lorry.Joshua's personal trainer, Latif Ayodele, and strength coach, Sina Ghami, died in the crash.A second defendant Abubakar Adamu, 35, the driver of the stationary lorry the car collided with, denies a charge against him of obstructing the free flow of traffic.Inspector Christopher Ajayi Taiwo of the Ogun State Motor Traffic Division told the court that by the time he arrived at the scene, both the damaged Lexus and the stationary lorry had been removed.But debris from the crash and soya beans scattered on the road from the lorry's load were found by officers, he added. The only items recovered from the Lexus were a logbook, painkillers and an energy drink, which were found near the driver's side, Ajayi said.Image source, Social MediaImage caption, The former heavyweight champion was a passenger in the crash, which killed his team members Latif Ayodele (left) and Sina Ghami (right)The court heard police has yet to take a statement from Joshua following the crash.During cross-examination, Kayode's lawyer questioned Ajayi over the lack of statement, to which he replied that "efforts are ongoing" and that he had not contacted Joshua because he "didn't have his number".The trial was adjourned until 10 September.Joshua, who was born in Watford, has family roots in Sagamu - a town in Ogun state, near the crash site.After the collision, the boxer posted a tribute to Ghami and Ayodele on social media."I didn't even realise how special they are," he wrote."I'll just be walking with them and cracking jokes with them, not even knowing God kept me in the presence of great men."100% it's tough for me, but I know it's even tougher for their parents."You may also be interested in:BBC Africa podcasts

articles.title: Feminist activist and journalist Gloria Steinem dies, aged 92
articles.summary: Her foundation said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City, "surrounded by many who loved her".
articles.body: Gloria Steinem, who became a leader of the women's liberation movement in the US, has died aged 92. In a post on Instagram, her foundation said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City on Wednesday, "surrounded by many who loved her". Steinem, who was a writer and magazine editor, co-founded the Women's Action Alliance - a group dedicated to fighting sexism - more than 50 years ago.She started her career as a journalist in New York and went on to co-found Ms. magazine, one of the first publications to focus on women's issues other than housekeeping and beauty.During the 1970s, Steinem was a vocal campaigner for women's reproductive rights, among other causes.She herself obtained an illegal abortion in London when she was 22 years old, and years later celebrated the US Supreme Court's 1973 ruling in the case of Roe v Wade, which granted women the constitutional right to abortion. Nearly half a century later she witnessed the reversal of this decision.She also spoke out in favour of the legalisation of same-sex marriage, as well as equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.Born on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, she had a difficult childhood and did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.After university in the late 1950s, she went to India on a research scholarship and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.She then moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. Her big break came through an exposé of Playboy Bunny working conditions. Eventually she became a columnist for New York Magazine, before founding Ms. magazine in 1972. Famously eschewing marriage, she went on to tie the knot in 2000 to David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist and father of actor Christian Bale. He died three years later from brain lymphoma.In 2013, then-President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honour in the US.Her foundation said "she continued working for equality until the very end"."Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humour."Her foundation said she lived her last years being in community and writing - welcoming guests into her home for "Talking Circles" - a tradition that will continue.Her commitment to her home becoming a centre for social justice movements, and a forthcoming book An Unexpected Life, are "among many gifts Gloria has given the world with the hope they have ripple effects for generations to come", the foundation said.Tributes flowed on Thursday after the news of her death, with writers and feminists commenting on Instagram with gratitude, some of them saying she had changed their lives.Meghan Markle "celebrated the life and legacy of my friend and mentor", along with pictures of the pair on Instagram."You all know her many accolades and the way in which she helped shape the world for woman and all people", Markle said, but added that beyond their work together, Steinem "privately, was even better than you would imagine".Steinem spent Thanksgiving with Markle's family, introduced the younger woman to one of her best friends, loved "our children with her whole heart, counseling me during hard times, and giving extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivaled cheekiness and wit", she said.Markle now wears "with pride" a bracelet Steinem gave her that says "we are linked, not ranked".Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and 2016 presidential candidate said Steinem was "one of the architects of the entire structure of women's equality, I mean tearing down those obstacles to young women being able to participate where their talents and hard work took them"."Gloria was at heart an optimist," Clinton told CBS Mornings on Thursday. "Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that's a moral choice, and she made it every day."

articles.title: Astronomers Detect a 10-Sided Structure in Saturn's Atmosphere
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://www.sciencealert.com/astronomers-spot-an-uncannily-geometric-10-sided-structure-in-saturns-atmosphere
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49549877
Points: 66
# Comments: 26
articles.body:
Polar projection of Saturn's southern hemisphere from Hubble data, revealing the decagon. (NASA, ESA, A. Sánchez-Lavega (Basque Country University, EHU))
Saturn, apparently, has been hiding its talents.For decades, humanity has puzzled over the gas giant's enormous hexagon swirling around its north pole – a six-sided atmospheric structure unlike anything else known in the Solar System.Now, it seems, that bizarre feature is not an isolated incident – and Saturn may have a propensity for polygons, rather than a passing whim.Lurking around the planet's south pole, astronomers led by Agustín Sánchez-Lavega of the University of the Basque Country in Spain have spotted another giant polygon – and this one has ten sides."This discovery suggests that the hexagon is not as extraordinary as previously thought and that, in fact, the conditions in Saturn's atmosphere are such that polygonal waves can form in both hemispheres surrounding the polar regions," Sánchez-Lavega told ScienceAlert.
Saturn's most prominent and well-known feature is its magnificent system of icy rings, but the hexagon at its north pole would have to be a pretty close second.It was first discovered in images from the Voyager probes in 1980 and 1981: a vast, six-sided atmospheric wave swirling around the pole at about 78.5 degrees latitude.In the intervening decades, both the Hubble Space Telescope and the Cassini-Huygens Saturn probe also captured the strange feature, suggesting that it has remained stable for at least 44 years.It's a weather phenomenon, but why it has such an almost perfect polygonal shape remains a mystery. And although scientists also thought Saturn's southern subpolar jets might produce a similar feature, none revealed itself across multiple searches.Then, in 2024, polygon  lightning struck for the second time.In images from amateur astronomers, a dark, undulating line was visible around the planet's south pole.Work in 2025 confirmed it. While creating polar projections from images of Saturn taken by astronomers Trevor Barry of Broken Hill Observatory in Australia and Jean-Paul Oger of the French Astronomy Association, the team finally saw it: Ten sides, forming an unmistakable polygon around the pole.Hubble observations showing the emergence of Saturn's south-polar decagon between 2023 and 2025. (Sánchez-Lavega et al., Sci. Adv., 2026)High-quality images from the Hubble Space Telescope confirmed it and allowed the team to trace it back to 2023."The discovery of the wave really did come as a surprise, as neither earlier images of Saturn taken by the Hubble Space Telescope nor those captured by the Cassini spacecraft whilst orbiting the planet between 2004 and 2017 had shown it," Sánchez-Lavega said.Centered around 60 degrees south, the decagon appears to be a vast atmospheric wave riding on one of Saturn's powerful eastward jet streams. The jet itself races around the planet at roughly 420 kilometers (260 miles) per hour, while the decagon moves at a comparatively leisurely place of around 10 kilometers per hour.Like the hexagon, the decagon doesn't appear to be just a pattern sitting across the visible cloud tops. Observations at different wavelengths revealed traces of its shape at different altitudes and latitudes, suggesting a vast, vertically layered structure embedded in Saturn's atmosphere.Fundamentally, it is the same kind of phenomenon as the hexagon, but – difference in side count notwithstanding – the two polygons are not mirror images of each other.Saturn, seen in natural color by the Cassini spacecraft in 2016. Its famous hexagon is visible around the north pole. (NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute)"In addition to the difference in the number of sides," Sánchez-Lavega explained, "the decagon is situated at a less polar latitude than the hexagon in the southern hemisphere, and is perhaps not as robust, as we have seen that it has formed."There are so many questions about these differences. Why did the decagon only form a few years ago, compared to decades of stability for the hexagon? Why are their latitudinal positions different?And why does the southern polygon have ten sides, compared to the north's nature-preferred six?"It may be linked to the difference in latitude, to the background wind structure, or perhaps even to the presence of a high-pressure vortex at nearby latitudes that could be forcing the formation of the wave," Sánchez-Lavega told ScienceAlert.There's even a plausible suspect.Just north of the decagon is a roughly 4,000-kilometer-wide anticyclone – a high-pressure vortex the researchers call a Red Spot – smaller, temporary analogs of  Jupiter's famous storm. Intriguingly, the decagon appears most pronounced near the vortex and least distinct on the opposite side of the planet.Simulations of three decagon formation scenarios. (Sánchez-Lavega et al., Sci. Adv., 2026)The researchers conducted simulations to determine whether this storm – or some other disturbance – could have played a role in the formation of the decagon.None of their scenarios, however, was able to reproduce the observed decagon exactly.And, of course, there's this little snag."The hypothesis that a nearby anticyclone at that latitude is driving the oscillation is an attractive one," Sánchez-Lavega said. "The same thing happened with the hexagon when it was discovered in 1980, but then the nearby vortex disappeared, and the hexagon remained."So for now, the answer is tantalizingly out of reach. Currently, the decagon is still there – observing how it changes over the coming months and years could reveal much more about how it formed.Saturn is tilted on its axis as it orbits the Sun every 29.5 years, giving the planet long seasons lasting about 7.5 years each. Its southern hemisphere is now moving through spring towards summer, tilting increasingly towards the Sun.Related: Amazing New Photos of Saturn's Moons Have to Be Seen to Be BelievedThe increase in solar radiation hitting the southern hemisphere – and the decagon – could cause some interesting changes. And as the south pole tilts further into view, astronomers will have an increasingly good vantage point from which to watch them unfold."We need to understand how the decagon evolves – in other words, whether in the coming years it will become unstable and break up, or, conversely, become more stable and robust as solar radiation increases," Sánchez-Lavega said.Saturn's hexagon has endured for at least 44 years; we only learned of its existence well after it was established.With the decagon, scientists now have a front-row seat to how Saturn builds its polygons in real time – and whatever happens, it's going to be one heck of a show.The research has been published in Science Advances.
This article was fact-checked by Fiona MacDonald and edited by Fiona MacDonald. While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human. If you spot a mistake, please let us know.

articles.title: Ferrari upgrade a step but not all we need - Hamilton
articles.summary: Lewis Hamilton says an upgraded Ferrari engine for this weekend's Italian Grand Prix is a "step forward but not the whole amount we need".
articles.body: Hamilton and team-mate Charles Leclerc have both won one race this season, with the Briton 59 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes."To win this weekend, the whole collective has to come together. Everything has to flow from the beginning," said Hamilton."There is a first ahead of me, in the sense of if I was to win I go into new territory winning for the first time in Ferrari at Monza. It would be phenomenal. "The pressure's high. You want to do it for the team. Many of them will come to this race. The tifosi come out in huge numbers with a passion that's unmatched. "And my mum's here. I don't think she's been to Monza, and certainly not (while I was) with Ferrari. I wanted her to experience this and bring any lucky dust she can bring."Ferrari's hopes of a home victory are boosted by the fact that Italian Antonelli will have a grid penalty for exceeding his permitted number of engine parts and is likely to start at the back.Hamilton said: "There is big gap between the top teams and the rest. Kimi will start from the back but with the power he has, and the performance he has, he should slide through that pack pretty easy and it's probably why they chose this race to do that."So achieving eighth or sixth should be relatively easy. We have to focus on maximising our weekend and try and take the energy from the tifosi to hopefully push us to the front."Antonelli's grid penalty was inevitable at some point after reliability problems earlier in the year meant they would need to exceed his allowance of four engines for the season.They chose this weekend because they calculated it was the most optimal race to do it, both in terms of the effect of a new engine on a track dominated by straights, and managing their engine pool through the rest of the year.Team-mate George Russell will also have an engine penalty, most likely in Azerbaijan in two races' time.Antonelli said: "I am very much looking forward to this weekend despite starting from the back. I will be able to enjoy it more than I did previously and hopefully we will still be able to have a good race."In some ways it helps to release pressure, although I would very much rather fight for pole and start at the front."It makes me a bit more relaxed going into the weekend. I think this track can be very good for us but we have to take into account that McLaren, Ferrari, even Red Bull can be good this weekend."There are other tracks where it is possible to overtake but this one is very energy starved and there are a lot of places where you can race differently and it gives us the best chance to climb through the field."Antonelli referred to energy starvation because the hybrid engines will be without their battery power for a higher percentage of the lap in Monza than at most races this year, because of the long straights and the lack of opportunity for recovery.Drivers are expecting a difficult and frustrating weekend, and for slipstreaming, which saves energy by reducing drag, to become a major feature in qualifying and the grand prix.Antonelli said he expected speed would flat-line on the straights but not drop significantly, and that the situation would be "better than many expected".Hamilton arrived at Monza for media day on Thursday in his new Ferrari F40, an iconic 1980s supercar, which he described as "a dream car of mine".He explained why the particular model he chose was so important to him, and a surprise resonance he discovered to his race number, which is 44.The seven-time champion said: "I have been looking for one for a while. I wanted one with low mileage and a story behind it. Lots have come up at auction but not particularly special. Or the paint's been redone. I wanted to find the most authentic one."I found this one that a guy bought it and drove it 69km from Maranello to his home and parked it and never drove it again."Then the decision is, 'Do you keep it as an art piece, all dusty, or clean it up?' That took a while to decide."I might be wrong but none of the Ferrari drivers in history have ever arrived in the coolest car in history."When they were taking the car apart... it has 44 stamped on the engine. I couldn't believe it. So it feels very much fate."He chose to drive it to the track, he said, "because I thought it was an opportunity to highlight the history of Ferrari in their own country and their race."

articles.title: Balrogg: Demonically compacting (up to 15%) lossless Vorbis/Opus recompressor
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://github.com/iczelia/balrogg
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49549778
Points: 83
# Comments: 11
articles.body:
balrogg losslessly recompresses Ogg Vorbis and Opus files. Archives are
typically 8-12% smaller than .ogg files and 3-8% smaller than .opus files.
Releases are not backwards or forwards compatible until v2.0 is reached.
balrogg is licensed under GNU GPL version 3. See COPYING. Report
issues to Kamila Szewczyk k@iczelia.net. The project is hosted at
balrogg -b e *.ogg *.opus
balrogg --progress -9 e music.ogg music.blr
e compresses and d expands. balrogg detects the codec. With -b, every
remaining path is processed using the available cores and memory. Encoding
appends .blr; decoding removes it. Larger inputs run first.
-p or --progress displays a progress bar on stderr for encoding and
decoding, with each Vorbis tuning trial identified separately. Use
--progress-lines for logs. Batch progress uses separate lines labeled with
Use your package manager or download a binary from GitHub Releases. To build a
The project uses C99 and only the C and math libraries. The Opus parser under
src/opus is derived from libopus.
Enable ASan and UBSan for tests
Build the portable mixer only
Target Windows 95 on an i486 (MinGW, 32-bit)
Run ./bootstrap first when building from a Git checkout. It requires autoconf
-1 through -9 select effort; the default is -9. Through -4, each level
adds a residue-model stage and affects decoding. Higher levels only expand the
parameter search, so -4 through -9 decode at the same speed.
Vorbis tuning evaluates the complete file at each selected setting. The best
candidate is retained in the destination file, with at most the best and current
candidate present during a trial.
Results for a five-megabyte music file follow.
8.3 percent smaller at 6.4 MB/s
4.0 percent smaller at 4.2 MB/s
9.8 percent smaller at 2.9 MB/s
4.8 percent smaller at 2.4 MB/s
The encoder refuses files it cannot reproduce exactly, including files with
bad checksums, invalid page sequences, unsupported Vorbis features, or no final
Vorbis packets with extra padding or alternative floor subclass choices retain
normal floor and residue compression. Classword corrections and padding are
modeled separately. Shortened packets (packet peeling) use an adaptive byte model.
Opus support is limited to one mono or stereo logical stream with channel
mapping family 0. Packets, including OpusHead and OpusTags, are limited to 61,440
bytes; extended frame headers and padding are supported within that limit.
Chained and multichannel Opus files are refused. Refusals
produce a diagnostic and exit status 1.
Malformed, unsupported, or unrecognized input
Batch mode returns the highest nonzero status reported by any file.
Each file uses one thread and requires seekable input and output files.
Vorbis model pages are allocated only when used, without relying on deferred
Supported hosts apply a 2 GiB process memory cap to reject unreasonable
allocations. Set BLR_MEMCAP to another size in MiB, or to 0 to disable the
Archives are portable across hosts. Windows builds use MinGW as follows:
A Windows 95 build uses a small KERNEL32 runtime and targets i486.
win95-check verifies the loader baseline, PE flags, and KERNEL32 imports.
An MS-DOS build uses DJGPP and needs an i386 with a DPMI host such as CWSDPMI.
DOS batch mode replaces the extension and runs serially. song.ogg becomes
song.blr, then expands to song.ogg or song.opu for Opus.
